<translation>
<pb n="10"/><note>A decorative woodcut initial N marks the beginning of the dedication.</note>

**THERE IS NO ONE WHO WOULD DENY THAT LORD** Philipp, Count <note>of Gleichen</note>, your father, on account of his most celebrated virtues and the singular piety he showed toward God, ought to be celebrated with the praises of a Hero and with Latin <note>original: "Ausonio"</note> song. However, since I am not endowed with such great eloquence that I am able to adorn his departed spirit according to his dignity, and yet I have entered into this arena, I pray that no one assigns this to me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even modest talents, even if they do not attain all things. It has pleased me to dedicate this poem to you, generous Counts, although it is a slight <note>original: "Leuidense"</note> gift, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you, who have in no matter yet declined from your paternal virtues, continue in this way, you will one day be celebrated with a similar Eulogy. Therefore, take care that you do not depart from your father's footsteps by degenerating from them. From Mühlberg <note>original: "Mulburgo"</note>, the 5th of the Ides of May, in the year from the birth of the Virgin,

1544.

***

### FUNERAL POEM ON THE DEATH OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS AND FAMOUS COUNT, etc.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial L marks the beginning of the poem.</note>

**L**et the elegy now put on mournful garments again,
And may you wish to hold the name that is properly yours.
Philipp, born of the high lineage of the Gleichens, has departed
From the living, he who was a father among the rest.
Therefore, a new grief occupies the brothers from that moment, and now
Again they moisten their cheeks and their entire faces with tears.
And so at home, in the buildings of the ancestral citadel, Sigismund <pb n="11"/> mourns his brother, full of mournful love.
But you, Ernst, having set out for the homes of Speyer <note>original: "Spirenses penates"</note>,
Groan at the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
Just as you were recently following the pious arms of the Saxon <note>the Elector of Saxony</note>,
Fighting with joined forces, O Hessian, alongside yours <note>Philipp of Hesse</note>.
In the meantime, cruel fate snatched away at home your brother,
Whose name was Grace <note>referring to Johann, implying 'grace of God'</note>, by an unjust death.
So now also, while the Emperor is holding a council,
Which I pray brings the grateful gifts of safety and peace.
While you are visiting this council with the Duke of Saxony,
You lose Philipp at home in a similar manner.
Therefore, Ernst, you rightly pour forth heavy tears,
And the cause for your weeping is just and heavy for you.
You also, sons, saddened by the death of your parent,
Weep, and a heavy grief holds your hearts.
A just cause produces immense complaints for you,
Which he who finds fault with has no true reason.
Until now you wept for your deceased mother and your uncle Johann,
Now you weep for both along with your father.
And now each sad citadel mourns its snatched away
Father, and the river Ohra <note>original: "Ora"</note> mixes its waters with tears.
What need is there for many words? All things are full of grief,
And every subject has reason to rightly weep.
We also, who inhabit the neighboring banks of the Wipper <note>original: "VVcite"</note>,
Weep for you, famous Philipp, with a complaining lyre <note>term: "cheli"</note>.
We weep and sing the proclamations of your praise with these
Verses, though they be unpolished and rough.
</translation>

<summary>Wendelin von Helbach dedicates a Latin funeral poem to the sons of the deceased Count Philipp of Gleichen, lamenting the family's successive losses. The text notes the absence of Count Ernst, who was attending the Diet of Speyer with the Elector of Saxony at the time of his brother's death.</summary>

<keywords>Count Philipp of Gleichen, Wendelin von Helbach, funeral elegy, Sigismund of Gleichen, Ernst of Gleichen, Speyer, Mühlberg, Ohra river, 1544</keywords>

<pb n="9"/><meta>continues from previous page: against Heraclitus and Cratylus</meta> who recognized nothing except what was subject to the senses, we establish that very same certainty. Indeed, the sciences of things considered universally ought not to exist because the extreme mutability and mortality of those things is converted by the mind’s intuition into eternal and perpetual constancy in actual fact and in every part, since no contemplation of our mind, however accurate, could provide that. Rather, they exist because things understood universally are released from the bonds of individual things, by which they are made unstable, and they embrace only the essence and its innate affections, which carry no mutation in themselves.

## XVIII.

Regarding the opinion of some that the <term>ousiae</term> <gloss>essences or substances</gloss> of things are perpetual, and the propositions formed from them are necessary, because they have been from eternity in God Most High and Great as in one who knows them, and as an idea and their primary cause: we do not think this is at all sufficient. For since all things are and have been in God by that reasoning, all individuals and even all the announcements which we call <term>contingent</term> <gloss>propositions that could be true or false</gloss> would exist with exactly equal eternity and certainty.

## XIX.

Although in truth Universals begin to exist at the same moment as the <pb n="10"/> individuals, nevertheless, by the order of nature regarding their existence, these universals are prior to them. For they can have their existence as universals from nowhere else than from individuals. However, if you look at their essence, you will find them to be prior to the individuals themselves, because they assist the constitution of singular things and communicate their <term>quiddity</term> <gloss>the "whatness" or essential nature</gloss> to them.

### XX.

From these things which we have established so far, it also becomes manifest in what way the treatment of Universals belongs to different faculties. It is indeed the task of the <term>Metaphysician</term> <gloss>philosopher of first principles</gloss> to investigate whether that Universal which is undeservedly attributed to Plato exists anywhere, or plainly nowhere. But it is the task of the <term>Logician</term> to discuss this universal form, which we have called a <term>being of reason</term> <gloss>ens rationis; a concept existing only in the mind</gloss>, and the accidents which flow from it by a certain deliberation of the soul. However, it belongs to the remaining disciplines to dispute concerning the subject matter itself, and the properties following its nature, with all mental intelligence removed.

### XXI.

But indeed the Universals—which some call by the name of <term>predicables</term> <gloss>categories of relationship between subject and predicate</gloss> and others call the five voices (though less aptly)—are only five in number: namely, Genus, Species, Differentia <note>The text ends here, continuing with Differentia on the next page.</note>
</translation>

<summary>This text defends the stability of universal scientific knowledge by distinguishing the unchanging essence of things from their mutable individual forms. It also categorizes the study of universals across different academic disciplines, including metaphysics and logic.</summary>

<keywords>universals, metaphysics, logic, essence, quiddity, Plato, Aristotle, predicables, five voices, being of reason</keywords>

<pb n="54"/><meta>continues from previous page: Oppianicus</meta>, who had set his heart on Sassia’s money, decided he must seek a remedy from within his own home for that delay which was being brought against the marriage. For while he had an infant son by Novia, his other son, born of Papia, was being raised by his mother at Theanum in Apulia <note>modern Teano Apulo</note>, which is eighteen miles away from Larinum. Suddenly, without any reason, he summoned the boy from Theanum, something he had previously not been accustomed to do except for the public games or on feast days. The wretched mother, suspecting no evil, sent him. While he had pretended that he was setting out for Tarentum, on that very day the boy, although he had been seen in public healthy at the eleventh hour <note>about 5:00 PM</note>, was dead before nightfall, and on the next day, before it was light, he was cremated. And it was the rumor of the people that reported this great grief to the mother before anyone from the household of Oppianicus did so. When she heard at one and the same time that not only her son but even the duty of the funeral rites had been snatched from her, she came to Larinum immediately, breathless with exhaustion, and there performed the funeral anew for the son who was already buried. Not yet ten days had intervened when that other infant son was killed. And so Sassia immediately married Oppianicus with a heart now rejoicing, confirmed in the highest hope. Nor is it a wonder, seeing that she was won over not by wedding gifts, but by the funerals of sons. Thus, while others are usually more desirous of money for the sake of their children, he judged it a pleasant thing to lose his children for the sake of money. I sense, judges, that because of your humanity you are violently moved by these great crimes as they are briefly demonstrated by me. With what spirit then do you think those men were possessed, who not only had to hear about these matters, but even to judge them? You are hearing about a man in whose case you are not the judges; about a man you do not see; about a man you can no longer hate; about one who has satisfied both nature and the laws, whom the laws punished with exile and nature with death. You hear this not from an enemy, you hear it without witnesses, <pb n="55"/> you hear it when those things which could be said most copiously are spoken by me briefly and in passing. They heard about a man concerning whom they were required to give their verdicts under oath; about a man whose nefarious and wicked face they gazed upon in person; about a man they hated because of his audacity; about one whom they considered worthy of every punishment. They heard from the accusers; they heard the words of many witnesses; they heard while every single matter was spoken of weightily and at length by Publius Canutius, a most eloquent man. And is there anyone who, having learned these things, could suspect that Oppianicus was overwhelmed by a trial and that an innocent man was circumvented? I shall now speak of the remaining matters in a heap, judges, so that I may arrive at those things which are closer and more joined to this case. I beg you to keep in memory that it is not my purpose to accuse the dead Oppianicus, but, since I wish to persuade you that the judgment was not corrupted by my client, I use this as the beginning and foundation of the defense: that Oppianicus, a most wicked and guilty man, was rightfully condemned. When he himself had given a cup to his wife Cluentia, who was the paternal aunt of this Habitus, she suddenly cried out in the middle of her drinking that she was dying with the greatest pain; nor did she live longer than she spoke, for she died in the midst of this very speech and outcry. And in addition to this so sudden death and the voice of the dying woman, all other things which are usually the signs and traces of poison were present in the body of that dead woman. And by the same poison he killed his brother, Gaius Oppianicus. Nor is this enough: although in the parricide <note>the murder of a close relative</note> of a brother itself no crime seems to have been omitted, nevertheless, to approach this nefarious deed, he first fortified his way with other crimes. For when Auria, his brother's wife, was pregnant and the birth already seemed to be approaching, he killed the woman with poison, so that along with her, <summary>Cicero recounts the series of domestic murders committed by Oppianicus to facilitate his marriage to Sassia and secure his inheritance. He argues that Oppianicus’s eventual conviction was the inevitable result of his clear and numerous crimes rather than bribery.</summary>
<keywords>Oppianicus, Sassia, Larinum, poisoning, infanticide, Cluentia, legal defense, Roman trials, Publius Canutius</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="17"/>...<note>continues from previous page: ...neither the grammarians nor the sophists could satisfy him when he asked what Chaos was, according to Hesiod.</note> Therefore, a much greater necessity is incumbent upon us to examine it accurately, since almost the entire hinge of the controversy turns upon it. According to Vossius, it is a "Vast Chasm" <note>original: "Vastus Hiatus"</note> from the ancient <term>chao</term> <gloss>to gape</gloss> instead of <term>chaio</term>, which according to Hornius, was formed from the Mosaic <term>Tohu</term> <gloss>formless</gloss> or <term>Bohu</term> <gloss>void</gloss> by the change of a single letter. <margin>In the Etymological Dictionary. History of Philosophy, Book II, Chapter XI.</margin> But in the mind of Riccioli, it descends from <term>para to cheisthai</term> <gloss>from pouring out</gloss>, a derivation which pleased the Stoics especially (according to Philo in <italic>On Incorruptibility</italic>) and Pherecydes according to the author Achilles Tatius. <margin>Cited place, Question V, page 201. Introduction to the Phenomena of Aratus, Chapter III.</margin> In this way, it will signify a confusion and a mixture or aggregation of many things together. 

But writers vary greatly in its meaning, just as they do in its origin. The Gentiles (except for Aristotle, who interprets it as "place") seem generally to have established that it denotes unbegotten matter existing before all the Gods, or, as Plato says, "before all things were made"; certainly the "principle of Natural Bodies" <note>original: "principium C. N."</note> which almost all who mention it agree is indicated by it. However, what sort of thing that was, and how it was constituted and arranged, is no more agreed upon among them than among clocks <note>a proverbial expression for total disagreement</note>. Regarding this, as well as the order in which individual elements <margin>Cited place, page 202 and following. Physical Positions Miscellaneous VI.</margin> or bodies were separated or distinguished from it, one may consult Riccioli, or our own Roeschelius. 

Burnet pursues this in such a way that he establishes "first-born" things like Chaos, and its twins, Night and Tartarus—that is, the upper and lower body. And indeed, he makes the former a dark air, impenetrable to the rays of the sun; the latter he makes Tartarus, or the abyss. Then he posits that pregnant Night likewise brought forth twins: namely, Earth and Aether, or the sublunary Heaven—that is, the region of purer air. In these matters, I think everyone perceives that the most ingenious author <note>Thomas Burnet</note> grants much of his own to Aristophanes. For, besides the fact that there appears in him neither hide nor hair <note>original: "nec vola, nec vestigium"</note> of a distinction between aether and heaven, nor can an atmosphere be conceived at that time when the terraqueous globe was being formed (since no vapors existed); furthermore, Night and Tartarus are not said by him to be begotten from Chaos, but to have existed simultaneously with Chaos. Finally, he ascribes "immense reaches" <note>original: "immensos sinus"</note> to Erebus, whom he joins with the abyss and tartarus—reaches which certainly he could only state incongruously regarding the terraqueous-aerial sphere, which is scarcely like a point in respect to the Universe. All these and similar inconveniences vanish of their own accord if it is said that Aristophanes held <italic>Night and Tartarus and Erebus</italic> not as diverse offspring of Chaos, but as parts of the same, or rather adjuncts or attributes. So that Chaos signifies matter, Night signifies darkness and the privation of light, Tartarus signifies a horrendous confusion, and Erebus signifies a vast void or interval <pb n="18"/> and denotes them as such. It is as if he wanted to say that Chaos was a vast and immense, as well as formless, emptiness—not otherwise than the author of the Book of Wisdom says, that "God made the world from invisible and formless matter"; or, as the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>St. Paul</note> speaks, that "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from things invisible, things visible might be made." Or, if one must speak from the corpuscular philosophy (supported by experience and most firm reasons), that "First Matter" and an infinite force of atoms occupied an immense space.

<margin>Book I, On the Heavens, Chapter III. Chapter II, cited above, page 94.</margin>
§. XVI. These things are also clearly conformable to the Mosaic narrative, and agree excellently with the sayings and traditions of both the Greek and barbarian philosophers; we shall not be overly laborious in citing these, since Master Tentzelius has already taken up this entire province. Rather, we urge this: that Aristophanes explicitly declares that the race of Gods did not exist before Love had mixed all things. That the stars must be understood by "the race of Gods" <note>original: "Deorum genus"</note> is proved more clearly than the midday sun by the phrasing "race of immortals" <note>original: "γένος ἀθανάτων"</note>, which none of the Ancients—whether Pythagoreans, Platonics, or Peripatetics—ever applied to sublunary things. This is so much the case that, although Pseudo-Hermes says and establishes that "nothing in the world dies," he nevertheless does not use the word "immortal" <note>original: "ἀθάνατον"</note>. The places by which this assertion could be demonstrated are infinite; however, let two suffice. One is from Aristotle, who says that "all nations attribute the highest place to the Gods, because that which is immortal is linked to the immortal" <note>original: "ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον"</note>; the other is from Ocellus Lucanus, who asserts with an elegant simile that "the course of the Moon is the isthmus of mortality and immortality." 

Nor do the Mythologists and Cyclic Poets say or teach anything else; they all proceed in explaining Theogonies in such a way that they narrate the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no intervening space of time. Regarding Plato and the Platonics, the same is most evident, such that to wish to declare it laboriously would be to lose one's effort. <margin>Book VI, 6. VI.</margin> Nevertheless, we cannot help but add from Proclus that he calls the "maker and producer Gods" of animals "new and recent"; elsewhere, however, he asserts that the "Orphic egg" and "the Being of Plato" are the same thing <note>original: "τὸ Ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν, καὶ τὸ τοῦ πλάτωνος ὄν"</note>. These latter points not only show that the ancients understood by the "egg" nothing other than Chaos itself, but they simultaneously reveal the foundation or occasion of the opinion concerning the pre-existence of anti-mundane matter. 

Namely, because whatever Gods there were besides the Supreme God (whom they called "One," "Good," "beyond essence" <note>original: "ἀνουσίαον"</note>, and not endowed with essence)—such as the stars and demons, and indeed even the Mind and Soul of the World—they believed these to be beings produced by the Supreme God. And they believed these recently produced Gods received matter, from which they would fashion sublunary bodies, as already prepared and existing. They could not help but establish eternal Matter, because before time (which began as soon as the mundane bodies were produced), there was mere eternity.

§. XVII. The fact that Aristophanes says Night first brought forth a "wind-egg" <note>original: "ovum subventaneum"; an unfertilized egg</note> does nothing against the truth; it only shows that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, and could not follow the incubation or brooding of Divine Love. Thus, he adorned the sentiment according to the capacity of his own wit. So this single difficulty cannot possibly prevent us—having dismissed Burnet's archaeology—from subscribing to the opinion sufficiently demonstrated by Hugo Grotius, Edmund Dickinson, Jacob Tollius, and Adam Tribbechov.

</translation>

<summary>This text examines the etymology and philosophical origins of the concept of Chaos, linking Greek mythological accounts (especially Aristophanes) to the Mosaic creation narrative. The author argues that ancient depictions of Chaos, Night, and the "Orphic egg" were poetic interpretations of the formless matter described in Genesis.</summary>

<keywords>Chaos, Mosaic narrative, Aristophanes, Plato, etymology, cosmogony, first matter, Night, Tartarus, Erebus, Thomas Burnet, Hugo Grotius, Theogony</keywords>

History of Philosophy, Book II, Chapter XI.</margin> But in the mind of Riccioli, it descends from <term>para to cheisthai</term> <gloss>from pouring out</gloss>, a derivation which pleased the Stoics especially (according to Philo in <italic>On Incorruptibility</italic>) and Pherecydes according to the author Achilles Tatius. <margin>Cited place, Question V, page 201. Introduction to the Phenomena of Aratus, Chapter III.</margin> In this way, it will signify a confusion and a mixture or aggregation of many things together. 

But writers vary greatly in its meaning, just as they do in its origin. The Gentiles (except for Aristotle, who interprets it as "place") seem generally to have established that it denotes unbegotten matter existing before all the Gods, or, as Plato says, "before all things were made"; certainly the "principle of Natural Bodies" <note>original: "principium C. N."</note> which almost all who mention it agree is indicated by it. However, what sort of thing that was, and how it was constituted and arranged, is no more agreed upon among them than among clocks <note>a proverbial expression for total disagreement</note>. Regarding this, as well as the order in which individual elements <margin>Cited place, page 202 and following. Physical Positions Miscellaneous VI.</margin> or bodies were separated or distinguished from it, one may consult Riccioli, or our own Roeschelius. 

Burnet pursues this in such a way that he establishes "first-born" things like Chaos, and its twins, Night and Tartarus—that is, the upper and lower body. And indeed, he makes the former a dark air, impenetrable to the rays of the sun; the latter he makes Tartarus, or the abyss. Then he posits that pregnant Night likewise brought forth twins: namely, Earth and Aether, or the sublunary Heaven—that is, the region of purer air. In these matters, I think everyone perceives that the most ingenious author <note>Thomas Burnet</note> grants much of his own to Aristophanes. For, besides the fact that there appears in him neither hide nor hair <note>original: "nec vola, nec vestigium"</note> of a distinction between aether and heaven, nor can an atmosphere be conceived at that time when the terraqueous globe was being formed (since no vapors existed); furthermore, Night and Tartarus are not said by him to be begotten from Chaos, but to have existed simultaneously with Chaos. Finally, he ascribes "immense reaches" <note>original: "immensos sinus"</note> to Erebus, whom he joins with the abyss and tartarus—reaches which certainly he could only state incongruously regarding the terraqueous-aerial sphere, which is scarcely like a point in respect to the Universe. All these and similar inconveniences vanish of their own accord if it is said that Aristophanes held <italic>Night and Tartarus and Erebus</italic> not as diverse offspring of Chaos, but as parts of the same, or rather adjuncts or attributes. So that Chaos signifies matter, Night signifies darkness and the privation of light, Tartarus signifies a horrendous confusion, and Erebus signifies a vast void or interval
pages.18:
and denotes them as such. It is as if he wanted to say that Chaos was a vast and immense, as well as formless, emptiness—not otherwise than the author of the Book of Wisdom says, that "God made the world from invisible and formless matter"; or, as the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>St. Paul</note> speaks, that "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from things invisible, things visible might be made." Or, if one must speak from the corpuscular philosophy (supported by experience and most firm reasons), that "First Matter" and an infinite force of atoms occupied an immense space.

<margin>Book I, On the Heavens, Chapter III. Chapter II, cited above, page 94.</margin>
§. XVI. These things are also clearly conformable to the Mosaic narrative, and agree excellently with the sayings and traditions of both the Greek and barbarian philosophers; we shall not be overly laborious in citing these, since Master Tentzelius has already taken up this entire province. Rather, we urge this: that Aristophanes explicitly declares that the race of Gods did not exist before Love had mixed all things. That the stars must be understood by "the race of Gods" <note>original: "Deorum genus"</note> is proved more clearly than the midday sun by the phrasing "race of immortals" <note>original: "γένος ἀθανάτων"</note>, which none of the Ancients—whether Pythagoreans, Platonics, or Peripatetics—ever applied to sublunary things. This is so much the case that, although Pseudo-Hermes says and establishes that "nothing in the world dies," he nevertheless does not use the word "immortal" <note>original: "ἀθάνατον"</note>. The places by which this assertion could be demonstrated are infinite; however, let two suffice. One is from Aristotle, who says that "all nations attribute the highest place to the Gods, because that which is immortal is linked to the immortal" <note>original: "ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον"</note>; the other is from Ocellus Lucanus, who asserts with an elegant simile that "the course of the Moon is the isthmus of mortality and immortality." 

Nor do the Mythologists and Cyclic Poets say or teach anything else; they all proceed in explaining Theogonies in such a way that they narrate the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no intervening space of time. Regarding Plato and the Platonics, the same is most evident, such that to wish to declare it laboriously would be to lose one's effort. <margin>Book VI, 6. VI.</margin> Nevertheless, we cannot help but add from Proclus that he calls the "maker and producer Gods" of animals "new and recent"; elsewhere, however, he asserts that the "Orphic egg" and "the Being of Plato" are the same thing <note>original: "τὸ Ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν, καὶ τὸ τοῦ πλάτωνος ὄν"</note>. These latter points not only show that the ancients understood by the "egg" nothing other than Chaos itself, but they simultaneously reveal the foundation or occasion of the opinion concerning the pre-existence of anti-mundane matter. 

Namely, because whatever Gods there were besides the Supreme God (whom they called "One," "Good," "beyond essence" <note>original: "ἀνουσίαον"</note>, and not endowed with essence)—such as the stars and demons, and indeed even the Mind and Soul of the World—they believed these to be beings produced by the Supreme God. And they believed these recently produced Gods received matter, from which they would fashion sublunary bodies, as already prepared and existing. They could not help but establish eternal Matter, because before time (which began as soon as the mundane bodies were produced), there was mere eternity.

§. XVII. The fact that Aristophanes says Night first brought forth a "wind-egg" <note>original: "ovum subventaneum"; an unfertilized egg</note> does nothing against the truth; it only shows that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, and could not follow the incubation or brooding of Divine Love. Thus, he adorned the sentiment according to the capacity of his own wit. So this single difficulty cannot possibly prevent us—having dismissed Burnet's archaeology—from subscribing to the opinion sufficiently demonstrated by Hugo Grotius, Edmund Dickinson, Jacob Tollius, and Adam Tribbechov.

<pb n="10"/>### XL.

An agreement is furthermore considered either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or is added immediately to a contract.

### XLI.

The former is called a <term>naked pact</term> <gloss>nudum pactum; an agreement without legal force</gloss>, but the latter are called not naked; since these do not rest upon the naked terms of an agreement, but either adhere to a contract or have a supporting law, everyone sees that they cannot be held in the class of naked pacts. <note>Cited from Bachovius in his notes on the Disputations of Treutler.</note>

### XLII.

And these may also not inconveniently be called <term>clothed</term> <gloss>vestita; legally enforceable</gloss>; for although these words do not appear in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists; moreover, where the matter is established, we ought to be flexible regarding the words, by the argument of <term>law 17</term>, Digest concerning the laws.

### XLIII.

A naked convention is that which stands at the limit of the consensus. <note>Original: "stat placiti fine."</note> <term>Law "si tibi" 27</term>, Code concerning letting and hiring. Or, what is the same thing, that which consists in the pure and simple limits of a convention.

### XLIV.

And it is called such because it is naked of a cause or a business transaction, <term>the said law "solent" 15</term>, Digest concerning prescribed words. This also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract, whence it is also called a simple convention in <term>law "avia" 6</term>, Code concerning the law of dowries, and merely a pact in <term>law "major" 23</term>, Code concerning pledges and mortgages.

### XLV.

For example, if it is agreed that you sell me your house, this convention stands in the naked terms of the consensus: but if indeed it is agreed concerning the thing and the price, that convention is no longer <pb n="11"/>called naked, because a business transaction has been added which produces a civil obligation, and a contract has been celebrated, which is called buying and selling, in the beginning of the law concerning buying and selling and the law on agreed pacts, 72, at the beginning, Digest concerning the contracting of a purchase.

### XLVI.
Thus if I bargain with you that you give me money as a loan, or that you exchange your Cornelian estate for my buildings, so far nothing has been done beyond a naked convention and a naked consensus. But as soon as you count out the money to me, or deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my buildings to you, a business transaction intervenes beyond the convention, and in that case a loan is contracted. At the beginning of the law regarding the modes by which an obligation is contracted by a thing. This indeed is an exchange. <term>Law "naturalis" 5, paragraph 1</term>, Digest concerning prescribed words.

### XLVII.
It is doubted whether the name of "pact," when uttered simply, signifies a naked pact? I affirm this through the <term>law of the Law of Nations 7, paragraph 5</term>, Digest concerning pacts. Those feeling the contrary are moved by the above-mentioned law on deliveries, 20, there "not by naked pacts," Code concerning pacts. But <term>Hunnius</term> satisfies these in his resolutions on <term>Treutler</term>, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.
A naked pact, moreover, is either express or tacit, which is to say it is gathered from the deeds of the contracting parties, and is said to be entered into by the thing itself in <term>law 2</term>, Digest concerning pacts, and <term>law 32</term>, Digest on partnership. We have one example of this in <term>law 2, paragraph 1</term>, Digest concerning pacts: he who has returned a security to a debtor is understood to have tacitly bargained not to sue. Another is in <term>law 3</term>, Digest under the said title, where he who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, but not the debt itself.
</translation>

<summary>This section distinguishes between naked pacts, which lack legal enforceability, and clothed pacts or contracts that carry civil obligations. It explains how a simple agreement becomes a contract through the addition of a specific transaction, such as payment or delivery.</summary>

<keywords>pactum nudum, naked pact, contract, civil obligation, buying and selling, loan, exchange, tacit agreement, Bachovius, Hunnius, Treutler</keywords>

<pb n="14"/><note>continues from previous page</note> John, the matter is narrated in such a way that it appears the lashes were inflicted upon Christ by Pilate’s own person, not by his soldiers, since mention of them is only made later in verse 2. Blessed Gerhard indicates that Bede, while adhering too literally to the text, hesitated on this opinion. But who would so easily believe that a man of such great standing, established in such dignity and authority among both Romans and Jews, would humble himself so far as to carry out this duty himself, which was to be dispatched by soldiers and <term>lictors</term> <gloss>official attendants</gloss> as their own proper task? It is rather more probable that this butchery was performed chiefly by those who were specifically commissioned and destined by Pilate to carry it out. However, the scourging is attributed here to Pilate himself, the Governor of Judea, as the principal moral cause, because the entire matter was conducted by his order and command. Thus, it is not absurd, but very appropriate, to explain the words of the Evangelists in this way. For is it not so, according to the common rule, that what one does through another or others should be considered and said to have been done by oneself?

XXVII. Furthermore, investigating the ministerial cause, we judge it not irrelevant to ask who and what kind of men were specifically admitted to scourge JESUS? If we look at the more corrected Greek codices here, we do not find their mention made separately in the text regarding this; yet we gather reasonably from the words, both preceding and following, that Roman soldiers and lictors—called by some <term>Brutiani</term> or <term>Brutii</term>—and these being gentiles, were the principal actors of this tragedy. For the added small word referring to the Jews, *Eis* <gloss>to them</gloss>, which is read in some copies after the word *tradidit* <gloss>he delivered</gloss>, is not genuine; hence, as Erasmus notes, it somewhat obstructs the sense.
<margin>
Annotations on Matthew chapter 27.
</margin>
For (he adds) Pilate did not deliver JESUS to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of punishment. Since it was they who previously seized Christ, bound him when seized, presented him bound to judgment, scourged him when presented, afterward clothed him in purple when scourged, crowned him when clothed, mocked him when crowned, struck him when mocked, led him away when struck, and crucified him when led away: just as we see this emphasized not once, but repeatedly, in the history of the entire passion.

XXVIII. But a doubt might perhaps arise for someone: did the Jews not reach out their own helping hands to the Heathens in this business? Certainly, with Judas the betrayer leading the way, they delivered Christ, seeking nothing else than that JESUS should be removed from their midst by the gentiles and finally lifted onto the cross after various tortures. Therefore, who among us ever doubts that the greatest blame for the entire passion, and thus also for the scourging, redounds upon the Jews as the morally efficient causes? Indeed, that the Jews performed the role of a physical cause in any part of the work, we neither read nor believe: especially since the SAVIOR himself, suffering patiently, predicted this concerning himself to his disciples on his final journey to Jerusalem, that it would come to pass that the Chief Priests and Scribes would deliver the Son of Man to the gentiles to be mocked and <term>eis mastigōsai</term> <gloss>to be scourged</gloss>. Compare Mark and Luke. You will see in both places that it is predicated of the nations, or (which is the same in these and many other places) the gentiles, and by no means of the Jews: <term>mastigōsousin</term> <gloss>they will scourge</gloss> and <term>mastigōsantes auton</term> <gloss>having scourged him</gloss>. Whence, so that this most true prediction of the TRUTH might be fulfilled at the same time, the gentiles alone had to scourge JESUS.
<margin>
Matthew 20 verses 18-19, chapter 15 [verses] 39-40, chapter 18 verses 32 and 33.
</margin>

XXIX. But even if we inspect the mind of the Jews themselves, it is easily established why they themselves did not wish to afflict JESUS with lashes. For since according to the divine law it was not permitted for Jews to inflict more than forty blows, or, as they themselves wrongly interpreted it, thirty-nine; hence, undoubtedly out of their most bitter <pb n="15"/> hatred against CHRIST, this punishment seemed too *lenient* if it were to be imposed by their own people upon this JESUS, whom they blasphemed as a *seducer*. They preferred, therefore, to choose gentiles to inflict this punishment, since they were restricted by no certain number and were accustomed to beat the accused *beyond measure*, and sometimes even *unto death*. Indeed, they did not intend the scourging for its own sake, but *only* demanded the crucifixion. Whence, not content with that punishment inflicted by Pilate, they also cried out for Christ to be punished by the cross, nor did they cease crying out until they obtained by the very deed that which they so greatly sought. They did not want *life*, they wanted *death*, and that to be paid for by the cross: which capital punishment, however, they were not permitted to carry out, although the *Romans carried out the same among the Jews at their pleasure*. To which their own confession, uttered with one voice before Pilate, especially pertains: *It is not lawful for us, they say, to put anyone to death*; understand this primarily, as authors of no small renown understand it, by the punishment of the cross. So restricted even at that time was the power of the Jews under the Romans. Indeed, perhaps the Jews refused to offer themselves as associates to the Romans in scourging Christ for this reason too: because they thought anyone of their people would be contaminated if they merely entered the praetorium with the Passover imminent, and much more so, therefore, if they became an assistant in punishments within the same. See *John 18*.
<margin>
John 18 verse 31; verse 18.
</margin>

<margin>
Matthew 27 verse 27. Mark 15 verse 16.
</margin>

XXX. But what of it? For what reason it was done by them matters little for us to know. We return more properly to the act of scourging itself. We gathered before from the text of Scripture that it was chiefly commanded by Pilate to his pitiless soldiers and attendants that they should scourge Jesus. Exactly how many those lictors were, we have not said, nor can we say; especially with Scripture and antiquity being silent. Beyond controversy, however, more than one—indeed many, if not most—were present at this act, who aided the business of scourging with their help and labor. The place where the scourging was to be instituted was determined to be the *court or praetorium, the house in which the provincial Governor not only lived, but also administered the law*. For the soldiers of the Governor had withdrawn there, with the entire cohort called together and assembled in that place.

<margin>
Lipsius, book 2 on the Cross, chapter 4, page 63.
</margin>

XXXI. There indeed, Jesus was forced to experience the individual fates of those to be scourged. Why shall we deny here that *he was stripped of his clothes*, we who have heard above that this custom remained *most common* among the Romans in this infliction of punishments? We also quite willingly grant some credit to that opinion by which it is asserted that Jesus *was bound to a column*; not so much because *Lipsius* sought to confirm this rite with certain examples and the testimony of others, but because the pious and ancient Fathers of the religion did not clearly doubt to affirm such a thing concerning the column of the scourged Savior. Clearly and excellently, the most prudent of Poets sang in his own age:
<margin>
Prudentius, Enchiridion of the New Instrument, concerning this column. See Library of the Fathers, Volume 4, page 924.
</margin>

->Bound within these halls the Lord stood, and annexed<-
->To the column, he gave his back, like a slave, to the lashes.<-
**He even continues:**
->The venerable column still stands, and the temple holds it.<-

<margin>
Volume 2, part 2, Delights of the human race, chapter 3, section 3, page 342.
</margin>

With which agrees what *Blessed Jerome* recites concerning *Paula* in her Epitaph to *Eustochium*: *There was shown to her, he says, on Mount Zion a column supporting a portico, stained with the blood of the Lord, to which he is said to have been bound and scourged.* Bede himself testifies that in the time of *Bede*, it was in the middle of a church. But what is said concerning this column being placed in a temple, we judge to be not undeservedly suspected as at least doubtful, if not entirely false. Meanwhile, whether such a column existed in the temple or not, it is enough that it existed in the praetorium at the time when Christ was bound to it. Hence *Hieronymus Drexelius* depicts this column thus: *By the Roman rite, Jesus was fastened with ropes to a two-foot column, which...*
</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the legal and physical circumstances of the scourging of Jesus, arguing that Roman soldiers rather than Pilate himself performed the act. It also explores the involvement of the Jews and the tradition of Christ being bound to a column during his punishment.</summary>

<keywords>Pilate, scourging, Roman soldiers, lictors, Jewish law, crucifixion, praetorium, column of the flagellation, Prudentius, Saint Jerome, legal jurisdiction</keywords>

Beyond controversy, however, more than one—indeed many, if not most—were present at this act, who aided the business of scourging with their help and labor. The place where the scourging was to be instituted was determined to be the *court or praetorium, the house in which the provincial Governor not only lived, but also administered the law*. For the soldiers of the Governor had withdrawn there, with the entire cohort called together and assembled in that place.

<margin>
Lipsius, book 2 on the Cross, chapter 4, page 63.
</margin>

XXXI. There indeed, Jesus was forced to experience the individual fates of those to be scourged. Why shall we deny here that *he was stripped of his clothes*, we who have heard above that this custom remained *most common* among the Romans in this infliction of punishments? We also quite willingly grant some credit to that opinion by which it is asserted that Jesus *was bound to a column*; not so much because *Lipsius* sought to confirm this rite with certain examples and the testimony of others, but because the pious and ancient Fathers of the religion did not clearly doubt to affirm such a thing concerning the column of the scourged Savior. Clearly and excellently, the most prudent of Poets sang in his own age:
<margin>
Prudentius, Enchiridion of the New Instrument, concerning this column. See Library of the Fathers, Volume 4, page 924.
</margin>

->Bound within these halls the Lord stood, and annexed<-
->To the column, he gave his back, like a slave, to the lashes.<-
**He even continues:**
->The venerable column still stands, and the temple holds it.<-

<margin>
Volume 2, part 2, Delights of the human race, chapter 3, section 3, page 342.
</margin>

With which agrees what *Blessed Jerome* recites concerning *Paula* in her Epitaph to *Eustochium*: *There was shown to her, he says, on Mount Zion a column supporting a portico, stained with the blood of the Lord, to which he is said to have been bound and scourged.* Bede himself testifies that in the time of *Bede*, it was in the middle of a church. But what is said concerning this column being placed in a temple, we judge to be not undeservedly suspected as at least doubtful, if not entirely false. Meanwhile, whether such a column existed in the temple or not, it is enough that it existed in the praetorium at the time when Christ was bound to it. Hence *Hieronymus Drexelius* depicts this column thus: *By the Roman rite, Jesus was fastened with ropes to a two-foot column, which...*

> Often the sick do not dare to speak, indeed they can scarcely do so, which must be deduced from the vehemence of the pains, or from a paralytic state of the organs dedicated to speech.

> Fever is present, insofar as the circulation of the humors, on account of sluggish nerves and the abundance of morbid matter, does not succeed according to desire; hence it happens that they conceive a fermentation or internal motion.

Light will be shed upon this opinion by the *Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever* by the most distinguished Lord Licentiate J. C. Wolff of Zerbst, formerly my most pleasant roommate, held at Wittenberg under the most excellent Lord Doctor Berger, Public Professor there and indeed my venerable preceptor. 

Moreover, for a more moderate degree of fermentation, the sick person does not feel its distresses.

A proclivity toward sleep is also an effect of the viscosity, thickness, and scarcity of the animal spirits and other liquids, or even of the compression of the brain. Nevertheless, somnolence is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term> <gloss>migraine</gloss>, as the previously praised Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs, insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood—relaxing from a constrictive motion both on account of the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy—pass through the small canals so slowly that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? Appetite is the offspring of the animal spirits; therefore, with the use of these denied, nausea arises. What is more, the corrupted gastric lymph is not suitable for dissolving food. The stomach, thus burdened and now sufficiently weak, contracts itself spasmodically and ejects the indigested mass again, which we call <term>Vomiting</term>. Whence a tumor on the surface of the head derives its birth, let it be sought from the preceding section. It should be noted moreover that it does not seem improbable to me that such a tumor can sometimes be nourished by caries of the skull itself.

### XI.
But as to why <term>Hemicrania</term> sometimes remits, or even torments the sick person only at certain interpolated intervals of time, <pb n="13"/> and from this a *periodic* pain results (the kind of examples one may read in Tulp, Linden, Bellini, and others); this depends upon various vicissitudes of the fluid surrounding us, and upon the peculiar constitution of the head introduced by the causes mentioned in §. IX. For in such a way we easily conceive that the offending matter, consumed in the passage of time, is restored anew, and creeps again into the injured part (always retracing its tracks like a folded paper), until it grows into so great a mass that it once more attempts a distension of the parts named so often, whence the disease puts on its former face.

XII. If we recall to mind all that has been said with a little more curiosity, what great *dangers* do we not see present for the sick? And what even greater ones do we fear, not without the support of reason? We do not hesitate to affirm that <term>Hemicrania</term> is a most dangerous disease, in whatever way it conducts itself. Since the affected part is most sensible and must bring aid to the economy of the body, and the producing causes exist as extremely grave. Indeed, the disease is most difficult to cure, both because, before it can be removed, its various causes must be torn out by the roots, and because scarcely any remedy is found equal to reducing the solid parts that have been twisted <term>p. n.</term> <gloss>contrary to nature</gloss> back to their <term>st. n.</term> <gloss>natural state</gloss>. But above all, the fact that only half of the head is affected makes the evil persistent. For a remedy, although it may wash over the affected place, will nevertheless work sparingly, seeking an exit where it finds the least resistance of all. I pass over the fact that substances taken in are not specifically determined here or there, but are distributed through the whole body by the law of circulation. Wherefore *External Hemicrania*, where medicines immediately touch the affected part, bids us be more confident, unless caries of the skull be joined to it. In respect to the duration of the disease, sex, age, the temperature of the air, and the idiosyncrasy of the body, various and different prognoses must also be formed. According to the greater or lesser number of symptoms, the evil must be called more fierce or more mild. I knew a friend (which is relevant to mention here) who contracted <term>Hemicrania</term> with a languor of the limbs on that side upon which he had lain during the night, which was happily resolved shortly, and, if I am not mistaken, within eight days. Alas, how much more difficult a cure do little worms nesting in the brain make, while small stones and calculi generated in the same simply refuse it! For confirmation of this, see the *Dissertation on Incurability* <note>original: "Atherapeusia"</note> 
</translation>

XVII. He who denies that being insofar as it is being is the object of Metaphysics, because all things treated in this discipline cannot be reduced to it—such as first principles, axioms, hypotheses, and first definitions, the doctrine of the first substance and its operations and attributes—let him also deny that the natural body insofar as it is natural is the object of Physics. For not all things treated in Physics are natural bodies: for example, matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so forth. Although, indeed, not everything that this or that person says belongs to a particular discipline.

XVIII. He who said that he who wishes to use abstractions in the remaining philosophical disciplines besides Mathematics abstracts the mind from the truth—because things must be known as they are found in the nature of things, not as certain things are usually or can be abstracted from them—was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is great dispute among the ancients whether virtue can be learned; some affirm it is given by nature to the good and denied to the wicked; others that it is perceived through use and doctrine. Plato seems sometimes to side with the former, sometimes the latter. But there is no doubt that both a nature that is not depraved in itself, and precepts, and exercise both establish and perfect virtue. The ancients called these <term>Physis</term> <gloss>Nature</gloss>, <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Reason/Doctrine</gloss>, and <term>Askesis</term> <gloss>Exercise/Training</gloss>. These are as necessary in virtue as in the arts, or even in crops, where there is need for rich soil, good seeds, and the diligence of the farmer. See Ludovicus Vives <note>Spanish humanist scholar</note> on chapter 1, book 19 of The City of God, column 1141; add Augustine in the said book, chapter 4, column 1148. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> passim; Plutarch in the booklet Whether Virtue Can Be Taught <note>original: "εἰ διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή"</note>, page 370.

XX. Everyone always wants what is good: Plato in the Hipparchus. For all good things are useful: the same in the Meno.

XXI. Poverty, the sister of a good mind according to Petronius in the Satyricon, page 94, seems preferable to riches. For she thoroughly teaches all arts wherever she touches someone, says Plautus in the Stichus. Add Seneca, epistle 15, and Theocritus. For usually Necessity and Sobriety themselves accompany her, and she renders men attentive and circumspect, whereas prosperity and opulence give birth to negligence. Hence the intellect is sharpened, from which the arts come. Indeed, as Apuleius says, she never inflated anyone with pride, never depraved anyone with lack of restraint, never made anyone wild with tyranny; she neither wants nor can have the delights of the belly and the loins. Truly, these and other outrages are usually the nurslings of riches. And although we read that even the greatest crimes have been committed by the poorest men, many were not actually poor, but beggars; Aristophanes provides this distinction in the Plutus, page 11:

> For the life of a beggar <note>original: "πτωχoῦ"</note>, which you speak of, is to live possessing nothing,
<pb n="13"/>but that of a poor man <note>original: "πένητος"</note> is to live sparingly and attending to works,
> so that nothing remains for him, yet surely nothing fails him.

### XXII. Hesiod teaches in these verses that the care of human affairs lies with the Spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note> by permission of the supreme Commander:

> These are the noble spirits upon the earth,
> holy, protectors of mortal men who ward off evil,
> who surely watch over judgments and cruel deeds,
> clothed in mist, wandering everywhere over the land.

It is likely, therefore, that some of these Spirits, like Ambassadors or Tribunes, take care of peoples and regions. Theodoretus records that these are Archangels in his commentary on Daniel chapter 10, as cited by Besoldus. Certainly, it makes it believable that Saint Michael presides over my Poland because, before the victory against the Lithuanians—which was obtained without a single Pole being killed—he was seen in Poland, as histories testify; hence at last a Basilica was built to him at Lublin. What of the fact that this kingdom extends toward the vast North? And from there, according to the word of Scripture, comes evil; that is, the greatest part of the <term>Alastores</term> <gloss>avenging spirits/demons</gloss> are stabled there. Whence Nicephorus Gregoras writes in his scholia on Synesius’s On Dreams, page 383, that the Chaldeans believe the Prince of the Outer Darkness <note>original: "Orcum"</note> holds the inheritance of the extreme and adjacent land which fell to him by lot: the ruler of the outermost and terrestrial portion.

### XXIII. Among men, he who is elated by the gift of fortune and opulence, and raised even to the changeable platform of a kingdom and a dangling tribunal, lives with rarely any access and with witnesses far removed in certain inner chambers of his dignity, says Apuleius in On the God of Socrates.

And among the Persians, the person of the King is hidden under the appearance of Majesty, as Justinus testifies in book 1, page 10, and Herodotus in Clio. They seem to have received this custom from the Chaldeans; for among them, Ninus the son of Semiramis, content with the Empire worked out by his parents, laid aside the study of war, and as if he had exchanged sexes with his mother, he grew old rarely seen by men in a crowd of women. His descendants also followed that example and gave responses to nations through intermediaries: Justinus in the cited place, page 4. They themselves, of course, indulged only in the pleasures of the body, and especially those which are immersed in matter beyond others, which the senses of touch and taste provide; they led a life not unlike that of a sea-lung <note>a species of jellyfish or sea-creature with minimal movement</note>. Far more rightly, Emperor Leo says in the Tactica, chapter 16, section 21, page 245: Those who are aloof and inaccessible, and who command their servants to rebuff those who approach them, naturally fail in many great matters. Nor is there reason for Apuleius to say in the cited place that familiarity breeds contempt and that rarity procures admiration for things. Let us hear Synesius in his Oration on Kingship, page 20, discussing it thus, as Petavius translates: *Up to now, no one has despised the Sun, although what is there that is seen more frequently?* Therefore, the King, if he wants to be a true one, and cannot otherwise
</translation>

It concludes with a critique of reclusive kingship, advocating for accessible leadership.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Physics, Virtue, Poverty, Saint Michael, Poland, Lublin, Kingship, Apuleius, Synesius, Aristophanes</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="14"/>### XXX.

Nor does it stand in the way that the Church in this life is subject to immense hardships and is disfigured by many scandals, and is still weak, carrying about many signs of guilt, whence it has need of constant prayer, as Psalm 32, verse 6 testifies, and concerning which it is said in the Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6, verse 12: "forgive us our debts." For it is adorned with the remission of sins, with the Son of God sanctifying Himself for it, John 17, verse 19. And His merit covers its remaining filth, applying His own justice to it and granting it the Holy Spirit, who kindles a new light and life in the hearts of the faithful. This adornment is that gilded clothing in which, according to Psalm 45, verse 10, the queen stands at the right hand of this king; and the same Psalm affirms in verse 14 that this glory is internal and cannot be seen by human eyes.

### XXXI.

But others are called putrid and dead members, and they are dry and sterile trees, Ezekiel 20, verse 47; <term>συκῆ ἄκαρπος</term> <gloss>unfruitful fig tree</gloss>, having nothing <term>εἰ μὴ φύλλα μόνον</term> <gloss>except leaves only</gloss>, Matthew 21, verse 19. They are the foolish virgins who, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them, Matthew 25, verse 2. They are the <term>Zizania</term> <gloss>tares/weeds</gloss>, and the sons and seed of the Devil, Matthew 13, verse 38; Genesis 3, verse 15; namely, men who are neither reborn nor holy, even if they agree with the doctrine regarding the foundation. For they live without repentance and faith, nor are they quickened and governed by the spirit of Christ, even though they move in the external society of the godly. But as for those in whom Christ performs nothing, who would call them members of Christ and the Church, except dead ones?

### XXXII.

But if they are not only indifferent hypocrites, but also disagree with the foundation and the doctrine of truth, and become either defenders or approvers of false doctrine that overturns the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 3, verse 11 <note>The source cites verse 5, but the context refers to the foundation of Christ in verse 11</note>; and if they stubbornly persevere in those manifest errors, having been condemned by the judgment of the true Church according to the norm of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings: then we assert that they are to be held not even as dead members, but altogether as <term>αναθέμασι</term> <gloss>accursed things</gloss> <pb n="15"/>and blasphemers, and that they are outside the Church, even if they dare to claim for themselves the title and name of the Church, as the Papists <note>original: "Pontificij"</note> diligently do. Because it is written, Galatians 1, verses 8 and 9: "If anyone teaches another Gospel, <term>ἀναθέμα ἔστω</term> <gloss>let him be accursed</gloss>."

### XXXIII.

However, it is manifest from the example of the Apostles that the saints can also have some errors, provided they do not overturn the articles of faith (for some build gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation, while others build wood, hay, and stubble, as Paul testifies in 1 Corinthians 3, verse 12). In the Apostles, both before and after the resurrection—even though they had seen with their own eyes the beginnings of a new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ—there was such darkness and weakness that they still dreamed that the Kingdom of the Messiah would be political, Acts 1, verse 6, and many wished for Levitical rites <note>original: "cultus Leviticos"</note> to be retained, Acts 15.

### XXXIIII.

And the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss> by which many are afflicted is far too blind and wretched, if we think there is no weakness in us, that we are ignorant of nothing, but are perfect and all-knowing. For it is most true what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And in verse 12: "We see now through a mirror and in an enigma."

### XXXV.

Nor does it stand in the way that the Church in this life is subject to immense hardships and is disfigured by many scandals, and is still weak, carrying about many signs of guilt, whence it has need of constant prayer, as Psalm 32, verse 6 testifies, and concerning which it is said in the Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6, verse 12: "forgive us our debts." For it is adorned with the remission of sins, with the Son of God sanctifying Himself for it, John 17, verse 19. And His merit covers its remaining filth, applying His own justice to it and granting it the Holy Spirit, who kindles a new light and life in the hearts of the faithful. This adornment is that gilded clothing in which, according to Psalm 45, verse 10, the queen stands at the right hand of this king; and the same Psalm affirms in verse 14 that this glory is internal and cannot be seen by human eyes.

## Question III.

### Does quantitative number apply to Intelligences?

Those substances which Theologians call Angels, Metaphysicians name Intelligences. And concerning these, there is a controversy here: Whether a quantitative number can be attributed to them. We stand manfully on the side of the negative, intending to use such a shield as this: Where there is no quantity, there is no quantitative number. In intelligences, there is no quantity. Therefore. Do you doubt the minor premise? You do rightly: for to always doubt is to always inquire into a greater truth. But do you attack it? You may attack it, provided you do not capture it. For does quantity not apply solely to material and corporeal things? Do you deny it? You strike against Philosophical principles; you rise up against Aristotle himself; against truth itself. Look at the species of quantity: Continuous is that whose parts are joined by some common boundary; Discrete, on the other hand, consists of parts neither joined nor fitted together by any such boundary, as Aristotle says in the book of Categories on quantity. Where, I ask, are there any parts in Intelligences? If these existed, they would surely make the substance of the Angels either partible or divisible, certainly the intelligences themselves would have an extension of parts, certainly they would consist of a body, and certainly they would participate in matter along with form, all of which are absurdities. I add also this: Quantitative number is counted among the common sensibles, Aristotle, book 2 on the Soul, chapter 6, text 64. If, therefore, intelligences are sensible, they must certainly be perceived by sense. Otherwise, if the thing that falls under sense is removed, the sense must necessarily be removed. But sense does not exist except in a body, and it is occupied with bodies, Aristotle, book of Categories on quantity. Who endowed with sound reason would ever <pb n="10"/> have called Angels bodies? Therefore, quantitative number ought not to be attributed to them. Do you infer that an Intelligible quantity, though not a predicamental one, is given in Angels, namely so that our intellect may conceive one thing in them which is not another? You proceed poorly. For as things are, so they are conceived; this is the distinction that lies between the divine and human intellect. Specifically, the divine Intellect makes things conform to its own concept; the human intellect, however, is itself conformed to things. How, then, could you form a quantity for yourself where there is no quantity at all? How could you conceive of one part distinct from another where no parts are given at all, and thus how could distinct parts be given? Certainly, when you conceive a thing in this way, your intellect represents to you not the thing, but a figment of the brain and imagination.

### Are there five Intellectual habits?

This question is taken from the 6th book of the Nicomachean Ethics, where the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> discusses the intellectual habits at sufficient length. It must be noted above all others that these habits are of two kinds: some are instrumental, which serve the principal ones as ministers, and these are Grammar, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Logic; some are principal, concerning which the present question is proposed. We have said with the Philosopher that these are five in number, namely *Intelligence, science, wisdom, prudence*, and *Art*; we recognize neither more nor fewer. But if the hectic fever is simple, which is our subject, we shall turn ourselves immediately to its containing cause, namely the filth foul with dryness, and the salt-sulfurous fumes licking away the moisture of the whole body: which things indicate their own alteration by moistening and cooling, as well as an <term>epicratic</term> <gloss>gradual or gentle</gloss> evacuation. Then we shall also think to serve the strengths, which, diminished by the defect of the substantial moisture, exist as the cause of the containing cause, and by their own right demand their conservation and reparation. Moreover, these indications must be administered in such a way that while we are solicitous for one, we do not neglect the other; since it is certain that both indications, taken from the strengths and the cause of the disease, walk with equal pace.

### §. 22.

From Surgery, there is nothing that benefits those with hectic fever. For bloodletting and purging are equally harmful to all diseases from depletion, of which kind hectic fever is one, as <term>Forestus</term> <note>Pieter van Foreest, 1521 to 1597, a Dutch physician</note> agrees with us, who in <term>book 4, Observation</term> relates that he noted a Noble Matron with hectic fever, who, when a vein had been cut by an empiric <note>an untrained or experimental practitioner</note>, died shortly after. Another man seized with hectic fever, having disregarded the prohibitions of Forestus at the persuasion of a surgeon and a wandering quack, also admitted bloodletting, and the following day, after one pill of precipitate <note>a chemical solid, often mercuric oxide</note> was taken from the medicaster <note>a pretender to medical skill</note>, he was extinguished on that same day.

### §. 23.

From Pharmacy, many highly praise metallic remedies, which, being more noble, are said to restore health to almost every sick person, let alone one with hectic fever. But what <term>Sennert</term> <note>Daniel Sennert, 1572 to 1637, a German physician</note> affirms in <term>On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chymists, chapter 18, regarding Spirit of Salt</term>, salt, and similar things, which can be administered more safely than metallic ones; that if used too often they can inflict the greatest damage, while they consume the natural humidity in the parts by drying it out, and therefore their use must be cautious in dry bodies (and such are the bodies of those with hectic fever); this can be said with even better right regarding the metallic remedies, with which many boast they have cured hectic patients, and which are in common use everywhere. On the same foundation, <term>Bravo de Sobremonte</term> in his <term>Medical Resolutions</term> disapproves of the rashness of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, 1493 to 1541, Swiss physician and alchemist</note>, who in every fever, and thus also in hectic fever, uses a single diaphoretic <note>a medicine that induces sweating</note>: which is against the indication that demands nutrition, not a violent dissipation of moisture. He also cannot help but find fault with <term>Helmont</term> <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont, 1580 to 1644, a chemist and physician</note>, because he uses the same diaphoretic <pb n="15"/> of Paracelsus, which is surely drying and heating, and consumes the strengths no less than the hectic fever itself: although he solemnly affirms in his book on fevers that it performs its effects insensibly and without sweat, and cures a hectic patient within the course of a Moon.

### §. 24.

<term>Poterius</term> <note>Pierre de la Poterie, a 17th century French physician</note> also gives his approval to this, when he testifies from his own experience in <term>book 2, On Fevers, chapter 25</term>, that he cured a fifty-year-old man who had labored for four years under a slow fever of the hectic kind with <term>Magnetic Sugar</term> <note>a chemical preparation, likely containing iron or minerals</note>: and restored another of the same sort to health within a month, having given his <term>antihectic</term> <note>a remedy against hectic fever</note> twice a day in a conserve of Roses. <term>P. J. Faber</term> <note>Pierre Jean Fabre, 1588 to 1658, a French physician and alchemist</note> joins himself as a companion to this man in asserting the utility of metallics for hectic patients, who recounts the cure of a desperate hectic fever by the use of <term>acid Spirit of Salt</term> and <term>Tincture of the Sun</term> <note>a preparation of gold</note> extracted with rectified <term>Oil of Salt</term> in his <term>Cures of Various Diseases, Cure 14</term>. I also know those for whom dry salts are in use for the purpose of essentially moistening the wasted body of hectic patients. Others praise the <term>Balsam of Life</term>, as they call it, which they prepare thus: they take two and a half ounces of Salt and two drams of the purest Gold. They melt them, pulverize them, extract them with Spirit of Salt, and distill it off to the consistency of an oil. This they drop into one dram of pulverized <term>Salt of Pearls</term>. Mix it in a marble mortar, dry it over a slow fire and gradually regenerate it until it acquires a purple color. They administer five to ten grains in a restorative broth quite often: and from this they hope that the substantial moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by an essentially moistening substance substituted in its place.

### §. 25.

But far be it from a Physician, walking with both legs of experience and reason, to use drying agents in place of essentially moistening ones, which are indicated by hectic fever. For although hectic patients cured in that way have often become somewhat fat and seemed plainly delivered from the disease; nevertheless, the unhappy outcome, not rarely and not long after, has revealed what was the strength of that cure: namely, that when the remnants of the spirits have been made more fixed, the remaining serous and excrementitious moisture is left behind, putrefies, and from a simple hectic fever joined with a putrid one it becomes a combined disease, because the governance of nature was intercepted by the service of the spirits being hindered by the said drying and fixation. We embrace a sounder opinion on curing hectic fever, as much as possible, together with Sennert. Certainly, he says in <term>On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chymists, chapter 18, page 324</term>: there are diseases in which more is gained by nutrition than by medicine: such is Hectic Fever,

But if the hectic fever is simple, which is our subject, we shall turn ourselves immediately to its containing cause, namely the filth foul with dryness, and the salt-sulfurous fumes licking away the moisture of the whole body: which things indicate their own alteration by moistening and cooling, as well as an <term>epicratic</term> <gloss>gradual or gentle</gloss> evacuation. Then we shall also think to serve the strengths, which, diminished by the defect of the substantial moisture, exist as the cause of the containing cause, and by their own right demand their conservation and reparation. Moreover, these indications must be administered in such a way that while we are solicitous for one, we do not neglect the other; since it is certain that both indications, taken from the strengths and the cause of the disease, walk with equal pace.

### §. 22.

From Surgery, there is nothing that benefits those with hectic fever. For bloodletting and purging are equally harmful to all diseases from depletion, of which kind hectic fever is one, as <term>Forestus</term> <note>Pieter van Foreest, 1521 to 1597, a Dutch physician</note> agrees with us, who in <term>book 4, Observation</term> relates that he noted a Noble Matron with hectic fever, who, when a vein had been cut by an empiric <note>an untrained or experimental practitioner</note>, died shortly after. Another man seized with hectic fever, having disregarded the prohibitions of Forestus at the persuasion of a surgeon and a wandering quack, also admitted bloodletting, and the following day, after one pill of precipitate <note>a chemical solid, often mercuric oxide</note> was taken from the medicaster <note>a pretender to medical skill</note>, he was extinguished on that same day.

### §. 23.

From Pharmacy, many highly praise metallic remedies, which, being more noble, are said to restore health to almost every sick person, let alone one with hectic fever. But what <term>Sennert</term> <note>Daniel Sennert, 1572 to 1637, a German physician</note> affirms in <term>On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chymists, chapter 18, regarding Spirit of Salt</term>, salt, and similar things, which can be administered more safely than metallic ones; that if used too often they can inflict the greatest damage, while they consume the natural humidity in the parts by drying it out, and therefore their use must be cautious in dry bodies (and such are the bodies of those with hectic fever); this can be said with even better right regarding the metallic remedies, with which many boast they have cured hectic patients, and which are in common use everywhere. On the same foundation, <term>Bravo de Sobremonte</term> in his <term>Medical Resolutions</term> disapproves of the rashness of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, 1493 to 1541, Swiss physician and alchemist</note>, who in every fever, and thus also in hectic fever, uses a single diaphoretic <note>a medicine that induces sweating</note>: which is against the indication that demands nutrition, not a violent dissipation of moisture. He also cannot help but find fault with <term>Helmont</term> <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont, 1580 to 1644, a chemist and physician</note>, because he uses the same diaphoretic
pages.15:
of Paracelsus, which is surely drying and heating, and consumes the strengths no less than the hectic fever itself: although he solemnly affirms in his book on fevers that it performs its effects insensibly and without sweat, and cures a hectic patient within the course of a Moon.

### §. 24.

<term>Poterius</term> <note>Pierre de la Poterie, a 17th century French physician</note> also gives his approval to this, when he testifies from his own experience in <term>book 2, On Fevers, chapter 25</term>, that he cured a fifty-year-old man who had labored for four years under a slow fever of the hectic kind with <term>Magnetic Sugar</term> <note>a chemical preparation, likely containing iron or minerals</note>: and restored another of the same sort to health within a month, having given his <term>antihectic</term> <note>a remedy against hectic fever</note> twice a day in a conserve of Roses. <term>P. J. Faber</term> <note>Pierre Jean Fabre, 1588 to 1658, a French physician and alchemist</note> joins himself as a companion to this man in asserting the utility of metallics for hectic patients, who recounts the cure of a desperate hectic fever by the use of <term>acid Spirit of Salt</term> and <term>Tincture of the Sun</term> <note>a preparation of gold</note> extracted with rectified <term>Oil of Salt</term> in his <term>Cures of Various Diseases, Cure 14</term>. I also know those for whom dry salts are in use for the purpose of essentially moistening the wasted body of hectic patients. Others praise the <term>Balsam of Life</term>, as they call it, which they prepare thus: they take two and a half ounces of Salt and two drams of the purest Gold. They melt them, pulverize them, extract them with Spirit of Salt, and distill it off to the consistency of an oil. This they drop into one dram of pulverized <term>Salt of Pearls</term>. Mix it in a marble mortar, dry it over a slow fire and gradually regenerate it until it acquires a purple color. They administer five to ten grains in a restorative broth quite often: and from this they hope that the substantial moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by an essentially moistening substance substituted in its place.

### §. 25.

But far be it from a Physician, walking with both legs of experience and reason, to use drying agents in place of essentially moistening ones, which are indicated by hectic fever. For although hectic patients cured in that way have often become somewhat fat and seemed plainly delivered from the disease; nevertheless, the unhappy outcome, not rarely and not long after, has revealed what was the strength of that cure: namely, that when the remnants of the spirits have been made more fixed, the remaining serous and excrementitious moisture is left behind, putrefies, and from a simple hectic fever joined with a putrid one it becomes a combined disease, because the governance of nature was intercepted by the service of the spirits being hindered by the said drying and fixation. We embrace a sounder opinion on curing hectic fever, as much as possible, together with Sennert.
