Let it be known to each and every person inspecting this present document, and specifically to those whom it concerns, will concern, and whom the business written below touches, might touch, or could concern in any way in the future. That in the year of the Nativity of the Lord one thousand five hundred twenty-four, in the twelfth indiction <note>a fifteen-year cycle used for dating in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, on Tuesday, which was the fifth day of the month of April, in the first year of the pontificate of the most holy father in Christ and our lord, Lord Clement VII, by divine providence Pope. In the presence of me, the Notary Public, and of the witnesses written below, specifically called and requested for this purpose, there appeared in person the honorable Lord Wolfgang Schultheiss, a priest of Strasbourg, in his own name, and also in the name of the venerable lords Matthew Zell of Kaisersberg, pastor of Saint Lawrence; Anton Firn, pastor of Saint Thomas; Johann Nubling, chaplain of the chapel of Saint Erhard of the churches of Strasbourg; Lucas Hackfurt, Conrad Spatzinger, and Alexander, formerly a member of the Order of Saint John <note>the Knights Hospitaller</note>, priests, likewise personally appearing before me, the notary, and the witnesses written below. He held and kept in his hands a certain written sheet of appeal or provocation, which—with the mind and intention of provoking, appealing, protesting, and seeking <term>apostuli</term> <gloss>formal letters of appeal sent to a higher court</gloss>, and doing other things as he said were more broadly contained in the same sheet—he delivered and assigned to me, the Notary Public written below, according to the aforementioned tenor. Lest any force be done, etc. After the interposition of this sheet of provocation, appeal, and <pb n="20"/>petition for <term>apostuli</term>, the said Lord Wolfgang Schultheiss, in his own name and in the name of the aforementioned lords, the principal appellants, requested from me, the Notary Public written below, that one or more public instrument or instruments be made and completed, as many as should be necessary for him or for any of the others. These things were done at Strasbourg, in the parsonage of the parish of Saint Lawrence of Strasbourg, in the year of the Lord, indiction, day, month, hour, and pontificate as stated above, being present there the honorable and discreet men Lord Wilhelm Beltinger, assistant in divine services, and Melchior Schell, sacristan of the Church of Saint Lawrence in Strasbourg, witnesses called and required for the preceding matters.

And I, Michael Schwencker of Gernsbach, of the Diocese of Speyer, by sacred imperial authority a Notary Public. Because I was present and personally intervened in all and singular the preceding matters while they were thus done and acted as is set forth, together with the aforementioned witnesses, and I saw and heard them so done. Therefore, I have taken note of this present public instrument, faithfully written by the hand of another at my direction, and have completed, published, and reduced it into this public form. And I have signed and subscribed it with my accustomed and usual sign, name, and surname.

### XXVII.

Likewise: if he does not administer justice to the vassal, he is constrained by the same loss.

### XXVIII.

And regularly, if the lord commits a <term>felony</term> <gloss>a serious breach of the feudal contract</gloss> against the vassal, for which the vassal would have lost the fief had he committed it, the lord loses the ownership of the feudal property.

### XXIX.

However, since we have made mention chiefly of that loss of a fief which deprives the vassal, it is not inconvenient to add here that there are some cases in which the vassal does not lose the fief, even though the <term>fidelity</term> <gloss>loyalty or allegiance</gloss> which joins both the vassal and the lord is not maintained or offered.

### XXX.

As, for example, if the lord of the fief is excommunicated, outlawed, a condemned heretic, guilty of <term>lese-majeste</term> <gloss>treason or an offense against the sovereign</gloss>, etc.

### XXXI.

Likewise: if the lord should command anything to be done by the vassal <pb n="17"/> against decency, an impossibility, or some other immoderate command, the vassal is freed from obedience.

->To whom a lost fief should devolve.<-

### XXXII.

When fiefs are lost for various reasons, the question is: do the fiefs <term>open up</term> <gloss>become available for reclamation</gloss> to the lord in every way and without distinction? Or does it go now to the lord and now to others, according to the variety of the causes? The latter is more true.

### XXXIII.

It is asked whether there is a free power of <term>refuting</term> <gloss>renouncing or giving up</gloss> a fief, or whether it must depend on the consent of the lord? Which seems uncivil: for it is permitted to renounce gains.

### XXXIIII.

Therefore, when a fief is renounced, it returns to the lord in the case where it is a new fief, notwithstanding that a loss might fall upon the sons as a result; but in the case where it is a paternal or ancient fief, it devolves to the male children, or to the <term>agnates</term> <gloss>relatives through the male line</gloss> if those children are lacking.

### XXXV.

A brother renouncing a fief in favor of a brother to whom it was afterwards assigned, and who died without heirs, is not excluded from the fief.

If, moreover, after all these things, the pulses, having suddenly risen into a swelling <note>a high or bounding pulse</note>, do not fall back into smallness nor become weak, a crisis is immediately to be expected. A solution is imminent *through sweat* if there is shivering, suppression of urine, a soft and wavy pulse, loose skin, if the exterior parts are hot, and a hot vapor breaks out. *Through urine*, if signs of the other excretions are absent, and there is a burning of the private parts, heaviness of the pubes, and especially a copious flow of purulent and vitreous urine on the indicating day. *Through an abscess: If a sense of weariness is perceived, abscesses arise chiefly at the joints and around the jaws,* as <term>Hippocrates</term> teaches in <term>Aphorism 31, Section 4</term>. Likewise: *Those for whom the bowels are disturbed near the beginnings, but the urine is scanty, in the progress of time the bowels are indeed dried up, but thin urine abounds; in these, abscesses at the joints occur,* the same author observing in <term>Coan Prenotions 619</term>. *Through diarrhea: If,* says <term>Hippocrates</term> again in the <term>Coan Prenotions</term>, *for one drawing breath with difficulty with a cough-inducing breath, there is a belch bringing back and rolling inward; it announces the bird's labor* <note>a metaphorical or technical reference to a specific type of struggle or respiratory sound</note>. <term>Coan 142</term> writes: *Those for whom belches, flatulence, and sounds of the belly with inflation are present, in them the bowels are disturbed.* *Through vomiting* it happens to those whom loathing of the stomach vexes, with a biting at the mouth of the stomach and frequent spitting, <term>Coan 142</term>. <term>Galen</term> says in <term>On Crises, Book 3, Chapter 11</term>, that a sign of critical vomiting is when the lower lip quivers. When the solution occurs through other excretions, for example through a flow of hemorrhoids or the menses, or through several at once, these also manifest through their own signs, which can be seen in the works of Practitioners.

XVI. It is terminated lethally, and death is signified to be near at hand, when livid spots <note>bruising or cyanosis</note> occur in this fever; <term>Coan 66</term>. If it is not treated correctly, it easily degenerates into a <term>hectic</term> <gloss>a slow, wasting fever</gloss>. <pb n="10"/>Stubborn affections of the brain, for example sleeplessness, deliria, tremors, convulsive movements, and long-clinging weaknesses of the nervous parts, not uncommonly follow an imperfect crisis through hemorrhage, as *Willis* notes in *Chapter 9, On Fevers*. These things suffice concerning the signs.

### XVII. I return to the definition, the last words of which are: *which arises either from bile alone, or with other humors putrefying together in the larger vessels.* By which words the difference of the <term>Causus</term> <gloss>burning fever</gloss> is partly expressed: For, by reason of the cause, one burning fever is from bile alone, which suddenly tends toward its peak with violence of all symptoms, and is otherwise called *exquisite* or *legitimate*. Another is from other humors mixed together, and is called *spurious* <note>notha</note>. Moreover, bile can be mixed and putrefy together with *phlegm* <note>pituita</note>, from which a *phlegmatic burning fever* arises, which has very mild symptoms, moves more slowly to its peak, and sometimes worsens toward evening: Or with *melancholy* <note>black bile</note>, and then signs of melancholy are present: Or with *blood*, as <term>Galen</term> seems to suggest in <term>Commentary 4, Aphorism 59</term>, when he teaches that *burning fevers have yellow bile overflowing in the veins together with the blood;* and these fevers, by reason of the preeminence of the putrefying humor, are called sometimes <term>synochoi kausodes</term> <gloss>continual burning fevers</gloss>, sometimes <term>kausoi synecheis</term> <gloss>continuous burning fevers</gloss>. Or if *scorbutic serum* is present, a scorbutic burning fever arises. In all these differences, malignancy not uncommonly supervenes.

### XVIII. Partly the immediate cause is noted. In explaining the series of causes, I shall follow the common path of the Practitioners, and I shall divide the causes of this affection into immediate and mediate. The immediate cause is *bile, either alone or putrefying with other humors*. The mediate causes are *Natural, Non-natural, and Preter-natural things*. <pb n="613"/>and recollection.

Explanation of the text.
The inscription of the book *On Memory and Recollection* indicates its subject matter; the single chapter is completed in two parts.

The First Part
Treats of memory.
I. To remember <note>original: "memorari"</note> and to recollect <note>original: "reminisci"</note> are not the same: because those with good memories, such as the ingenious, are not necessarily good at recollecting.
II. Memory is not of the future or the present, but of the past: because hope or opinion belongs to the future; sense perception to the present: but memory belongs to a past act: which is neither sense perception nor opinion.
III. Memory is an affection of something once time has passed.
<margin>Corollary. Supposition.</margin>
IV. Only those things that perceive time remember.
V. Understanding does not occur without a <term>phantasm</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss>: and therefore the intellect does not understand without continuous time.
VI. Memory is an affection of the primary sensitive faculty. He proves this because it belongs to that faculty to know time; therefore memory belongs to it: for the sense perceives motion, time, and magnitude: whence he admits memory to belong to the intellect accidentally: insofar as it receives a phantasm from the senses.
VII. These sayings are proved because even non-intelligent beings remember, such as brute animals.
VIII. Not all animals possess memory.
IX. Although the species <note>the formal likeness or mental representation</note> of a thing may be present: yet memory is not regarding the species, but regarding the absent thing: he proves this because if a painting or a seal represents a past thing, so does the species in the imagination: he proves this first because those in great motion do not remember, such as the drunk or the sick: because the species are hindered. 2. Children do not remember: because species are hindered due to fluxibility. 3. The elderly do not remember well; because due to excessive dryness, they do not receive the species well. 4. Because those who understand quickly retain and remember poorly.
X. Memory is not of that species: for then it would be of the present.
XI. It seems that memory is of the present: because memory belongs to the sense itself: now sense is of the present. 2. Because a species is in the imagination just as a painting is on a wall: now the painting is present to the one seeing it. 3. If the common sense can be of the absent; then also the exterior sense.
XII. The preceding are resolved; because although the species exists as a certain thing present in the mind: yet insofar as it is representative of another, it is thus of an absent thing: he explains the mode of representing diverse species as in the text.
XIII. Memory increases and is preserved through frequent meditation: for the soul is made more capable if it remembers many times.

The second part, on recollection.
XIV. Recollection is not memory, nor is it sensing or understanding something anew: the second is proved; because memory does not occur when one understands or senses something anew: therefore neither does recollection; the antecedent is clear because memory requires the interruption of past time: and thus memory supposes a prior act or habit: But it differs from memory because in recollection, forgetfulness intervenes.

XV. To remember or to recollect is not to know something repeatedly: but to know that one has previously known or seen this.
XVI. The mode of recollecting occurs through this: that just as one motion of the soul occurs after another: so it apprehends one after another: And thus when we recollect, we are moved from one act to another by meditating, through the similar or the contrary.
XVII. Why do we sometimes recollect easily from a long time ago: and not what was done yesterday or the day before? He responds that this is because recollection occurs through the apprehension of something that is effective for apprehending.
XVIII. First corollary: we certainly recollect from that principle from which the things to be recollected began. Second corollary: we recollect well-ordered things more easily than disordered ones.
XIX. Why can one wishing to recollect sometimes not do so: and then later, without seeking, recollect spontaneously? He responds because the one wishing has many apprehensions that are not effective for that recollection: and spontaneously thereafter comes the apprehension that is effective for apprehending.
XX. One wishing to recollect should think of the places in which he has been.
XXI. The best mode of recollecting is through division, as in "that week I was there," by dividing through the days I may easily find what I did from one to the other.
XXII. Why do those having the principle of recollecting not recollect? He responds because that principle is indifferent to many things.
XXIII. Why do we sometimes recollect defectively? It is responded that just as things occur in natural matters, so also they do in matters of the will.
XXIV. Time contributes to recollecting: so that one knows past time to be past: yet both memory and recollection occur without a fixed time: although things are understood in proportion to the time.
XXV. It happens that one errs in recollection, and this is on the part of the thing and on the part of the time.
XXVI. Memory differs from recollection: because although animals other than man remember; they do not recollect; the reason for which is that recollection occurs with discourse <note>reasoning or sequential thought</note>.
XXVII. Recollection is a bodily affection: the first sign of this is: because many wishing to recollect and not being able to are disturbed: especially in the melancholic: and it is just as in the angry; whose motions they cannot easily calm: and because of strong imagination, we do not cease from the memory of certain things.
XXVIII. The second sign is; because those having heavy upper parts remember poorly. The third sign is because children and the elderly are poor at remembering: children due to excessive motion, the elderly due to lack of motion.

Annotation
1. Primary sensitive faculty, that is, the common sense.
16. Order contributes most to memory: Whence one about to commend something to memory / should always study to review it in the same order: otherwise if he orders it now this way, now that way / he will confuse himself.
These precepts which Aristotle has handed down concerning memory, <pb n="614"/> younger writers have followed more accurately: the Rhetoricians whom they call Orators have enriched them: as may be seen in Cicero and Fabius: for artificial memory consists primarily in places, images, their comparison, and the order employed: for in our time some have handed down artificial memory.
12. Antiphon, indeed of less sound mind / thought those things were truly done / which were imaginary to himself.
23. We err "alone" <note>original: "Solo"</note>. Read "we summon alone" <note>original: "solae cifamus"</note>: he means / if we wish to recollect a name: and because it ends in "-bertus," I pronounce "Engelbertus," when it is "Eckbertus."
24. Aristotle says times and magnitudes are proportioned, let it be a. b. c.
<note>A triangular diagram labeled with points a, b, c at the vertices, and f, d, h, k, m, e along the sides and interior.</note>
the triangle of time and h. i. k. the triangle of the thing: and adapt it to the text / and you will find what you seek: except that someone uses letters both for Aristotle and the translator: you use them thus. as is the proportion of a. b. to b. c. such is h. i. to i. k.: and so consequently when applied.
25. Error occurs in memory, while one thinks he remembers / when he does not remember: and while he does not think he remembers / while he exercises memory.
28. Dwarf, pygmy <note>original: "pumilio"</note>, so Aristotle wishes. to be like dwarfs / because they are of small stature / and have large heads, according to that distich of Martial:
If you only look at the man's head: you would believe him Hector
If you see him standing: you would think him Astyanax.

## Single Question.
### Whether memory and recollection differ:
### Article I.

Note I. That we may proceed in reverse order, this is the mode of remembering: while one sees (for the sake of example), then a species and likeness of the king is imprinted in the soul, just as a seal imprints its form in wax: that species is reserved in the soul: and he who saw it can think of him: and then he is said to remember: This being supposed, know that the way of memory is its reception: for the memorative power itself is called memory: similarly the organ reserving the species is called memory: and fourthly, memory is used for the act of remembering: and thus we speak here of memory: And thus memory is twofold, i.e., intellectual and sensitive. ¶ And six things are required for memory, namely three representatives and three things represented according to Buridan: the things represented in the prior example are the king seen, the vision, and the past time in which he saw: of all these, it is necessary that the soul have species, images, and likenesses / if it wishes to remember.
Note II. That foundation being laid, the difference between remembering, recollecting, and forgetting can easily stand: For if species are strongly imprinted and totally reserved in the soul; so that immediately upon noticing, they immediately move the power to repeated knowledge of the thing: And through these species memory occurs: Either these species are weakly imprinted, or lost through length of time or another cause and corrupted and totally abolished and removed from the power of corporating species: and then we are said to forget: Or they are only weakened, not inwardly lost / but confused and fragile, they still adhere slightly in the memorative organ / not sufficient by themselves to move the power / except with the apprehension of another, and with help: by which it may be elevated and actuated: and then through these species we recollect: Take the symbol: you saw a painting on a wall: after an interval you return, where part of the painting is deleted, and part remains: now from the part of the painting remaining, you discourse to the knowledge of the deleted part: so it happens in recollection. ¶ Corollary. Recollection does not presuppose total forgetfulness / but partial: but relearning presupposes total forgetfulness. ¶ Corollary. Thus is Averroes to be understood: that recollection occurs with interrupted memory, namely by partial forgetfulness: this is the mind of Brussels and Eisenach: Always add, however, that generally memory extends itself to recollection.

Note III. From these things the definition of memory given by Aristotle is clear. Memory is the affection or habit of something once time has passed: it is the judgment of past acts by way of pastness: The doctors do not agree here, to which power memory belongs: Aristotle concludes it to be an affection of the primary sensitive faculty, i.e., the common sense: Avicenna in the 6th book of *Natural Philosophy*, part 5, chapter 6, denies memory to be in the intellect: William of Ockham in question 12 of the fourth book denies memory to be in the intellect: he is moved by this / because for memory, complex knowledge <note>propositional knowledge</note> is required: but sense does not know complexly: Also because in remembering, the power is reflected upon its own act: but no sense reflects upon its own act: more on these in Scotus, distinction 45 of the fourth book, question 3. But Gregory of Rimini strongly resists in distinction 2, question 2, article 2, doubt 3: because first, memory is of the common sense regarding sensibles: and accidentally or consequently it is in the intellect: yet memory of intelligibles is primarily in the intellect: Ockham does not stand in the way because Gregory and d'Ailly in question 3 of the first book show well that sensitive knowledge is complex, concerning which see the prologue of the *Logic*. Secondly, although the exterior sense may not be reflexive / because no one sees himself seeing: yet the common sense is indeed reflexive over the exterior senses: because it perceives itself seeing: Wherefore we have posited a twofold memory: sensitive and intellectual.

Note IV. From this the definition of recollection is clear: Recollection is the resumption of knowledge lapsed from memory from some principle retained in memory: which take as in the second note. ¶ It follows that one wishing to recollect must have recourse to some rememorative principle / from which another follows in order: so that he may thus find what is sought: And it does not matter whether it be natural order or customary: just as when I cannot say some verse of a psalm or a poem / unless I recount some preceding ones: Wherefore rightly Aristotle preaches...
</translation>

<summary>This text provides a scholastic commentary on Aristotle's theories of memory and recollection, distinguishing between the passive retention of images and the active process of recovery. It discusses the physiological requirements for memory and cites various medieval and Renaissance authorities including Buridan, Ockham, and Averroes.</summary>

<pb n="12"/>a severe and long-lasting <note>original: "grauem, & diuturnum"</note> disease. It would be a rather long story if I wished to recount everything that he asserts happened to him during his illness. At last, after many years, in the sixth year of Pope Nicholas V, he returned to the Curia so that he might go to the tomb of our Savior. Naked and destitute—for he had fallen among thieves on the journey—he stayed with some members of the Curia who were my neighbors and most honorable men, to whom he had previously been known. <pb n="11"/>civil law may come from Laws, Plebiscites, Senate Decrees, the edicts of Princes, and the authority of the Learned <note>original: "Prudentum"</note>. From Law 7, the beginning of the Pandects <gloss>Digest</gloss> *On Justice and Law*, it is not sufficiently clear to which of these parts our action owes its birth. There is no doubt that its formulated words and the solemn formula, by which it was necessary to be proposed in antiquity, are to be referred to the learned in Law, by the argument of Law 2, paragraph 6, of the Pandects *On the Origin of Law*.

### §. VII.

The proximate efficient cause or foundation is a Right established in another’s thing <note>original: "Jus in re aliena"</note> or a servitude, whether personal or real; or rather the harm and injury which is inflicted when one person strives either to entirely deprive another of the exercise of a servitude due to him, or at least acts as an impediment so that he cannot exercise his Right quietly. For since an action is a complaint <note>original: "quærela"</note>, according to the final Law of the Pandects *On Summoning into Court*, and since no one can complain unless he suffers an injustice which he desires to be corrected by a Judge, it follows that the foundation of the Confessory action is not so much the Right in another’s thing itself, as it is the injury committed regarding that Right.

### §. VIII.

This action can be attempted by one who, possessing a Right in another’s thing belonging either to himself or to his property, is either entirely deprived of its exercise or at least hindered in its quiet use. For just as a person claims <note>original: "vindicat"</note> a corporeal thing who, being the Owner <note>original: "Dominus"</note>, lacks the exercise of Ownership power while another is the possessor, similarly it is lawful to use the Confessory action for one whose exercise of a Right in another’s thing has been either completely misappropriated or at least whose quiet use has been interrupted by the act of another. Moreover, since <pb n="12"/> servitudes are of either persons or things (Law 1, Digest, *On Usufruct*), it is manifest that this action is given both to him who has a right in another’s thing through himself, and to him who has it through his property. Therefore, when *Ulpian* <note>famous Roman jurist, c. 170–223 AD</note> says in Law 2, § 1, and Law 6, § 3, *If a servitude be claimed*, that the action is competent for no one other than the Owner of the estate, it is clear he is speaking only of Real servitudes, since in personal ones a Right in another’s Thing is sufficient without an estate. But if there are several Owners of the dominant estate, they each claim the whole <note>original: "in solidum"</note> and not just a part (Law 6, § 4, *If a servitude be claimed*). It is not given to a USUFRUCTUARY <note>one who has the right to use and enjoy the fruits of another's property</note> (Law 1, beginning; Law 5, § 1, *If a Usufruct be sought*); for although he also holds a right in another's thing, because the dominant estate does not belong to him by right of ownership, he cannot claim a servitude belonging to that estate, though he can sue those hindering the Usufruct. This, however, is to be understood regarding the direct claim; for that he can take action by a useful action <note>an equitable legal remedy adapted from a direct one</note> is declared by Law 1, § 4, *On Remissions*. Though some interpret this regarding a fructuary who, as if a proxy for the Owner of the property, claims the servitude in his name; others prefer to settle this conflict by thinking that the opinion of *Julian* <note>Salvius Julianus, Roman jurist</note> reported in the said Law 1, § 4, Digest, *On Remissions*, was rejected by *Marcellus* in Law 1, *If a Usufruct be sought*, and by *Ulpian* in Law 5, § "whether". Furthermore, since it happens that he who has a Right in another’s Thing is either entirely deprived of the exercise of his right, or indeed exercises it but not securely and quietly, it follows that this action is given to the Owner whether he is possessing or not possessing (Law 6, § 1, *If a servitude be claimed*); to the latter so that one may recover lost possession, to the former so that he may exercise the servitude securely (by the argument of Law 5, final §, *If a Usufruct be sought*).
</translation>

<keywords>Confessory action, servitude, jus in re aliena, Usufructuary, Roman Law, Ulpian, property rights, legal injury, dominant estate</keywords>

<pb n="10"/>19. It is clear that this reasoning concludes nothing more than that the Angels did not exist before the third day; it by no means proves they were created on that day.
20. Therefore, since none of these opinions rest upon certain foundations, we conclude with Origen in book 1 of On First Principles <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>:
> It is part of the Church's preaching that there are certain Angels of GOD; but when these were created is not clearly enough distinguished.

## APHORISM 3.

->*Angels are spirits, intelligent and wise, good, holy, powerful, destined for the ministry of GOD, for the salvation of men.*<-

### I. EXPOSITION.

1. Since the human tongue stammers regarding things removed from the senses, some sort of description may suffice us for the Angels—those most blessed minds which are furthest removed from the senses—and let it be this one which our aphorism has just provided.
2. It describes the Angels as they were from their first origin, and establishes their *Genus* as *Spirits*.
3. It attributes to them *accidents* or concreated *Qualities*, such as intelligence, wisdom, goodness, holiness, and power. We wish all these predicates to be understood restrictively and within their own kind, not absolutely. For as soon as you compare these to the spirituality, intelligence, goodness, etc., of GOD, a difference presents itself as great as that which lies between the infinite and the <pb n="11"/>finite, between the essential and the accidental, between the creative and the created, and between immutable and mutable holiness, goodness, and the rest.
4. *Their duty is described as twofold: one is considered with respect to GOD, the other with respect to men.*

->CONFIRMATION.<-

5. Scripture itself confirms this nature of the Angels, and indeed I. *that they are Spirits*. 1. By calling them *Spirits* simply, in Psalm 104:4, and Hebrews 1, *last verse*: "Are they not all (Angels) ministering spirits?" 2. By *denying them matter*, because they do not have flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12, nor flesh and bones, Luke 24:39.
6. II. It attributes *concreated qualities* to them: and the woman of Tekoa says that *Angels are Intelligent*: "My lord," she says, "is wise according to the wisdom of an Angel of GOD, to know all things that are on the earth," 2 Samuel 14:20.
7. They are called *Good* by the Creator Himself. For "GOD saw everything that He had made, and behold, all things were very good," Genesis 1:31. Since Angels were made by GOD (as stated above in aphorism 1), they are therefore good by the goodness of creation, as Theologians like to say.
8. They are called *Holy*, Luke 9:26, Acts 10:22.
9. They are *Powerful* in strength, Psalm 103:20; to say nothing here of the wonderful works of the Angels, which sufficiently demonstrate their power (mentioned above in aphorism 1, thesis 9), and the names of principalities, powers, virtues, and thrones which they are assigned in scripture.
10. III. The *Duty* which they perform with respect to GOD is the celebration of His name. For the Cherubim and Seraphim sing: "Holy, Holy, Holy," etc., Isaiah 6:3. And the execution of His commands. Hence "thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stand before him," Daniel 7:10. Psalm 103:20-21 speaks of both of these duties.
</translation>

<pb n="195"/><meta>continues from previous page: teaches the perfect merit of Christ</meta> and the full cause through which regeneration is given to us. The discussion in Romans 3 and Ephesians 2 regarding gratuitous justification <note>justification by grace rather than works</note>, from which this regeneration of ours flows, pertains to this. Next, the doctrine of the <term>communicatione idiomatum</term> <gloss>communication of properties</gloss> is manifest here: for the Son of Man, insofar as he is man, did not descend from heaven, nor was he in heaven before the ascension; and before his conception in the womb of the virgin, that Son of Man was not even a man. Therefore, it is clear that the language is figurative <note>original: "improprium", meaning not used in its literal or narrow sense</note>, and is spoken of the whole person on account of the other nature to which these things are proper. For the <term>logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> was the Son in heaven before he was incarnated, and as the same <term>logos</term> he descended from heaven to assume flesh; these things are attributed here to the Son of Man through communication—that is, to the man Christ—because he is the same as God, and the Divine and human natures constitute the same person. Hence the predicates are exchanged, and it is said that God suffered, and redeemed the Church with his own blood; and conversely, the man Christ is in heaven, and "before Abraham was, I am," and similar things. See Cyril 32. 
<margin>Communication of properties.</margin> 
<margin>Romans 3:21; Ephesians 2:8</margin>
<margin>Acts 20</margin>
<margin>John 8:57</margin>

*And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.*

He shows how the merit of the Son of God becomes useful to us, namely through his death and our faith, which firmly <pb n="196"/> apprehends that merit. He uses an argument from a likeness. He took the likeness from Moses in Numbers 21 concerning the bronze serpent, which, lifted up by the command of the Lord, saved those gazing upon it against the bites of the fiery serpents. 
<margin>Numbers 21:8, 9</margin>

The explanation is added by the Lord Christ himself, which shows how the members correspond to each other. The <term>antitypa</term> <gloss>antitypes or spiritual fulfillments</gloss> here are Christ and the serpent; the lifting up and the death of Christ; gazing at the serpent and firmly apprehending Christ by faith; the bite of the serpents and the power of sin; this temporal life and eternal salvation. From this, a fitting and timely allegory is taken. First, the bronze serpent was established by God as the author when things were desperate among the Israelites; so Christ was given as mediator when things were desperate among us. For no suitable one was found among men, or even among the Angels. Next, the bronze serpent heals those struck by serpents; Christ heals those struck by the serpent Satan, he himself having become the serpent for the serpent, as if you were to say the poison of the poison. Thirdly, it benefits by sight alone; so Christ heals us by faith alone. Fourthly, the mystery of the cross is manifest in the lifting up. Things lifted up are seen more easily and are of use to more people. So the merit of Christ is set forth in public for all nations; hanging, he consecrates the air, who by walking had already sanctified the earth; stretching out his hands, he calls together <margin>Antitypes</margin> <margin>Allegory</margin>
</translation>

<keywords>regeneration, justification, communication of properties, Christology, bronze serpent, allegory, atonement, faith, crucifixion</keywords>

<pb n="11"/>and when this constitution was removed, according to a constitution of Marcus Antoninus, a special praetor, who is also called "tutelary," was appointed so that he might give tutors to those of senatorial rank after an inquiry, just as other praetors do, and might demand security and compel them to the administration of the office. Paragraph 3 of this title. Custom finally did away with this constitution of Marcus, whereby at Rome either the Urban Prefect gave tutors—namely to the children of <term>illustres</term> <gloss>high-ranking officials</gloss>, Law 1, Code on the guardianship and curators of illustres—or the praetor did so according to his jurisdiction; but in the provinces, the governors gave them, or the magistrates did so by order of the governor. Paragraph 4 of this title. Justinian later changed this custom again and entrusted that right to the <term>defensores civitatum</term> <gloss>defenders of the cities</gloss> together with the bishop of the same city or other magistrates. Paragraph 5 of this title; Law 30, Code on the Episcopal Audience; Cujas in his later notes on this. 

Today, however, the ordinary magistrate of each place gives a tutor, and not only when a guardianship has ended as in civil law—Law 5, "If a tutor," Code on the risk of tutors; final paragraph of this title—but also every year, according to the constitution of Charles V published in the year 1548, he demands an account from the tutors. Canon law does not resist this, Clementine 1, "On religious houses," chapter 1, "On sick clerics." By Saxon law, however, the nearest heirs demand an account every single year. Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term> <gloss>Territorial Law</gloss>, article 23; Fachsius, difference 17; Reinhard, difference 7. (e) because it belongs neither to <term>imperium</term> <gloss>supreme power</gloss> nor to jurisdiction. Law 6, paragraph 2, on guardianships; Law 23 at the end, on the excuses of tutors; but it belongs to him alone to whom either the law, a decree of the Senate, or the Prince has granted it. The beginning of the Institutes on this title; Law 1, paragraph 2; Law 8, on tutors and curators; Law 1, on the office thereof. The Dissertation of the Doctors after the gloss on the said Law 6 attributes this to <term>mixtum imperium</term> <gloss>mixed power</gloss>. Muscornius in his treatise on jurisdiction says otherwise, that it belongs sometimes to jurisdiction and sometimes to <term>imperium</term>. Bellonus, in the first of his Supputations, 2, establishes that it belongs to permission. (f) and therefore a tutor cannot be given to a spendthrift nor to a madman—paragraph "Of madmen," who can give tutors by will; Pragmatic Question 3, numbers 33, 63—nor to a minor—said question, numbers 8, 10—nor to a mute or a deaf person. Law 1, paragraph "A mute," on guardianships. According to Brunnus on the said paragraph "A mute," this also holds for one who contracted such a defect after the guardianship was assumed, because of the reasoning in the said paragraph "A mute." Dissertation of Pia<pb n="12"/>gius, said question 3, number 49, whom Manzius follows with doubt in his second question 2, number 1. Nor can it be given to one suffering from a perpetual illness, since he himself is under care. Paragraph 4, on curators. Nor to a cleric—chapter "They are denied," distinction 88—unless he wishes to undertake it voluntarily. Law "Generally," with the following <term>Authentica</term> <gloss>Justinianic novella</gloss>, Code on bishops and clerics. Nor to a slave, because he is considered as dead by civil law—Law 32, on the Rules of Law. Nor to a debtor or a creditor. <term>Authentica</term> of the minor, Code on those who give tutors. Nor to a husband. Law "A husband," Code on guardianship. It is otherwise by Saxon law, by which a wife is found under the guardianship of her husband; Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term>, article 31. 

These persons therefore being excepted, guardianship can be conferred upon anyone; and since it is a public office—beginning of the Institutes on the excuses of tutors—it is so necessary that a tutor can even be compelled by the taking of pledges. Law 5, Code on those who give tutors. Saxon law also proves this, Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term>, article 47, where the gloss is accepted. Final law in the beginning, Code on the administration of tutors; by the argument of Law 28, Code on decurions, book 10. And indeed it is performed for free, unless the tutor is poor. Law 33, "From tutors," final paragraph on the administration of tutors; Law 15 supports this, but also if he has had excuses to present or others, about which in the following disputation. (g) Not only by virtue of office but also at the petition which relatives, kinsmen, and friends provide out of free will. Law 2, "Those who seek tutors"; Laws 4, 5, 10, Code on the same. Or they are bound to provide one, such as a mother, unless she wishes to be excluded from succession according to the <term>Senatusconsultum Tertullianum</term> <gloss>Senate decree on maternal inheritance</gloss>. Said Law 2, paragraph 1, even if she is a natural mother. Final law, Code on guardianship; and all who are called to the succession of a deceased ward. Law 10, Code on legitimate heirs. Likewise freedmen. Said laws. (h) Law 6, paragraph 1, on guardianships; for time is not a way of introducing or removing an obligation. Law 4, on servitudes; Law 44, paragraph 1, on Obligations and Actions, such as silently exists between a ward and a tutor, even a legitimate one, because the giving of a tutor is a legitimate act. Law 77, on the Rules of Law. (i) Said law, paragraph 1.

<margin>Title 21.</margin>
### IX.

In these ways (a) a tutor having been appointed is bound (d) to interpose (c) his authority (b) while present (e), and indeed purely (f), immediately (g) in the very business (h) which is being conducted with the ward (i), since without it nothing is considered to have been done (k).
</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the historical evolution of dative guardianship from Roman law under Marcus Antoninus and Justinian to contemporary Saxon law. It outlines the legal disqualifications for being a tutor and the mandatory nature of the office as a public duty.</summary>

<keywords>guardianship, dative tutor, Roman law, Saxon law, Landrecht, legal disqualifications, civil law, Charles V, jurisdiction, authority</keywords>

<pb n="13"/><meta>continues from previous page: On one side of the entrance stands a tower, square in shape and five paces in width,</meta> built in a square, covered with silk cloths of the highest value, and surrounded on all sides by railings, outside of which the onlookers stand. To this tower or shrine, a certain small door provides access, joined by another where, on one side, twenty and on the other, twenty-five books are bound quite preciouslly, which contain the life and laws of Muhammed and his companions. In the lowest part of the tower, the praised man <note>referring to Ludovico di Varthema</note> adds that the sepulchre of Muhammed is shown underground, in which likewise are buried certain of his friends, namely Ali <note>original: Haly</note>, Othman, Abu Bakr <note>original: Abubecer</note>, and Umar <note>original: Homar</note>; the last two of whom were companions of Muhammed. These things, I say, Varthema testifies as an eyewitness. Furthermore, as for the fact that others have commonly persuaded people that Muhammed’s sepulchre hangs from a magnet under the vault of the temple, or was driven by a lightning bolt to the underworld—perhaps more out of hatred for the religion than a zeal for truth—the very consistent talk of men returning every year from Medina to Egypt, and an accurate ground plan <term>ichnographia</term> <gloss>a scale map or floor plan</gloss> of the entire temple received with an explicit depiction of the monument, teaches that this wanders from the truth. Prosper Alpinus also mentions this in the following manner: It was built next to the sepulchres of his father-in-law and son-in-law, of simple but precious stone; then it was fortified by a square enclosure, the wall of which closest to the tombs is of lower construction and contains a diamond inserted into the internal face of the wall. They proclaim this diamond to be the most noble in size and appearance of all that the sun sees, and by the reflection of the rays gathered from the sun, it strikes the chest <note>or coffin</note> of the lying Muhammed as if with a celestial glow. An intermediate partition adorns a veil splendid with gold and gems. The Emperors at Byzantium <note>the Ottoman Sultans in Constantinople</note> solemnly transmit this to Medina, and when it is carried through the city of Cairo as a public spectacle, the Viceroy and Nobles of Egypt, then some tens of thousands of people, follow it reverently outside the gates. Outside these enclosures of the sepulchre, the monument <pb n="14"/> of Fatima, the daughter of Muhammed, is seen, as well as some cases for sacred books. Philipp Lonicer, Doctor of Sacred Theology, adds his own vote regarding the site, writing of the Sepulchre of Muhammed: When Muhammed had died, the <term>Sculperi</term> <gloss>perhaps a corruption of a title for disciples or carriers</gloss> or disciples carried his corpse to Modinum or Medina, and there, as he himself had commanded, a sepulchre was dug for him in the middle of the temple. The body was enclosed in a wooden chest and then covered with marble, at a height nearly that of a man. Two tablets stand out from the sepulchre, one higher fixed at the head, the other lower applied to the feet. The sepulchre is covered by a vault or canopy; a cloth, which they call waved <note>watered silk or moiré</note>, of green color is placed upon it. This sepulchre is the one that the Turks and Ethiopians seek with great devotion and in great numbers, promising themselves the remission of sins if they kiss it. These words are inscribed on the marble: THIS IS THE SEPULCHRE OF MUHAMMED. The Armenians at one time, having driven tunnels underground for nearly eight <term>stadia</term> <gloss>about one mile</gloss>, had set their minds on stealing the corpse of Muhammed. But their snares having been miraculously detected, they were betrayed and paid the penalty for their crime with their heads. Afterward, they fortified the sepulchre, enclosed on all sides by iron grates, lest the body of the Prophet be snatched from them by theft, or snares, or even some fraud. For they claim that he prophesied in his will that the corpse would by no means be left there beyond a thousand years, and that then would be the end of his religion and empire. Thus far Lonicer.

It happened once, however, that a certain Leader, or Prefect of the Caravan <note>original: Corovana</note>, as they call it, of Damascus, came into conversation with the Overseer of this sepulchre, or a certain Priest of the Mosque: where the Prefect of the Caravan said to the Muhammedan Priest: I earnestly ask you to show me the corpse of this Prophet; if you do this, you shall carry away three thousand ducats from me as a reward! The Priest, having heard these things, responds to the Leader: What is this rashness, that with your eyes, with which in this theater of the world so many <note>the sentence continues on the next page</note>
</translation>

It details the surrounding monuments of his companions and daughter, the precious silk veils sent from Constantinople, and a failed attempt by Armenians to steal the body.</summary>

The definition by <term>Meisner</term> in his *Dissertation on the Supreme Good*, chapter 4, page 350, where he says nobility denotes a dignity in a series of certain families arising especially from military virtues, is essential; yet it is not so perfect as that of <term>Andreas Tiraquellus</term> in *On Nobility*, chapter 6, §. 1: "Nobility is a quality bestowed by the sovereign power, by which someone is shown to be accepted above the commoners." #### Concerning
# The Division of Nobility
# On the Classification of Nobility.

§. 1. Not just one division of Nobility occurs. <term>Plato</term> divided it into four species, the first of which is of those born of famous, good, and just ancestors. Secondly, he called those noble whose parents had been noble and princes. Thirdly, he wanted those to be called noble whose ancestors had been celebrated in fame and opinion, and that either from clearly performed military deeds or from the crowns of contests. Finally, he judged the most excellent kind of Nobility to be when someone excelled by the greatness of his own mind. Compare Plutarch, book 10, *Against Nobility*.

§. 2. <term>Aristotle</term> distinguishes between the Nobility of the Race and that of the State along with Private nobility in book 1 of the *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, chapter 5; so much so that he says the splendor of the former consists in being indigenous and very ancient, and having the first leaders as illustrious; and also that many from that race have stood out as distinguished in those things which are sought after. Private nobility, however, is from either men or women and the legitimate procreation from them.

§. 3. <term>Gregory of Nazianzus</term> makes a threefold kind of nobility: one which drew its origin from above, as are all who are created in the image of God; the second, which proceeds from blood; the third is recognized from virtue and vice. Oration 18; compare Oration 28.

<pb n="551"/><meta>continues from previous page: but Aegyptus had fifty male children by many wives.</meta> Brother Danaus had just as many daughters. Since they were contending with one another for the kingdom, Danaus, by the work of his daughters, killed the sons of Aegyptus except for one or two; for he had received an oracle that slaughter was imminent for him by one of them. Stricken with fear, and by the advice of Minerva, he first fashioned a ship named by him from the number of his daughters a <term>penteconter</term> <gloss>a fifty-oared galley</gloss>, as if you were to say a ship of fifty oars, in which he fled after placing his daughters aboard. Landing thence in Rhodes, he dedicated a statue of Lindian Minerva. From here he also betook himself to Argos, and Helanor, who was then reigning at Argos, handed over the kingdom to him (but he, having taken possession of that region, called the inhabitants Danaans after his own name). But because that region labored under a scarcity of water, since Neptune in anger had dried up the springs of Inachus because he had testified that the land belonged to Minerva, he meanwhile sent his daughters out to fetch water. One of these, Amymone, searching for water, threw a weapon at a deer and struck a sleeping Satyr. Therefore, having been awakened from sleep, he was seized with a wondrous desire to possess the girl. But at the arrival of Neptune, the Satyr took to flight. Amymone, however, lay with him, and Neptune showed her the springs of Lerna. Not only things that exist in fact, but also those held in hope <note>such as future harvests or unborn livestock</note> can be sold: however, among other things, sacred and spiritual items are excepted, which cannot be sold by themselves without sacrilege and <term>simony</term> <gloss>the buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges</gloss>. A pact of resale and the resale itself, if done without fraud, is approved by law. A sale under a <term>Lex Commissoria</term> <gloss>a forfeiture clause where the seller may rescind if the price is not paid</gloss> or an <term>addictio in diem</term> <gloss>an adjudication to a better bidder within a certain timeframe</gloss> are considered absolute.

### XVI. Other Onerous Contracts.

Not only a real <term>census</term> <gloss>a ground rent or annuity tied to property</gloss>, but also a personal one is licit; not only an irredeemable one, but also a redeemable one, both on the part of the buyer and the seller. <term>Dry exchange</term> <gloss>a bill of exchange used to hide a usurious loan</gloss> cannot produce a just profit. The justice of real exchange, whether local, manual, or by letters <note>bills of exchange</note>, is easily maintained. A contract of partnership can be made so that one party provides the capital and the other the industry <note>labor or skill</note>. For a game to be valid, among other things it is required by its nature that the risk be equal on both sides; and for a wager, the condition of the parties must be equal. A lessor must primarily ensure the preservation of the thing leased. A depositary is sometimes held liable for <term>light fault</term> <gloss>minor negligence</gloss>, according to *Law 12, Digest on deposits*. A <term>commodatum</term> <gloss>gratuitous loan for use</gloss> cannot be reclaimed by itself before the time for which it was granted has elapsed. If the thing lent perishes by chance without the fault of the borrower, the loss falls to the Owner, according to the *Final Law, Digest on loans for use*. A <term>precarium</term> <gloss>a grant of use at the will of the grantor</gloss> is not ended by the death of the person granting it. A non-sworn <term>suretyship</term> <gloss>guaranteeing a debt</gloss> of a wife for her husband is void. Even rights can be pledged or mortgaged.

### XVII. Injury and Restitution.

Injury is the violation of another's right: one type is real, which is committed by the unjust laying on of hands; another is verbal, which is committed through words, letters, writing, or an insulting picture, according to *Law 15, Digest on injuries and libelous pamphlets*. One is slight, another is atrocious, which type must be determined from the act, the place, the person, and other circumstances, as in the *paragraph on atrocious, Institutes on injuries*. To one who is willing, no injury is done, except <pb n="15"/> where positive or natural law resists the surrender of the right: hence, one who drags a cleric to a secular tribunal against his will still commits an injury. Indeed, an inflicted injury is repaired either by satisfaction or by restitution. Restitution is an act of commutative justice <note>justice governing private transactions</note>, necessary for salvation not as a matter of means, but only by precept: which is as much Divine as it is natural; partly affirmative, partly negative. The obligation of restoring arises either from an unjust taking or from the thing taken itself: hence restitution differs greatly from payment, since the obligation of paying proceeds from contracts.

-> THE END <-

Artificial, or reasons and arguments. All of these, according to the nature of this theme, are so arranged that, on one hand, they directly and expressly establish <term>kata thesin</term> <gloss>by way of proposition</gloss> the antiquity and <term>theopneustia</term> <gloss>divine inspiration</gloss> of the points which we seek; on the other hand, they act <term>kat’ arsin kai athetesin</term> <gloss>by way of removal and rejection</gloss>, insofar as they deny that the Tiberian Masoretes were the authors of the points and remove them from consideration, or are altogether silent regarding them. Hence, having now finally cited the testimonies, we shall subjoin the following reasons for establishing the antiquity and divine inspiration of the points.

§. 3. To obtain the truth of our assertion, we urge I. *The most certain danger of uncertainty and ambiguity*. For if we maintain that the vowel points were finally added by the Rabbis after the lapse of several centuries: would we not render the clarity of meanings and the origin of words exceedingly ambiguous, indeed plainly uncertain? Truly, the Hebrew idiom, in proportion to its rather narrow constraints, does not abound in so many primitive and radical words, and for that reason is forced for the most part to represent and explain several quite different things by a single derivative. For I ask, let them explain to me whether the diversity of meanings depends on the consonants alone, or indeed on the vowels? It cannot depend on the consonants alone, because the same consonants occur under very diverse meanings of words. The matter becomes clearer by examples. Thus, if <term>hvh</term> <note>הוה</note> is pointed as <term>havah</term> <note>הָוָה</note>, it means *he was*; but in this way, <term>hovah</term> <note>הֹוָה</note>, it denotes *calamity*. In another way, <term>havvah</term> <note>הַוָּה</note>, it signifies *substance*. Likewise, if <term>bqr</term> <note>בקר</note> is pointed as <term>baqar</term> <note>בָּקַר</note>, it denotes *he searched*; if <term>baqqer</term> <note>בַּקֵּר</note>, *to search* or *search!*; if <term>boqer</term> <note>בֹּקֶר</note>, *morning*; if <term>baqar</term> <note>בָּקָר</note>, *cattle*, and similar things. Who indeed would conveniently distinguish between these words descending from one root, and discern one meaning from another, unless the diversity of vowels came to one's aid?

§. 4. To this we urge II. *The inevitable office of the points*. For that well-worn saying is also valid here: <pb n="16"/>spoken words are symbols of the passions in the soul, and written words are symbols of the spoken words <note>original: "τὰ ἐν τῇ φωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβολα, καὶ τὰ γραφόμενα τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ"</note>, as Aristotle says in *On Interpretation*, chapter 1. Indeed, a prior and more powerful account is held of vowels than of consonants. For since vowels are an essential part of reading and writing, and constitute the chief part: who would think that the primordial language lacked these, especially since every language that is destitute of them is rendered maimed, mutilated, and imperfect? Therefore, vowels are not only called <term>tenuot</term> <gloss>motions</gloss> by the Hebrews, and <term>ta phoneenta</term> <gloss>the voiced things</gloss> by the Greeks; but they are also elsewhere called the souls of words, which vivify them, and just as in other languages, they hold the sovereignty. Furthermore, every speech, for the recording of which literature serves, consists of words, words of syllables, and syllables of consonants and vowels. If, therefore, no syllable can consist without vowels, so also no speech. And what is more, not even a letter can be uttered without vowels. Hence Johannes Isaac, a converted Jew, said most excellently: that he who reads the Scripture without points and accents is like a man riding a <term>achaliniton</term> <gloss>unbridled</gloss> or unruly horse. There are some who call the <term>immot ha-qeriah</term> <gloss>mothers of reading</gloss> <note>vowel letters such as Aleph, He, Waw, Yod</note> to their aid here, on the grounds that they can supply the turns of the vowels. That for several thousands of years, a necessary means of interpreting Scripture was lacking; because, as for the pronunciation, so also for the certain and indubitable recording of sacred matters, vowel points are irrefutably required. 2. That the Holy Scripture is offered up to be corrupted by enemies; for if the points were not divinely handed down, it will certainly be easy to interpret a word otherwise than is right. 3. For it does not speak of the interpretation and controversies of Scripture according to the whim of the Church, but specifically of private injuries and offenses. But let it be so: let us grant to some Papist objectors that it can also be understood in a broader sense regarding injuries which are done to the whole Church and to God himself, namely, through the perverse interpretation of Scripture and heresies. We ought indeed to hear the Church; but she is not to be heard simply and in all things, but only insofar as she follows Christ the head and the Holy Spirit as leader, speaking in the word, by interpreting and judging. No less must the leaders and pastors of the churches be reverently obeyed in the Lord (2 Thessalonians 3:3, 14; Hebrews 13:17); yet not absolutely, but conditionally, insofar as and as long as they hear the voice of the supreme Shepherd, Jesus Christ, correctly set forth his word, and keep themselves within the boundaries of their calling. However, one must not believe or obey simply and in all things without any <term>dokimasia</term> <gloss>testing or examination</gloss>—that is, without an examination of interpretations, dogmas, and rites proposed by others according to the norm of the divine word, and without any discernment from all sides as if with closed eyes; just as the Pharisee readers and interpreters were partly to be heard, insofar as they sat in the chair of Moses (Matthew 23:2), and partly not to be heard, but avoided, insofar as they brought forth the leaven of their own doctrine and human traditions, infecting the sound sense of Scripture (Matthew 16:6, 12).

<pb n="14"/><meta>continues from previous page: should invite us to...</meta> such great sobriety that we would not even allow drunkenness to be named among us. AP. Above all, let the most shameful deeds and most foolish habits of drunkards steer us away from the immoderate custom of drinking. For from what outrages do they abstain? They cast off all shame, are inflamed by illicit lust, bring forth the secrets of the mind, wallow in filth, walk with no moderation of step, stagger, vomit in the manner of beasts, <margin>Drunkards</margin> and pursue all the best people with slanders; <margin>Isaiah 5.</margin> they do not regard the work of God, nor consider the works of His hands. Indeed, when they have weakened the body with immense gorging and are exhausted from perpetrating works of darkness, they collapse as if lifeless, <margin>Chrysostom On Prayer, book 2.</margin> lying prostrate on the ground like pigs, so that it can most truly be said: A DRUNKARD IS A LIVING CORPSE. Finally, let profane men and Heathens <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> move us, who utterly condemned this detestable and abominable vice; so much so <margin>Athenaeus, book 10.</margin> that Solon <note>Solon was an Athenian lawmaker known for his wisdom.</note> felt a prince should be punished with death if he were caught drunk. And among the Indians, it was not permitted for a king to reach the point of drunkenness by drinking. Among the Persians, however, this was granted to the king on only one day, on which they sacrificed to the Sun. NEPH. And I remember reading that Pittacus of Mitylene, <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> not the least of the Seven Sages of Greece, passed a law that if anyone committed any outrage while drunk, he should be punished with a double penalty. AP. If, therefore, those who were ignorant of God so greatly condemned, avoided, and punished this crime, what I ask you do you think we Christians ought to do? NEPH. Let us labor so that we are never intoxicated with wine, in which there is <term>asotia</term> <gloss>dissoluteness or debauchery</gloss>; let us despise and avoid drunkenness, which takes away the heart and memory, which dissipates the senses and confuses the intellect, and which makes a beast out of a man, an invalid out of the robust, and a fool out of the wise. <margin>Ephesians 5; Hosea 4; Augustine; Origen.</margin> <margin>Ignatius, epistle 11 to the Ephesians.</margin> Let us instead burn with a zeal for sobriety and temperance; and let us reflect that now, even now, are the final times; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest we despise the riches of His goodness and patience <pb n="15"/> and endurance. Let us also remember that our bodies are the temple of God and an instrument of the Spirit who dwells within us. <margin>1 Corinthians 3; 2 Corinthians 6; Galatians 5.</margin> AP. Sobriety and temperance are fruits of the Spirit; but drunkenness and luxury <note>In this context, "luxury" refers to excess or lechery.</note> are the nurses and promoters of all vices, the receptacles of all kinds of filth. Just as smoke drives away bees, so does a hangover drive away the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. NEPH. And just as clouds and rain always follow the South wind, so do diseases of the soul and the animal <note>referring to the "animal spirits" or physical vitality</note> follow drunkenness. COM. Therefore, must one not drink at all? AP. Certainly, if moderation is absent. However, honor must be shown to the body, so that it may be fed with sufficient food, not immoderate and superfluous; <margin>Colossians 2.</margin> and we must take care lest we ourselves be found to be the murderers of our own bodies. COM. I understand at last that nothing is more ruinous to a man than intoxication. AP. Therefore, brother, heal this disease in yourself; separate this vice from you, and flee the company of wine-bibbers as if from a reef. TRIC. Oh! Are you not ashamed, Comasta, <note>The name Comasta likely derives from the Greek "komastes," meaning a reveler.</note> you who allow yourself to be corrupted by their persuasion? AP. Come, rise Comasta, let us depart; do not listen to these men. COM. Farewell, you drinking companions; I must depart and take care that I become a man: but if you are wise, take an example from me.

## THE END.

<margin>III. Member of this dispute.</margin>
It remains for us to weave in the form of a feudal judgment, which is shared with Civil Law: for a citation must be made, a petition exhibited, the lawsuit contested, and other things that belong to the Judicial order. <note>a.</note> Unless in certain cases something else is specially observed. <note>b.</note>

->XCIII.<-

As for instance in cases of evidence, where women are clearly not admitted to give testimony. <note>a.</note> Likewise, five witnesses are required to prove ingratitude. <note>b.</note> And if there is a dispute between the Lord and the Vassal, neither provides the <term>Iuramentum calumniae</term> <gloss>oath of calumny/good faith</gloss>, even if either party proffers it. <note>c.</note> Then, if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant is not immediately acquitted, but a defense is still granted to him through an Oath. <note>d.</note> Indeed, sometimes to the Defendant and sometimes to the plaintiff, according to the discretion of the Judge, an oath is given or remitted. <note>e.</note>

<note>a. section "On the old," at the end, Title 32, book 2, Feudal Law; and there Cujas, book 4, title 35; see also Law "from that," Digest on Witnesses; Novels of Leo 48. b. single chapter and there the Doctors, title 57, of said book 2, Feudal Law; otherwise two suffice, as in proving an Investiture, section "if anyone," title 26, book 1, Feudal Law. c. section "in which," title 33, book 2, Feudal Law. d. sections 2 and 3, title 4, and sections 1, 2, and 3 of said title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; section "Likewise it is pleasing," title 15, book 2, Feudal Law; noted by Borcholt chapter 7, no. 48. e. section "Oath," and the final section of said title 33, book 2, Feudal Law; noted by Cujas book 1, Feudal Law title 1, section "similarly," at the end, and book 4, title 36.</note>

->XCIV.<-

This defense by oath—or this oath enjoined or permitted for the sake of defense—is either simple, when one swears alone, just as a Lord against a Vassal, <note>a.</note> and a Vassal against a lord (if, namely, when a dispute over investiture has been raised, he can prove that he has possessed the fief for a year with the Lord's knowledge and without his contradiction); <note>b.</note> or it is due to a lack of evidence with twelve <term>Sacramentalibus</term> <gloss>oath-helpers</gloss>, that is, co-swearers, who <pb n="21"/> are taken from among kinsmen or others. <note>c.</note> He himself is also counted among the twelve, <note>d.</note> and they swear and affirm that they believe it to be true, having touched the most holy Gospels or consecrated weapons. <note>e.</note>

<note>a. section "if indeed a fief," title 4, book 1, Feudal Law; and there Cujas book 1, title 1, section "similarly." b. section "if however someone," at the end, Title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; Cujas in said section "similarly," and title 28. c. section "when however someone," in said title 4, book 1, Feudal Law; single chapter title 10, in said book 1, Feudal Law; section "Where nothing," title 33, book 2, Feudal Law; Borcholt notes chapter 2, number 18; said law 5 and law 12, how one ought to defend himself in the Lombard Law. d. Cujas book 1, title 24. e. said title 33; Cujas section "Likewise if a controversy," book 2, title 1, title 24, and title 28; chapter 2, at the end, title 2, book 2, Feudal Law.</note>

### XCV.

Another is the armed defense used in these books, which is instituted through a duel and singular combat. <note>a.</note> And yet another which was formerly permitted in a very superstitious manner by way of Trial <note>original: "Tentationis"</note> rather than defense, by touching glowing iron, and likewise by water-ordeals, <note>b.</note> called "exploration" by the Feudalists: both of which we rightly detest as being plainly contrary to humanity and piety. <note>c.</note>

<note>a. section "if a Soldier," with the gloss, title 27, and section 3, Title 39, book 2, Feudal Law; section 1, title 2, book 3, Feudal Law; in more correct books. b. See Münster everywhere, and other Histories here and there. c. Damhouder notes this in "Criminal Practice," chapter 42.</note>

### XCVI.

What if the peers, who were present at the time of investiture, later ceased to be Peers? If a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal, are they still considered suitable witnesses? Certainly, for whatever reason they may have ceased to be peers. <note>single chapter, Title 19, book 2, Feudal Law; where Cujas and others discuss this.</note>

### XCVII.

What if the Peers are absent or contumacious? Those who are absent are to be waited for, unless they are far away; <note>a.</note> but those who are contumacious are plainly to be ignored. <note>b.</note>

<note>a. gloss of Baldus and Laudensis, number 26; Alvarotto, Praepositus, Afflictis and others in chapter 1, Title 2, book 2, Feudal Law; Ardizone notes this in said chapter 138, section "Where indeed one possesses." b. Baldus in said chapter 1; argument from law "if to a legatee" section 1, Digest on fiduciary manumissions; Curtius part 2, member 2, on the fiefs of Laity, number 25.</note>

### XCVIII.

When a sentence has been passed, is it possible to appeal in feudal cases? It is variously debated; but the view that it is possible has prevailed, and specifically to the next superior, if there be one, or to the ordinary to whom the matter is subject.

<note>Text at the end of title 22, and section "Witnesses," title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; Raynaudus in said penultimate section.</note>

pages.21:
are taken from among kinsmen or others. <note>c.</note> He himself is also counted among the twelve, <note>d.</note> and they swear and affirm that they believe it to be true, having touched the most holy Gospels or consecrated weapons. <note>e.</note>

### XCV.

Another is the armed defense used in these books, which is instituted through a duel and singular combat. <note>a.</note> And yet another which was formerly permitted in a very superstitious manner by way of Trial <note>original: "Tentationis"</note> rather than defense, by touching glowing iron, and likewise by water-ordeals, <note>b.</note> called "exploration" by the Feudalists: both of which we rightly detest as being plainly contrary to humanity and piety. <note>c.</note>

### XCVI.

What if the peers, who were present at the time of investiture, later ceased to be Peers? If a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal, are they still considered suitable witnesses? Certainly, for whatever reason they may have ceased to be peers. <note>single chapter, Title 19, book 2, Feudal Law; where Cujas and others discuss this.</note>

### XCVII.

What if the Peers are absent or contumacious? Those who are absent are to be waited for, unless they are far away; <note>a.</note> but those who are contumacious are plainly to be ignored. <note>b.</note>

### XCVIII.

When a sentence has been passed, is it possible to appeal in feudal cases? It is variously debated; but the view that it is possible has prevailed, and specifically to the next superior, if there be one, or to the ordinary to whom the matter is subject.

<pb n="19"/>ought to be restored, whatever has come to him by occasion of the mandate, according to Law 10, paragraph 2, and Law 20, at the beginning, under the title "On Mandate" <note>original: "Mandati"</note>.

### XXXIII.

Regarding the case in section 30, the cause of the litigation there is the detention of property which Paul seeks back from Maevius. He assigns the reason for seeking it as being that he mandated Maevius to carry his property to Pomponius so that he might keep it; and if Pomponius refused, Maevius was to guard it until he [Paul] sought it back. Paul’s intention is based on Law 1, paragraph 12, under the title "On Deposit" <note>original: "Depositi"</note>, where an action of mandate, but not of deposit, is granted to him. We shall yet propose other examples.

### XXXIV.

The things said thus far have shown us actions arising from contracts; we must now look at a case where partly a contract and partly a wrong <note>term: "delictum" gloss: a civil wrong or tort</note> produces the action. For instance, Sempronius leased his house to Titius. This consensual business having been perfected, they go together to visit the leased house. But once they are inside the house, Sempronius, without any roundabout words, beats Titius with a club placed behind the door, out of a hatred previously conceived against him. Having greased him liberally <note>a metaphorical expression for a sound beating</note>, he throws him out of doors and no longer grants him the power of inhabiting the place. Because Titius has endured this with an unwilling stomach, he does not wish to bear the matter without any vengeance; thus he hastens to approach a judge and intends to sue Sempronius.

### XXXV.

Furthermore, because in the proposed case two facts or distinct acts offer themselves, why should not two separate legal remedies also be obtained to pursue a double goal or end of the intention? For two things are involved here, one of which is a contract and the other a wrong, which differ greatly and produce two separate petitions. A double object of grievance and offense, from the double fact and act performed, is brought into court. The first object of dispute 
<pb n="20"/>is the denied habitation of the house which the plaintiff <note>term: "actor"</note> claims; and for that reason, because it was so agreed between them that he should inhabit it for a certain price to be paid at a determined time, the plaintiff's intention is based on Laws 7, 8, and 9 of the Digest title "On Leasing and Hiring" <note>original: "locati conducti"</note>. The other matter of litigation or object which creates the lawsuit is the beating, for which the plaintiff seeks a civil remedy; he desires to bind the defendant <note>term: "reus"</note> to pay him such and such an amount, for the reason that, without any cause or occasion given, he received the plaintiff with quite injurious blows. Therefore, his intention is based on Section 10 of the Institutes title "On Injuries" <note>original: "de injuriis"</note>, and the estimatorty action of injuries is granted to him.

### XXXVI.

Another example follows, where only a wrong is vindicated, which shall be the following: namely, a certain shoemaker hired a musician living in Altdorf, so that he might cheer him and his companions with the help of music. Consent now being given by both parties, the musician came at the appointed time with his companions and played his strings as long as it was permitted to do so by the magistrate’s leave. The time having now elapsed, the musician refused to play any longer. Because this displeased the shoemaker, he did not stand long meditating on what should be done, but with one blow he broke his lute <note>term: "panduram"</note>. But truly, since the musician cannot endure this, he calls the shoemaker to the tribunal. But by what action can he proceed against him?

### XXXVII.

Here again the fact, whether promissory or of a wrong, must be sought, so that we may know what creates the lawsuit between the parties. That fact consists in this: that the shoemaker damaged the musician's lute. The musician desires to avenge the damage before a judge because the shoemaker performed this injurious act against the musician without any fault or occasion given; and so he intends to bind him to the payment of the damage caused. Surely the musician's intention is based on Section 13 of the Institutes title "On the Aquilian Law" <note>original: "de Leg. Aquil."</note>.
</translation>
