<pb n="17"/>to come to light, he demonstrated a human cadaver that had been filled quite liberally with wine a few hours before strangulation, and which was opened by the same Bartholin. For once this was dissected, neither were the lacteal veins visible anywhere, nor did the thoracic vessels abound with any chyle. He confirms that the heart indeed sought the wine, as much from the fearless mind despising death as from the fierce, bilious humor flowing out from the mammary vessels. Thus we recently saw it represent a milky color from milk during public anatomical demonstrations in a mastiff <note>original: "molosso"</note> well nourished with milk before strangulation, and dissected by the Most Noble Lord Doctor Faschius in the Anatomical Theater. For when this was opened, the lacteals, the <term>receptaculum chyli</term> <gloss>receptacle of the chyle</gloss>, and the thoracic duct came forth immediately so turgid, white, and glistening that everyone present was seized with stupor and the greatest admiration.

Various observations by authors confirm that the insertion of the thoracic lacteals varies in different subjects. Bartholin, departing slightly from Pecquet here, proves through various experiments that a solitary branch under the esophagus, thymus, thoracic artery, and left clavicle is poured into the left axillary vein. Pecquet, on the contrary, asserts that this thoracic duct is divided into two branches from the third spine of the back, of which the left tends toward the left clavicle and the right toward the right. Thus he expressly says in his <term>Anatomical Experiments</term> <gloss>Experimentis Anatomicis</gloss>, page 27:

> I should have sacrificed <note>an idiomatic expression for 'finished my task'</note> had not the straying path of the lacteals at the fork along the spine of the thorax repeatedly called my admiring eyes back to themselves with their persistent white swelling.

But there will be no one who does not assert along with Bartholin that either the illustrator added something to the true discovery, or it was the discoverer's conjecture. For the same man frankly confesses in his work <term>On the Thoracic Lacteals</term> <gloss>de Lacteis Thoracicis</gloss>, chapter 12, page 35, that when a bellows was applied to the lower parts, no trace of a vessel appeared on the right, nor could anything similar to this be seen or explored; a fact which <term>autopsy</term> <gloss>personal observation/dissection</gloss>, the most reliable guide, has also rightly taught us in several animals. Nor do we now deny that which the man of profound erudition, Adrian Auzotius, reports—that he saw this vessel preserved for many days having been tied on both sides—but we rightly maintain that nature revealed to him in a single subject that which it denied to the illustrious Bartholin in countless others. Therefore, Bartholin observed only a single insertion in six humans and most animals, except for one female dog, <pb n="18"/>in which he found a bifurcated insertion; he categorized this as a rare occurrence, since other vessels and their progression were also arranged differently in that same subject. It is therefore easily apparent from what has already been cited that nature plays in various ways here in the progression of the thoracic vessels.

If we consider its surface, it is sufficiently smooth, sleek, and soft, and it yields easily when pressed with the fingers, indicating that a certain moisture is contained within.

## CHAPTER VI

### Which brings forward the use, action, and many benefits of this duct.

Since all members in the human body are so arranged that they conspire toward one certain common benefit, and not even the smallest part seems to have been established in vain by the Creator of things, but each performs its own actions and has its own utilities with which it brings aid to the body in time of necessity, it does not seem foreign to the matter if we depict the benefit of this duct more at length and inquire a little more accurately into its genuine use.

Since, however, this canal for the most part corresponds with the Asellian lacteal veins, it must be said that its use also differs little from theirs, provided we have first well distinguished the point of origin and the point of termination. We therefore recognize no other use than that it receives the milky liquor from the receptacle of the chyle, further refines what has been received over the longer tract of its journey, and finally conducts the refined fluid to the thorax and the axillary branches. That this is its duty and that Nature gave it this action to perform is testified at length not only by men most skilled in anatomical matters—Pecquet, Bartholin, Rolfincius, Conringius, Schenckius, Wepferus, Ammannus, Paulli, Hornius, Deusingius, Mantellus, Mersennus, Auzotius, and others—but also by <term>autopsy</term> <gloss>dissection</gloss> and the diligent dissection of cadavers confirms the same.

Who will there be who, along with Riolanus, Leichnerus, Backius, and other anatomists, would any longer doubt that this duct carries chyle? For this is proven not so much by its transparent, bright white color, most similar to milk,
</translation>

Paolo Manuzio, son of Aldus, knowing nothing of that edition, likewise published it himself in Venice the following year. More correct than before, and with a very copious index, it was afterwards given to the public light in Geneva in the year 1569 by Francesco Porto of Crete.

Then in Oxford, twenty-five years later, it was published with erudite and copious notes by Gerard Langbaine <note>original: Gherardo Langbenio</note>. This was succeeded by the edition in quarto from Bologna, made in the year 1644, of the Greek text with three Latin versions: by Gabriel de la Pierre, Domenico Pizzimenti, and Piero Pagani; it was, however, by far inferior to the others already made. Tanneguy Le Fèvre <note>original: Tanaquillo Fabro</note> judged Gabriel de la Pierre a somewhat more successful translator; and for that reason he was the author of the reprint of Longinus in Saumur in the year 1663 in octavo, having added for that occasion some of his own brief notes, since he intended to make a fine and more complete edition. After these, Jacobus Tollius, by the comparison of many <term>MSS</term> <gloss>manuscripts</gloss>, having reported all the various readings and his <pb n="22"/> notes and those of others, gave us an edition the most ample and copious of all, printed in quarto in Utrecht in the year 1694.

*In the year 1710, with the greatest accuracy and labor, the celebrated* John Hudson *published the text with his new version, very rich in notes, variant readings, and three most copious indexes, having brought it to light in* Oxford *in a most elegant large octavo form, and dedicated it to two of his learned friends:* Mr. Henry Newton, *Envoy to the Court of* Tuscany *for her British Majesty, and the* Signor Abbot Anton Maria Salvini, *a Florentine Gentleman. However, we shall maintain the negative with Zoesius on the title of the Digest, *On the Undutiful Will*, number 26, through Law *fratris* 21, Code, *On the Undutiful Will*, § 1, and the Institutes on the same. For although in the Novellae the children of brothers are admitted with the brothers to the inheritance of a paternal uncle, this nonetheless proceeds if he dies simply intestate, and not also if the will is overturned through a complaint of undutifulness. Furthermore, children of brothers succeed to a deceased paternal uncle by right of representation only then if they were conceived while he was living; otherwise, they will not be admitted to the goods of one whom they do not touch by any kinship, by Law 1, § *si quis proximior*, Digest, *Whence Cognates* <note>original: "unde cognati"</note>. <margin>II.</margin> Secondly, all those things which we have said thus far concerning the majesty of Christ—true God and man, filling all things everywhere—possess this use and bring us this benefit: that in all afflictions we may approach our priest, Christ, with all the greater confidence, since he is present everywhere to us not only regarding his divinity, but also regarding his humanity, and we may implore his help. For whatever evil happens to us, it must not be felt that it occurs by chance and without his foreknowledge or will. He is truly with us; He sees and knows all things; He also rules and governs all things. And since he favors all those believing in him and invoking him out of faith, he does not concede or permit any adversity to happen to them unless he knows that very thing is healthy for them and useful for obtaining heavenly goods. Because if we are in danger in water, in fire, in prisons, or are overwhelmed by any calamity, we always can and should stir up our faith and invocation to God by this reasoning: that we know Christ, true God and man, is not absent and far from us in some peculiar place of this external heaven distant from us, perhaps having no care for us, but that he himself, in his humanity as much as his divinity, is with us in the water, in the fire, in prison, and in every calamity. And provided we embrace and invoke him with true faith, he will never let us perish.

<margin>III.</margin> Finally, the knowledge of the majesty of Christ—in that he is everywhere and fills all things not only by his divinity but also by his humanity—brings us also this use and this benefit: that we may walk all the more religiously in the fear and obedience of God, and avoid sins and crimes with all the greater diligence. For if that majesty, namely Christ, true God and man, acts perpetually among and around us, and <pb n="18"/> is present to us wherever we may be, and constantly gazes upon all our thoughts as well as our actions, certainly we ought to dread and revere such majesty deservedly, and live all the more cautiously. Very many people think that if they can so cover and hide those things which they do evilly that they reach the eyes and conscience of no man, they have looked after their own affairs well. Meanwhile, they do not consider that Christ himself is present, who sees all things and will without doubt not leave evil deeds unpunished. Who would not say that a servant is vehemently foolish who thinks it goes well for him if the things he does treacherously against his master remain hidden from the conscience and eyes of his fellow servants and the rest of the household, and meanwhile he does not care for the conscience and sight of his master, who is present and sees all things? Therefore, let us not confound or disturb the presence and sight of Christ our Savior, but rather treat it with honor and joy. And so that his presence may be more of a consolation to us than a terror and destruction, let us take care not to offend the present eyes of that majesty with sins and crimes,

->by which we may be governed by the favor and grace of Christ,<-

<pb n="9"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...conveniently ruled by a single Count or District-governor</meta> conveniently, nor could all cases be settled by him, they distinguished these into other smaller parts through <term>Centenae</term> <gloss>Hundreds</gloss>, or specific villages and districts, by a laudable institution. They assigned individual Overseers to each <term>Centena</term> <gloss>Hundred</gloss>, called <term>Centgraven</term> <gloss>Hundred-counts</gloss>, and joined to these again other assistants and deputies, who went by the name of <term>Centenarii</term> <gloss>Centenarians</gloss>, so that for the one to whom the Count alone was not equal, the task might become lighter with the burden divided among others. <term>Beatus Rhenanus</term> agrees with us in book 2 of <italic>German Matters</italic>, saying, the regions were distinguished by Hundreds, whence the name <term>Centenarius</term>. That magistrate, who presided over the Hundred, was subject to the Count. Moreover, just as we said a little before that traces of the ancient German districts exist among us today, so we must not think that the word <term>Centena</term> has entirely vanished through the passage of time. For near Heidelberg, by the witness of the same <term>Rhenanus</term>, a trace of the <term>Centena</term> still appears in several places, and the use of this word has remained even to our times.

§. 3. Indeed, in Franconia and the Palatinate, the word <term>Centena</term> today seems to have another meaning, while by <term>Centena</term> they understand criminal jurisdiction and <term>merum Imperium</term> <gloss>pure authority</gloss>, and thus the punishment of capital crimes. From this, what in other places is called <term>Hals-</term> <gloss>neck</gloss> or <term>hohe Gerechtigkeit</gloss> <gloss>high justice</gloss>, they call <term>Centgerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>Hundred-justice</gloss>. They name the one to whom such judgment belongs a <term>Centherrn</term> <gloss>Hundred-lord</gloss>; the assessors of the same criminal judgment, <term>Zentschöpffen</term> <gloss>Hundred-jurors</gloss>; and finally those who are subject to such judgment, <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term> <gloss>subjects of the Hundred</gloss>. Concerning this matter, let <term>Berneggerus</term> be consulted. But it is so far from the case that modern customs have imposed another meaning on the word <term>Centena</term> different from the old use, that it rather exactly reflects the most ancient institution of the Germans, by which they divided the districts into <term>Centenae</term>, or as we just said, and placed over each <term>Centena</term> a judge, whom they called a <term>CentGraffen</term>, with his <term>Centenarii</term> and <term>Scabini</term> <gloss>lay judges/jurors</gloss>. For what prevents one from being allowed to call a Count of a Hundred a <term>Zentherrn</term>, or a judgment held in a Hundred before the Count and <term>Centenarii</term> a <term>Zentgericht</term> <gloss>Hundred-court</gloss> or <term>Zentgerechtigkeit</term>? The <term>Scabini</term>, called by the Germans <term>Schöpffen</term> from the Teutonic word <term>schaffen</term> i. e. to care for, because the <term>Scabini</term> must diligently care that no injury is done to anyone in the Hundred, and must procure the advantage of the Hundred by all means, <pb n="10"/>so named (for they are mistaken, as many as derive that word either from the Hebrew <term>Shabbat</term> with <term>Besoldus</term>; or from <term>Scamnis</term> <gloss>benches</gloss>, on which they were accustomed to pronounce sentence, with <term>Becmannus</term>; or with others from elsewhere) who were given as assistants to the Count of the Hundred along with the <term>Centenarii</term>, what prohibits calling them <term>Zentschöpffen</term>; or calling the men who belonged to the same Hundred <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term>?

§. 4. We said in §. 2 that the <term>Centenarii</term> are to be derived from the <term>Centenae</term>, so that it might be clear that the opinion of those men—who are very many in number and of the greatest authority—does not please us, who wish our <term>Centenarii</term> to be understood as Counts of the Hundreds and so called from the number one hundred. For thus, to produce at least a single one from many, the famous <term>Berneggerus</term> says: <term>Zentgraffen</term>, as if you would say, Centenary Counts, that is, presidents and princes of the centumviral judgment <note>a court consisting of one hundred men</note>, who are also called <term>Centenarii</term> in the ancient laws of the Germans. But we assert that Mr. <term>Berneggerus</term> relies on a hypothesis that is not sufficiently certain, and that neither were one hundred Counts added to the Princes formerly elected in the council, nor are the Counts of the Hundreds themselves ever understood through the term <term>Centenarii</term>. For when that passage of <term>Tacitus</term> which he cites for himself says: <note>original: "Eliguntur in iisdem Conciliis & Principes, qui jura per Pagos vicosque reddunt. Centeni singulis ex plebe Comites, Consilium simul & autoritas, adsunt"</note> "Princes are also elected in the same Councils, who administer justice through the Districts and villages. One hundred companions from the common people are present for each, serving as both counsel and authority," <term>B. Reinesius</term>, a man never to be mentioned without praise, proved it convicted of a fault and showed that <term>Certi</term> <gloss>certain/fixed</gloss> should be substituted for <term>Centeni</term> <gloss>one hundred</gloss>. From this it is clear that he himself fell into a common error with others and, having presupposed this false hypothesis, fell with several others into a false opinion concerning the Centenary Counts. We know indeed from <term>Tacitus</term> and other authors that the Ancient Germans, if they were about to conscript a soldier, chose a hundred youths from individual districts. But what then? Is it to be gathered from there that one hundred companions were also joined to a civilian Prince? Surely the patrons of the contrary opinion seem to have gathered thus and compared <note>Greek: "kat’ allēlon"</note> that passage about the hundred youths elected from individual districts in time of war (and afterwards denominated from that hundred-fold number for the sake of honor, as <term>Tacitus</term> hints) to this one about the hundred companions. However, although this was, so to speak, their primary falsehood <note>Greek: "prōton pseudos"</note> and stood as the cause of such a significant error for them, those two places are very different.
</translation>

---

->§. 23.<-

Moreover, this depends on the will of the contracting parties, so that either a fixed day is determined, before the lapse of which the debtor does not have the freedom of paying, <note>By the argument of the cited paragraph 2 and Law 7, On Verbal Obligations</note> or the payment is deferred to an uncertain time. <note>By the argument of Law 48, Digest, On Verbal Obligations; Law 85, Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations.</note>

---

->§. 24.<-

Furthermore, since in both cases the entire weight is placed on the fact that the day is added in favor of the creditor, it is necessary that he act cautiously in determining it.

---

->§. 25.<-

For as far as it concerns a certain time, whenever <pb n="12"/> <note>Two handwritten diagonal ink strokes appear in the left margin, likely reader marks or a cancellation mark.</note> <margin>/</margin> <margin>/</margin> a day has been simply added to the instrument of obligation, it is presumed as many times to have been added for the sake of the debtor—namely, for the purpose that he may use the thing in the meantime as he pleases, and cannot be sued by the plaintiff during that middle period which is left free for him for paying. <note>By the argument of Law 117, Digest, On Rules of Law; Law 41, paragraph 1; Law 42, On Verbal Obligations; Law 44, paragraph 1, Digest, On Obligations and Actions; paragraph 2, Institute, On Verbal Obligations.</note> From which it simultaneously follows that he is able to pay even before the day, although against the will of the creditor, <note>Law 70, Digest, On Payments; Law 50, Digest, On Obligations and Actions</note> provided however that general caution is applied, so that the payment is offered without any detriment to the creditor, and not at an inopportune time or place. <note>Law 39, Digest, On Payments; Law 122, principle, Digest, On Verbal Obligations.</note>

->§. 26.<-

Hence, if every faculty of paying within the established day ought to be taken away from the debtor, those words must especially be employed from which it clearly appears that it was intended by the contracting parties that the debtor wished to renounce this favor legally belonging to him, and to confer the same upon the creditor; lest, of course, the agreement—which otherwise is held as hateful since it hinders liberation from debt—might be interpreted more openly against the creditor, in whose power it was to dictate the law.

Finally, there is the dispute and protest of the Jews regarding the changing of the writing. For if it had been without the <term>yod</term> and <term>vav</term> <note>Hebrew letters forming "this is"</note>, the writing would have remained ambiguous, and the crowd of high priests would have had a handle and opportunity for excusing themselves concerning its explanation.

XIII. *Jesus* <note>original: "Iησȣ͂ς"</note> is Hebrew in its origin, said to come either from <term>Yehoshua</term> or from <term>Yeshua</term>. For he who was called <term>Yehoshua</term> in Haggai and Zechariah is called <term>Yeshua</term> elsewhere, in Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7; and Joshua, or <term>Yehoshua</term>, is elsewhere called <term>Yeshua</term> in Nehemiah 8:17. It is derived, moreover, from the verb <term>yasha</term> in the <term>Hiphil</term> <gloss>causative stem</gloss>, which signifies to make safe, to save, to preserve, and to vindicate. He takes his name from the deed to be performed. In the same way we read many such things in scripture, such as *Jacob*, who was called the supplanter from <term>aqeb</term> <gloss>heel/overreach</gloss>, because he had supplanted his brother in the birthright. By a similar reasoning, Christ receives his name from the admirable and plainly stupendous work of salvation, so that he might be called *Jesus*, *Savior*, or *Soter* <note>original: "σωτήρ"</note>, which signifies more than the Latin *servator* <gloss>preserver</gloss>, as Cicero himself acknowledges in the *Second Action against Verres*: I saw that he was inscribed at Syracuse not only as the patron of that island, but even as its *Soter*. How great is this? So great that it cannot be expressed by a single Latin word. He is truly the *Soter* who has given salvation. From this was born the Greek *Iesous*, which is read and written with two syllables just like the Latin, with the letter S added. For the Greeks add the same to foreign names at the end.

XIV. Here, if anyone wishes, let him venerate the religion and subtlety of the *Jesuits*, who write JHESUS for JESUS, or IHS by abbreviation of three letters, and lest any superstition be lacking, they even place a cross above it. These good companions wrongly introduce the H into the Latin, not noticing that the aspiration H is present neither in the Greek nor the Hebrew language. For it is not a Latin word, but made in imitation of the Greek diction, whence it preserves almost the same inflection in the oblique cases. But this is nothing new for the Jesuits; indeed, I remember and know the name of a *Rector* of a Jesuit College in a quite celebrated place, who cried out loudly as he surveyed the register with a sort of feigned wonder, seeing Lutherans <pb n="16"/> and students who had placed Greek and Hebrew sentences alongside <note>their names</note>, though that good director could scarcely, or not at all, pronounce Latin. For when he was about to ask what my lodging was, he formed another word according to a foreign character: What is your *Quartirium*? <note>a corruption of the French 'quartier' or German 'Quartier'</note> But I most gladly forgive this on account of his liberality. Furthermore, Galatinus is a witness that some are found who judge the name *Iesous* to be the same as the tetragrammaton name *JEHOVAH*, such that a <term>Shin</term> is inserted <note>rendering it YHShVH</note>, which error is surely not slight. Who does not see that the letters are very different in the names <term>YHWH</term> and <term>Yeshua</term>? Who does not recognize a different and distinct signification? For the latter expresses salvation, the former the essence of God. Therefore, the root from which each arises is different. Read on this the Blessed Chemnitz in his *Harmony of the Gospels*, and the Blessed Meisner in his *Christology*.

### XV. The Nazarene.

By this national name JESUS is so called, from Nazareth, a city of Galilee and the homeland of his parents. Regarding the application of this name to Christ, a threefold difference of exposition is given. To some, he is called a Nazarene as if separated and consecrated to the Lord, from Judges 13:7 and Genesis 49:26. For others, the eleventh chapter of Isaiah, verse 1, provides support. A third group joins both passages. And here different people look to different roots. There is the root <term>natsar</term> <gloss>to guard, to fashion, to plant</gloss>; there is also <term>nazar</term> <gloss>to separate, to sanctify</gloss>. Whence <term>nazir</term> and in Chaldean <term>nazira</term>, a Nazarene. We do not deny that both apply to the Lord, yet we feel that he had this name here derived from the city and the common homeland. It is also written in various ways. Sometimes as *Nazoraios* in Matthew, Luke, and John; but Mark exhibits it with another termination, *Nazarenos*, as it is also found elsewhere. It is therefore used promisingly, just as I say *Essaios* or *Essenus* <gloss>an Essene</gloss>. We do not deny that it is also found written as *Nazarenos* <note>with an epsilon instead of alpha</note>, since that could have happened due to the negligence of painters or the corruption of the Greek language, as, alas! in Greece itself the inhabitants do not know Greek. We shall add this monument of that fact from Crusius, who collects the letters of learned men and reports some in the third book of his *Turco-Graecia*, page 216 and following, from which it will suffice to have noted even this single following one:

Lord Theodosius, dear brother-in-law, and brother in holiness, and lord-priest, greetings in Christ. Know, Lord Theodosius, that since we took up our dwelling after the exile of my wife: with a good death my mother died...
</translation>

<keywords>etymology of Jesus, Soter, Jesuit orthography, Nazarene, Hebrew roots, linguistic corruption, Martin Chemnitz, Balthasar Meisner, Martin Crusius</keywords>

Just as the movement of an eagle, a serpent, and a ship is smooth and without noise; so are the arts of men hidden and secret in seducing her who is an <term>Almah</term> or virgin. IV. It is equally difficult to know whether she who still hides with her parents is an <term>almah</term> <gloss>virgin</gloss> and has not granted herself to a man, as it is to know the way of an eagle in the sky, etc. V. The guarding of virgins is difficult because the arts of men, by which they lay snares for them, are concealed, etc. <note>Compare the celebrated Saubert's dissertation on this passage, chapter 2; and Spanheim's Evangelical Doubts 34, section 18 and following. Add to this Leonhard Hutter, Common Places, Diexodus article 23, latter question, pages 864 and 865; Jakob Martini, book 3 on the Three Elohim, chapter 43; and the Blessed Walther, Vindication of the saying in Jeremiah 31, chapter 5, verse 22, against his opponent, page 73 and following.</note> However, let us assume that in that passage of Proverbs a comparison of a harlot and an adulteress is established; nevertheless, the word <term>almah</term> could signify a virgin there and be taken <term>doxastikos</term> <gloss>according to opinion</gloss> or <term>eironikos</term> <gloss>ironically</gloss>. Nor is that manner of speaking unusual in the Sacred Codex, that someone is called not by what they truly are, but what they seem or are believed to be, or what they sell themselves as, or what they had been before. Whence also our Blessed Luther says:

> The Jews would gain nothing, he says, except this: that the name <term>almah</term> signifies such a young woman there whom everyone considers a virgin, and who wears a virgin’s wreath and name, and presents herself as a virgin, although she is a harlot. Such an abuse of the name by no means removes its proper and genuine signification even in that place, as all endowed with a healthy mind will easily understand.

Therefore, we have so far proved that this passage of Proverbs does nothing to support the sense which the Jews attribute to the word <term>almah</term>. And since these same people, refusing to yield to divine truth, explain the same word in Isaiah 7 in that perverse sense and simultaneously appeal to the cited place in Proverbs, they do what most lazy Sophists are accustomed to: when they dispute about some controversial matter, they take the very thing in controversy as proven and thus deceive their adversary. We conclude now with a once great theologian as well as philosopher, Master Doctor Jakob Martini, that the word <term>almah</term> in our passage signifies nothing else than a virgin hidden, concealed, and secret from the sight of men, and thus entirely untouched, regarding whose modesty and integrity there is no doubt, especially when the letter <term>He</term> is placed before it, which, as Galatinus rightly advises, makes the word signify <pb n="16"/> determinately. For it is worth noting, says the praised author, that in the whole *Holy Scripture* this word <term>ha-almah</term> <gloss>the virgin</gloss>, written articulately with the letter <term>He</term>, is found only three times, and is always used for a virgin: *Genesis 24 verse 43, Exodus 2 verse 8, and Isaiah 7 verse 14*. Since therefore the first two to whom <term>ha-almah</term> is attributed were virgins, who will doubt that this word used in the same way by Isaiah in his prophecy denotes a pure virgin, since the Jews cannot demonstrate from any other place that <term>ha-almah</term> is used for a married woman. Finally (which even Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, known as Rashi</note> relates), that sign given by Isaiah ought to have been truly miraculous; but for a young woman to conceive by a man (and thus with the loss of virginity) and bear a son is no miracle, since it happens naturally and thus occurs daily. Let the Jews concede then, whether they will or no, that the sign given by the Prophet was none other than that, contrary to the custom of nature, a virgin would conceive and bear a son by the miracle of God alone. <note>Blessed Jakob Martini, cited book 3, page 243 and following.</note>

->**Harah**<- <gloss>pregnant / conceiving</gloss>

Chaldean: **me’adya** which is from **‘adi**, from which comes the feminine participle **me’adya**. Syriac: **hablata** <note>original: ܚܒܠܬܐ</note> a present participle, which marks the upper point in the letter <term>Lamed</term>, from the root **habal** <note>original: ܚܒܠ</note> to conceive. Arabic: **tahbalu** <note>original: تَحْبَلُ</note> 3rd person perfect singular feminine future from the root **habala** and **habila** <note>original: حَبَلَ & حَبِلَ</note> she conceived. Ethiopic: **tetsannas** <note>original: ትፀነስ</note> 3rd person feminine singular future from the root **tsannasa** <note>original: ፀንሰ</note>: she conceived. Persian: **abestan** <note>original: آيستَن pro آبستَن</note> whose harmonic root will be **abal**: he subdued. Our Hebrew word is a singular feminine noun from the root **harah**: she conceived. It is well known that the Prophets are accustomed to describe things which are still in the future, even a long time after, with words signifying the present tense because of that most certain and undoubted confidence. Just as in this place he says the Virgin is already pregnant, although she was to become such a long time afterward. But what do the Rabbis say to this word? Their defender Abarbenel...
</translation>

It emphasizes that the promised birth must be a supernatural miracle rather than a natural occurrence to qualify as a prophetic sign.</summary>

<keywords>Isaiah 7:14, Almah, virginity, Hebrew philology, Jakob Martini, Martin Luther, Biblical prophecy, miracle, Abarbenel, etymology</keywords>

<pb n="3"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta>the day had dawned; on this day, he said, the ancients were accustomed to desire and pray that they might be allowed to <term>annare perannare</term> <gloss>pass through the year and complete the year</gloss> happily, and they took diligent care that they did not even name things dire, sad, or funereal; but rather spoke only good words, abstained from all quarrels, and spoke only joyful and friendly things among themselves.

However, although this honor of invoking <term>Anna Perenna</term> <gloss>the Roman goddess of the new year and the cycle of time</gloss> was not held as cheap or contemptible, the cult of Janus was nevertheless preferred over her. For we find in the archives of antiquity that Janus was invoked first in all sacrifices and prayers, and was accustomed to be placed before the other gods, and even before Jove himself. For because he first built temples for the gods in Italy and instituted the rites of the sacred ceremonies, he earned a perpetual place in the prayer of sacrifices. And since in all things the first and last parts have the greatest force, they wished Janus to be the leader in sacrificing, as Cicero says (<italic>Book 1, On the Nature of the Gods</italic>).

We, who are called and are Christians, are so far from simply subscribing to the formulas of the heathens—as if we did not have others equally good or better—that we instead seriously condemn all that erroneous material which the idolatry of the Gentiles attracted. We judge that only that which seems derived and composed from the "Year" <note>referring to the word "Annus" in Anna Perenna</note> should be retained in this particular vow. For if we who make the vow obtain it by our prayer, each one of us will have cause to congratulate himself and rejoice after the course of the year.

And we know that vows of this kind were cared for in the shrines, chiefly by the <term>Flamines</term> <gloss>priests assigned to specific deities</gloss>. But what did those who sat at the helm of the Republic do around this time? Consuls and Senators were ordained: once ordained, they entered upon their duties and, for the sake of a favorable omen <note>original: "auspicii gratia"</note>, performed a ceremonial tasting <note>original: "delibabant", referring to a symbolic beginning of a task</note>. This can be seen in the election of the father of Symmachus, a man of wonderful eloquence and knowledge. While he was in the country and in retirement, digesting the injury of a lost home, the Senate summoned him to a new honor by frequent votes and finally by sending orators. And it was then the Calends, by which the year is opened, as <pb n="4"/> his son himself testifies and rejoices (<italic>Book 1, Epistle 44</italic>). To this the rhythmic describer of the <term>Fasti</term> <gloss>the Roman religious calendar</gloss>, Naso <note>Ovid</note>, subscribes, and he politely introduces this rite when he says:

> With unsoiled garments they go to the Tarpeian heights,
> And the people themselves are the same color as their festival.
> Now the new <term>fasces</term> <gloss>bundles of rods symbolizing authority</gloss> lead the way, the new purple shines;
> And the new weight is felt by the conspicuous ivory <note>referring to the curule chair of the magistrates</note>. (<italic>Fasti, Book 1, verse 10</italic>)

Indeed, it was also the custom on that very day to taste, and as it were to imbue and auspiciously begin, one's duties. Drusus, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take his omens; Nero took his omens on the Calends of January; the Emperor Maximianus immediately made what he had hoped for in the future a finished matter. Regarding the former, Tacitus, the writer of Augustan history, testifies (<italic>Book 4, Annals, chapter 36</italic>); Suetonius testifies regarding the second (<italic>chapter 46</italic>); and the Panegyrist regarding the latter. Nor is the custom and habit of Christians far removed from this time, who, in certain places, around these same turnings of the year, integrate and restore their councils of senates. And they seem to do this more correctly than the ancients. For we believe that at that time was born the eternal Son of God, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> of the eternal Father, who by his merit and satisfaction designated and appointed us as heavenly citizens and nobles. We leave to others the custom of tasting and imbuing business and the occupations assigned to each as <term>aparchas</term> <gloss>first-fruits</gloss>, and, so to speak, in use: knowing that the paternal grace of God, earned by our prayer, can, if He wills, make every month and every day of the month prosper for us, and that a certain inception of work on the first or any other day does not help us at all.

Which the most praised divine Emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius also seem to have acknowledged, who wished by a salutary rescript that the days of the January Calends be devoted to leisure and be an <term>apodeixis</term> <gloss>demonstration or display</gloss>: a thing which is not usually unknown to the priests of the law and the scholars of the arts <note>original: "lyris", literally "lyres"</note>. (<italic>Novellae 8, Law "Omnes Dies" 7, chapter on Holidays XII, book 3</italic>). Perhaps so that they might attend to divine worship and sacred matters...
</translation>

<summary>This text compares ancient Roman New Year customs, such as the invocation of Anna Perenna and Janus and the inauguration of magistrates, with Christian traditions. The author argues that while Christians reject pagan idolatry, they maintain the practice of beginning the year with prayer and administrative renewal, emphasizing God's grace over superstitious omens.</summary>
<keywords>New Year, Anna Perenna, Janus, Ovid, Cicero, Roman Law, Christian adaptation, Magistrates, Calends, Religious Rites</keywords>

### LXIII.
Of those works, some are internal, others external.

### LXIIII.
Internal works are to acknowledge the depravity and corruption of nature, to confess oneself guilty of divine wrath and eternal punishments, and to grieve for sins from the soul.

### LXV.
To flee for refuge to the mercy of God offered in Christ, and to firmly and certainly resolve that through Him the remission of sins and the right of entering the heavenly inheritance are given.

### LXVI.
To devote oneself entirely to the obedience of God, and to apply oneself to this with the whole mind, so that all plans and actions of life may serve the glory of the divine name and the utility of the Church.

### LXVII.
External works, however, are those which strike the eyes and the exterior senses.

### LXVIII.
These consist either of words, such as teaching the <term>evangelium</term> <gloss>Gospel</gloss>, calling upon God in dangers, giving thanks to the same for benefits, and putting forth a confession of faith.

### LXIX.
Or of deeds: such as hearing the word, using the <term>sacramenta</term> <gloss>sacraments</gloss> ordained by God, giving <term>eleymosinae</term> <gloss>alms</gloss>, and devoting the body for the <pb n="14"/> assertion of truth and the glory of Christ, if there be need, through martyrdom.

For if these <note>internal works</note> are done without those <note>external ones</note>, they are nonetheless pleasing to God: if those <note>external ones</note> are undertaken without these <note>internal ones</note>, they are so far from being approved by God that they are a greatest abomination.

->LXXII.<-
For to worship God without the interior, sincere affection of the heart is to lie.

->LXXIII.<-
For to testify to that which is not so belongs to the act of deceiving.

For whatever is not from faith, although it may have the appearance of good, is nevertheless so far from being approved by God that it is reputed as sin.

<translation>
<pb n="18"/><meta>continues from previous page: Indeed, truly,</meta> since you expect someone magnificent, what is more magnificent than this King, whom the Angels applaud from the heavens, whom Kings adore in the cradle, offering him gold, frankincense, and myrrh, the gifts of kings. If you desire one who fights and triumphs, what is stronger, what is more glorious than this Hercules, who already in the cradle has tamed the ancient serpent, and was born and revealed for this purpose: that he might destroy the works of the devil, and restore to its place whatever the fury of the infernal Prince had shattered. Here you see a lamb, indeed, but one who is to take away the sins of the world; a lamb, but one who is at the same time the greatest Lion of the tribe of Judah. You believe that the dry rod of Aaron <note>the brother of Moses, whose staff miraculously budded</note> blossomed, put forth leaves, and bore fruit; why do you not also believe that a virgin could give birth? You believe that the great Goliath was slain by little David, that the lion was torn apart by Samson, and the Philistines were routed; why do you not also believe that the head of the serpent was crushed by this little Hercules in the cradle, the seed of the woman? Omnipotence performs what human impotence cannot, and what lack of faith cannot grasp. Truly, Saint Augustine <note>the influential North African theologian, 354 to 430 AD</note> rightly judges these cradles more venerable than your temple in Jerusalem, repeating:

> *O manger, more venerable and holy than the very temple of Solomon! And though the temple of Jerusalem shines with gold, though it may glitter with Cherubim, the ark of God, lampstands, tables, and golden vessels; though it be adorned with the most spacious courts, with sacrifices, and the ministry of priests, it is nonetheless inferior to the manger of Bethlehem.*

Your fathers in the desert endured many deadly plagues from fiery serpents; and when Moses had raised a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign, whoever among the struck looked upon it was healed. Behold, truly, here in the cradle lies hidden the tamer of those fiery serpents, and the bronze serpent himself, who was later raised up on the sign of the cross: look upon him and live! But alas, you seed of the snake, seed of vipers, you do not wish to recognize the blessed seed of Abraham, the seed of the woman. The most holy Infant complains of you unbelievers: *The <pb n="19"/> ox has known his owner, and the donkey the manger of his lord; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood.* <note>Isaiah 1:3</note> After the Jews, approach the cradle of our Hercules, you born of the gentiles, whom this infant—long desired by the nations—has called a people, when you were not a people. The Magi, whether Persians or Chaldeans, go before you and, with a star as their guide, approach the Savior of the nations as well. *Truly those cradles do not shine with precious paintings, here purple and scarlet do not radiate, nor whatever the* Seres <note>the Chinese, famous in antiquity for silk</note> *taught the hand to spin with learned skill, whatever* Babylon *wove with ingenious comb, whatever the* Tyrians *dyed, whatever the* Phrygians *embroidered, whatever the* Milesians *shore;* nevertheless, those cradles are no less the cradles of the King of Kings and Lord of Lords, the King who shall break the kings of the earth with a rod of iron. If you believe, gentiles, that Minerva <note>goddess of wisdom</note> was born from the brain of Jupiter; believe also that this God was born of God. If you believe that Jupiter, through a golden shower, made Danaë pregnant; believe also that the Spirit of God overshadowed the virgin, so that she might carry a womb and bear a son. If you believe that your Hercules subdued the immense monsters of men and beasts, overcame the Erymanthian boar, crushed the bull in a wrestling match with Antaeus, routed the Stymphalian birds, fought with the Amazons, conquered the three-bodied Geryon, tamed the horses of Diomedes, cleansed the stable of Augeas, struggled with the dragon of the Hesperides, fought against the Lernaean Hydra and the three-headed Cerberus; believe also that this our celestial Hercules has conquered the world, death, the devil, and hell, and has trampled his and our enemies under his feet, cast out evil spirits with a word, calmed the winds and waves with a command, healed lepers, the deaf, and the blind with a touch, and by a simple order put to flight every kind of disease and death.

I have called, after the Christians, even the Jews themselves; I have called the gentiles to the cradle of our Hercules. It is time that I myself approach. Grant, Boy Jesus, that I may from a distance only [see] your manger...
</translation>

<summary>This section compares the infant Christ to the mythological Hercules, arguing that his humble cradle is more powerful than Solomon's Temple or the feats of pagan heroes. The author addresses Jews and Gentiles, urging them to recognize the spiritual triumphs of Christ over the devil and death as superior to classical myths.</summary>

<keywords>Christology, Hercules, typological interpretation, Solomon's Temple, Jewish-Christian relations, classical mythology, Saint Augustine, miracles</keywords>

<pb n="11"/>, and likewise those of the Prophets, and the remaining books of the Old Testament, you have then destroyed the whole of the sacred scripture of the Old Testament. For when all the parts are removed, the whole itself is taken away. I, however, shall so demonstrate the true divinity of those very books to you from the books themselves, that you will not depart without most justified confusion: And then I will also demand of you, that if you are able and willing, you show the contrary. I shall observe the same method in the books of the New Testament, and I will offer you the saying of John 21, verse 24: This is the disciple who testifies of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true. But then I will add a collation of the Old and New Testaments and of parallel sayings, and the mutual testimony of the books concerning themselves, and finally I will ask of you: Do you believe that from all these any single thing is true, or do you hold all those things as false? Let that Papist <note>The author refers to his opponent, Johannes Pistorius, who converted to Catholicism.</note> assert: Tell it to the Church: if he acknowledges it as true, I have what I want. But if he denies it, he destroys the primary foundation of all the Pontiff’s followers. Whatever you answer, Pistorius, it will pertain to the ignominy of this argument of yours. 5. That faith which Pistorius describes here is not justifying faith, but historical faith, which many have lacked, and can lack without the loss of salvation. For that number of Biblical books, or the order of the same, contributes nothing to the righteousness of faith, provided that you sincerely believe what scripture proposes to be believed concerning Christ the redeemer. See thesis 24 of the 1st disputation.
29. Note here on page 15 the extreme impudence of Pistorius, expressly writing: That our opinion concerning the perfection and sufficiency of Holy Scripture leads away by degrees to the denial of the whole of sacred scripture, and makes men Turks <note>A common early modern term for Muslims.</note> and Epicureans <note>Here meaning atheists or those living only for pleasure.</note>. His argument is such: Those who believe nothing except what is held in sacred scripture are led away by degrees to the denial of the whole scripture, and turn out Turks and Epicureans. The Lutherans believe nothing except what is held in sacred scripture. Therefore, the Lutherans are led away by degrees to the denial of the whole scripture, and turn out Turks and Epicureans. Who would not judge such an impudent Apostate most worthy of the hatred of all? For are not to believe and to deny contraries? How then do they meet in the Lutherans alone? For whoever believes the unique scripture certainly does not deny it. And he who denies it, <pb n="12"/> does not believe. Concerning the Papists, the conclusion is most true: a thing which shall be most clearly demonstrated in its own place.

30. Argument 2. Nothing is to be believed except what stands written in the word of God. But nowhere is it found in scripture that nothing is to be believed except what stands openly <note>original: "bekandtlich"</note> in scripture. Therefore, not even this itself ought to be believed, page 16.

31. I respond. There are 4 terms <note>A logical fallacy where a syllogism has four terms instead of the required three.</note>. The proposition speaks generally of that which stands in any way in the word of God, whether expressly, that is, in distinct words, or implicitly, that is, through a certain, firm, and necessary consequence. And to this extent it is true. The assumption speaks only of that which stands openly. Hence the argument is narrower than the question, when it ought to be either broader or equally broad. 2. Pistorius’s assumption is most false, which is evident from thesis 4, and especially from these most clear testimonies: Do not turn aside to the right or to the left, Deuteronomy 5, verse 32. To the law and to the testimony. If they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them, Isaiah 8, verse 20. Let him be anathema, who shall have preached another Gospel, Galatians 1, verse 8. Not to teach other doctrine <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν"</note>, 1 Timothy 1, verse 3, and chapter 6, verse 3. This pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection that follows human functions, commending them with a particular sweetness.

### XLIII.

Therefore, just as theoretical happiness surpasses practical happiness, so too does theoretical pleasure excel over practical pleasure.

Furthermore, from what has preceded, this also is clear: that Aristotle saw both the excellence and the dignity of human nature, as well as its corruption. This is evident when he confesses that a desire for divinity and immortality is implanted in man by nature, yet he says that divinity does not belong to man insofar as he is man. However, he did not know the cause of this, much less the manner of obtaining immortality through the MESSIAH; for this is entirely owed to revelation, as the most learned Zwinger has most beautifully noted in his commentary on chapter 7 of Book 10 of the Ethics. <note>Theodor Zwinger the Elder (1533–1588) was a famous Swiss scholar who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>

### XLV.

Nor is there any reason why we should reject Aristotle's doctrine concerning human happiness simply because it is less in agreement with our Christian religion.

### XLVI.

For besides what we said <pb n="15"/> above, <margin>Sermon to the Young on How They Might Profit from Greek Literature.</margin> that the philosopher disputes on this matter as a philosopher, his opinion ought to be commended to us on this name alone: because the philosopher either says the same things—that is, things congruent with heavenly truth, where the consensus is profitable—or he says different things, where the comparison is profitable, to use the words of Saint Basil the Great, a witness in this matter beyond all exception.

### XLVII.

Finally, the philosopher does not contradict himself, even though in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asserts that practical happiness is the highest good, while in the last book he maintains and contends that <term>theoretikēn eudaimonian</term> <gloss>theoretical happiness</gloss> is superior to it.

### XLVIII.

For just as in the first book, regarding practical happiness, he respects the <term>syntheton anthrōpon</term> <gloss>composite man</gloss> <note>the human being as a union of body and soul</note>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the <term>noun</term> <gloss>intellect</gloss>, which he calls <term>malista anthrōpon</term> <gloss>most of all the man</gloss> <note>the essential or highest part of a human being</note>.

### XLIX.

From all of this, finally, I judge it to appear more clearly than the midday light, as the saying goes, that what Cicero used to say is most true: that all the authority of philosophy—that is, the doctrine of life and morals—consists in procuring a blessed life, and for that reason its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.

For we see that in the states of all Republics, various kinds of men are found, who of their own accord depart as if into diverse classes, so that the illustrious and wealthy constitute one; the weaker and poor another; and finally a third, those who walk the middle path and exist as a temperament <note>a balancing element</note> between the illustrious and the poor. But by what method these classes are to be composed, so that the city may be rendered quiet and every part of the city may enjoy its own happiness—this is the task, this is the labor.

<margin>Aristotle, Politics, Book 5, Chapter 1</margin>
The illustrious or wealthy persuade themselves that while they excel the rest in splendor, they are simply superior, and that by right and merit, unequal things are owed to them as unequals. Conversely, the poor, measuring all things by liberty, concede no inequality. By this vain persuasion of men—as if his own right is not attributed to each—the states of Republics are most greatly changed, which was long ago excellently proven by Aristotle.

Writers record of Solon <note>the famous Athenian lawmaker</note> that, in order to make the citizens familiar to him and be declared a legislator by them, he said: He would bring laws equal for all; and from this, by the greatest zeal and will of all, the judgment of making laws was permitted to him. For the common people thought he spoke of the mean of the matter <note>arithmetic equality</note>, to borrow this from the schools; the Aristocrats thought he spoke of the mean of the person <note>proportional equality based on merit</note>. If the citizens persist in these precipices, nor wish to remit anything of their own right which they boast of so laboriously, it is easily evident that contentions of this sort are joined with the internal slaughter of the Republic, nor do they cease before one side is oppressed.

Truly neither side, whether the poor or the wealthy are considered, is accustomed to seek equality and inequality from true principles. It is a common assertion of Philosophers that virtue alone makes a distinction between the commoners and the illustrious; so that the latter may shine forth among the rest, while the former live content with their humbler lot. But who may persuade minds of this, which, too blinded by love of self, are driven hither and thither? Nor is the matter so clear that it holds no further doubt.

<margin>Aristotle, Politics, Book 6, Chapter 3</margin>
Aristotle himself, dealing with Democracy, confesses that it is extremely difficult to so order the people that all participate equally in the communion of rights. For although the weaker look to nothing else by this equality of theirs than that they not be oppressed by the wealthier; nevertheless, you will notice the diverse purposes, zeals, propensities, inclinations, inventions, arts, and rules of the more powerful.

Lest we dwell longer on this question, and to explain in few words the mind of the Philosopher, which is found more than once in his <term>Politics</term> <gloss>Aristotle's work on the state</gloss>, <pb n="13"/> these things must be added: namely, that harmony can be obtained between the poor and the rich if the legislator always has a greater care for the middle citizens than for the extremes, for then the Republic will be contained as if in an equilibrium. But if this proceeds less according to wish, another way must be attempted: namely, that the rights themselves be properly mixed, so that both parties preside over affairs and concede a little to each other in turn. Let there be added also other offices of humanity and signs of benevolence, whether in gesture or in conversation; let one promote the advantages of the other and turn aside disadvantages; perhaps in this way such a Republic will fare well enough, while no one can complain that they are either oppressed or despised, but all live among themselves with equal right.

What we have said thus far concerning the mixing of the Popular state with the Aristocratic, Greek and Latin writers explain more fully beyond the <term>Politics</term> of Aristotle and Plato, treating Democratic and Aristocratic matters even to the point of nausea. For to repeat our opinion again: among the ancients, a Popular state was never found unless tempered by the arts of the Aristocrats. Let us not speak at present of the changes and various trials by which the Attic Republic <note>Athens</note> was vexed. Therefore, Thucydides, Demosthenes, and Isocrates must be turned over diligently. In Roman history, Halicarnassus <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</note>, Plutarch, and Dionysius are to be commended; but none surpasses the labors of Livy in thoroughly learning the characters of the Aristocrats.

§. 13. The signs for recognizing the state of a Republic are not rarely confused. If the power of Kings were contained in external apparatus and splendor, surely the King of Poland would surpass all Princes of Europe in Majesty, whom the leading men venerate like servants. But his power is closed within narrow limits. Indeed, it is a small thing that is permitted to him in Ecclesiastical matters: it is a crime to condemn a knight to death except in the assembly. Concerning the waging of war and the entering of treaties, there is a common care with the Senate: he cannot even in the Senate, without the consent of the rest of the nobility, promulgate new laws, command an extraordinary tax, mint money, name a successor, and other things which most adorn the Royal dignity. And to finish in a few words: the rights of Majesty are exercised by the aristocrats rather than by the King. Cromer <note>Marcin Kromer, a Polish historian</note> has followed this out diligently and successfully.

You will cast aside and despise those things which oppose these arts, and you will judge them not only unworthy of the man you ought to present yourself as in the future, and such as we all augur you will be, but utterly unworthy of a human being. You have always lived laudably before this; there was modesty in the boy, there is integrity in the youth, there is a perfect reckoning of punishment <note>likely referring to a sense of justice or moral consequence</note> and a knowledge of things to be sought and things to be avoided. What seemed to be lacking was an opportunity in which you might show yourself. The greatest opportunity of all has been granted by divine providence through the singular counsel of the Supreme Pontiff Paul IV, who, since he is the uncle of your parent, and since he has loved you not a little from your early age, and since he has been accustomed to embrace all his kin with an incredible affection, nevertheless followed certain other things in honoring you. He gave honor not to kinship or family, but to you yourself, who strive to illuminate the family name; and as the beginnings present themselves, the outcome will prove the effort. Behold, Alfonso, you have a field in which your virtue—acquired through vigils and now confirmed by the habit of acting well—may run forth. This is that province for which you were training yourself, toward which your cares looked, a province most worthy of your talent, your best thoughts, and your studies. Show the excellence not only of your will but also of your industry, and bring forth from your soul those noble qualities which you have gathered since childhood so that you might reflect the ancient glory of your race and your present domestic virtue. It is not, believe me, a labor for one who thinks well to <pb n="25"/> do well. For that which is placed within ourselves does not depend on anything else, nor is it taken from the outside; in this, what stands in the way of the reality following the will? Now virtue itself invites, itself allures and moves those studious of it with every goodwill and every reward, and I do not doubt that the excellent force of your mind will overcome all difficulties and all human things. Therefore, I indeed congratulate you for your own sake regarding that highest grade of honor to which the divine wisdom of Pope Paul has raised you; but I am moved somewhat more by the public interest, which has been handed over and commended to you along with that dignity. You will protect it throughout your life—it being a thing that often, and now indeed especially, lacks the help of such men—and there will be placed in you a most firm defense against injustice and impiety. If these things seem great and glorious to you, you ought to so establish and moderate your mind that you refer nothing to yourself, and arrogate nothing to yourself, or expect nothing from yourself. Consider that all things have flowed from God, who is the perennial and eternal fountain of all good things. For we, as ourselves, are nothing; but we can be something, and even very much, as we are from God and through God. Farewell.

<pb n="138"/>On the impediments of this work on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have already determined for you the impediments of this work in general. Now, however, we shall address you in more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall relate all those impediments to you more openly, most fully, and in order. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his complete organs, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself, such as if he were blind or had his limbs amputated, since he is not assisted by the members by whose mediation this art is perfected, acting as ministers to nature. If indeed the artist's body were weak and sick, such as the bodies of those with fever, or of lepers whose limbs fall away, and of those laboring at the ends of life, and of old men already of a decrepit age, he will not reach the completion of the art. By these natural bodily infirmities, therefore, the artist is hindered in his intention.

On the impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have set before you one chapter in which we related in absolute and manifest discourse the impediments depending on the part of the artist's body. It remains for us to relate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have natural talent <note>original: "ingenium"</note>, and a soul searching subtly into natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the artifices which are able to follow nature in the properties of its action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Just as there are many who have a stiff neck, void of talent in every investigation, who can scarcely understand common speech, and likewise learn common works with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many to have a soul easily believing any fantasy, but what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastical, deviating from reason, full of error, and remote from natural principles, since their brain, filled with many fumes, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. There are also, besides these, others who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinions, and from will to wills, just as those who now believe this, and want the same, without any foundation of reason. Yet a little after that, they believe another thing similarly, and want another thing. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely finish the smallest part of that which they intend, but rather leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth from natural things, no more than beasts, such as those captured in mind, the insane, and children. There are others who despise science and do not think it exists: whom this science likewise despises, and repels them from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves, serving money, affirming this wonderful science themselves, but they fear to interpose the expenses. Therefore, although they affirm it and investigate it according to reason, yet they do not arrive at the experience of the work because of the greed for money. To these, therefore, our science does not come. For how would he who is ignorant or has neglected to investigate the science reach it easily?

On external impediments hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments delaying the end of this art which are from radical principles according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is expedient, therefore, that we finally relate the impediments coming from without, and from the fortunes and cases happening by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, some shrewd and talented men, not at all ignorant of the works of nature and of nature herself, in which it is possible <pb n="139"/> to be followers of principles and works, whose investigation is also not fantastical in all things which are regulated by the movements and actions of nature beneath the lunar circle. These men, however, being oppressed by extreme poverty, are forced to postpone this excellent mastery <note>original: "magisterium"</note> due to the lack of means. There are also many others besides those just mentioned, curious men, detained by the various cares and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business, from whom our precious science again flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the impediments are that distract from this art.

<note>A decorative drop cap C marks the beginning of the conclusion.</note> We conclude, therefore, from what has already been said, that it is necessary for the artist of this work to be learned and perfect in the sciences of natural philosophy, because however much money and naturally deep talent he has, and desire in this artifice, he will not acquire its end unless he has attained natural philosophy through doctrine. For what is not attained through natural talent is aided in its defect through doctrine. It is necessary, therefore, for the artist to be helped by the highest scrutiny and industry. For because of doctrine, however much science he has acquired, unless he is also helped by natural industry, he will not be invited to such precious banquets. For in an instant he would correct his error through his industry, for which he would not know how to apply a remedy if he were founded on doctrine alone: and likewise he would aid an error in an instant from science acquired through natural doctrine, which he could not avoid through industry alone: since art is helped by talent, and talent likewise by art. And it is likewise necessary for him to be of a constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to attempt now this, now that: because our art does not consist in, nor is it perfected in, a multitude of things. For there is one stone, one medicine, in which the mastery consists, to which we add no foreign thing, nor do we diminish it, except what we remove as superfluous in preparation. It is also necessary for him to apply himself diligently to the work until its consummation, so that he does not leave the work cut short: because he would acquire neither science nor profit from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss. It is also expedient for him not to be ignorant of the principles and main roots of this art, which concern the essence of the work: since he who is ignorant of the beginning will not find the end. And we shall tell you all those principles in complete discourse, and also sufficiently open and manifest to the prudent, according to the requirement of this our art. It is likewise expedient for the artist to be temperate and slow to anger, lest suddenly, because of an impulse of anger, he scatter and destroy what has already been begun. Likewise, let him guard his money, nor let him as a presumptuous man distribute it vainly, lest by chance if he has not found the art, he be left in misery and the despair of poverty: or lest by chance, when he has already approached the end of this mastery through his investigation, his expenses are consumed, and the wretched man violently leaves the true end because of poverty. Just as those who at the beginning of their investigation prodigally destroy their whole treasure, when they are near the end, they have nothing further with which to work. Whence such men are buried in sorrow in two ways: both because they scattered their money on useless things, and because they lose the most noble science which they would have discovered immediately. For it is not necessary to consume your goods, since for a low price (if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art and have rightly understood those things which we have handed down to you) you will arrive at the completion of the mastery. If therefore you lose your money by not attending to our warnings, which we have written for you open and manifest in this little book, do not unjustly gnaw at us nor enjoin blasphemies upon us, but impute it to your ignorance and presumption. Therefore, this science does not well suit a poor or indigent man, but rather is...
</translation>

<summary>This text details the physical, mental, and external impediments that prevent an alchemist from achieving the Great Work, emphasizing the need for a sound body, a rational mind, and sufficient financial resources. It concludes by stressing that the "mastery" requires a balance of natural talent and formal education in natural philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, impediments, natural philosophy, talent, doctrine, industry, poverty, one stone, mastery</keywords>

Since that distinction is arbitrary, which they attribute to the Egyptian inventors, the distinction of the <term>trigones</term> <gloss>astrological triangles</gloss> also depends solely on human whim, as Kepler agrees in chapter 6 of his *Book on the New Star*. Every effort of this contrived fiction, by which he attempted to establish the elementary qualities of individual triangles, will also be in vain. Furthermore, the objections that most people raise against the efficacy of the <term>dodecatemoria</term>, Gassendi also raises in *Physics*, section 2, book 6, chapter 2, page 724. Abdias Trew candidly confesses this error of the Astrologers in *Medical Astrology*, disputation 1, thesis 36: <note>original: "Quod quatuor qualitatibus elementaribus pollere & differre ab invicem inferunt Astrologi, majori faciunt absurditate, quam si asinum iisdem qualitatibus pollere cum equo dicant, quod uterque, & ut Homerus loquitur, μώνυξ sit."</note> That the Astrologers infer these signs possess and differ from one another by four elementary qualities, they do with greater absurdity than if they said a donkey possesses the same qualities as a horse because both, as Homer says, are <term>monyx</term> <gloss>single-hoofed</gloss>. And yet some Astrologers attribute so much to this fiction that they fill both sides of their weather forecasts with it, predicting a future that will be warmer or colder according to how many planets are found in notably hot or cold signs. The ancients rather looked to the figure of the signs; many monuments of the Arabs testify that for driving away scorpions, the sign of Scorpio rising was badly affected, namely on account of an occult sympathy, which they believed in, regarding which see thesis 14.

<translation>
<pb n="10"/>### XXXI.

That it has drawn its origin from <term>pituita</term> <gloss>phlegm</gloss> is established by a phlegmatic nature, a whitish color of the joint, an obtuse and persistent pain with <term>oedematous</term> <gloss>fluid-filled</gloss> swelling, from food previously ingested, and finally from a paroxysm returning <sup>a</sup> every single day.
<sup>a</sup> Pereda in Paschal, book 1, chapter 61.

### XXXII.

Gout rarely arises from <term>melancholia</term> <gloss>black bile</gloss>; if, however, it draws its origin from the dark humor, it is bad, both because it disturbs much more than others, and because it lasts longer and does not yield so easily to medicines. The signs by which it is betrayed are a deep pain with heaviness, a blackish color, a cold and dry temperament, an age verging toward senility, and cycles of exacerbations returning on the fourth day; the urines are for the most part thin and watery in the beginning, afterwards dark and moderately thick, and what settles in them is sometimes dusky, sometimes indeed mixed, as witnessed by Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta</note>, book 3, chapter 78.

### XXXIII.

Finally, if gout should proceed from various mixtures of the humors, mixed signs will arise in various ways.

### XXXIV.

As far as the prognosis is concerned, it becomes known from the nature and condition of the aforementioned things. Generally, however, it must be affirmed that all gout is difficult to cure.

### XXXV.

Nevertheless, young people can be cured, <sup>a</sup> even if they have held it by hereditary right, as well as those <sup>b</sup> in whom <term>tophaceous</term> <gloss>stone-like</gloss> calluses have not yet appeared congealed around the joints, who love labor, and have an obedient bowel; these, having certainly obtained a prudent Physician, will be able to be saved.
<sup>a</sup> Felix Plater, in Observations, book 2, page 473. <sup>b</sup> Hippocrates, aphorisms 6, 49 and 55.

### XXXVI.

On the contrary, old men can scarcely be cured who have <pb n="11"/> such hardened calluses around the joints, of which the Poet <note>Ovid</note> says:
> Medicine knows not how to loosen the knotty gout.
Together with those who live luxuriously and have a dry bowel, as Galen teaches in book 10 of On the Composition of Medicaments According to Places, chapter 2. Nor can those be cured in whom <sup>a</sup> it is hereditary from a native imbalance of the brain and weakness of the joints, unless they have timely encountered this evil in their youth.
<margin><sup>a</sup> Hippocrates, book 2, On Diseases of External Parts.</margin>

### XXXVII.

Gouty pains are moved for the most part in Spring and Autumn, as Hippocrates teaches in aphorism 55 of book 6. In whomsoever gouty diseases occur, they end after the inflammation has subsided in a space of 40 days, provided (as Galen says in his commentaries) the Physician has not wandered in his work, and the patient has obeyed him in all things.

### XXXIIX.

In other respects, by reason of its path and exit, this evil is for the most part terminated in four ways: for it is either resolved, and this quite often; or it is matured, but rarely; or it is sometimes hardened; or it is transferred to the noble members <note>the vital organs</note>, whence for many it has ended in dropsical disease, and for some in asthma, as Aëtius witnesses.

### XXXIX.

From these things already said, it appears that gout draws its origin from different causes, and is also ended in different ways: by reason of origin, one is hot, as that which comes from blood and bile; another is cold, as that which arises from phlegm and black bile; another obtains a mixed nature, according to the proportion of the causing matter; one exists as curable, but another in no way so.

Gout rarely arises from <term>melancholia</term> <gloss>black bile</gloss>; if, however, it draws its origin from the dark humor, it is bad, both because it disturbs much more than others, and because it lasts longer and does not yield so easily to medicines.
