<pb n="9"/>is commanded in place of a fine. Thus the Phocians were accused by the Thebans and, in a common council of Greece, condemned to pay such a great sum of money that it could not be paid; at length, in desperate circumstances, since they were deprived of their fields, children, and wives, they were driven to plunder that most famous Temple of Apollo which was at Delphi, from which there later broke out the greatest wars, by which all Greece was subjected to the yoke of the Macedonians. Regarding this, Justin <note>Justin, Roman historian</note> says in Book 8, chapter 1: A no less light danger is to be feared from that avarice which is seen in private matters, when specifically either individual magistrates or the entire order of magistrates drag the goods of private individuals to themselves by force, fraud, and under some pretext.

## XIII.
Indeed, since this **Avarice** exists as a frequent cause of ruin above others, a King will act most safely if he exacts small taxes in parts, with the consent of the states, after the necessity of the financial matter has been demonstrated; if he preserves ordinary taxes and does not easily command new ones. Adam Conzen <note>Adam Contzen, Jesuit political theorist</note> says in Book 9 of his *Politics*, chapter 8, §. 4: Especially since no vice is found more foul in Princes and those governing the Commonwealth than **Avarice**. *For to hold the Commonwealth for profit is not only base, but also wicked and nefarious*, says Cicero. Indeed, it is even repugnant to nature itself; hence the same author says:

> To take something away from another, and to increase one's own advantage by the disadvantage of a man, is more against nature than death, than poverty, than pain, than the other things which can happen either to the body or to external things. For it destroys the fellowship and society of men: For if we are so disposed that each one plunders or violates another for the sake of his own gain, that society of the human race, which is most according to nature, must necessarily be broken apart.

## XIV.
An equal, indeed an almost greater plague than **Avarice** is accustomed not rarely to be produced in Commonwealths by the **Ambition** of those who wield the scepters; from which, as if from a Hydra <note>literally "a Lerna of evils"</note> of evils, besides wars, of which it is the torch, infinite other evils also leap forth, and it is often accustomed to bring the greatest plague and destruction to the ambitious themselves. For although **Avarice** also exists as a frequent cause of war, yet <pb n="10"/> Ambition is far more persistent in it. Indeed, their own wicked causes snatch each man into battles, yet the lust for dominating holds the leadership, says *Adam Conzen, Book 10 of his Politics, chapter 8.* Hence *Thucydides* rightly said: The cause of all evils is the desire for power arising from ambition. And *Polybius*, a most weighty writer, says: After some city has overcome and struggled out of many and great dangers, and has now ascended to leadership and power: It is manifest that where successful fortune, not applied moderately, has fixed its seat in it, luxury creeps into the morals, and Ambition and stubbornness into the minds of men, both concerning the magistracy and concerning others: When these evils have once grown strong, they will exist as the beginning of a change for the worse, starting from honors sought or denied through Ambition.

XV. Moreover, many do not judge themselves blessed in every part unless they can enlarge their Kingdom by adding new provinces to the old ones, ignorant that according to *Seneca, epistle 113*, to rule oneself is the greatest Empire. Nor do they attend to the most certain destruction of their own provinces resulting therefrom: For while they are not content with their own limits and gape for more provinces, they often lose those things which they have already placed in safety. For example, the states of Greece, which while they each desired to rule, they all lost their empire. *Justin, book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, from the mouth of Truth is that saying of *Thucydides* in the description of the *Corcyraean sedition*: The cause of all evils is the desire for power and Ambition. From these affections all calamity is born. Thence arose atrocious wars continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the created world. Inflamed by this, Alexander pursued all Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is said to have once said: if two ways lay open; one to the underworld, the other to the throne, he would choose that one which led to the underworld. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but yet it shows the most miserable ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, climb onto a slippery peak, tottering, agitated by lightning and winds, where they can neither stand firm nor depart.
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss Avarice and Ambition as primary causes for the corruption and downfall of states. Using historical examples like the Phocians and Alexander the Great, the author argues that greed and the lust for power lead to social fragmentation and the eventual collapse of kingdoms.</summary>

<keywords>Avarice, Ambition, political corruption, Thucydides, Cicero, Adam Contzen, Greek history, taxation, greed, desire for power</keywords>

<pb n="20"/>transparent medium, such as under water or radiating through glass, is called <term>ANACLASTICA</term> <gloss>refraction</gloss>. In this doctrine Euclid, Ptolemy, Vitello, and Kepler are distinguished.

XLVIII. <term>SCENOGRAPHICE</term> <gloss>scenic design or stage-painting</gloss> has no common kinship with Optics, indicating how we may fashion images that are neither out of proportion nor deformed, specifically regarding distances and heights; it is otherwise called <term>PERSPECTIVA</term> <gloss>perspective</gloss>. The German Lencker, Ubaldus, and Giovanni Battista Benedetti have prescribed this for us.

XLIX. You might not incongruously call <term>PICTORIA</term> <gloss>the art of painting</gloss> either its daughter or sister; it is the true and genuine art in which Zeuxis, Apelles, and Parrhasius once excelled, and in our age, Dürer. Whatever artistry they possess in their paintings, they owe solely to mathematical proportions, as Dürer himself sufficiently proves in his most learned German work. Indeed, other artisans—sculptors, goldsmiths, architects, military commanders, captains, and musketeers—cannot do without it for the skillful firing of projectiles at fixed targets.

L. I come finally to <term>CANONICA</term> <gloss>the study of musical ratios</gloss> or <term>MUSICA</term> <gloss>music</gloss>, specifically <term>Harmonica</term> <gloss>the science of harmony</gloss>, which is the science of sound measurable by number. This involves contemplating and practicing harmony or the order composed of sounds and intervals, having considered the ratio of appearing harmonies and applying the judgment of the senses everywhere, so that, according to Plato, the ears might seem to have been placed before the mind. Whatever this Theory of Harmony teaches, it demonstrates all things by mathematical principles. Among the ancients, many excelled in this, such as Euclid, Aristoxenus, Ptolemy, and Boethius, the musicians.

LI. But from those theoretical foundations, another, <term>PRACTICA</term> <gloss>practical music</gloss>, composes songs which possess grace in sound or harmony and elegance in singing. In this, many emulate the supreme artist Orlando <note>likely referring to the composer Orlande de Lassus</note>.

LII. Finally, even <term>ASTROLOGIA</term> <gloss>astrology</gloss> does not wish to be separated from the mixed mathematical disciplines. For Astronomy itself is present as either servant or mistress, teaching to what good those astronomical observations and contemplations can be put if we look to the distinction of times, in which it has wonderfully and uniquely aided in chronological <pb n="21"/> matters. Indeed, from a diligent consideration of the sites, positions, and configurations of the stars and planets, it divines certain events through conjecture. This includes both things in the elements, such as storms and the like, which we call <term>PROGNOSTICA</term> <gloss>prognostication</gloss>, and things concerning humans, such as life, diseases and death, temperament, character, morals, and the like, which is called <term>GENETHLIACA</term> <gloss>the casting of nativities</gloss>. It often divines truths, often falsehoods, often vanities, and often impieties. It need not be rejected if the many superstitions of the Arabs and many other less solid minor precepts are pruned away, and only those things are retained which admit either reason or experience, or both together.

LIII. In this class, others also number <term>CHIROMANTIAM</term> <gloss>palmistry</gloss> and <term>METOPOSCOPIAM</term> <gloss>metoposcopy, the art of reading foreheads</gloss>. The former teaches the method of recognizing signs and characters in the human hand and of judging them skillfully; the latter is the art of divining from the forehead. We have primary patrons and writers for these: Taisnier, Johannes de Indagine, Rothmann, and Thaddaeus Hagecius.

LIV. But we do not wish to either highly commend or too sharply attack these at this point, lest we slip beyond this mathematical scope into the camp of the Physicists for disputes regarding signatures <note>referring to the Doctrine of Signatures, the belief that plants or objects resembling body parts can treat them</note>.
</translation>

<keywords>refraction, perspective, painting, music theory, harmony, astrology, palmistry, metoposcopy, Albrecht Dürer, Johannes Kepler</keywords>

In that prior state of Nature, it is something distinct from all accidents, by which this man is an individual man, so much so that those accidents suppose and follow singularity rather than constituting it; and Socrates is Socrates even if all accidents were abstractly removed by the mind. Therefore, the statements of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote the Isagoge, an introduction to Aristotle's Categories.</note> are to be understood either concomitantly, because the collection of accidents follows (as has been said) the individuation of substance, or notificatively, because through them, as notes and signs, we recognize the individual. See Zabarella <note>Giacomo Zabarella, a 16th-century Italian Aristotelian philosopher.</note> in several places, and in book 1, chapter 2. See also Jacobus Martini, <term>Metaphysical Exercises</term>, book 1, theorem 5.

->IV.<-

**We therefore state, not without fitness, that form—not a peculiar form, but the specific and communicated form—possesses within itself the power of individuating matter.**

We have not yet sufficiently investigated in a clear manner what that thing is through which a man is what he is, as Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a prominent Renaissance scholar.</note> says in his <term>Exercises</term>, section 6, number 1. But our Theorem says that this thing is form. Since the office of form is to bestow being, quiddity <gloss>the essence or "whatness" of a thing</gloss>, and the totality of that quiddity—according to the testimony of Armando de Bello Visu <note>Armandus de Bellovisu, a 14th-century Dominican theologian.</note> in Treatise 2 <term>On Causes</term>, chapter 142—a distinction must be considered between "giving being" and the "act of a thing." This being is twofold, and consequently the act is twofold: one is the being of <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence</gloss> or <pb n="10"/>essence; the other is of <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>existence</gloss> or existence. Wherefore, "act" can also be taken in two ways: first, for the degree of essence which form attributes, insofar as the form of an animal constitutes the animal, and the form of a man constitutes the man; second, for the act of existence outside the soul, which form likewise bestows. However, it is not just any form that does this, but only that ultimate and specific form which is directed toward nothing else than making the thing exist individually. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary theologian of the Scholastic tradition.</note> explains this no less skillfully than elegantly in the first part of the <term>Summa</term>, Question 3, articles 2 and 3, and in other places, when he says: "Being is the actuality of form." For form implies potentiality before it is placed into being; therefore, being is compared to essence as act is to potency. Because of this, we see that the form of an animal—or any other general form—constitutes the proper essence of that thing, such as the essence of an animal or a plant; yet it cannot bestow actual existence without the help of the specific form, which alone both constitutes the essence of the species and makes the thing exist in act. And this is what all philosophers have commonly been accustomed to say in abundance: that a general form gives an act, but an imperfect one, while the specific form supplies a perfect act that requires no other form for existing. Just as it is contracted in man through that same form, it is perfected to such a degree that no other form can be given,</translation>

<pb n="9"/><meta>continues from previous page: supreme Prince</meta>

### X.

The decree of Charles the Fat <note>original: "Carolus Crassus", reigned 881-888</note> *concerning the Roman expedition*, dated to the year 890, is untrustworthy and devoid of both credit and truth. Even if this were not evident from the clause added to the decree, which clearly betrays a defect, the mere insertion of the word *Fief* <note>original: "Feudi"</note> and the rest of the character of the style, which is inconsistent with that age, would brilliantly demonstrate it.

***

### XI.

The *decree on tournaments* by Henry the Fowler <note>original: "Henricus Auceps", reigned 919-936</note>, the first King of the Saxons in Germany, dated to the year 938, is a forgery. This is because the style is repugnant and does not suit the logic of the times, and also because it names circles not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet established, such as Burgraviates, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, to say nothing of other signs of falsehood.

***

### XII.

The origin of the Electors <note>the prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire</note> is incorrectly ascribed to the age of Otto the Great <note>reigned 936-973</note>, as *Christoph Gewold*, a Bavarian Councilor and otherwise a very learned man, does. He undoubtedly followed *Martinus Polonus*, who is believed to have been almost the first author of that opinion.

***

### XIII.

The tradition of *Frederick Barbarossa* <note>original: "Fridericus Aenobarbus"</note> being trampled underfoot by Pope *Alexander III* <note>original: "Alexandro Magno", likely referring to Alexander III's victory over the Emperor</note> is deservedly to be exploded; just as that which the common people hand down regarding his death—that he was submerged in a river—should be counted among fables. For the contrary is clear from the *Diary of Thageno*, in which no such thing is related. Only *Otto of Saint Blasien*, as far as I know, stands <pb n="10"/> for the common opinion. Others, whoever are more accurate, are either silent or disagree.

### XIV.

That Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinum"</note>, was devoured by mice is false. The argument concerning the tower visible today in the Rhine <note>the Binger Mäuseturm or Mouse Tower</note>, which they commonly bring forward to confirm their opinion, is utterly absurd and least of all sustains the dignity of proof.

### XV.

It is a common opinion that the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was carried off by a poisoned host given by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of Saint Bernard <note>the Cistercians</note>. This is not without merit of doubt, because Conrad Vecerius, who described his life most diligently, related no such thing.

### XVI.

It cannot be proven by certain and indubitable records that the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy beyond the Jura, or Arles. Nor can the assertors of the contrary opinion bring forward or demonstrate a diploma <note>an official charter or deed</note> of such alienation, although it is otherwise well known that he was a little too liberal not only toward the French, but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

### XVII.

<margin>
Germany chapter 28, in the book On the Origin of the Bohemians.
</margin>
They are absurd who think the Bohemians received their name from some King Bohemus. To this also belongs the error of those who write that they were a Gallic people, among whom are Cornelius Tacitus and Johann Matthias von Sudeten, to whom Melchior Goldast otherwise owes much. But there are just causes which encourage us to disagree with them
</translation>

<summary>The author refutes several historical myths and forged documents, including the "decree on tournaments" of Henry the Fowler and the legend of Archbishop Hatto's death by mice. He also questions the tradition of Frederick Barbarossa's humiliation by the Pope and the origins of the Bohemian name.</summary>
<keywords>Charles the Fat, Henry the Fowler, Frederick Barbarossa, Hatto of Mainz, Henry VII, Charles IV, Bohemia, historical criticism, forged documents, tournaments, Electors</keywords>

Who Samson was can be gathered from the preceding, namely a <term>Nazirite</term> <gloss>one consecrated to God</gloss>, who from birth was dedicated to God as a redeemer of Israel. What a Nazirite or the <term>Naziriteship</term> <gloss>the state of being a Nazirite</gloss> is, is described at length in Numbers 6; the narrowness of the page prevents bringing all of that here. Let the eager reader look there. Nevertheless, many and the chief points of the Naziriteship seem able to be referred to these three heads: (1) That they should not drink wine or <term>sicera</term> <gloss>strong drink</gloss>, or anything else that could intoxicate. Among the Jews, as <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli, 1499–1562, a Reformed theologian and commentator.</note> Peter Martyr notes in his commentary, <term>sicera</term> was the name for water that was poured onto pressed grapes after the wine had been squeezed out, which, when it had finished fermenting, retained some flavor of wine; it was the same as that which we call secondary wine, and which in Upper Saxony is called <term>Lauer</term> <gloss>press-wine or tart wine</gloss>. (2) That they should not shave their heads, but nourish their hair throughout the whole Naziriteship. (3) That they should not contaminate themselves with funeral mourning, not even at the death of a father. Paul also seems to have had such a vow in Acts 21. Thus Samson was a holy and public person from his very first birth, and he was such even in death. (2) Concerning what Samson did, some things have already been said in the teaching on the object; namely, after he had judged the Israelite people for some time, having been captured and blinded by the Philistines, he was cast as a private citizen into prison. There he recovered the grace of God and the virtue of his Naziriteship, and thus in his recovered vocation he redeemed the people of Israel and liberated his fatherland from the enemies by whom it was oppressed. He fought bravely, conquered, and sealed the victory with his own death. (3) Where this act was done, the sacred history teaches: namely in some public place, where the Philistines had gathered to celebrate a feast to their <term>deaster</term> <gloss>petty god or idol</gloss> Dagon, where God was mocked and Samson, that chosen Prince of God, was held in derision. Not a few think this house was the temple of Dagon itself, on account of its size, which is not to be presumed in a <pb n="19"/> private house: for three thousand people were in the upper part of the house. Therefore, the place was not narrow; which proves all the more that those extraordinary strengths were so immense that they must be estimated as plainly incomparable. (4) By what aids he did it is clear from his prayers, namely by supernatural aid, by the special grace of God and by plainly divine assistance. (5) Finally, it must be seen how that man of God, judge of the people and thus a public person, liberated his people, and took vengeance for the deprivation of his eyes and through this the injury inflicted upon himself and God. Namely, he seized the occasion given to him: for when he saw that all hope of victory without his own death was vain, he preferred to perish in a mutual destruction rather than leave the glory of God stained, his fatherland without liberty, and his enemies without vengeance. Thus he sought victory with death accompanying it as if called to it, and he preferred to return the life he had laid down and been granted to GOD and his Fatherland rather than retain it unjustly.

->§. 19.<-

Therefore, Samson did not properly kill himself, as he would have done if he had run himself through with a sword or dashed his head against a column; but he permitted himself to be overwhelmed along with the enemy. Nor did he kill himself by moral imputation, because he primarily intended to kill the Philistines and seek vengeance for his eyes. Secondarily, however, and only permissively, he involved himself in the same slaughter which he could not escape. Which was surely a matter of great fortitude, as <note>Cornelius a Lapide, 1567–1637, a Jesuit exegete known for his vast commentaries.</note> Cornelius a Lapide says on this passage. Not incongruously, therefore, <note>Saint Ambrose, c. 339–397, Bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church.</note> Ambrose says concerning him in Epistle 70 on this passage:
> *Samson conquered himself in death; and although he was indeed incomparable in this life, yet in death he conquered himself, and bore an insuperable spirit, so that he despised and held as almost nothing the end of life which is fearful to all.*

Let this question of the moderns close the number: namely, whether the damage which is claimed under the Aquilian Law is a true or a <term>quasi-delict</term> <gloss>as if a crime</gloss>? ## COROLLARIES.

### I.
Whether we can perform a <term>manumission</term> <gloss>freeing of a slave</gloss> before a deputy of a Proconsul is greatly debated; we think that the act of manumission can be carried out before him.
<note>François Hotman in the 2nd amicable response, 1, speaks against it; Cujas, book 1 of observations, chapter 1, and book 15 of observations, chapter 19.</note>

### II.
A father, by reason of paternal power, can claim a son according to the Law of the Quirites <note>a</note> <gloss>ancient Roman civil law</gloss>. But it is asked whether a mother can do the same? Which we deny. <note>b</note>
<note>a) Law 1, paragraph "through this," Digest on the claim of property. b) Argument from Law "mother" 38, Digest on thefts. The gloss on the second to last law on freedom by trust disagrees.</note>

### III.
An argument from contracts to last wills proceeds affirma- <pb n="20"/> tively, if the reason is equal everywhere and the same in both cases.
<note>Everhardus of Middelburg, on the contrary regarding last wills. Schneidewin on the title of the Institutes on the removal of the Fufia Caninia Law, number 8.</note>

### IV.
The question is uncertain whether a minor under 25 years of age can be a judicial <term>procurator</term> <gloss>legal representative</gloss>? We are more inclined toward the negative view, approved by the votes of the more frequent Doctors, <note>a</note> especially since it has been granted by the authority of a Papal decree. <note>b</note>
<note>a) The Doctors on the Law "of demanding" 12, Code on procurators, and on the Law "minor," Digest on the same. b) Chapter "and generally," outside on procurators in the 6th; differences of Cujas, book 22, observations, chapter 16, whom Pacianus follows in century 2, question 10.</note>

There is no less doubt among the interpreters of the law: whether besides the <term>actiones bonae fidei</term> <gloss>actions of good faith</gloss> enumerated in paragraph 28 of the Institutes on actions, others of the same kind may be found? We similarly deny this: thinking that a most absolute and perfect enumeration of all good faith actions is contained therein.
<note>Common Doctors as reported by Schneidewin on the said paragraph, number 8; in the same place where Donellus speaks elegantly. Cujas on 11, observations 28. Lorius in the treatise on actions, axiom 20; differences of Corasius on the said paragraph.</note>

### VI.
Very often we see that beauty alone serves as a dowry for girls. Hence we think it is accepted by the Doctors for a peculiar reason: that in the case of a maiden's face being injured, an account can be taken of the deformity and the visible scars.
<note>Ravennas on the Law "from this," Law 3, Digest on if a quadruped is said to have caused damage; whom Albericus commends in the same place.</note>

->THE END.<-

For this reason the most illustrious Prince, FREDERICK IV, in that same year of [15]89, in order to investigate Krentzheim’s doctrine, presented in the assembly of priests the Table of the Lutherans concerning the difference between the Dogmas of Luther and Calvin and others, printed at Wittenberg in the Year of our Lord 1575. He kindly exhorted him to return a written response that was express, simple, and direct on each point. Acts pages 7, 82. He did this, albeit unwillingly, acting correctly in the same manner as the theologians of Rostock, Oels, Frankfurt, and Saxony judged, using the phrases and words of our people <margin>(i)</margin> and he delivered this confession of his to the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE on nearly the last day of September. Acts pages 82, 24b, 25b, 65b, 98; Report page 26. FREDERICK IV then took care to have it delivered on the fifteenth day of the following April in the year [15]90 to the Rostock theologians; in the month of January of the year [15]91 to the Oels theologians, with the addition of two orations of Krentzheim delivered in the General Assembly by the mandate of FREDERICK IV in excuse of Calvinism; and finally in the month of April to the Frankfurt Academy. All of these men, turning this confession and the remaining writings over with the greatest diligence from head to heel <note>from beginning to end</note>, condemned Leonhard Krentzheim in the transmitted judgments and annotations of Calvinism regarding the articles of the Holy Supper and the Person of Christ. Acts pages 24b, 28, 43, 65, 92, 98.

> (i) He speaks indeed with us, yet he holds with the Calvinists; the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau. Acts pages 19, 21.

### X.

The theologians in the villages of Bärsdorf and Cuniz judged Krentzheim no differently, and in the sight of all, when the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, moved by their prayers towards this year of [15]91, called the Pastors of the Duchy of Legnica with Krentzheim into a public trial which was instituted on the fifteenth day of January, they were constant in this opinion in both speech and writing. Acts page 87. Indeed, our man responded at length to the chapters brought against him and attempted to clear himself of the crime, but the Prince in no way approved of the response; instead, he sent the statement of his contrary will, exhibited in writing, once again to the Academy at Frankfurt. Krentzheim, having been summoned to the Court on the twentieth day of June, by permission of the Judge, who was the Prince's Prefect, carried home the opinions and questions of this University sent back from Frankfurt on the third day of May of that same year, and at seven o'clock on the following morning, he brought them back <pb n="11"/>adorned with a written and plausibly colored response. *Acts pages 102, 103.* Truly, this plausible response was vehemently rejected by everyone, because both the explanations and the modes and formulas of explaining the Article on the Holy Supper, which *Martin Gosky*, formerly Pastor of St. Mary’s Church, had excerpted from Krentzheim’s orations held in the assemblies of Pastors and read aloud publicly in the presence of all the Pastors, proved and showed him to be altogether suspect. Therefore, the Frankfurt theologians were consulted a third time by the Most Illustrious Prince through letters written on the eleventh day of July, but since Krentzheim had responded with little integrity even in this writing to those things which were asked, they could not find rest, but on the thirty-first day of June, having transmitted their judgments to the Prince, they anew judged him suspect of Calvinism. *Acts pages 109, 110b.*

XI. Scarcely had this judgment been sent back when not only did the reformation instituted by the Administrator of the Electorate of Saxony, Frederick William, reach the ears of the Most Illustrious Prince, but at the same time he was made more certain that certain letters of Leonhard Krentzheim written to Master Urban Pierius—Pastor at Wittenberg and General Superintendent of the Electorate of Saxony, but vehemently suspect of Calvinism <note>k</note>—had been found in his study and were being kept in the desk of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM. Incited by these things, the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE decided to refer this controversy to the Saxon theologians as well; but so that Krentzheim might be evidently convicted of errors, the Most Illustrious Prince first twice requested his letters from the Administrator most affectionately; having obtained them by a second letter, he read them through eagerly and simultaneously detected in them the most certain signs of perverse doctrine. *Acts page 116.* Therefore, after FREDERICK IV saw that this discord could in no way be suppressed by tolerating and delaying it, but would cause great detriment to the Church unless it were timely put to rest, in letters worked out on the 6th day of February in the year [15]93 to the Most Illustrious Duke of Saxony, Frederick William, he called Master Martin Mirus and Master Georg Müller from Saxony to settle this controversy. *Acts pages 141, 142.* Furthermore, by the order and mandate of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM, Master Aegidius Hunnius, formerly a most celebrated Doctor and Professor of Theology in this Academy of Wittenberg, and Wolfgang Mamphrasius, Superintendent of Wurzen, departed for Legnica. To these men, our man was ordered to give an account of his doctrine in a public colloquy on the very large stone floor of the Castle, where Duke FREDERICK IV had summoned his counselors, two delegates from Oława, leading men from the Equestrian Order and the city council, and all the Pastors of this Duchy, with many from the lowest common people looking on. This took place in the same year, on the 1st and 2nd of April, New Style...
</translation>

Understand this as privation compared with privation and others, namely blindness compared with deafness, poverty, silence, a cow, a stone, etc.

<margin>XX.</margin>
XX. There are indeed those who—as it may be permitted to advise <term>diexodikōs</term> <gloss>at length</gloss>—call <term>diaphoronta</term> <gloss>differing things</gloss>, that is, things that are different and repugnant, "Disparates." But neither of these designations is suitable, since neither is equal to the breadth of Disparates. For the former is narrower than is just, as it does not embrace all forms of Disparates. For a Difference and a Univocal <note>having a single, consistent meaning</note> have a Genus, and they differ through something of their own—namely, a Specific Difference. But in truth, certain Disparates contain neither of those. For God and prime matter are indeed reckoned among Disparates; yet they neither have a Univocal Genus, nor do they differ through something of their own. For the entire essence of God is distinguished from the essence of prime matter; hence they are named by Metaphysicians not as "different," but as "diverse." Of this kind is also the name <term>hetera tō eidei</term> <gloss>diverse in species</gloss>, which is ascribed to Disparates from the Metaphysics of Aristotle.

<margin>Commentary on Ramus’s Dialectic, chapter 13, book 1, pages 228 and 235.</margin>
Yet the latter designation is much broader; for by it (as Downame <note>George Downame, a logic commentator</note> rightly observes) Opposites are also contained, since "repugnant" refers not only to the former but also to these. Hence, by the nature of the thing clashing, the "opposition" of some things together and at once in one Subject is said to be the repugnance of things not permitting themselves to exist in respect to the same thing.

<margin>XXI.</margin>
XXI. So much for the Nominal Definition and Division of the Disparate, to which its Real Definition was to be subjoined. For without this, it will not happen that its nature becomes known to the mind.

<margin>Section 1, chapter 10, book 2, Posterior Analytics.</margin>
For that is hitherto believed to be the <term>logos ho ti esti</term> <gloss>logical discourse of what a thing is</gloss>, by which, what a thing is, is placed before the eyes of the human intellect.

<margin>XXII.</margin>
XXII. But we cannot grant a full supply of that definition to any one person, inasmuch as its parts do not suffice for us for its constitution. For the Genus and Difference of the Disparate, properly so called, are lacking, as it is practically an exile from the house of the Categories <note>the Aristotelian Predicaments</note>. For the First Notions <note>direct concepts of things</note> do not receive it into their flock, nor is that which is first denoted by that concept merely Categorical. For beyond this, it includes the Divine and Transcendent, yet it contains none <pb n="10"/> according to the actual thing <note>in reality</note>, and thus the Disparate exists as indifferent to them.

<margin>XXIII. Section 1, chapter 13, book 2, Posterior Analytics.</margin>
XXIII. But we shall nevertheless strive with the greatest effort, if in any way possible, that we might <term>thēreuōmen ta en tō ti esti katēgoroumena</term> <gloss>hunt for the things predicated in the "what it is"</gloss>, or Synonymous Thoughts <note>Noemata</note>, to weave together a Logical Discourse by which, approaching as closely as possible to a Definition, we may place the "whatness" of the Disparate before our eyes.

<margin>XIX.</margin>
XXIV. Therefore: 1. A Disparate is a Notion. Because it is an idea or image formed by the intellect, which presents something to the mind. 2. A Disparate is a Second Notion <note>a concept of a concept</note>. Inasmuch as it is a concept representing a first concept, or representing a thing by means of a first concept. 3. A Disparate is a Dialectical or Logical Second Notion. Since it is produced by an intellect cultivated by Dialectic or Logic. 4. A Disparate is an Incomplex <note>simple/single</note> Dialectical Second Notion. Since it is brought about so that it belongs to the first operation of directing the intellect. 5. A Disparate is a General Incomplex Dialectical Second Notion. Since it is produced for the sake of representing a first concept—not only one that is Categorical, Divine, or Transcendent, but any one of those. 6. A Disparate denotes a first concept, or by means of this, a thing. For it is in the register of Second Notions. 7. A Disparate denotes a first concept which is able to be repugnant <note>incompatible/clashing</note>. For a nature diverse from one Disparate to another Disparate is perceived. 8. A Disparate denotes a first concept which can be repugnant (not only to one, but by this very fact to more or) many. For it can be thought of as clashing not with one at least, but with many and almost infinite things. 9. A Disparate denotes a first concept which can be repugnant to many equally, that is, in like manner, equally, by a like reason, by the same mode of clashing, or while the same kind of repugnance remains everywhere. For the bare power of a Disparate to fight with many is not enough for its nature. For it is necessary that the reason for clashing be everywhere equal and the same. Therefore, although one of the Disparates can fight with many; yet in whatever manner it can be repugnant to a second, in the same manner it can be repugnant to a third, a fourth, and the rest. 10. We have "hunted down" two <term>katēgoroumena</term> <gloss>predicates</gloss>, or two thoughts. For one is a General Incomplex Dialectical Second Notion; the other is the designation of a first concept that can be equally repugnant to many. 11. Neither are not <term>ta en tō ti esti katēgoroumena</term> <gloss>the things predicated in the "what it is"</gloss>, or Synonymous Thoughts. That is, both can be affirmed essentially of the Disparate. 12. A General Incomplex Dialectical Second Notion is likened to a Genus. For just as...

# PARADOX VII.

## Although the <term>lunula</term> <gloss>little moon or lune</gloss> (a part of the circle) was reduced to a square space long ago by Hippocrates of Chios, the <term>quadrature</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss> of the circle has nevertheless not yet been discovered to this day.

### DECLARATION.

<term>Tetragonism</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss>, or the quadrature of the circle, has been attempted thus far by two primary ways: either geometrically through lines, or arithmetically through numbers. In the former way, the <term>lunula</term> was reduced to a square space long ago by Hippocrates of Chios, but the circle has in no way been able to be squared, neither geometrically nor arithmetically, to this day.

### DEMONSTRATION.

No one, if they have properly understood his demonstration, will deny that the quadrature of the <term>lunula</term> was most correctly discovered by Hippocrates of Chios, for it is as follows: Let there be drawn circle *a, b, c, d*, and upon its diameter *b, c* let there be established a square *b, e, f, c* whose diagonal <pb n="13"/> is *b, d, f*. <note>See Figure VI</note> Let there also be dropped a semidiameter *g, i, d*, perpendicular to *b, e*, which will bisect both the semicircle *b, d, c* and the diagonal *b, d, f* at point *d*. Therefore, with center *d* and interval *d, b*, let another circle be described through points *b, e, f*, and let the straight line *d, c* be connected. Moreover, since in the right-angled triangle *b, e, f*, the side *b, f* subtends the right angle *b, e, f*, its square will be double the square of *b, e* or *e, f* by the 47th proposition of the first book of Euclid. And consequently, the circle *b, e, f* will be double the circle *a, b, d, c* by the 2nd proposition of the twelfth book of Euclid, and the semicircle *b, e, f* will be double the semicircle *b, a, c*, and the quadrant *b, g, d, c* will be equal to that same semicircle *b, a, c*. Therefore, when the common segment *b, g, c, i* is taken away, the <term>lunula</term> *b, a, c, g* remains, equal to the triangle *b, i, d*. If that triangle is squared by the last proposition of the second book of Euclid, the <term>lunula</term> *b, a, c, g* will be squared. But that the circle has not been reduced to a square space to this day, neither by lines nor by numbers, is clearly evident from the most recent writings of geometers. Hippocrates indeed persuaded himself that by the same reasoning with which he had completed the quadrature of the <term>lunula</term> (a part of the circle), the whole circle could also be squared, and therefore he attributed the discovery of <term>tetragonism</term> or the quadrature of the circle to himself. But in truth, as ingeniously as he had recalled the <term>lunula</term> to a square space, he wandered so foully in squaring the circle, as is plain to anyone from Father Caspar Schott’s *Technica Curiosa*, Book VIII, section 1, on my pages 600 and 601, and Christopher Clavius’s *Mathematical Works*, Volume II, Book VIII, page 189. Indeed, Blancanus says in *Aristotle’s Mathematical Places* that it is credible that Hippocrates recognized this fallacy (which he used in squaring the circle) and concealed it on account of the subtlety of the discovery. It has happened no differently in the most recent attempts at the quadrature of the circle, in which, once properly examined, a false reasoning is generally detected, so that many today judge <term>tetragonism</term> to be absolutely impossible; see the *Acts of the Erudite of Leipzig* for the month of September in the year 1687, page 524. Therefore, although the <term>lunula</term>, a part of the circle, was reduced to a square space long ago, the quadrature of the circle has nevertheless not been discovered to this day. Which was to be demonstrated.

For no sooner did Holofernes <note>referring here to the leader of the Huns or the suitor Etherius</note> come into the sight of URSULA than he already put on a heavenly mind: no sooner did he greet her presence in his soul than he changed his mind toward divine things: no sooner did he kiss her hand with a chaste kiss than he changed the decree of war into peace. And nothing further remains, except that the treaties of virginal peace be confirmed by the end of life itself. Be present therefore, fierce spirit of the barbarians! and sign the kiss of perpetual peace with the blood of those making the pact, and grant that privilege to the banks of the Rhine, that they may glory in the peace concluded by Saint URSULA even unto our own age.

-><-

But why do we implore barbarian minds with anxious prayer? Of their own accord they conspire for the slaughter of Christians, to whom no enemy is greater than one marked with the Christian name: they desire above all to satisfy the thirsty sword with the blood of those whose life is hostile to them: they judge those unworthy of the earth who deny that there are many gods in heaven.

As URSULA stood with Etherius; so for the faith, and for the love of virginal peace, she saw her fellow-soldier Virgins fall from their station and their life: with the same spirit that she embraced her heavenly spouse; with the same she received the fatal weapon: with the same love that she panted for this peace, with the same she breathed her last in testimony of peace. She breathed her last! that soul, truly corrupted <note>undone or broken</note> by the weapon, which could be conquered by no siege engines: the Virgin fell as a prey to the barbarian hand, she who by an inviolable vow decreed to always stand in the perpetual greenness of Virginity. She gave her blood, she who devoted the whitest milk of Virginity to the Heavenly powers alone.

But it was fitting for the Virgin that in one kiss she should join both Laurels of Virginity and Martyrdom <pb n="13"/>together. offering is surely the pious gifts of our tongue; c

which no one, except the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Sacrosancto Flamine"</note> of <term>Jehovah</term>, d knows how to fashion so that they please, or how to render them fit. <margin>a Mark 9:49; 1 Corinthians 3:13.</margin>

Let this, therefore, be for us today as a sacred anchor, let it be like the gift which our minds have determined to sacrifice to the Supreme Being; let it purge and remove all filth, let a most sweet scent accompany our mouths, and let a fragrance rise to heaven with good breaths. the holy altar of the Lord beforehand with the ruddy blood. b So now, let us sprinkle the altar with the rosy blood of Christ the Savior before WE place ourselves upon it; which is nothing else than to pour out thanks to the celestial Father from the heart in the name of Jesus alone: He, without a doubt, will have gathered all the fruit of our lips and noted our voices with His ear. Moreover, the clear voice of the Law commanded 
<margin>c Sirach 35:9.</margin> 
that one approach the gifts with happy countenances above all, with eyes without a cloud, and with serene foreheads and faces: c so we too are commanded to bring these libations of ours into the holy dwellings with a joyful and good spirit,

and with cheerful cheeks to give the honor of praise to the Lord. d Afterward, it was a great sacrilege for a son of Ephraim <note>referring to the Israelites</note> to diminish

the gifts which they wished to slaughter with a sacrificial hand: e thus it will by no means be helpful for us to have secretly diminished the gifts which we have begun to offer to the Thunderer <note>original: "Tonanti", referring to God</note> at present. ### XXI.

Therefore, parents succeed to their children who die without children of their own, if the brothers and sisters of the deceased have also died, in equal shares <term>in capita</term> <gloss>per capita; by heads</gloss>. If the brothers and sisters are still living and were joined to the deceased from both sides <note>from both the father and the mother</note>, they also share per capita; but if only the children of such brothers or sisters remain, they succeed by the right of representation <term>in stirpes</term> <gloss>per roots; by lineage</gloss>.

### XXII.

Parents of different lines, from the paternal and maternal sides, who are established in the same degree of kinship, even if they are unequal in number, do not divide the inheritance by an individual portion <term>pro virili portione</term> <gloss>a man's share</gloss>, but rather by account of the lineage. Today, they divide the inheritance of the deceased without distinction of the types of goods left behind.

### XXIII.

It is well known in law that brothers and the children of brothers joined to the deceased from only one side are excluded from the inheritance by all ascending relatives.

### XXIV.

An adoptive father cannot be the heir to his adopted son whom he no longer has under his legal power, even though a son of that kind may succeed to him.

### XXV.

I would say differently regarding one into whose power an adopted person passes; to him, just as to one who adopts a person already of legal age <term>arrogatori</term>, the succession is granted in the goods of the adopted grown son, just as it is to a legitimate and natural father.

### XXVI.

Natural parents succeed to their natural children whom they have legitimized by a subsequent marriage, or by a decree of the prince, or by an offering to the local senate <term>oblatione curiae</term>, just as if they were natural and legitimate.

### XXVII.

By the same reasoning that natural and illegitimate children succeed their parents, so these parents in turn succeed them. Specifically, the natural father and his ancestors succeed to two ounces <note>two-twelfths of the estate</note> of his natural son's estate, while the mother and her ancestors from the maternal line succeed to the whole <term>in solidum</term>.

### XXIIX.

I believe it is not in doubt that those born from incest and condemned union, if they cease to be among the living, have neither father, nor mother, nor any ancestor as a successor.

### XXIX.

These points concern the succession of those standing in the direct line. When these are lacking, those in the collateral line succeed, whose succession is extended as far as the tenth degree.

### XXX.

But whether the succession of agnates <note>relatives through the male line</note> in an ancient fief is limited to certain degrees, or proceeds into infinity, the opinions of the Doctors of Law vary because of conflicting texts, which I think should be reconciled by a rule of distinction.

### XXXI.

Brothers and sisters who are <term>amphithaleis</term> <gloss>born of the same father and mother</gloss>, joined from both sides, exclude those joined from only one side <pb n="7"/> from the inheritance of a predeceased brother. They take per capita; but when they concur with the children of predeceased brothers who were joined from both sides, these children, and no more distant relatives, are called to the succession by right of representation <term>in stirpes</term>.

### XXXII.

Is a half-brother by the same father <term>frater consanguineus</term> also excluded from the fief by those joined from both sides in feudal law? The accepted opinion is that he is to be admitted to the fief of the deceased along with a brother joined from both sides.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed one another in a paternal fief, but in a new fief it is not so; instead, the fief reverts to the lord. Sisters are incapable of succeeding in either case.

### XXXIV.

If only the children of brothers joined from both sides remain, and no uncles survive, are they called to the succession of the deceased uncle per capita or <term>in stirpes</term>? It has been established in both the new and old law that they are called per capita, and this is true.

### XXXV.

If the deceased left no brothers, sisters, or their children joined from both sides, but only uterine brothers <note>same mother</note> or paternal brothers <note>same father</note>, then these are admitted to the brother’s inheritance.

### XXXVI.

Inheritances are not granted such that paternal goods go to paternal relatives and maternal to maternal, as in the old law; but if paternal and uterine brothers exist together, the inheritance of the deceased is divided equally among them. If only one group exists, they obtain the entire inheritance.

### XXXVII.

Those adopted by ancestors from both the paternal and maternal lines succeed one another collaterally, as do those adopted as adults <term>arrogati</term>, although the latter are by no means included under the name of "cognates" <note>blood relatives</note>.

### XXXIIX.

Collateral relatives connected to each other by a natural bond through the father enjoy no right of succession. However, it is certain in law that those joined through the maternal line succeed one another, even if one is natural and the other legitimate.

### XXXIX.

Illegitimate children <term>spurij</term> born of one and the same father but of different mothers are prohibited from succeeding one another; however, no one would affirm this regarding illegitimate children born of the same womb <term>homogastriis</term>.

### XL.

There is no succession between incestuous brothers, nor between those adopted by a stranger.

### XLI.

After brothers and the children of brothers, those who are closest in degree are called per capita, so that those equal in degree are admitted equally without distinction of sex.

### XLII.

So much for the succession of those touching the deceased by kinship; to whom

<translation>
<pb n="682"/>barricaded doors and guarded their families, whom I could sometimes see from atop my horse, huddled together in the courtyards in anxious suspense. From the distance, one occasionally heard the cries of distress from women and children when unscrupulous marauders had forced access to their hiding places and were plundering them or taking them captive.

In their outward appearance, the <term>Pâlem</term> <gloss>a local ethnic group</gloss> do not differ significantly from the <term>Somraï</term> and <term>Gâberi</term>; they are strong, well-built, often tall figures with a more or less black skin color, which generally shows no nuances tending toward reddish or yellowish tones, and they likewise seem for the most part to understand the <term>Bagirmi</term> language.

The sky had become heavily overcast, and thunder rolled on all sides as we set up our night camp at the feet of some <term>Delêb</term> palms <note>Borassus aethiopum, a tall fan palm</note> without any other tree cover. I spent half the night performing surgical treatment on the wounded. I stitched the flesh wounds with horsehair and bandaged the more serious injuries as well as possible. However, many had penetrating chest and abdominal wounds or open shoulder and hip joints, and some gave up the ghost during the night.

The next morning (June 1st), we set out an hour before sunrise and crossed, also in a roughly easterly direction, a lowland with lush grass growth that was described to me as a <term>Komodûgu</term> <gloss>riverbed or watercourse</gloss>. At its deepest points, it showed swampy ground and here and there small puddles of water; according to the people, it is said to run north toward <term>Mul</term> and northwest to the <term>Ba Ili</term> <note>a river in the region</note>. We had passed a similar grass-rich, treeless valley, abundant with water in summer, which seemed to extend from southeast to northwest, toward evening the day before. Both of these, as well as the valley-like lowland near <term>Murki</term> and another located south-southwest of <term>Gundi</term> which we saw later, seem to be parts of the swamp network from which the <term>Ba Ili</term> eventually develops. An hour after sunrise we turned south, passed numerous scattered and barricaded homesteads that already belonged to <term>Gundi</term>, moved beyond the center of this main settlement of the <term>Tummok</term> tribe, and made camp at 8 o'clock in the morning. Immediately, everyone went into the <pb n="683"/> surroundings to look for roofs and coverings from huts, poles and fences, wooden mortars and other household utensils—in short, all the necessary requirements for a dwelling. The impudent slaves of the King and his highest dignitaries also came back richly laden, but my people had only looted a piece of straw fence, which was at most enough for the wall of a hut, and for the time being we had to content ourselves with a dwelling made of leafy branches. While the morning had been gloomy with a weak southeast wind, the sky cleared up around midday, so that I indulged in the hope of a rain-free night. But the rains had become so frequent over time, and I could so little afford damage to my meager belongings, that when neither <term>Almâs</term> nor <term>Hammu</term> <note>Nachtigal's servants</note> had succeeded in finding a hut roof in the vicinity by afternoon, I lay down to sleep not without worry.

An evil night followed, the beginning of which has remained in my memory as particularly repulsive. Without suspecting it, we had erected my provisional hut on a termite mound that had not yet risen above the level of the surrounding ground, and during the night the hated little creatures paid me a most unwelcome visit. I had hardly spent half an hour in restless sleep on my bed—which was always laid out directly on the ground—I had been suffering from severe rheumatic pains since <term>Somraï</term>, when I awoke and felt a strange sensation on the skin of my entire body. At first, I tried to ignore it and go back to sleep, but since my pains promised me no rest anyway, I decided to get up and light a lamp. The latter was no easy procedure, for although I had made a lamp out of a small bowl of butter by means of a scrap of <term>Châm</term> <gloss>calico or cotton cloth</gloss> rolled into a wick, our cooking fire had gone out, and I had to ignite dry rags using the priming powder of one of our flintlock muskets. At last I had light, and now, by the dim glow of the primitive lamp, I saw my bed flooded by thousands upon thousands of white termites, a great many of which I had already crushed. My shirt and the surface of the bedcover were covered with the insects squashed into a pulp, and ever new swarms of them...
</translation>

<pb n="88"/>Regarding these feuds, it is like this: the feuds of women are the lowest of all; therefore, if one person has entered inside and another also enters, they will undoubtedly kill one another without hesitation. Regarding what was said about someone entering by paying five hundred <term>karshapana</term> <gloss>a silver or copper coin of ancient India</gloss>, that is also true; it is surely necessary for her clothes and ornaments. Regarding what was said about cleaning the house after seven days have passed, that is also true; whether it is done earlier or later, what conflict could there be in that? Regarding what was said about not examining the men who come and go, that is also true; since she is not a common prostitute, if the men coming and go were to be examined, who would ever enter her house? Then the assembly granted her those five supreme conditions, and she was enjoyed by the assembly. As the <term>Licchavis</term> <gloss>a prominent noble clan</gloss> of Vaishali began to enter her house to take their pleasure as they wished, some of them, due to their great attachment to sensual objects, became free of desire the very moment they saw her. Others became so by touch alone; none of them performed the act of a man with her. She thought, "These are not real men; I must prepare a scheme." She then resided in various regions 

<leaf-break/>

Amrapali <note>original: Amra Skyong ma, "Protector of Mangoes"</note>, who was extremely beautiful, youthful, and possessed the sixty-four arts, was fit only for a god to enjoy. He <note>the minister Sakyong</note> said, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, let us go to Vaishali. You shall take pleasure and delight with her." He replied, "The <term>Licchavis</term> of Vaishali have been our enemies who have long caused us harm and attacked us; they will surely try to harm you." The King said, "Wise one, men are possessed of a hero's heart; let us go." He said, "Your Majesty, if you place such great importance on a matter of no purpose, then go." He entered a chariot and set out for Vaishali together with Sakyong. Having gradually reached Vaishali, Sakyong stayed in a pleasure grove. The King entered the house of Amrapali, and after some time, the sound of a bell arose. The <term>Licchavis</term> of Vaishali became agitated and a clear cry went out, "Wise ones, one of our enemies has entered, sound the bell!" A great noise arose, and King Bimbisara <note>original: Gzugs can snying po</note> asked Amrapali, "Fair lady, what is this?" "Your Majesty, they are searching the houses." "For what reason?" "For the sake of Your Majesty." "What should be done? Shall I flee?" "Your Majesty, do not be displeased. Your Majesty, since it takes seven days to search the houses, please take your delight and enjoy yourself for these seven days. Enjoy yourself as you wish, and after seven days, I will know the right time."

<pb n="89"/>He played with her, delighted with her, and took his pleasure as he wished. After some time, Amrapali became possessed of a sentient being <note>she became pregnant</note>, and she said to King Bimbisara, "Your Majesty, a sentient being has entered me." He gave her a fine muslin cloth and a signet ring and said, "If it is a girl, she is yours. If it is a boy, wrap him in this muslin, hang this signet ring around his neck, and bring him to me." He then left, entered his chariot, and set out with Sakyong while the bells were ringing. They said, "Wise ones, the enemy has emerged! Pursue him!" Five hundred <term>Licchavis</term> with arrows like spokes of a wheel pursued King Bimbisara. When Sakyong saw them, he said, "Your Majesty, the <term>Licchavis</term> of Vaishali are coming. Your Majesty, shall I fight with them or shall I drive the chariot?" He replied, "I am exhausted; I will drive the chariot. You alone must fight with them." As he began to fight with them, the people of Vaishali recognized his face 

<leaf-break/>

They said, "Wise ones, whoever our enemy is, he is this one's father!" and they beat him even more. When the boy later told his mother what had happened, she thought, "The <term>Licchavis</term> of Vaishali are very fierce and skilled; there is a danger that he might be killed." While she was thinking this, she saw many merchants carrying goods who were going to Rajgir <note>original: Rgyal po'i khab, "The Royal Residence"</note> and said, "Stamp your containers with this signet ring and you will go without having to pay customs duties. Also, take this boy to the royal palace, hang this signet ring around his neck, and leave him at the gate of Rajgir." They agreed, saying, "We shall do so." She gave the boy a pearl necklace and said, "Son, when the King is gathered for business, leave the pearl necklace on your feet and sit in his lap as if afraid. If someone says, 'This boy does not know how to be afraid,' you must say, 'Is there any son who is afraid of his father?'" He gradually reached Rajgir with the merchants. They bathed him, put the signet ring on him, and left him at the gate of the royal palace. He went to where the King was 
</translation>

<summary>This page describes King Bimbisara's secret visit to the courtesan Amrapali in Vaishali and the resulting birth of a son. To protect the child from the hostile Licchavi clan, Amrapali sends him to the King's palace in Rajgir with tokens of his royal parentage.</summary>
<keywords>Amrapali, Bimbisara, Vaishali, Licchavis, Rajgir, Sakyong, pregnancy, signet ring, merchants</keywords>

<pb n="386"/>The stays of the words are one thousand and eight. Having reached that or even one hundred together with eight, having performed the recitation, and having stayed in fasting for a day and a night, offer the rosary to the Sage on the seventh day. Recite just as before. Make the measurement equal to that. Then, recite fully over the rosary. Staying in that very place at night, on a ground spread with <term>kusha</term> grass, the knower of mantras should sleep there. Whatever dreams are seen, if virtuous dreams are seen, the dreams are certainly a sign. Success <term>siddhi</term> should be accomplished by that. If Buddhas, Hearers <term>shravakas</term>, or Solitary Realizers <term>pratyekabuddhas</term> are seen in the dream, the practitioner of mantra will achieve results. Perform that ritual with certainty. If one sees the form of a monk or the various beautiful images of a Brahmin, if those dreams are seen, the rosary should be offered in that way. The practitioner who accomplishes all the purposes of mantra will achieve them without a doubt. From the Basic Ritual of the Noble Lady Tara with Braided Hair Up-bound, from the Vast Pitaka of the Bodhisattvas, a Extremely Extensive Mahayana Sutra: The Chapter on the Ritual of the Counting Rosary, the Tenth from the Infinite Rituals of the Cloth Painting and the Robe, is complete. Then, the Blessed One Shakyamuni looked again at the great mandala of the assembly possessed of all things and spoke to the Great Bodhisattva, the Noble Lord Avalokiteshvara: "Great Being, there are ritual distinctions for completing the chapters of your knowledge-mantras and the ritual preparations for the fire offering <term>homa</term>."
<leaf-break/>
Avoiding living creatures, and that which is well-joined with sand. Then, the rim is like a lotus, in the form of a mandala on all sides. Or, with effort, make it four-sided with three petals. The peaceful <term>shantika</term> and the increasing <term>paushtika</term> rituals are also correctly proclaimed here. For wrathful magic <term>abhichara</term>, in the center of the ground, make a <term>vajra</term> <gloss>ritual thunderbolt</gloss> with two points or three points. The fire pit <term>kunda</term> should be two cubits <term>hasta</term> in width. Prepare it likewise in a clean direction. Perform it likewise on the banks of a river. In the directions of a single teaching, or in a cemetery or an empty house, the fire offering should be well-prepared. Likewise on the peak of a mountain, or always in an empty temple, or likewise in a great monastery. Whatever the directions for accomplishment are, they were spoken by the Supreme Person. For all fire offering rituals, those places are mentioned. Sitting upon a bundle of <term>kusha</term> grass the size of a cubit, the knower of mantras should specifically perform the fire offering ritual there. By staying in that very place, there is no doubt of swift success. By facing East or North, perform the peaceful and increasing rituals. The wrathful rituals are in the South; the mantra practitioner should avoid that <note>this likely refers to the direction to be avoided for peaceful works</note>. Facing East is the success of peace, and facing North is for increasing. By that, always begin the recitation of the knowledge-mantra. Use Bilva, Arka, Slada, and Nyagrodha wood for the increasing rituals. For wrathful magic, dry wood, and those that are acrid, sour, or sharp. All those should be avoided; they were always forbidden by the Sages. For the peaceful and
<pb n="387"/>increasing rituals, moist wood is very auspicious. Likewise, for wrathful rituals, use dry wood. If those acrid, sour, and sharp ritual sticks <term>samidh</term> are not available, one should always examine the wood. Examine if it has two tips. With <term>kusha</term> grass that is green, oily, and similar in appearance to the neck of a peacock, always spread the <term>kusha</term> grass in a circle. For peaceful and increasing rituals, it is like emerald. Likewise, sinful <note>wrathful/destructive</note> actions are always done with dry substances, but here the Supreme Conqueror has forbidden them. With pure, stainless water, always avoiding worms, perform the sprinkling for purification on all sides. Turning to the right, ignite the fire with diligence. Perform the rinsing of the mouth according to the ritual. Using the root of pure grass, make a lamp of proper measure. Then, forming a fist, ignite the fire with effort. Do not do it with the wind from the mouth, nor ever with the hem of a garment. Clearly avoid the lower robe and upper robe. It is not with the delight of extinguishing it by the wind of the hands or other clothes. Use a clean fan or clothes; one may even fan with a jewel. By this correct arising of wind, the fire is made even. The knower of mantra should ignite the fire. Having meditated for the sake of the fire offering, then with the hand that is not the right <note>the left hand</note>, perform the purification sprinkling there. Then, give three ladlefuls of cow's butter into the fire. Then, prostrate. To all the Buddhas and
<leaf-break/>
mixed. For the peaceful ritual, the color is white; it is always praised by the Supreme Conquerors. If one performs a fire offering with white fire, the mantras will be accomplished. Likewise, one who desires success in the increasing ritual always uses white. Black, the color of smoke, and also grey-yellow are for sinful <note>wrathful</note> acts. By these three colors being transformed, these are the three types of success. Other colors, like the color of a cloud, or on that ground of the teaching, the mantra practitioner will have no success. If one sees such a similar color, or a fire burning with various types of colors, the rituals should be started again. The recitation should be done once more. If the mantra is accomplished, by seeing the ritual of the action, enter the fire offering again. For the dismissal and the invitation, the mantra of the fire should be <unclear>eight syllables obscured</unclear> spoken. Having previously examined well, request this mandala to depart. The rituals of invitation are to be performed in that very place. The activities of the fire are likewise in form. Begin in the presence of the cloth painting <term>pata</term>. The previous Tathagatas have said that the mantras will be accomplished there. All the rituals praised by the Conquerors should be performed in that very place. Other rituals are to be performed; specifically the sinful <note>destructive</note> rituals which are criticized by the Supreme Conquerors and which conflict with or are despised by the world. Rising, and the Universal Monarchs, and the stages <term>bhumis</term> of the Bodhisattvas...

<pb n="107"/>one will become invulnerable to all adversaries, unfriendly people, wicked beings, and sins. At no time and in no place will fear arise, and one will be completely liberated. Henceforth, one will never be stained by the taints of sin. If one mixes <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pills with sesame oil and smears it on the face and forehead, then goes before a king, the king will embrace one like a son in his lap, one will obtain great joy, and all fears of the king's wrath will be pacified. If smeared over the entire body, even if the body is worthy of execution, it will not be struck by weapons, for they will break into pieces. If an arrow is shot, it will not land on the body and the bow will break. <translation>
<pb n="352"/>Medicine is food to be eaten, and water is that which is always to be drunk. One will not be overcome by old age or death, and will always be protected. Make a crown from the hair of a thief, and there join the syllable <term>HUM</term> <gloss>the seed syllable of the enlightened mind</gloss> which arises. The <term>Yogi</term> <gloss>practitioner of yoga</gloss> in the course of their conduct holds the skulls of the five Buddhas. By making a skull the size of five fingers, one wears it as a crown. From the nature of Method and Wisdom, the hair girdle is twice-encircled. For the sake of offering the hair, carry ashes. One holds these through the conduct of a <term>Yogi</term>. The sound of the <term>Damaru</term> <gloss>small hand-drum</gloss> is the recitation. Knowing the meditation on the <term>Khatvanga</term> <gloss>ritual staff</gloss> is Wisdom itself. By the conduct of the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>ritual scepter</gloss> and the skull, these are the recitation and meditation. Greed, delusion, fear, and anger: the fruit of shame should be completely abandoned. Having abandoned duality by oneself, perform the conduct without any doubt. Having given the gift of the body, then perfectly perform the conduct. By analyzing what is suitable and unsuitable, therefore, one should not give ordinary gifts. Food and drink should be eaten just as they are found. Because of concepts of "pleasant" and "unpleasant," do not act out of mere attachment. The conduct of what is edible and inedible, and likewise what is drinkable and undrinkable, and the praises of where to go and where not to go: these should not be made into concepts. Any disciple who has found accomplishment is perfectly <unclear>…</unclear>

<leaf-break/>

When she shows her clothes to the teacher, he should perfectly show his trident <note>original: "rTse-gsum"</note>. To one who shows her breasts, he should perfectly show the joining <note>the space between parts</note>. To one who shows her teeth, he should perfectly show his mouth. To one who shows a frown, he should be told to loosen his topknot. To one who shows her forehead, he should perfectly show his back. To one who shows the soles of her feet, he should play with <unclear>…</unclear>. By the gesture and the response to the gesture, they are distinguished by the <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond/vow</gloss>. To that, the <term>Yogini</term> <gloss>female practitioner</gloss> says: "O, the son has great compassion! If he shows a rosary in his hand, he is saying 'Let us gather'." If the rosary is clearly presented, he is a good ascetic staying in the <term>Samaya</term>. That which is called the outer gathering, dwelling in the sphere of good conduct: in that gathering, whatever the <term>Yogini</term> says, all of it should be done. "O Blessed One, what are the places of gathering?" The Blessed One replied: "The <term>Pitha</term> <gloss>Seat</gloss> and the <term>Upapitha</term> <gloss>Near-Seat</gloss>, the <term>Kshetra</term> <gloss>Field</gloss> and the <term>Upakshetra</term> <gloss>Near-Field</gloss>, the <term>Chandoha</term> <gloss>Gathering Place</gloss> and the <term>Upachandoha</term> <gloss>Near-Gathering Place</gloss>, likewise the <term>Melapaka</term> <gloss>Meeting</gloss> and the <term>Upamelapaka</term> <gloss>Near-Meeting</gloss>, the <term>Pilava</term> <gloss>Crossing</gloss> and the <term>Upapilava</term> <gloss>Near-Crossing</gloss>, the <term>Smashana</term> <gloss>Charnel Ground</gloss> and the <term>Upasmashana</term> <gloss>Near-Charnel Ground</gloss>. These are the twelve stages. The Lord of the ten stages <note>the ten Bhumis of a Bodhisattva</note> himself: this should not be spoken of by others. O Blessed One, the places <pb n="353"/> and so forth, what are they?" The Blessed One replied: "The Seat is explained as Jalandhara. Likewise is Oddiyana. The Seat is Kollagiri. Likewise is Kamarupa. The Near-Seat is called Malava. It is also Sindhunagara. The Field is explained as Mummu ni; the Field is the number of the creators. Devikotta is likewise a Field; the Field is the number of the <unclear>…</unclear>. The Near-Field is called Kuluta. Likewise Arbuda, and the peak of Mount Godavari. The Near-Fields are thus summarized. The <term>Chandoha</term> are Harikela and those born within the salt ocean, Lampaka and Kanchi, and likewise Saurashtra. The Near-<term>Chandoha</term> are Kalinga, the Island of Gold, and Konkana; these are stated in brief. The <term>Pilava</term> is both in the city and those dwelling at the edge of the village: Caritra and Kosala, and the city of Vindhyakumara. O <term>Vajragarbha</term> <gloss>Vajra Essence</gloss> of great compassion, the Near-<term>Pilava</term> is near to those. The <term>Smashana</term> are the attained assembly and the edge of the great ocean. The garden, the wall, and the edge of the pond are called the Near-<term>Smashana</term>. For the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings, the <term>Vajra</term> of the <term>Yogini Tantra</term> is the excellent gathering of the <term>Yoginis</term>, even during the day itself."

<leaf-break/>

Sentient beings will fall under that power. This is the seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Settlement of Signs and Places.

Then, the wheel of the <term>Yogini</term> will be explained. Meditate on the <term>Bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> in the realm of space. As for the visualization in the center, according to what is appropriate for the preceding wheel, the deities arise just as they are. The wheel is first Earth and Water. According to what is appropriate, Fire, and the great Wind of the deities; and how the meditator also arises. The wheel itself is born from the source of phenomena <note>original: "Chos-’byung"</note>. The two <unclear>…</unclear> are without fault. They become one from the filaments, and are called the exterior of the triangle. In the center of that, meditate on the nature of the fifteen dead seats <note>refers to the fifteen yoginis surrounding the central deity</note>. Upon that is the Moon. Upon the Moon is the seed syllable itself. Afterwards, press down with the Victor over Maras <note>Buddha</note>. From the union of the two comes Great Bliss. <term>Ali</term> <gloss>the vowel series</gloss> abides in the form of the Moon. <term>Kali</term> <gloss>the consonant series</gloss> appears in the form of the <unclear>…</unclear> <note>likely the Sun</note>. From the union of the Moon and Sun, the Goddess <term>Gauri</term> and the others become famous. The Moon is endowed with the Mirror-like Wisdom. The seventh of the seven is endowed with Equanimity. The seed syllable and hand-emblem of one's own deity should be called the Discriminating Wisdom. All becoming one is Effort. The perfect, pure Sphere of Reality <note>original: "Chos-dbyings"</note>: by the ritual spoken by the wise, the five aspects <unclear>…</unclear>
</translation>

It further lists the twenty-four sacred sites (Pithas and auxiliary locations) for tantric gathering and begins a technical description of the Yogini mandala visualization involving elemental forces and wisdom types.</summary>
<keywords>Vajra, Yogini, Pitha, Mandalas, Tantric Conduct, Secret Signs, Sacred Geography, Five Wisdoms</keywords>

<pb n="10"/>adorned by the wheel <note>original: cakra</note> of <unclear>...</unclear>, she is a turbulent mass of her own light. 
Homage to her who is majestic with great joy, whose crown is a spreading garland of light. 
By her laughing and mocking <term>Tuttare</term>, she brings demons and the world under her power. 
Homage to her who is able to summon all the hosts of protectors of the earth. 
By the syllable <term>Hum</term> of her shaking, frowning brow, she completely liberates all those in poverty. 
Homage to her whose head is adorned with a crescent moon, all her ornaments blaze intensely. 
From the midst of her hair-knots, <term>Amitabha</term> <gloss>Infinite Light</gloss> eternally radiates great light. 
Homage to her who dwells within the center of a blazing garland like the fire at the end of the <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss>. With her right leg extended 
<leaf-break/>
and her left leg tucked, she is surrounded by joy. She completely destroys the armies of enemies. 
Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth with her palms and stamps it with her feet. 
With the syllable <term>Hum</term> and a frowning expression, she shatters the seven levels <note>referring to the seven subterranean or worldly realms</note>. 
Homage to the blissful, virtuous, and peaceful one, she whose field of experience is the peace of <term>Nirvana</term>. 
Properly endowed with <term>Svaha</term> and <term>Om</term>, she is the very destroyer of great sins. 
Homage to her who is surrounded by great joy, she who completely shatters the bodies of enemies. 
Arranging the speech of the ten-syllable mantra, she is the very <term>Tara</term> arising from the <term>vidya</term> <gloss>knowledge-mantra</gloss> <term>Hum</term>. 
Homage to <term>Ture</term> who stamps her feet, she who is the very seed-syllable in the form of <term>Hum</term>. Mt. Meru, 
<pb n="11"/>Mandara, and the Vindhya mountains, as well as the three worlds, are made to tremble by her. 
Homage to her who holds in her hand the sign of the deer <note>the moon</note> in the form of a celestial lake. 
By reciting <term>Tara</term> twice and the syllable <term>Phat</term>, she clears away all poisons without exception. 
Homage to her whom the kings of the host of gods, the gods themselves, and the <term>kinnaras</term> <gloss>celestial musicians</gloss> rely upon. 
By the majesty of her joyful armor, she clears away disputes and bad dreams. 
Homage to her whose two eyes are like the sun and the full moon, radiating an intensely clear light. 
By reciting <term>Hara</term> twice and <term>Tuttare</term>, she clears away very violent infectious diseases. 
Homage to her who is endowed with the power of peace by the arrangement of the three "thatnesses" <note>the three syllables Om Ah Hum or the three bodies of a Buddha</note>. The hosts of <term>don</term> <gloss>malevolent spirits</gloss>, <term>rolang</term> <gloss>zombies</gloss>, 
<leaf-break/>
and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss> are destroyed by <term>Ture</term>, the most supreme one. 
This is the praise of the root mantra and these are the twenty-one homages. 
Whosoever possesses intelligence and is endowed with supreme devotion to the Goddess, if they recite this upon rising at dusk or at dawn, 
Their remembrance will bestow all fearlessness. 
All sins will be completely pacified, and all lower realms will be destroyed. 
One will quickly be empowered by seventy million Buddhas, and achieving even greater than this, 
One will proceed to the ultimate state of Buddhahood.

It then transitions into the benefits of reciting the praise, promising protection from fear, purification of sins, and the attainment of enlightenment.</summary>
