If the yogi who maintains it in this way gains stability in the natural state, the delusions of the mental afflictions are purified and the result of Buddhahood is attained. Thus he spoke. 

Again, this was offered to the great scholar Nyima Drakpa, arranged according to the thirty letters of the alphabet: 
<term>Ka</term>: The self-arising realization of the unborn. 
<term>Kha</term>: Within the state that is clear like the sky. 
<term>Ga</term>: That awareness which is without denial or proof. 
<term>Nga</term>: Is the state of knowing that I have no true existence. 
<term>Ca</term>: Through practice that is without fabrication. 
<term>Cha</term>: Until the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> is attained. 
<term>Ja</term>: Accomplish the meaning of acting for the <leaf-break/> benefit of others. 
This song of experience on the thirty letters of the alphabet was written as it dawned in the mind. Thus he spoke. 

Again, in the year of the Pig, when the Interior Minister <term>Nangso</term> <gloss>a local administrative title</gloss> Sonam Gyalpo passed away in Lhalung, his wife and son, the <term>Chomze</term> <gloss>religious practitioners</gloss>, requested that the master come to lead the funeral rites. At that time, his schedule did not allow it, so he sent a relic that had emerged from his own teeth, along with this series of instructions to comfort the minds of the Minister’s wife and son: 

To the Triple Gem, the reliable objects of refuge, I bow and go for refuge. To the Lord, mother, and son who have had a deep karmic connection since previous times, please listen. Wherever one looks on the earth, under the sky, in the cardinal or intermediate directions, in the center or the periphery, for all sentient beings of the three realms, there is no time of escape from the suffering of death; it is the destination for everyone. Father <leaf-break/> and mother alike, rising up in succession, there is no end to the depths of suffering. Now that you have found this precious human body, cast away all mundane affairs and exert yourself in the Dharma; this is your eternal purpose. All these temporary affairs are of an illusory nature; whatever you do will not help, so meditate on impermanence within your being. Abandon the affairs of this life and accomplish your eternal purpose. If you are to achieve the great goal, do it now, for there is no knowing what will happen in the next life. At this time when you have your own autonomy, abandon distractions and busywork, and exert yourself in the practice of these profound instructions of the self-arising Great Perfection! This will lead to happiness here and joy in the next life. As for your current kingdom, protect it with the Dharma of a loving mind. If you benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you. Hold these instructions of the <term>Be-ban</term> <gloss>the bee-monk</gloss> Pema Lingpa in the center of your heart! Around the pig month, I will be there; at that time, priest and patron shall have a detailed discussion.

<note>The following describes the lineage successor.</note> When the Great Knowledge-Holder <term>Metok</term> <gloss>Flower</gloss> was performing alms-gathering, at a delightful place called Bi in the southwest border of the monastery of Pema Lingpa, he gave this introduction through poetry to the Khampa mendicant Rinchen Zangpo: 

The unconditioned nature of mind is the great sky. The natural conceptualizations of elaboration are a continuous chain. The six objects and the ground display illusory forms. Does the Khampa see that which, being without truth, destroys the path to happiness, like the moon in water or a mirage? 

So he spoke, and the other replied: 
Upon the ground of firm, unchanging faith, the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion flourish. I pray that the fruit of compassionate needs and desires may ripen. 

In response, he spoke this again: Like the king of birds <note>the Garuda</note> with wings <leaf-break/> spread wide. 

Aha! Having studied and contemplated in a non-sectarian way, the furthest reaches of the doubting mind were cut. Knowing what to adopt or reject regarding Dharma and non-Dharma, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Spurred by the reminder of impermanent death, having developed renunciation and weariness toward the delusive nature of cyclic existence, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Knowing that all worldly actions and deeds are without point, resting in the state of non-action, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Seeing the suffering of all who possess wealth, yet finding that having no wealth is a great ornament for the mind, possessing the noble wealth of contentment, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Taking awareness as the support for one's own benefit, training in the Bodhichitta that benefits others, turning the minds of oneself and others toward the Dharma, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! The expanse of reality is free from conceptual elaboration, and awareness is unborn and free from extremes; having reached the limit of realizing the View, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! The natural state of bliss, clarity, and non-thought, where the object and subject of meditation <leaf-break/> are one. 

Relying on the teacher, the pure vision that awakens the karmic potential of the fortunate is the main priority for certain yogis who dwell in the land of Tibet. I ask you to offer a brief praise to them. This time, I, a yogi, have arrived at Bumthang, which is difficult to reach. I have met one such as you, the Lord Pema Lingpa, who is difficult to meet. You have granted the instructions of the Profound Dharma, the Gathering of All Intentions. I have tasted the sacred substances that bring liberation through tasting. I am happy, aha! I am joyful, aha! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have come upon the path of empty-clarity without grasping. From the mountain pass of naked seeing, free from extremes, I looked toward the unobstructed, translucent state, and I met the guru of the spontaneously present natural state. I requested the oral instructions on the inseparability of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six senses. Through the pure merit of former times, I have met such an essence of the realization of the All-Good <term>Samantabhadra</term>. Through the power of the prayers I make now, may we never be parted throughout the eon. I am happy!

(3) Table of the Eight Negations from the <term>Madhyamaka Shastra</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Middle Way</gloss>

No Arising: The myriad phenomena do not arise. Why? Because the world sees it with their eyes. For example, at the beginning of an eon, grain does not arise. Why? Because apart from the grain at the beginning of the eon, the grain of today cannot be found. If today’s grain existed apart from the initial grain, there would be arising, but this is not actually so. Therefore, there is no arising.

No Ceasing: The grain at the beginning of the eon does not cease. Why? If it ceased, there should be no grain today, but there is actually grain. Therefore, there is no ceasing.

No Permanence: The myriad things are not permanent. Just as when a grain produces a sprout, the seed is transformed and destroyed; therefore, there is no permanence.

No Interruption: The myriad things are not interrupted. Just as from a grain there is a sprout, therefore there is no interruption; if there were interruption, there would be no continuity.

No Unity: The myriad things are not one. Just as the grain does not become the sprout, and the sprout does not become the grain. If they were one, but they are actually not; therefore, they are not one.

No Difference: The myriad things are not different. If they were different, why distinguish the sprout, stalk, and leaf of grain, and not call them the sprout, stalk, and leaf of a tree? Therefore, they are not different.

No Coming: The myriad things do not come. Like the sprout within the grain, it comes from nowhere. If it came, the sprout should come from elsewhere, like a bird coming to perch in a tree; but it is not actually so. Therefore, there is no coming.

No Going: The myriad things do not go out. If there were a going out, one should see the sprout going out from the grain, like a snake going out from a hole; but it is not actually so. Therefore, there is no going out.

<pb n="52"/><meta>continues from previous page: ...the stages of the Lesser Vehicle. "Supreme" refers to surpassing those causes.</meta> Because obstacles are exhausted and virtues are perfected, the fruit of enlightenment reaches the ultimate stage; therefore, he is called the "Most Supreme." "Action" <note>original: "業" <term>karma</term></note> refers to a general summary of the actions and functions of the three wheels <note>the three modes of action: body, speech, and mind</note> of all Buddhas. This means the most supreme of actions, or that the actions themselves are most supreme. Both interpretations are acceptable. This refers specifically to the mental action of universal knowledge, the supreme physical action of unimpeded form, and the supreme verbal action of compassionate rescue. "The one who is supreme" refers to the person who possesses these virtues; namely, the Buddha.

Second, distinguishing by the two benefits <note>self-benefit and the benefit of others</note>: "Most supreme action" is a general heading, while "universal knowledge" and the other terms are specific markers showing the virtue of self-benefit. Within this, the internal aspect is the wisdom of universal knowledge, and the external aspect is the unimpeded form. The <term>Srimala Sutra</term> <gloss>Lion's Roar of Queen Srimala</gloss> says: "The Tathagata's <gloss>Thus Gone One</gloss> form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise." This follows that same meaning. "Saving the world" and the other phrases specifically show the virtue of benefiting others. The one in whom both benefits are perfected is the Buddha.

Third, distinguishing by the three virtues: "Most supreme action" is the general label. "Universal knowledge" shows the Buddha's merit of Great Wisdom. "Form is unimpeded" clarifies the Buddha's merit of Great Meditative Concentration <note>original: "大定" <term>Samadhi</term></note>. This means that by relying on concentration, he initiates supernatural powers and manifests form without hindrance. <pb n="53"/> Third, "saving the world" and so on, clarifies the Buddha's merit of Great Compassion. The <term>Mahayana-samgraha</term> <gloss>Summary of the Great Vehicle</gloss> clarifies the merits of the Buddha's Enjoyment Body <note>original: "受用身" <term>Sambhogakaya</term></note> by speaking only of these three.

Fourth, explaining according to the text: Here, only the Reward Body <note>original: "報身" <term>Sambhogakaya</term></note> and Transformation Body <note>original: "化身" <term>Nirmanakaya</term></note> are clarified, because the Dharma Body <note>original: "法身" <term>Dharmakaya</term></note> is included within the Dharma Jewel. "Most supreme" is as explained in the first interpretation. Regarding "universal knowledge" in action, there are two types. First is universal knowledge of true wisdom, which concerns the Mind as Suchness <note>original: "心眞如門"</note> and its constant merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Second is universal knowledge of conventional wisdom, which concerns the Mind as Samsara <note>original: "心生滅門" <gloss>the gate of birth and death</gloss></note> and the differences in dependent origination. Both the principle and the phenomena are perceived equally; this is unerring universal knowledge.

Regarding "form is unimpeded," the Tathagata's physical body is sovereign and without obstacle. This has many varieties, as explained in the "Inconceivable Dharma" chapter of the <term>Avatamsaka Sutra</term> <gloss>Flower Adornment Sutra</gloss>. Now, I will briefly distinguish four types:
1. The lack of hindrance between the large and the small. This means every single sense organ pervades the entire Dharma Realm <note>the entire universe</note>, yet it does not destroy the nature of the various organs, nor does the text suggest the appearances of the organs become confused. 
2. The lack of hindrance in mutual function. This means the various organs perform each other's functions without obstructing one another.
3. The lack of hindrance between principle and phenomena <note>original: "理事無礙"</note>. This means that while the manifested form is brilliant, it does not obstruct the fact that its entire substance is empty of nature. This profound principle...
</translation>

It specifically explores the concept of "unimpeded form," referencing the Avatamsaka Sutra to explain how a Buddha's physical manifestation transcends ordinary limitations of size and function.</summary>

<pb n="61"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta>Therefore, he qualifies the Lord of all <note><term>Sarvesha</term></note> as <term>Hamsa</term>. This Lord of all has the form of a mantra with the sequential structure of <term>Hamsa</term>. As it is stated in the <term>Prapanchasara</term>: "That consciousness-only essence is called <term>Tattva</term>. From the proximity of light, desiring to manifest, it becomes dense and at some point attains the state of a point <note><term>Bindu</term></note>. Splitting in time, that <term>Bindu</term> becomes twofold. The <term>Bindu</term> is the right part, and the left part is the creative emission <note><term>Visarga</term></note>. Thus, the right and left parts are distinguished as male and female. The sound <term>Ham</term> is said to be the <term>Bindu</term>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as <term>Sah</term>. The <term>Bindu</term> is called the Person <note><term>Purusha</term></note>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as Nature <note><term>Prakriti</term></note>. The <term>Hamsa</term> consists of both Person and Nature; this entire world is composed of that." 

This is clearly stated in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "In the void within the thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with a divine gateway, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two syllables of <term>Hamsa</term>, resides that which resembles pure crystal and is radiant with pure moon-like luster," and so on. Here, the phrase "above the two syllables of <term>Hamsa</term>" is very clear. Alternatively, it means he is known or famous by the name <term>Hamsa Parama</term>. For this reason, the author himself in the forty-eighth verse has mentioned the name <term>Hamsa</term> by saying, "Some call this the form of <term>Hamsa</term>." Or, it may be understood through a compound where <term>Hamsa</term> is at the end; by deleting the middle term as in the rule of <term>shaka-parthiva</term>, the term <term>Hamsa Parama</term> is established. This means he is known by the name <term>Paramahamsa</term>. Thus it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This one, in the form of <term>Paramahamsa</term>, is joined with all moving and unmoving things." 

The phrase "the continuous flow of waves of every kind of happiness" <note>original: "sakala-sukha-santana-lahari-parivaha"</note> means that <term>sakala-sukha</term> is happiness in every way; its <term>santana</term> is its expansion; that itself is a series of waves <note><term>lahari</term></note> which is poured forth <note><term>pari</term></note> everywhere, meaning it is revealed as something that lasts through subsequent time. Thus, in the form of a series, he is characterized by all-pervading happiness of every kind. As previously stated, this <term>Hamsa</term> is situated below the Supreme Shiva. 43

<pb n="62"/># The Description of the Six Chakras
## Verse 17

The Shaivites call it the Place of Shiva; the groups of Vaishnavites call it the Supreme Person;
Others call it the place of Hari-Hara; while still others, who are devotees of the honey at the two lotus-feet of the Goddess, call it the place of the Goddess;
And yet other great sages call it the pure abode of both Nature and Person. 44

Therefore, he qualifies the Lord of all <note><term>Sarvesha</term></note> as <term>Hamsa</term>. This Lord of all has the form of a mantra with the sequential structure of <term>Hamsa</term>. As it is stated in the <term>Prapanchasara</term>: "That consciousness-only essence is called <term>Tattva</term>. From the proximity of light, desiring to manifest, it becomes dense and at some point attains the state of a point <note><term>Bindu</term></note>. Splitting in time, that <term>Bindu</term> becomes twofold. The <term>Bindu</term> is the right part, and the left part is the creative emission <note><term>Visarga</term></note>. Thus, the right and left parts are distinguished as male and female. The sound <term>Ham</term> is said to be the <term>Bindu</term>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as <term>Sah</term>. The <term>Bindu</term> is called the Person <note><term>Purusha</term></note>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as Nature <note><term>Prakriti</term></note>. The <term>Hamsa</term> consists of both Person and Nature; this entire world is composed of that." 

This is clearly stated in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "In the void within the thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with a divine gateway, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two syllables of <term>Hamsa</term>, resides that which resembles pure crystal and is radiant with pure moon-like luster," and so on. For this reason, the author himself in the forty-eighth verse has mentioned the name <term>Hamsa</term> by saying, "Some call this the form of <term>Hamsa</term>." Or, it may be understood through a compound where <term>Hamsa</term> is at the end; by deleting the middle term as in the rule of <term>shaka-parthiva</term>, the term <term>Hamsa Parama</term> is established. This means he is known by the name <term>Paramahamsa</term>. Thus it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This one, in the form of <term>Paramahamsa</term>, is joined with all moving and unmoving things." 

The phrase "the continuous flow of waves of every kind of happiness" <note>original: "sakala-sukha-santana-lahari-parivaha"</note> means that <term>sakala-sukha</term> is happiness in every way; its <term>santana</term> is its expansion; that itself is a series of waves <note><term>lahari</term></note> which is poured forth <note><term>pari</term></note> everywhere, meaning it is revealed as something that lasts through subsequent time. Thus, in the form of a series, he is characterized by all-pervading happiness of every kind. As previously stated, this <term>Hamsa</term> is situated below the Supreme Shiva. 43

**THERE IS NO ONE WHO WOULD DENY THAT LORD** Philipp, the Count your father, on account of his most celebrated virtues and the singular piety he showed toward God, ought to be celebrated with the praises of a Hero and with Latin <note>original: "Ausonio"</note> song. However, since I am not endowed with such great eloquence that I am able to adorn his departed spirit according to his dignity, and yet I have descended into this arena, I pray that no one assigns this to me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even modest talents, even if they do not achieve everything. It has pleased me, generous Counts, to dedicate this poem to you, although it is a slight <note>original: "Leuidense"</note> gift, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you, who have not yet declined from your ancestral virtues in any matter, continue in this way, you will one day be celebrated with a similar eulogy. Therefore, give your effort so that you do not wander away by degenerating from your father's footsteps. From Mühlberg <note>original: "Mulburgo"</note>, the 5th of the Ides of May, in the year from the birth of the Virgin,

1544.

### AND RENOWNED COUNT, etc.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial L at the beginning of the poem.</note>

**L**et the elegy now put on mournful garments again,
   And may you wish to hold the name that is properly yours.
Philipp, born of the high lineage of the Gleichens, has departed
   From the living; he who was a father among the rest.
Therefore a new grief occupies the brothers from that moment,
   And now again they moisten their cheeks and their whole faces with tears.
And so at the ancestral home, in the buildings of the Sigismund castle,

full of mournful love, he grieves for his brother.
But you, Ernst, having set out for the home of Speyer <note>original: "Spirenses penates"</note>,
Groan at the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
Just as you recently followed the pious arms of the Saxon,
Fighting with joined forces, O Hessian, with yours.
Meanwhile, a brother whose name is Grace <note>refers to Johann, whose name implies "God is gracious"</note>, cruel fate
Snatched away at home in an unjust death.
With the Emperor <note>original: "Cesare"</note> also holding a council now,
Which I pray may bring the grateful gifts of safety and peace.
While you were visiting this with the Duke of Saxony, you now
Lose Philipp at home in a similar manner.
Therefore, Ernst, you rightly pour out heavy tears,
And there is a just and heavy cause for you to weep.
You also, sons, saddened by the death of your parent,
Weep, and a heavy grief holds your hearts.
A just cause brings forth great lamentations for you,
Which anyone criticizing would have no true reason.
Until now you wept for your departed mother and your uncle Johann,
Now you weep for both of them along with your father.
And now each sad castle mourns its snatched-away
Father, and the Ohra <note>a river in Thuringia</note> mixes its waters with tears.
What need is there for many words? Everything is full of grief,
And every subject has cause to rightly weep.
We also, who inhabit the nearby banks of the Weite <note>refers to the river Wyhra or similar local waterway</note>,
Weep for you, famous Philipp, with a complaining lyre <note>term: cheli; gloss: a lyre or lute</note>.
We weep and sing the proclamations of your praise in these
Verses, though they be unpolished and rude.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...against Heraclitus and Cratylus</meta>
<note>the philosopher Heraclitus argued all things are in flux, while Cratylus argued that language cannot fix the meaning of changing things</note> we establish that very same certainty. For the sciences of things considered universally ought not to exist because the total mutability and mortality of things is, by an intuition of the mind, converted into eternal and perpetual constancy in actual fact and in every part; no contemplation of our mind, however accurate, could provide that. Rather, it is because things understood universally are released from the bonds of individual things, by which they are made unstable, and embrace only the essence and its innate properties, which carry no mutation in themselves.

## XVIII.

For as to what some believe—that the <term>ousiae</term> <gloss>essences or substances</gloss> of things are perpetual, and the propositions produced from them are necessary, because they have been in God, the Best and Greatest, from eternity as in a knower, an idea, and their primary cause—we judge this to be by no means sufficient. Since by that reasoning all things are and have been in God, all individuals would also exist with exactly equal eternity and certainty, as would all those statements which we call contingent <note>propositions that are only true by chance or circumstance rather than logical necessity</note>.

## XIX.

But although at the same moment Universals begin to be with in-
</translation>

<translation page="10">
dividuals, yet in the order of nature, as far as their existence is concerned, these individuals are prior to them. For universals cannot have existence from anywhere else than from individuals. However, if you look at their essence, you will find it to be prior to the individuals themselves, because they assist the constitution of singular things and communicate their <term>quiddity</term> <gloss>the "what-ness" or essential nature</gloss> to them.

### XX.

From these things which we have established so far, it also becomes manifest in what way the treatment of Universals belongs to different faculties. Indeed, it is the task of the Metaphysician to investigate whether that Universal exists anywhere—which is undeservedly attributed to <term>Plato</term> <gloss>referring to the theory of ideal Forms existing independently</gloss>—or plainly nowhere. But it is for the Logician to discuss this universal form, which we have called a <term>being of reason</term> <gloss>ens rationis; a concept existing only in the mind</gloss>, and the accidents which flow from it by a certain reflection of the mind. To the remaining disciplines, however, it belongs to dispute about the subject matter itself and the properties following its nature, once all mental understanding is removed.

### XXI.

But truly the Universals, which some call by the names of <term>predicables</term> <gloss>classes of logical predicates</gloss> and others call the five terms (though less aptly), are only five: namely, Genus, Species,
</translation>

<summary>This section argues that universals derive their stability by abstracting essence from individual changes and defines the different roles of metaphysics and logic in studying them. It introduces the five standard predicables, beginning with Genus and Species.</summary>
<keywords>universals, essence, stability, God as cause, metaphysics vs logic, ens rationis, predicables, Genus, Species</keywords>

For as to what some believe—that the <term>ousiae</term> <gloss>essences or substances</gloss> of things are perpetual, and the propositions produced from them are necessary, because they have been in God, the Best and Greatest, from eternity as in a knower, an idea, and their primary cause—we judge this to be by no means sufficient. Since by that reasoning all things are and have been in God, all individuals would also exist with exactly equal eternity and certainty, as would all those statements which we call contingent <note>propositions that are only true by chance or circumstance rather than logical necessity</note>.

## XIX.

But although at the same moment Universals begin to be with in-

dividuals, yet in the order of nature, as far as their existence is concerned, these individuals are prior to them. For universals cannot have existence from anywhere else than from individuals. However, if you look at their essence, you will find it to be prior to the individuals themselves, because they assist the constitution of singular things and communicate their <term>quiddity</term> <gloss>the "what-ness" or essential nature</gloss> to them.

From these things which we have established so far, it also becomes manifest in what way the treatment of Universals belongs to different faculties. Indeed, it is the task of the Metaphysician to investigate whether that Universal exists anywhere—which is undeservedly attributed to <term>Plato</term> <gloss>referring to the theory of ideal Forms existing independently</gloss>—or plainly nowhere. But it is for the Logician to discuss this universal form, which we have called a <term>being of reason</term> <gloss>ens rationis; a concept existing only in the mind</gloss>, and the accidents which flow from it by a certain reflection of the mind. To the remaining disciplines, however, it belongs to dispute about the subject matter itself and the properties following its nature, once all mental understanding is removed.

Therefore, a much greater necessity lies upon us to examine this accurately, since nearly the entire hinge of the controversy turns upon it. History of Philosophy, Book II, Chapter XI.</margin> But in the mind of Riccioli, it descends from <term>para to cheisthai</term> <gloss>from being poured</gloss>, a derivation which pleased the Stoics especially, according to Philo’s <term>On Incorruptibility</term>, and Pherecydes according to the author Achilles Tatius.

<margin>In the place cited, Question V, page 201. Introduction to the Phenomena of Aratus, Chapter III.</margin>
In this way, it will signify a confusion and a mixture or aggregation of many things together. But just as in its origin, so also in its meaning, writers vary greatly. The Gentiles, except for Aristotle, who interprets it as a place, seem commonly to have determined that it denotes an unbegotten matter existing before all Gods, or, as Plato says, before all things were made; certainly a *natural principle* from which, nearly all who mention it agree equally, it is indicated. However, what kind of thing that was, and how it was constituted and arranged, is no more agreed upon among them than among clocks. Regarding this, as well as the order in which individual elements <margin>In the place cited, page 202 and following. Physical Positions, Miscellaneous VI.</margin> or bodies were separated or distinguished from it, one may consult Riccioli, or our own Roeschelius. Burnet carries this out in such a way that he establishes the first-born, like chaos and its twins, as Night and Tartarus, that is, the upper and lower body. And indeed, he makes the former a dark air, impenetrable by the sun's rays; the latter he makes Tartarus, or the abyss. Then he posits that the pregnant Night likewise brought forth twins, namely, Earth and the Ether, or the sublunary Heaven, that is, the region of purer air. In these matters, I think no one fails to see that this most ingenious Author grants a great deal of his own to Aristophanes. For, besides the fact that there appears neither hide nor hair in him of a distinction between ether and heaven, nor could an atmosphere be conceived at that time when the terrestrial globe was rounded, with no vapors existing: furthermore, Night and Tartarus are not said by him to be generated from Chaos, but to have existed simultaneously with Chaos. Finally, to Erebus, whom he joins with the abyss and Tartarus, he ascribes immense reaches, such as could certainly only be incongruously declared of the terrestrial-aerial sphere, which behaves scarcely like a point in respect to the Universe. These and other similar inconveniences all expire of their own accord if it is said that Aristophanes held *Night, Tartarus, and Erebus* not as different offspring of Chaos, but as parts of the same, or rather as adjuncts or qualities. Thus Chaos would signify matter, Night would signify darkness and the privation of light, Tartarus would signify a horrendous confusion, and Erebus would signify a vast emptiness or space.
</translation>

<translation page="16">
<meta>continues from previous page: ...space.</meta>

It is as if he wished to say that Chaos was a vast and immense, and likewise formless, emptiness, not otherwise than the Author of the Book of Wisdom says, that God made the world out of invisible and formless matter; or, as the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>The Apostle Paul</note> speaks, that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things might be made. Or, if one must speak from the corpuscular Philosophy, supported by experience and the strongest reasons, that the Primary Matter and the infinite Force of atoms occupied an immense space.

<margin>
Book I on the Heavens, Chapter III.
Chapter II, as cited above, page 94.
</margin>
§. XVI. These things are also plainly conformable to the Mosaic narrative, and agree excellently with the sayings and traditions of both the Greek and barbarian Philosophers; in citing which we shall not be overly laborious, since Master Tentzelius has already occupied this entire province. Rather, we urge this point: that Aristophanes expressly declares that the race of Gods did not exist before Love had mixed all things; that by these "Gods" the stars ought to be understood is proved clearer than the midday sun by the phrase <term>genos athanaton</term> <gloss>the race of immortals</gloss>, which none of the Ancients, whether Pythagoreans, Platonists, or Peripatetics, ever applied to sublunary things—to such an extent that, although the pseudo-Hermes says and establishes that nothing in the World dies, he nevertheless does not employ the word <term>athanaton</term> <gloss>immortal</gloss>. The places by which this assertion could be demonstrated are infinite: yet two may suffice: One from Aristotle, who says that all nations attribute the highest place to the Gods, because <term>as the immortal is linked to the immortal</term>; the other from Ocellus Lucanus, who asserts with an elegant simile that the moon’s course is the Isthmus of mortality and immortality. Nor do the Mythologists and Cyclic Poets say or teach anything else, for they all proceed in explaining Theogonies in such a way that they narrate the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no interval of time interposed. Regarding Plato and the Platonists, the same is most evident, so that to wish to declare it laboriously would be to lose one’s effort.

<margin>
Book VI, Chapter VI.
</margin>
Yet we cannot help but add from Proclus that he calls the Gods who are makers and producers of animals "young and recent"; but elsewhere he asserts that the <term>Orphic egg</term> and <term>Plato’s Being</term> are the same thing. These latter points not only show that the ancients understood nothing other than Chaos itself by the egg, but simultaneously reveal the foundation or occasion for the opinion regarding the pre-existence of pre-mundane matter. Namely because, whatever Gods besides the supreme God—whom they called the One, the Good, <term>anousiaon</term> <gloss>beyond being</gloss> and not endowed with essence—such as the stars and demons, indeed even the mind and the Soul of the World itself, they believed to be beings produced by the supreme God. They believed these recently produced Gods received Matter, from which they might fashion sublunary bodies, as already prepared and existing. They could not help but establish eternal Matter, because before time began—which started at the same moment the Mundane bodies were produced—there was pure eternity.

§. XVII. That Aristophanes says Night first brought forth a "wind-egg" <note>an unfertilized egg</note> does not hinder the truth and shows only that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, nor could he reach the incubation or brooding of Divine Love: therefore he adorned the opinion according to the capacity of his own genius. Thus this single difficulty can by no means bring it about that, setting aside Burnet's archaeology, we should not subscribe to the opinion sufficiently demonstrated by Hugo Grotius, Edmund Dickinson, Jacob Tollius, and Adam Tribbechovius.
</translation>

### XL.
Furthermore, an agreement is considered either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or as it is added immediately to a contract.

### XLI.
The former is called a naked agreement <note>original: "nudum"</note>, while the latter are said to be not naked; since these do not rest upon the naked terms of an agreement but either adhere to a contract or have an assisting law, anyone can see that they cannot be held in the class of naked agreements. *Bachovius in his notes on the Disputations of Treutler.*

### XLII.
And these may also not inconveniently be called "clothed" <note>original: "vestita"</note>; for although these words do not appear in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists; moreover, where the matter is established, we ought to be flexible regarding the words, *by the argument of law 17, Digest concerning laws.*

### XLIII.
A naked convention is that which stands at the limit of the consensus. *law "si tibi" 27, Code concerning letting and hiring.* Or, what is the same thing, that which consists in the pure and simple limits of a convention.

### XLIV.
It is so called because it is naked of a cause or a business transaction <note>original: "a causa seu negotio"</note> *the said law "solent" 15, Digest concerning prescribed words.* This also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract, whence it is also called a simple convention in *law "avia" 6, Code concerning the Law of dowries,* and merely an agreement in *law "major" 23, Code concerning pledges and mortgages.*

### XLV.
For example, if it is agreed that you sell me your house, this convention stands in the naked terms of consensus: but if it is agreed concerning the thing and the price, it is no longer naked

<summary>This page defines "naked" versus "clothed" agreements, explaining that a naked agreement lacks a formal legal cause or transaction.</summary>
<keywords>pactum nudum, pactum vestitum, Bachovius, Treutler, consensus, contract</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="11">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
that convention is called, because a business transaction has been added which produces a civil obligation, and a contract has been celebrated, which is called buying and selling, at the beginning of the law concerning buying and selling and the law regarding agreed pacts 72, at the beginning of the Digest concerning the contracting of a purchase:

### XLVI.
Thus, if I bargain with you that you give me money as a loan, or that you exchange your Cornelian estate for my house, so far nothing has been done beyond a naked convention and a naked consensus. But as soon as you count out the money to me, or you deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my house to you, a business transaction intervenes beyond the convention, and in that case a loan is contracted. At the beginning of the law regarding the ways in which an obligation is contracted by a thing. This indeed is an exchange. Law "naturalis" 5, paragraph 1, Digest concerning prescribed words.

### XLVII.
It is doubted whether the name of "agreement" <note>original: "pactum"</note>, when uttered simply, signifies a naked agreement? Which I affirm through the law of the "Law of Nations" <note>original: "Jurisgentium"</note> 7, paragraph 5, Digest concerning agreements. Those feeling the contrary are moved by the above-mentioned law "traditionibus" 20, there "not by naked agreements," in the Code concerning agreements. But Hunnius satisfies these in his resolutions on Treutler, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.
Moreover, a naked agreement is either express or tacit, which is to say it is gathered from the deeds of the contracting parties, and is said to be entered into by the thing itself in law 2, Digest concerning agreements; law 32, Digest on partnerships. Of which we have one example in law 2, paragraph 1, Digest concerning agreements: he who has returned the security bond to the debtor is understood to have tacitly agreed not to sue. Another in law 3, Digest under the said title: where he who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, but not the debt itself.

<summary>This page explains how a business transaction transforms a naked agreement into an obligation and distinguishes between express and tacit agreements.</summary>
<keywords>buying and selling, loan, exchange, obligation, tacit agreement, Hunnius, Treutler, pledge</keywords>
</translation>

### XL.
Furthermore, an agreement is considered either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or as it is added immediately to a contract.

### XLI.
The former is called a naked agreement <note>original: "nudum"</note>, while the latter are said to be not naked; since these do not rest upon the naked terms of an agreement but either adhere to a contract or have an assisting law, anyone can see that they cannot be held in the class of naked agreements. *Bachovius in his notes on the Disputations of Treutler.*

### XLII.
And these may also not inconveniently be called "clothed" <note>original: "vestita"</note>; for although these words do not appear in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists; moreover, where the matter is established, we ought to be flexible regarding the words, *by the argument of law 17, Digest concerning laws.*

### XLIII.
A naked convention is that which stands at the limit of the consensus. *law "si tibi" 27, Code concerning letting and hiring.* Or, what is the same thing, that which consists in the pure and simple limits of a convention.

### XLIV.
It is so called because it is naked of a cause or a business transaction <note>original: "a causa seu negotio"</note> *the said law "solent" 15, Digest concerning prescribed words.* This also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract, whence it is also called a simple convention in *law "avia" 6, Code concerning the Law of dowries,* and merely an agreement in *law "major" 23, Code concerning pledges and mortgages.*

### XLV.
For example, if it is agreed that you sell me your house, this convention stands in the naked terms of consensus: but if it is agreed concerning the thing and the price, it is no longer naked

<summary>This page defines "naked" versus "clothed" agreements, explaining that a naked agreement lacks a formal legal cause or transaction.</summary>
<keywords>pactum nudum, pactum vestitum, Bachovius, Treutler, consensus, contract</keywords>
pages.11:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
that convention is called, because a business transaction has been added which produces a civil obligation, and a contract has been celebrated, which is called buying and selling, at the beginning of the law concerning buying and selling and the law regarding agreed pacts 72, at the beginning of the Digest concerning the contracting of a purchase:

### XLVI.
Thus, if I bargain with you that you give me money as a loan, or that you exchange your Cornelian estate for my house, so far nothing has been done beyond a naked convention and a naked consensus. But as soon as you count out the money to me, or you deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my house to you, a business transaction intervenes beyond the convention, and in that case a loan is contracted. At the beginning of the law regarding the ways in which an obligation is contracted by a thing. This indeed is an exchange. Law "naturalis" 5, paragraph 1, Digest concerning prescribed words.

### XLVII.
It is doubted whether the name of "agreement" <note>original: "pactum"</note>, when uttered simply, signifies a naked agreement? Which I affirm through the law of the "Law of Nations" <note>original: "Jurisgentium"</note> 7, paragraph 5, Digest concerning agreements. Those feeling the contrary are moved by the above-mentioned law "traditionibus" 20, there "not by naked agreements," in the Code concerning agreements. But Hunnius satisfies these in his resolutions on Treutler, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.
Moreover, a naked agreement is either express or tacit, which is to say it is gathered from the deeds of the contracting parties, and is said to be entered into by the thing itself in law 2, Digest concerning agreements; law 32, Digest on partnerships. Of which we have one example in law 2, paragraph 1, Digest concerning agreements: he who has returned the security bond to the debtor is understood to have tacitly agreed not to sue. Another in law 3, Digest under the said title: where he who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, but not the debt itself.

<summary>This page explains how a business transaction transforms a naked agreement into an obligation and distinguishes between express and tacit agreements.</summary>
<keywords>buying and selling, loan, exchange, obligation, tacit agreement, Hunnius, Treutler, pledge</keywords>

the matter is narrated in such a way that it appears the lashes were inflicted upon Christ by the very person of Pilate, not by his soldiers, since mention of them is made only in verse 2. Blessed GERHARD indicates that Bede, while adhering too closely to the literal text, remained stuck in this opinion. But who would so easily believe that a man of such great standing, established in such dignity and authority among both Romans and Jews, would humble himself so far as to carry out this duty himself, which was to be dispatched by soldiers and <term>lictors</term> <gloss>civil officers attending magistrates</gloss> as their own proper task? It is instead more probable that this butchery was performed chiefly by those who were specifically sent and designated by Pilate for its execution. However, the scourging is attributed here to Pilate himself, the Governor of Judea, as the principal moral cause, because the entire matter was carried out by his order and command. Thus, it is not absurd, but very appropriate, to explain the words of the Evangelists in this way. For is it not, according to the common rule of law, that what one does through another or others, he is to be considered and said to have done by himself?

XXVII. Furthermore, investigating the ministerial cause, we judge it relevant to ask: who and what kind of men were specifically admitted to scourge JESUS? If we look at the more corrected Greek manuscripts, we do not find their mention made separately in the text regarding this; yet we gather reasonably from the words, both preceding and following, that the Roman soldiers and <term>lictors</term>—called by some <term>Brutiani</term> or <term>Brutii</term> <gloss>a class of public servants of low rank</gloss>—and these being gentiles, were the primary actors of this tragedy. For the added small word looking toward the Jews, *Eis* <gloss>to them</gloss>, which is read in certain copies after the word *tradidit* <gloss>he delivered</gloss>, is not genuine; hence, as ERASMUS notes, it somewhat obstructs the meaning.
<margin>
Annotations on Matthew chapter 27.
</margin>
For (he adds) Pilate did not deliver JESUS to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of punishment. For these are the ones who earlier seized Christ, bound him when seized, presented him bound to judgment, scourged him when presented, clothed him in purple after he was scourged, crowned him when clothed, mocked him when crowned, struck him when mocked, led him away when struck, and crucified him when led away: just as we see this emphasized not once, but repeatedly, in the history of the entire passion.

XXVIII. But perhaps a doubt could arise in someone’s mind: did the Jews not extend their helping hands to the Heathens in this business? Certainly, with Judas the traitor carrying the torch before them, they delivered Christ, seeking nothing else than that JESUS might be removed from their midst by the gentiles and finally raised upon the cross itself after various tortures. Therefore, who among us ever doubts that the greatest blame for the entire passion, and thus also for the scourging, redounds upon the Jews as the morally efficient causes? However, that the Jews performed the role of a physical cause in any part of the work, we neither read nor believe: especially since the SAVIOR himself, suffering patiently, predicted this concerning himself to his disciples on his final journey to Jerusalem: that it would happen that the Chief Priests and Scribes would deliver the Son of Man to the gentiles to be mocked and <term>eis mastigōsai</term> <gloss>to be scourged</gloss>. Compare MARK and LUKE. You will see in both places that it is stated of the nations, or (which is the same in these and many other places) the gentiles, but by no means the Jews: <term>mastigōsousin</term> <gloss>they will scourge</gloss> and <term>mastigōsantes auton</term> <gloss>having scourged him</gloss>. Hence, so that this most true prediction of the TRUTH might be fulfilled at the same time, the gentiles alone had to scourge JESUS.
<margin>
Matthew 20:18-19; chapter 15:39-40; chapter 18:32-33.
</margin>

XXIX. Furthermore, if we look at the mind of the Jews themselves, it is established without difficulty why they were unwilling to strike JESUS with lashes. For, since according to the divine law it was not permitted for Jews to inflict more than forty blows, or, as they themselves poorly interpreted it, thirty-nine, with whips; hence, undoubtedly out of the most bitter 
</translation>

<translation page="15">
<margin>
John 18:31, 18.
</margin>
hatred against CHRIST, this punishment seemed too *mild*, if it were to be imposed by their own people upon this JESUS, whom they blasphemously called a *deceiver*. They preferred, therefore, to choose gentiles to inflict this punishment, since they were restricted to no fixed number and were accustomed to beat the accused *beyond measure*, and sometimes even *unto death*. Indeed, they did not intend the scourging for its own sake, but *only* demanded the crucifixion. Hence, not content with that punishment inflicted by Pilate, they cried out that Christ must also be punished by the cross, nor did they cease crying out until they obtained by the very deed that which they so greatly sought. Truly, they did not want *life*, they wanted *death*, and that to be paid for by the cross; yet it was not permitted for them to carry out this capital punishment, although the *Romans carried it out among the Jews according to their pleasure*. To this point their own confession, uttered with one voice before Pilate, especially pertains: *It is not permitted for us, they say, to put anyone to death*; understand this primarily, as authors of no small renown understand it, regarding the punishment of the cross. So restricted was the power of the Jews under the Romans even at that time. Indeed, perhaps the Jews also refused to offer themselves as associates to the Romans in scourging Christ because they thought any of them would be contaminated if someone, with the Passover imminent, even entered the <term>praetorium</term> <gloss>governor's headquarters</gloss>, and much more so if he became an assistant in punishments within the same. See *John 18*.

<margin>
Matthew 27:27.
Mark 15:16.
</margin>

XXX. But what of it? For what cause that was done by them matters little for us to know. We return more directly to the act of scourging itself. We gathered before from the text of Scripture that it was commanded by Pilate, chiefly to the cruel soldiers and attendants of Pilate, that they should scourge Jesus. Exactly how many those <term>lictors</term> were, we have not said, nor can we say; especially since Scripture and antiquity are silent. It is, however, beyond controversy that more than one, indeed many, if not very many, were present at this act, who aided the business of the scourging with their help and labor. The place where the scourging was to be instituted was established as the *court or praetorium, the house in which the provincial Governor not only lived, but also administered the law*. For the soldiers of the Governor had withdrawn there, with the entire cohort called together and assembled in that place.

<margin>
Book 2 on the Cross, chapter 4, page 63.
</margin>

XXXI. There, indeed, Jesus was forced to undergo the individual fates of those to be scourged. Why shall we deny here that *he was stripped of his clothes*, we who have heard above that this custom remained *most common* among the Romans in this infliction of punishments? We also not unwillingly grant some credit to that opinion by which it is asserted that Jesus *was bound to a column*; not so much because *Lipsius* strove to confirm this rite with certain examples and the testimony of others, but because the pious and ancient Fathers of religion did not entirely doubt to affirm such a thing concerning the column of the scourged Savior. Clearly and excellently, the most prudent of Poets sang in his own century:

<margin>
Prudentius, Enchiridion of the New Testament, concerning this column. See Library of the Fathers, Volume 4, page 924.
</margin>

->*Bound in these halls the Lord stood, and to a column*<-
->*Attached, he gave his back, like a slave, to the whips.*<-
**Indeed, he continues:**
->*The venerable column still stands, and supports the temple.*<-

<margin>
Volume 2, part 2, Delights of the human race, chapter 3, section 3, page 342.
</margin>

With which agrees what *Blessed Jerome* relates regarding *Paula* in her Epitaph to *Eustochium*: *There was shown to her, he says, on Mount Sion a column supporting a portico, stained with the blood of the Lord, to which he is said to have been bound and scourged.* Bede himself testifies that in the time of *Bede* it was in the middle of the Church. But what is said concerning this column being placed in a temple, we judge to be at least deservedly suspect, if not entirely false. In the meantime, whether such a column existed in the temple or not, it is enough that it existed in the <term>praetorium</term> at the time when Christ was bound to it. Hence *Hieronymus Drexel* depicts this column thus: *By Roman rite Jesus was bound with ropes to a two-foot column, which...*

<summary>These pages discuss the legal and physical circumstances of Christ's scourging, arguing that while Pilate ordered it, the act was carried out by Roman soldiers rather than Jews to ensure a punishment exceeding Jewish law. The text also examines the tradition of the column to which Christ was bound, citing early church fathers and poets.</summary>
<keywords>Pilate, scourging, Roman law, Jewish law, praetorium, column of the flagellation, lictors, Prudentius, Jerome, Bede</keywords>

all muscles are marked by this character in general, so it happens especially to the muscles of the thorax, so that they can no longer lift the ribs; thus the equilibrium between the pressing air and our body is necessarily destroyed, which results in difficult breathing, accompanied step by step by anxiety of the <term>precordia</term> <gloss>the region of the heart and diaphragm</gloss>.

> Often the sick do not dare to speak, or indeed are scarcely able to, which must be deduced from the intensity of the pains, or from a paralytic state of the organs dedicated to speech.

> Fever is present insofar as the circulation of the humors, on account of sluggish nerves and a surplus of morbid matter, does not succeed as desired; hence it happens that they conceive a fermentation or internal motion.

Light will be shed upon this opinion by the *Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever* by the most illustrious Master Licentiate J. C. Wolff of Zerbst, formerly my most pleasant companion, held at Wittenberg under the most Excellent Master Doctor Berger, Public Professor there and truly a venerable preceptor. 

Moreover, depending on a milder degree of fermentation, the sick person may not feel its discomforts.

A proclivity for sleep is also an effect of viscosity, thickness, and a lack of animal spirits and other fluids, or even of a compression of the brain. However, <term>Somnolentia</term> <gloss>drowsiness</gloss> is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term> <gloss>migraine</gloss>, as the previously praised Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood—partly due to the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy, relaxing from a constrictive motion—pass through the small canals so slowly that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? Appetite is the offspring of the animal spirits; therefore, with the use of these denied, nausea arises. What is more, the corrupted gastric lymph is not suitable for dissolving food. The stomach, thus burdened and now sufficiently weak, contracts itself spasmodically and ejects the indigested mass again, which we call <term>Vomiting</term>. Whence a tumor on the surface of the head derives its birth, let it be sought from the preceding section. It should be noted moreover that it does not seem improbable to me that such a tumor can sometimes be nourished by caries of the skull itself.

### XI.
But as to why <term>Hemicrania</term> sometimes remits, or even torments the sick person only at certain interpolated intervals of time,

<keywords>respiration, fever, J. C. Wolff, Berger, animal spirits, nausea, vomiting, skull caries</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="11">
and that a *periodic* pain results from it (examples of which can be read in the works of Tulp, Linden, Bellini, and others); this depends on various changes in the fluid surrounding us, and on the peculiar constitution of the head introduced by the causes mentioned in Section IX. For in such a way we easily conceive that the offending matter, consumed over a stretch of time, is restored anew, and creeps back into the injured part (which, like a folded piece of paper, always retraces its old marks) until it grows into such a mass that it causes a new distension of the parts mentioned so often, whence the disease puts on its former face.

XII. If we recall all that has been said with a somewhat more curious mind, how great are the *dangers* we see present for the sick? And what even greater ones do we fear, not without the support of reason? We do not hesitate to affirm that <term>Hemicrania</term> is a most dangerous disease, in whatever way it behaves. Since the affected part is highly sensitive and must provide aid to the economy of the body, and the producing causes are exceedingly grave. Indeed, the disease is most difficult to cure, both because its various causes must be torn out by the roots before it can be removed, and because scarcely any equal remedy is found to reduce the solid parts that are twisted <term>p. n.</term> <gloss>praeter naturam; contrary to nature</gloss> and return them to their <term>st. n.</term> <gloss>status naturalis; natural state</gloss>. But above all, the fact that only half of the head is affected makes the evil stubborn. For a remedy, although it may bathe the affected part, will work only sparingly, seeking an exit where it finds the least resistance. I remain silent on the fact that substances taken in are not specifically determined here or there, but are distributed through the whole body by the law of circulation. Wherefore *External Hemicrania*, where medicines touch the affected part immediately, bids us be more confident, unless caries of the skull is joined to it. With respect to the duration of the disease, sex, age, the temperament of the air, and the idiosyncrasy of the body, different <term>prognostics</term> <gloss>forecasts of the disease's course</gloss> must also be formed. According to a greater or lesser number of symptoms, the evil must be called more fierce or more mild. I knew a friend (which is relevant to mention here) who contracted <term>Hemicrania</term> with a languor of the limbs on that side upon which he had lain during the night, which was successfully resolved shortly, and, if I am not mistaken, within eight days. Alas, what a more heavy cure do the little worms nesting in the brain require, while the little stones and calculi generated in the same place plainly reject it! For confirmation of this, see the *Dissertation on Incurability* <note>original: "Dissertatio de Atherapeusia"</note>

<summary>The author discusses the periodic nature of migraines and the difficulty of treating the condition due to its localized nature. He highlights the dangers of the disease and notes that internal causes, such as stones or parasites in the brain, make it nearly impossible to cure.</summary>
<keywords>periodicity, Tulp, Linden, Bellini, prognosis, external hemicrania, brain stones, incurability</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="12">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
observe order. The Politician, however, when he first deals with the city and the republic and afterwards with their parts and species, observes the synthetic Method.

XVII. He who denies that being as being <note>original: "ens quatenus ens"</note> is the object of Metaphysics, because all things treated in this discipline cannot be reduced to this—such as first principles, axioms, hypotheses, and first definitions, the doctrine of the first substance and its operations and attributes—might as well deny that the natural body as natural is the object of Physics. This is because not all things treated in Physics are natural bodies; for example, matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so forth. Moreover, not everything said by this or that person necessarily belongs to a specific discipline.

XVIII. He who said that anyone who wishes to use abstractions in the other philosophical disciplines besides Mathematics abstracts the mind from the truth—because things must be known as they are found in the nature of things, not as certain aspects are usually or can be abstracted from them—was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is a great debate among the ancients as to whether virtue is learned. Some affirm it is given by nature to the good and denied to the wicked; others believe it is perceived through use and instruction. Plato seems at times to agree with the former, and at times with the latter. But there is no doubt that virtue is established and perfected both by a nature that is not inherently depraved, and by precepts and exercise. The ancients called these: Nature, Reason, and Practice <note>original: Φύσιν, λόγον καὶ ἄσκησιν</note>. These are as necessary in virtue as they are in the arts, or even in crops, which require rich soil, good seeds, and the diligence of the farmer. Ludovicus Vives <margin>at chapter 1, book 19, City of God, column 1141; add Augustine in the said book, chapter 4, column 1148.</margin> references the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> throughout; see Plutarch's booklet *Whether Virtue Can Be Taught* <note>original: εἰ διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή</note>, page 370.

XX. All people always desire the good: Plato in *Hipparchus*. For all good things are useful: the same in *Meno*.

XXI. Poverty, the sister of a good mind according to Petronius in the *Satyricon*, page 94, seems preferable to riches. For she thoroughly teaches all arts wherever she touches a person, as Plautus says in *Stichus*. <margin>Add Seneca, epistle 15, and Theocritus.</margin> For most often Necessity and Sobriety accompany her, and she renders men attentive and circumspect; whereas favorable fortune and opulence give birth to negligence. From this, the intellect is sharpened, from which the arts arise. Indeed, as Apuleius says, she never inflated anyone with pride, never corrupted anyone with lack of restraint, never made anyone savage with tyranny. She neither wants nor is able to indulge the delights of the belly or the loins. Truly, these and other outrages are usually the nurslings of riches. And although we read that even the greatest crimes have been committed by very poor men, many of these were not actually poor, but beggars; Aristophanes provides this distinction in *Plutus*, page 11:

> For the life of a beggar, which you describe, is to live having nothing;
</translation>

<translation page="13">
but that of a poor man is to live sparingly and to attend to his labors,
possessing nothing in excess, but certainly lacking nothing.

### XXII. Hesiod teaches in these verses that the care of human affairs rests with the Genii <gloss>guardian spirits</gloss> by permission of the supreme Commander:

> These are the noble spirits dwelling on the earth,
> holy, warding off evil, guardians of mortal men,
> who watch over justice and cruel deeds,
> clothed in mist, wandering everywhere over the land.

It is therefore probable that certain Genii, like Ambassadors or Tribunes, care for peoples and regions. Theodoret relates that these are Archangels in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 10, as cited by Besold. Certainly, that Saint Michael presides over my Poland is made credible by the fact that he was seen in Poland, as history testifies, before the victory against the Lithuanians, which was obtained without a single Pole being killed. Hence, at last, a Basilica was built to him at Lublin. What of the fact that this most vast kingdom extends toward the North? And from there, according to the saying of Scripture, comes evil; that is, the greatest part of the <term>Alastores</term> <gloss>avenging spirits/demons</gloss> are stabled there. On this point, Nicephorus Gregoras writes in his scholia on Synesius' *On Dreams*, page 383, that the Chaldeans consider the Prince of the Outer Dark and of the adjacent earthly inheritance, which fell to him by lot, to be: the leader of the furthest and terrestrial portion.

### XXIII. Among men, he who is puffed up by the gift of fortune and opulence, and elevated even to the changeable platform of a kingdom and its hanging tribunal, will rarely live within reach, and with witnesses far removed, he dwells in certain inner chambers of his own dignity, as Apuleius says in *On the God of Socrates*.

And among the Persians, the person of the King is hidden under the appearance of Majesty, as Justin testifies in book 1, page 10, and Herodotus in *Clio*. This is because not all things treated in Physics are natural bodies; for example, matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so forth. Moreover, not everything said by this or that person necessarily belongs to a specific discipline.

He who said that anyone who wishes to use abstractions in the other philosophical disciplines besides Mathematics abstracts the mind from the truth—because things must be known as they are found in the nature of things, not as certain aspects are usually or can be abstracted from them—was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is a great debate among the ancients as to whether virtue is learned. Some affirm it is given by nature to the good and denied to the wicked; others believe it is perceived through use and instruction. Plato seems at times to agree with the former, and at times with the latter. But there is no doubt that virtue is established and perfected both by a nature that is not inherently depraved, and by precepts and exercise. The ancients called these: Nature, Reason, and Practice <note>original: Φύσιν, λόγον καὶ ἄσκησιν</note>. These are as necessary in virtue as they are in the arts, or even in crops, which require rich soil, good seeds, and the diligence of the farmer. But others are called putrid and dead members, and they are dry and sterile trees (Ezekiel 20, verse 47); a <term>συκῆ ἄκαρπος</term> <gloss>unfruitful fig tree</gloss> having nothing <term>εἰ μὴ φύλλα μόνον</term> <gloss>except leaves only</gloss> (Matthew 21, verse 19). and blasphemers. ### XXXIII.

It is manifest from the example of the Apostles that even the holy can hold some errors, provided they do not overturn the articles of faith. In the Apostles, both before and after the resurrection—even though they had seen with their own eyes the beginnings of the new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ—there was such darkness and weakness that they still dreamed the Kingdom of the Messiah would be political (Acts 1, verse 6), and many wished for Levitical rituals to be retained (Acts 15).

### XXXIIII.

And the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss> by which many are burdened is far too blind and unhappy, if we think there is no weakness in us or that we are ignorant of nothing, but are instead perfect and all-knowing. For it is most true what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And in verse 12: "We see now through a mirror and in a riddle."

### XXXV.

But the godly and those who are teachable, when admonished, return to the way. Just as it is certain that the Apostles finally cast away their dreams of a physical kingdom of the Messiah and the necessity of circumcision and other Levitical rituals once they received the Holy Spirit. They did not, like the stubborn Jews, contradict the Spirit against their conscience and against so many great testimonies of the truth.

### XXXVI.

Nor indeed, in discussing the Church in the manner described, do we dream of some Platonic Idea or a city existing nowhere on earth that consists only of an image in the mind. Nor do we believe she wanders in the dark among <term>Andabatas</term> <gloss>blindfolded gladiators</gloss>.

## Question III.

### *Whether a Quantitative Number applies to the Intelligences?*

Those substances which the Theologians call Angels, the Metaphysicians name Intelligences. And regarding these, it is here disputed: Whether a quantitative number can be attributed to them. We stand manfully on the negative side, using such a shield: Where there is no quantity, there is no quantitative number. In the intelligences, there is no quantity. Therefore. Do you doubt the minor premise? You do rightly: For to always doubt is to always inquire into a greater truth. But do you attack it? Attack it then, provided you do not overcome it. For does quantity not apply solely to materialized and corporeal things? Do you deny it? You strike against Philosophical principles; you rise up against Aristotle himself; against truth itself. Look at the species of Quantity: It is continuous, whose parts are joined by some common boundary; or discrete, whose parts on the contrary are neither joined nor fitted together by any such boundary, according to Aristotle in the book of Categories, on quantity. Where, I ask, do you see any parts in the Intelligences? If these were present, they would surely make the very substance of the Angels either partible or divisible; surely the intelligences themselves would have an extension of parts; surely they would consist of a body; surely they would participate in matter along with form—all of which are absurd. I add this also: Quantitative number is classified among the common sensibles, according to Aristotle in book 2 of On the Soul, chapter 6, text 64. If therefore the intelligences are sensible, they must surely be perceived by sense. Otherwise, if the thing which falls under the sense is removed, the sense must necessarily be removed. But sense exists only in a body, and is concerned with bodies, according to Aristotle in the book of Categories, on quantity. But who endowed with sound reason has ever called Angels bodies?
</translation>

<translation page="10">
Therefore, quantitative number ought not to be attributed to them. Do you infer that a quantity, even if not predicamental <note>referring to the ten Aristotelian categories or predicaments</note>, is nevertheless given in *Angels* as Intelligible, so that our intellect may conceive one thing in them which is not another? You proceed poorly. For as things are, so they are conceived, which is the distinction that exists between the divine and human intellect. For the divine Intellect makes things conform to its own concept; the human intellect, however, is itself conformed to things. How therefore will you be able to form a quantity for yourself where there is no quantity at all? How will you be able to conceive one part distinct from another where no parts are given at all; why then would they be given as distinct? Certainly, when you conceive a thing in this way, your intellect represents to you not the thing itself, but a figment of the brain and the imagination.

## Question IV.

### *Whether there are five Intellectual Habits?*

This question is taken from the 6th book of the Nicomachean Ethics, where the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> discusses intellectual habits at sufficient length. It must be noted above all others that these habits are twofold: some are instrumental, which serve the principal ones as ministers, and these are Grammar, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Logic; others are principal, concerning which the present question is proposed. We have said with the Philosopher that these are five in number, namely *Intelligence, Science, Wisdom, Prudence*, and *Art*; we recognize neither more nor fewer. If there are those who prefer more, I do not see by what argument they are led, unless perhaps they refer the aforementioned instrumental habits among the principal ones, or include them under the term of Art. But who is so blind that he does not see the distinction between both types of habits? Or who is so abandoned by all thought,
</translation>

J. Faber</term> <gloss>Pierre-Jean Fabre, 1588–1658, French physician and alchemist</gloss> joins him in asserting the same utility of metallic remedies for Hectic patients. In his *Cures of Various Diseases*, Cure 14, he recounts the use of acid Spirit of Salt and <term>Tincture of the Sun</term> <gloss>a preparation of gold</gloss> extracted with rectified Oil of Salt for a desperate Hectic case. I also know of those for whom dry salts are in use for the purpose of moistening the wasted body of Hectic patients in an essential way. Others praise the <term>Balsam of Life</term>, as they call it, which they prepare thus: They take two and a half ounces of salt and two drachms of the purest gold. They melt them, pulverize them, and extract them with Spirit of Salt, drawing it off until it reaches the consistency of oil. This they drop into one drachm of pulverized Salt of Pearls. They mix it in a marble mortar, dry it over a slow fire, and gradually regenerate it until it acquires a purple color. They administer five to ten grains of this in a restorative broth quite frequently; from this, they hope that the substance-forming moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by the substitution of an essentially moistening substance.

But far be it from a physician, who walks with both legs of experience and reason, to use drying agents in place of essentially moistening ones, which are indicated by Hectic fever. We embrace a sounder opinion on curing Hectic fever as far as possible, along with Sennert. # MARRIED MEN

In the name of the Lord, Amen. Let it be known to all and each who inspect these presents, and specifically those whom it concerns, will concern, or whom the business written below touches, might touch, or could concern in any way in the future. That in the year from the Nativity of the Lord one thousand five hundred twenty-four, in the twelfth <term>indiction</term> <gloss>a fifteen-year cycle used in dating</gloss>, on Tuesday, which was the fifth day of the month of April, in the first year of the Pontificate of the most holy father in Christ and our lord, Lord Clement VII, by divine providence Pope. In the presence of me, the Notary Public, and the witnesses written below, specifically called and requested for this purpose, there personally appeared the honorable Lord Wolfgang Schultheiss, a priest of Strasbourg, in his own name and also in the names of the venerable lords: Matthäus Zell of Kaysersberg, parish priest of Saint Lawrence; Anton Firn, parish priest of Saint Thomas; Johann Nubling, chaplain of the chapel of Saint Erhard of the churches of Strasbourg; Lucas Hackfurt; Konrad Spatzinger; and Alexander, formerly a member of the Order of Saint John <note>the Knights Hospitaller</note>, priests likewise personally appearing before me, the notary, and the witnesses written below. He held and kept in his hands a certain written schedule of Appeal or challenge, which—with the soul and intention of challenging and appealing, protesting, and seeking <term>Apostoli</term> <gloss>formal letters of appeal sent from a lower to a higher judge</gloss>, and doing other things as he said were more broadly contained in the same schedule—he delivered and assigned to me, the Notary Public written below, according to the prescribed tenor. Lest any force be done, etc.

After the interposition of this challenge, appeal, and
</translation>

<translation page="20">
# APPEAL

petition for <term>Apostoli</term> <gloss>letters of appeal</gloss> on the written schedule, the said Lord Wolfgang Schultheiss, in his own name and in the name of the previously mentioned lords who are the principal appellants, requested from me, the Notary Public written below, that one or more public instrument or instruments be made and completed, as many as should be necessary for him or for any of the others. These things were done at Strasbourg in the Parish House of the parish of Saint Lawrence of Strasbourg, in the Year of the Lord, Indiction, day, month, hour, and Pontificate as stated above, in the presence of the honorable and discreet men Lord Wilhelm Beltinger, an assistant in divine services, and Melchior Schell, sacristan of the Church of Saint Lawrence in Strasbourg, witnesses called and requested for the aforementioned things.

And I, Michael Schwencker of Gernsbach, of the Diocese of Speyer, a public Notary by sacred imperial authority. Because I was present and personally intervened in all and each of the aforementioned things while they were being done and conducted as described, together with the previously named witnesses, and I saw and heard them so done. Therefore, I have taken note of this present public instrument, faithfully written by the hand of another by my order, and from there I have finished it, published it, and reduced it into this public form. I have marked and signed it with my usual and customary sign, name, and surname.

<note>A purple circular library stamp of the National and University Library of Strasbourg partly obscures the bottom of the last paragraph.</note>

Having been requested and asked for the same and as a testimony of all the aforementioned.

->At Strasbourg, from the house of Wolfgang Köpfel<-
->near the horse market, 12 April<-
->THE YEAR 1524.<-

in the ancient contests of Greece, crowns made of parsley <term>apium</term> <gloss>celery or parsley</gloss> were customarily granted to the victors. Pindar is a witness that such was the use of parsley in the Isthmian and Nemean games. Aeneas also, having arrived in Italy, set out and arranged a table upon the ground covered with parsley. <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus,</note> *Roman Antiquities, book 1.* Similarly, Horace confirms that parsley was taken up for crowns in celebrating the birthday of Maecenas. *Odes, book IV, Ode 11.*

§. 18. Furthermore, they relate that crowns woven from flowers were placed upon the dead, as is testified with one voice by *Xenophon in the 5th book of the Expedition of Cyrus, the commentator of Euripides in the Phoenician Women, and Lucian in the dialogue On Mourning; and among the Church Fathers, Justin Martyr in the Second Apology, and Clement of Alexandria in the Instructor <term>Paedagogus</term>, book II, chapter 8.* Moreover, that tombs were sprinkled with flowers is indicated by *Sophocles in Electra, Plutarch in Numa, and Tranquillus <note>Suetonius</note> in Nero, chapter LIII.* For they used to bring leafy branches and flowers to the sepulchers, and scattered flowers at the funeral; a custom which the ancient Christians in the age of Prudentius did not disapprove of, and retained for some time, even though in the first centuries of the Christian era they not only did not apply crowns to graves,
