do not benefit others through the four correct analytical knowledges, and do not benefit others through great loving-kindness, and do not benefit others through great compassion, and do not benefit others through the eighteen unshared qualities of a Buddha, and do not benefit others through the fruit of a stream-enterer, and do not benefit others through the fruit of a once-returner, and do not benefit others through the fruit of a non-returner, and do not benefit others through the state of an <term>Arhat</term> <gloss>worthy one who has overcome all delusions</gloss>, and do not benefit others through self-enlightenment <note>referring to the path of a Pratyekabuddha</note>, and do not benefit others through the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and do not benefit others through the knowledge of all aspects, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of wisdom, do not act in accordance with the perfection of concentration, do not act in accordance with the perfection of diligence, do not act in accordance with the perfection of patience, do not act in accordance with the perfection of ethics, do not act in accordance with the perfection of generosity, and [do not act in accordance with] internal emptiness,
<leaf-break/>
do not act in accordance with, and do not act in accordance with the powers, do not act in accordance with the branches of enlightenment, do not act in accordance with the noble eightfold path, do not act in accordance with the noble truths, do not act in accordance with the meditative concentrations, do not act in accordance with the immeasurables, do not act in accordance with the formless absorptions, do not act in accordance with the eight liberations, do not act in accordance with the nine serial absorptions, do not act in accordance with the gateways of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, do not act in accordance with the superknowledges, do not act in accordance with the meditative stabilizations, do not act in accordance with the doors of <term>dharani</term> <gloss>incantations or mnemonic formulas</gloss>, do not act in accordance with the ten powers of a <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone One; a Buddha</gloss>, do not act in accordance with the four fearlessnesses, do not act in accordance with the four correct analytical knowledges, do not act in accordance with great loving-kindness, do not act in accordance with great compassion, and [do not act in accordance with] the [eighteen] unshared qualities of a Buddha
</translation>

<translation page="199">
do not act in accordance with the eighteen unshared qualities, and do not act in accordance with the fruit of a stream-enterer, do not act in accordance with the fruit of a once-returner, do not act in accordance with the fruit of a non-returner, do not act in accordance with the state of an Arhat, do not act in accordance with self-enlightenment, do not act in accordance with the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and do not act in accordance with the knowledge of all aspects, then they will remain on one of the two stages <note>referring to the lower paths as opposed to full Buddhahood</note>: that is to say, either the stage of a Hearer <note>Shravaka</note> or the stage of a Solitary Realizer <note>Pratyekabuddha</note>. Why is that? It is because these sons of noble family or daughters of noble family did not previously write down this profound perfection of wisdom, did not teach it, did not recite it, did not contemplate it correctly, and did not apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom. Because those sons of noble family or daughters of noble family on the Bodhisattva vehicle did not act in accordance with this perfection of wisdom, therefore those sons of noble family or daughters of noble family on the Bodhisattva vehicle [remain in that] state.
<leaf-break/>
and do not rely upon [it], and do not write down the perfection of concentration, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down the perfection of diligence, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down the perfection of patience, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down the perfection of ethics, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down the perfection of generosity, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down internal emptiness, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down external emptiness, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down internal and external emptiness, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down the emptiness of emptiness, do not teach it, do not recite it, do not contemplate it correctly, and do not rely upon it; and do not write down great emptiness, do not teach it, do not recite it...
</translation>

<summary>These pages outline the consequences of failing to practice or preserve the perfection of wisdom, warning that such neglect leads one to the lower stages of Hearers or Solitary Realizers rather than full Buddhahood. The text enumerates various Buddhist qualities and types of emptiness that must be correctly engaged with through writing, teaching, and contemplation.</summary>
<keywords>Perfection of Wisdom, Prajnaparamita, Bodhisattva, Shravaka, Pratyekabuddha, Emptiness, Buddhist path, merit, Dharma practice</keywords>

of her own hands, she is a mass of light that quivers. 
Homage to her who is majestic with extreme joy, 
Her crown emits a garland of light. 
By her laughing and mocking laughter with <term>Tuttare</term>, 
She brings the <term>maras</term> <gloss>demonic forces</gloss> and the world under her power. 

Homage to her who is able to summon 
All the hosts of guardians of the earth. 
With her frowning brow and the quivering syllable <term>Hum</term>, 
She completely liberates all those who are destitute. 

Homage to her who is crowned by a crescent moon, 
All her ornaments shine with great brilliance. 
From her hair-knot, <term>Amitabha</term> <gloss>the Buddha of Boundless Light</gloss> 
Continually creates a vast radiance. 

Homage to her who dwells within a garland of blazing fire, 
Like the fire at the end of the <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss>. 
With her right leg extended

<leaf-break/>

and her left leg tucked, she is surrounded by joy. 
She completely destroys the armies of enemies. 
Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth with her hand, 
Pounding it with her palms and treading with her feet. 
With a frowning face and the syllable <term>Hum</term>, 
She shatters the seven levels of the underworld. 

Homage to her who is blissful, virtuous, and peaceful, 
Whose domain is the peace of <term>Nirvana</term>. 
Properly endowed with the syllables <term>Svaha</term> and <term>Om</term>, 
She is the destroyer of great sins. 

Homage to her who is surrounded by perfect joy, 
She completely shatters the bodies of enemies. 
By the arrangement of the ten-syllable speech, 
The <term>vidya</term> <gloss>knowledge-mantra</gloss> is the liberator born from <term>Hum</term>. 

Homage to her who stamps her feet with <term>Ture</term>, 
Whose essence is the seed syllable in the form of <term>Hum</term>. 
She causes Mount Meru, Man-
</translation>

<translation page="11">
-dara and the Vindhya mountains, 
And all the three worlds to tremble. 

Homage to her who holds in her hand 
The symbol of the hare <note>The moon</note> in the form of a celestial lake. 
By reciting <term>Tara</term> twice and the syllable <term>Phat</term>, 
She clears away all poisons without exception. 

Homage to her whom the kings of the host of gods, 
The gods and the <term>kinnaras</term> <gloss>celestial musicians</gloss> rely upon. 
With the majesty of her armor and her joy, 
She clears away disputes and bad dreams. 

Homage to her whose two eyes 
Are like the sun and the full moon, shining with brilliant light. 
By reciting <term>Hara</term> twice and the syllable <term>Tuttare</term>, 
She clears away extremely fierce infectious diseases. 

Homage to her who by the arrangement of the three Suchnesses <note>Refers to the qualities of body, speech, and mind</note>, 
Is perfectly endowed with the power of peace. 
The hosts of spirits, <term>vetalas</term> <gloss>zombies</gloss>, 

<leaf-break/>

and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>, 
Are destroyed by <term>Ture</term>, the most excellent. 
This is the praise of the root mantra, 
And these are the twenty-one homages. 

Whoever is endowed with devotion to the Goddess, 
An intelligent person who recites this with great faith, 
Rising at dusk or at dawn, 
By remembering this, all fearlessness is perfectly granted. 
All sins are completely pacified, 
And all lower realms are destroyed. 

One will quickly be empowered 
By seventy million Buddhas. 
One will obtain greatness greater than this, 
And eventually proceed to the state of Buddhahood. 
By this, even the most potent and fierce poison, 
Whether consumed or encountered elsewhere,
</translation>

<summary>These pages contain the concluding verses of the Twenty-One Praises of Tara, detailing her power to destroy enemies, heal diseases, and grant protection. The text explains the spiritual benefits of reciting these praises, including purification of sins and the attainment of enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Tara, mantra, Hum, Tuttare, Ture, protection, healing, enlightenment, Tibetan Buddhism, prayer</keywords>

<translation page="19">
Father Apa, who is of great respect, and his son
Offered one piece of meat together with food, beer, and spirits once. May their people and wealth increase!
Kye! From this royal palace in the borderland region:
The emanation of virtuous gold, the Great One <term>Khoche</term> <gloss>a title of respect</gloss> Gendun,
The wise lady <term>Shecham</term> <gloss>noble lady</gloss> Drukl-mo, and Ugyen Wangdzom,
Together with their retinue, gave meat, food, and beer once. By this gift, may they obtain the virtuous Buddha!
Apa Naktrong, who has adopted all compassion,
From the great school of deep longing for the Holy Dharma,
Established this connection by offering food and beer once. May he be born in the field of Avalokiteshvara!
From Yulmo of the Wengkhar fortress in the beautiful land of water-ripples:
Sonam Tenpa, who has entered the path of the Holy Dharma, and
The "Gesar-flower" <note>original: "ge ser mtog"</note> Tashi Zangmo
Established a connection by offering food and spirits once. May they be born in the presence of Ugyen Pema!
The Master of Sages from the previous successive lineage,
The teacher Pema Karpo and the youth <term>Tagshar</term> <gloss>young man</gloss> Khipo, these two
Rendered service to the Dharma with food and spirits. May their merit increase like the limits of the sky!
From the district of Themkhang-bi, created as a cool grove:
The youth Kunzang, in the bloom of his youth,
Established a connection to the Dharma with food and spirits.
To the "Kumuda-flower" Karma Wangmo:
Her "small assembly" spirits and moon-like
Dharma is offered. May she be enriched with wealth that is never poor!
The elderly Tsang who knows how to speak, the Great One Gawa,
Offered service to the Dharma with food and beer once. May his life be long, without illness, and his enjoyments increase!
From the Tiger-Water Monastery on the secluded mountain,
Where the elephant of the mindful and conscious mind is tamed,
The renunciant who has opened the expanse of the Great Perfection <note>original: "rdzogs pa chen po"</note>,
Led by the teacher Sangdak Norbu:
The hermit meditator Tenzin Guru,
The renunciant who has abandoned and accepted, the meditator Tashi,
The meditator Karma who has abandoned worldly thoughts, and
The meditator Ngawang Trinley—all of them
Have great merit and offered to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Kuntuzangpo!
From Konbar in Yulmo, at the mouth of the descending elephant:
Pema Tsewang, great in Dharma and stature,
The pure-visioned Apa Druk Tsering,
The great-minded Apa Druk Phuntsok,
The heaven-appointed youth Kun-lay,
And others, together with food and spirits,
Each offered once. By this great blessing,
May their people, wealth, and food—these three—flourish and increase!
Of the meditator Tenzin Guru...

<leaf-break/>

These three rendered service with southern beer once. May their enjoyments be great and their people and wealth increase!
Ngawang Tenzin, who possesses intelligence and skill, and
Sonam Chodzom, of faithful and good thoughts—these two
Established a connection to the Dharma with southern beer twice.
Apa Tsewang, who possesses a good nature, and
The "Mañjuśrī-flower" Pema Wangmo,
Offered service to the Dharma with southern beer once.
Sonam Trinley, who is strong as a buffalo,
The perfect Bukri of unchanging faith, and
The "conch-sheet-flower" girl Sonam
Made a connection to the Dharma with southern beer twice. May they be born in the pure realm of Khechara!
Apa Thondup, the great treasure of knowledge,
Offered southern beer once to the profound Dharma.
Norbu Trinley, who is strong as a great lion,
Offered dried fish from the Indian river Bhati
Once and rendered service to the Dharma. By the merit of this virtuous request,
May all be victorious and obtain the Buddha-realm!
Kye! From the Tsenkhar Monastery on the white mountain-holder:
Apa Druk Norbu, of excellent power of speech, and
The "mountain-grove-flower" girl Chomo—
These two rendered service with southern beer once. May they be born in the land of Pema the Blissful!
From the rock-pile of Dovali, a land surrounded by rows of forest trees, beautiful with white wool:
Konchok, who has the power of enlightened activity,
Sithal Tashi, who has the strength of a thoroughbred horse,
The faithful woman Semcho Wangmo Lhamo,
The "soft-white-flower" Lhawang Dronma, and
The retinue, offered southern beer and one portion of meat. May they be born before the Buddha in the realm of bliss!
The youth Tshechu, like a tree trunk,
The youth Ngo-lay, like a sandalwood tree,
Each established a connection with southern beer once.
Apa Tsewang, Ngawang Druk Norbu,
Sonam Trinley, Ngo-lay, and Tshechu—
Joining together, they offered one breast of meat. By the great virtue of this single offering,
May they be born in the realm of Sukhavati!
The clear-fruited Drukkhyi Lhamo and
Also the "white-flower" girl Karmo
Established a connection to the Dharma with "assembly beer." May they obtain the rank of the Victorious Vidyadhara!
The hermit renunciant meditator Tsondru and
The very compassionate Rinchen Wangmo,
Together with southern beer and spirits...
</translation>

<translation page="20">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Led by them:
Drup Lhamo, whose own stream of being is distant <note>from worldliness</note>,
Dekyi Chodzom, of great love and compassion, and
The "saffron-flower" girl Yangdzin,
Established a connection to the Dharma with food and spirits. May they be born in Sukhavati in the future!
Kye! The Upper Kur region, beautiful with the white wool of its flowing rivers,
The perfect city of Tashi Drak:
The faithful mother Kunga Wangmo,
The "golden-flower" Norbu Dzompa, and
The charming Wangchen Thondup—these three
Offered southern beer and spirits twice.
They offered one portion of pork to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Pema Lingpa!
The great meditator Ugyen Tenzin, whose mind is emptied into the Holy Dharma,
And Dzompa Lhamo, who remembers the divine Dharma—these two
Offered food and spirits once. May they be born in the field of Kuntuzangpo!
Kye! The great field of the garden where the water and mountains are beautiful,
Yulmo Lekshig-gang, built in tiers:
The "silver-flower" Phagdor Wangmo
Offered food and beer once to the Dharma of the scriptures.
Her servants Ngak Tsering and
The great-hearted mother Sang-dron—these two
Offered the southern connection of "great rice" once. May they obtain the rank of liberation in the higher realms!
Apa Tsewang of unchanging faith,
The sandalwood tree youth Kol-lay, and
The beautiful and devoted girl Naka—
The father, son, and daughter <note>original: "pha pad gsum"</note>, with southern food, tea, and beer,
May they be born through miraculous birth in the presence of the Victorious One!
Mother Nyida, of great virtuous mind,
Offered the drink of fragrant tea once. May she be born in the presence of Ugyen Pema!
Kye! Formed upon the land of the great cool grove,
From the city of the great Domkhar in Yulmo:
Led by the very loving Dechen Wangmo,
The "Udumbara-flower" Tashi Wangmo,
The "Kumuda-flower" girl Pemo-la,
The "flower of supreme joy" girl Demchog-mo,
The "very clear flower" Tsewang Lhamo,
The "sky-flower" Thondup Zangmo, and
The "sun-flower" girl Khyimo-la—
These girls offered "assembly beer" once. By the power of this virtuous mandala,
May they obtain the supreme path of liberation and Great Bliss!
Kye! The park of Nangyer, a land of pleasant experience,
From the village of Chamakhardung formed upon the land:
The great-minded Apa Drukgal-la,
The skillful youth Dharma-la, and
The mother Yoka-mo, whose own stream of being is distant...

<leaf-break/>

Offered once. May they be born in the great realm of Tushita!
Those who performed the work of the paper <note>original: "sho gu"</note> from the forest trees:
Sonam Trinley, Norbu Trinley,
Nakpo-lay, Tamdrin Ngonser,
The great gate-keeper Tenzin Chodar, Dor-phun Tsok,
Rinchen Wangmo, Tashi Drukgyal,
The great gate-keeper Do-phen, Konchok Wangyal,
Tshechu-lay, and Na-lay—these eleven,
Having cast off the exhaustion and fatigue of their panting breath,
Offered the service of paper for the scriptures of the Victorious One.
By this offering, may they be born through miraculous birth in the presence of the Buddhas and receive prophecy!
Kye! From the very white eastern Tashi Gang-chen and
From the cool and very clear Yulmo Bhagi:
Trinley Norbu, who moves like the flight of a Garuda bird,
Offered southern beer from his faithful heart twice. May he be born in the realm of Abhirati!
The meditator Rigdzin, who realizes the meaning of Emptiness,
Established a connection by offering southern beer six times. May he be born in the Pema field of Chamara!
Now, "Well done, well done" to the patrons and their retinue!
"Happy, happy" to all those who established a connection!
To those who rendered service with a faithful heart
Upon the good ground of the white side of virtue:
By everything offered, whether of great or small substance,
By dedicating it to the path of enlightenment, may the ocean of existence
Be dried up without a body of fire <note>referring to the fires of suffering</note>, and may we beings,
Having cleared away the obstacles of the demons of wrong views,
See the great path that leads to Tushita!
Having seen it, I pray that we receive the prophecy!
Kye! The great miraculous scribes who bring things to maturation:
From Tashi Gang, Dungsam, Phimstang,
Wangkhar, and Kur-tod,
In the secluded mountain-holder of Samten Choling,
In the presence of the qualified Lama, the captain of beings,
All the secretaries assembled and constructed this.
First, upon the beautiful, soft, white beaten paper,
The emanation of the Victorious One, Pema Thuk-kha,
Constructed the first headings in the language of India.
The Wisdom Beings were invited to descend into the Commitment Beings.
The Lord of Enlightened Activity, Sherab Gyatso, and...
</translation>

<summary>
These pages list various patrons, meditators, and workers from regions like Yulmo and Kur-tod who contributed food, spirits, and labor (such as paper-making) to the production of the manuscript. Each entry concludes with a dedication of merit, wishing for the donors to be reborn in pure lands like Sukhavati or Tushita.
</summary>

<keywords>
patrons, Yulmo, Kur-tod, offerings, paper-making, dedication of merit, Sukhavati, Tushita, scribes, Pema Lingpa, Great Perfection
</keywords>

Apa Naktrong, who has adopted all compassion,
From the great school of deep longing for the Holy Dharma,
Established this connection by offering food and beer once. May he be born in the field of Avalokiteshvara!
From Yulmo of the Wengkhar fortress in the beautiful land of water-ripples:
Sonam Tenpa, who has entered the path of the Holy Dharma, and
The "Gesar-flower" <note>original: "ge ser mtog"</note> Tashi Zangmo
Established a connection by offering food and spirits once. May they be born in the presence of Ugyen Pema!
The Master of Sages from the previous successive lineage,
The teacher Pema Karpo and the youth <term>Tagshar</term> <gloss>young man</gloss> Khipo, these two

From the district of Themkhang-bi, created as a cool grove:
The youth Kunzang, in the bloom of his youth,

Her "small assembly" spirits and moon-like

The hermit meditator Tenzin Guru,
The renunciant who has abandoned and accepted, the meditator Tashi,

Have great merit and offered to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Kuntuzangpo!

Pema Tsewang, great in Dharma and stature,
The pure-visioned Apa Druk Tsering,

The heaven-appointed youth Kun-lay,

Each offered once. By this great blessing,

Sithal Tashi, who has the strength of a thoroughbred horse,

The "soft-white-flower" Lhawang Dronma, and

The youth Ngo-lay, like a sandalwood tree,

Also the "white-flower" girl Karmo
Established a connection to the Dharma with "assembly beer." May they obtain the rank of the Victorious Vidyadhara!
The hermit renunciant meditator Tsondru and
The very compassionate Rinchen Wangmo,
Together with southern beer and spirits...

Nakpo-lay, Tamdrin Ngonser,

Rinchen Wangmo, Tashi Drukgyal,

Having cast off the exhaustion and fatigue of their panting breath,
Offered the service of paper for the scriptures of the Victorious One.

Offered southern beer from his faithful heart twice. May he be born in the realm of Abhirati!

"Happy, happy" to all those who established a connection!

Upon the good ground of the white side of virtue:

Be dried up without a body of fire <note>referring to the fires of suffering</note>, and may we beings,
Having cleared away the obstacles of the demons of wrong views,
See the great path that leads to Tushita!
Having seen it, I pray that we receive the prophecy!
Kye! The great miraculous scribes who bring things to maturation:
From Tashi Gang, Dungsam, Phimstang,
Wangkhar, and Kur-tod,
In the secluded mountain-holder of Samten Choling,
In the presence of the qualified Lama, the captain of beings,
All the secretaries assembled and constructed this.
First, upon the beautiful, soft, white beaten paper,
The emanation of the Victorious One, Pema Thuk-kha,
Constructed the first headings in the language of India.
The Wisdom Beings were invited to descend into the Commitment Beings.

It will not be pacified; similarly, please understand also that it is so for attachment to desires. Just as someone afflicted by the disease of leprosy, tormented by worms moving beneath the skin, might rely entirely on the glow of a fire for the sake of comfort and experience a fleeting semblance of pleasure, yet the disease is not pacified—instead, the inflammation of lymph increases and the piercing pain grows worse—similarly, although one may feel a moment of satisfaction by indulging in the qualities of desire, thirst <note>craving</note> will expand further and remain insatiable. Therefore, please understand the nature of attachment to desires and reverse the thirst of attachment to desirable qualities from the very beginning.

Thus thirst will expand. After explaining the definitive cycle of attachment to desires, next is the explanation of the actual path. This includes an extensive explanation of the common vehicle path, and a brief presentation of the unique Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note> path and the entrance to the result. Regarding the first, identifying the object of meditation through a concise teaching, and explaining the stages of the five paths through an extensive explanation; regarding the first of those: To see the ultimate truth, constantly cultivate the correct mental engagement regarding all things. There is no other quality-possessing Dharma that is equal to this. The purpose is to see and realize the mode of being of the ultimate truth.

<leaf-break/>

Regarding the things comprised of matter and consciousness, they are produced by causes and conditions, and are thus <term>conditioned</term> <gloss>samskrita</gloss>. Furthermore, because the subsequent moment arises while the previous moment ceases, they are impermanent as they are constantly changing and perishing. In accordance with that, regarding correct mental engagement: all conditioned things except for the Truth of the Path are <term>contaminated</term> <gloss>sasrava</gloss>. This includes the five: the world as a vessel <note>the environment</note> comprised of the three realms, the physical senses, and the consciousness and mental factors which are contaminated. Feelings associated with suffering are the <term>suffering of suffering</term>. Feelings associated with pleasure are the <term>suffering of change</term>. Feelings associated with neutral states are the <term>suffering of conditioning</term>. Among these, even animals and the like know the <term>suffering of suffering</term>. The <term>suffering of change</term> is seen by those possessing intelligence. Although the <term>suffering of conditioning</term> is the basis of all suffering, others do not know it; it is realized by the <term>Noble Ones</term> <gloss>Aryas</gloss>. Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are empty," although "emptiness" is often used generally for the freedom from conceptual elaboration, here the aspect of emptiness within the Truth of Suffering refers to being empty of discordant causes. A creator being such as Ishvara or the theories of Time as a cause are impossible within the actual nature of things; one knows them to be empty of such a creator. One understands that things arise from the meeting of various harmonious and suitable causes and conditions.

<leaf-break/>

The nature of this—which includes uncontaminated wisdom, meditative concentration, and ethical discipline—is possessed of the power to abandon the afflictions and enables the attainment of the state of cessation. To generate certain knowledge in that way is the mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. Regarding the extensive explanation of the divisions of the five paths: there is the presentation of the stages of the path for ordinary beings and the presentation of the Path of the Noble Ones along with its result. Regarding the first, there is the teaching on the factors related to the Path of Accumulation and the teaching on the factors related to the Path of Application. Within the first: to show that on the Path of Accumulation one must dwell exceedingly in ethical discipline and wisdom: Even if men possess noble lineage, physical beauty, and great learning, if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline, they are not worthy of honor. Thus, whoever possesses these two qualities, even if they lack other qualities, should be honored. Even if a man belongs to a supreme lineage like the great Sal tree class of Kings or the great Sal tree class of Brahmins, and is physically handsome, healthy, and highly trained in the eighteen sciences and secular treatises, if he lacks the wisdom that knows the path to liberation and the mode of being, and lacks the ethical discipline of pure adoption and rejection, he is not an object of veneration for the world including the gods. Furthermore, if one possesses lineage,

</translation>

<translation page="15">
beauty, and learning, it goes without saying. Whoever possesses those two qualities—the wisdom of knowing the path to liberation and the mode of being, and the excellence of ethical discipline—becomes a supreme object of worldy offerings and veneration, even if they lack other qualities. Within that wisdom, there are three types: wisdom arising from hearing, from contemplation, and from meditation. In the context of the Path of Accumulation, the two wisdoms of hearing and contemplation are primary. Regarding ethical discipline, although there are infinite categories of Bodhisattva discipline, in this context it refers to the <term>Pratimoksha</term> <gloss>Individual Liberation</gloss> discipline. To show that those on the Path of Accumulation must equalize the conceptualizations of the eight worldly concerns: The Knower of the World <note>the Buddha</note> said: "Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and insignificance—equally regard these eight worldly concerns as not being the domain of your mind." The Knower of the World, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, taught that one must equalize these eight concerns. Specifically, gain of excellent resources and the poverty of not finding them; physical health and mental ease versus discomfort; hearing pleasant news versus unpleasant news spread by others; and direct praise versus blame.

<leaf-break/>

Since <note>non-virtue</note> will not arrive as a friend or helper, one should never perform sinful actions for the sake of others. Regarding the context of this verse: if one thinks that there is no need to abandon sinful actions because the result of committing them does not occur immediately: Though some sinful actions committed do not cut immediately like a weapon, when the time of death arrives, the results of those sinful actions will become manifest. Although the results of most sinful actions committed do not ripen and cut immediately like a wound from a sharp weapon, when the time of death, the intermediate state <note>bardo</note>, and future lives arrive, whatever the ripening results of those sinful actions are, they will be experienced and become manifest. If one asks how long it takes for the results of karma to ripen: there are two types—karma not certain to be experienced and karma certain to be experienced. Regarding the first, there is "done but not accumulated" and "not done but accumulated." Within "done but not accumulated," there are three levels: great, medium, and small. Entering the preparation for a virtuous or non-virtuous action but not reaching the main act is "small." Entering the preparation and stopping after half the main act due to regret is "medium." Entering the preparation and completing the main act, but developing intense regret before the conclusion is "done but not accumulated."

<leaf-break/>

Regarding "to be experienced in other lifetimes": these are the weaker actions that have been done and accumulated, for which the time of occurrence is uncertain. Depending on whether they meet with the awakening conditions of similar virtue or sin, the fact that they are uncertain to arise within two, three, or many lifetimes is what "to be experienced in other lifetimes" means. Even sinful actions that are certain to be experienced can be overcome by their remedies. The statement in this text that the results of sinful actions do not ripen immediately refers to the majority of karma, excluding "karma experienced in this lifetime." If one asks which will ripen first among both virtuous and non-virtuous actions committed that are ready to ripen: the Noble Ananda said: "Whichever is heavy, whichever is near, whichever is habitual, and whichever was done earlier—among those, the former will ripen first." The meaning is: among the virtuous and non-virtuous actions ready to ripen, the one with the greatest strength will ripen first. If the strength is equal, whichever virtuous or non-virtuous thought was most clear at the time of death and provided sustenance will ripen first. If the clarity is also equal, whichever had the greater force of habit will ripen first. If those are also equal, whichever virtuous or non-virtuous act was done first will ripen first, following the chronological order of when they were committed. If non-virtue is equal, and virtue...

</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the necessity of abandoning attachment to desires, the four aspects of the Four Noble Truths, and the importance of ethical discipline and wisdom over worldly status. It further explains the mechanics of karma, detailing how and when virtuous and non-virtuous actions ripen across lifetimes.</summary>
<keywords>desire, leprosy metaphor, four noble truths, suffering, emptiness, path of accumulation, eight worldly concerns, karma, ripening of results, ethical discipline, wisdom</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: they both seek mental peace</meta>
both possess a perspective based on attainment <note>grasping at concepts</note>. How is this different from the old interpretations? In fact, their error is even greater than others. The reason is that previously they held to the old interpretations of the Treatise on Numbers <note>the Abhidharma tradition</note>, and now they have also acquired a "new wisdom" of the Three Treatises <note>the Madhyamaka tradition</note>. This simply adds one more view to the rest. The Master says: "This is merely adding more weight to the load." It can be said that the more extensive their learning, the more numerous their delusions. 

The intention of the sutras and treatises is to rest the mind so it can reach the original source; this is why one is called a <term>shramana</term> <gloss>ascetic or seeker of the way</gloss>. Furthermore, one should rest the mind until one reaches the state of no-resting <note>a state beyond the effort of meditation</note>. 

Regarding the claim that the "Middle-Provisional" should not be refuted: one who embodies the Way realizes that this "provisional nature" is fundamentally the Way itself. There is no need to refute it. If you seek to refute it, are you not refuting the Way? You must look deeply into this meaning. The current talk of "refuting" is because people do not understand that the established provisional nature is originally the Way. Therefore, they treat the Way as the Non-Way. Now, we simply make them realize that the Non-Way is the Way; thus we call it "refuting." In reality, nothing is refuted. 

Second, one must know that nature <note>inherent nature or svabhava</note> is itself the provisional. Ordinary people are deluded and claim that the provisional becomes nature. The Buddhas observe that nature is always provisional. Therefore, it is said that all worldly truth <note>conventional reality</note>, when viewed by the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Come One; the Buddha</gloss>,

<summary>Jizang argues that adding new intellectual concepts to old ones only increases delusion. He explains that "refuting" the provisional is actually a method to reveal that conventional reality is inherently the Way.</summary>
<keywords>attainment, shramana, provisional nature, worldly truth, Tathagata</keywords>
</translation>

-><term>Gui</term><- <note>a signature or archival marker</note>

is always the supreme truth <term>paramartha-satya</term>. 

Third, one who embodies the Way knows that this Way has never been divided into "provisional" or "nature." Provisional and nature arise from two conditions <note>the dualistic perspective of the observer</note>. It is just as the single Way has never been "true" or "conventional" <note>the Two Truths</note>, yet arises from two conditions. 

Fourth, those who follow the teachings must recognize that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess an internal realization of unimpeded contemplation and an external mastery of limitless eloquence. They may speak of the provisional as nature, or speak of the provisional nature as being "non-nature." They may say nature is not nature, or that the provisional is nature. If you cling to a single piece of language, you will lose the complete meaning. Such a person is not a student of the Three Treatises.

<summary>The text emphasizes the non-duality of reality, explaining that divisions like "nature" and "provisional" are pedagogical tools used by Buddhas, rather than inherent properties of the Way.</summary>
<keywords>supreme truth, non-duality, Two Truths, unimpeded contemplation, Three Treatises</keywords>
</translation>

The reason is that previously they held to the old interpretations of the Treatise on Numbers <note>the Abhidharma tradition</note>, and now they have also acquired a "new wisdom" of the Three Treatises <note>the Madhyamaka tradition</note>. This simply adds one more view to the rest. The Master says: "This is merely adding more weight to the load." It can be said that the more extensive their learning, the more numerous their delusions. 

The intention of the sutras and treatises is to rest the mind so it can reach the original source; this is why one is called a <term>shramana</term> <gloss>ascetic or seeker of the way</gloss>. Furthermore, one should rest the mind until one reaches the state of no-resting <note>a state beyond the effort of meditation</note>. 

Regarding the claim that the "Middle-Provisional" should not be refuted: one who embodies the Way realizes that this "provisional nature" is fundamentally the Way itself. There is no need to refute it. If you seek to refute it, are you not refuting the Way? You must look deeply into this meaning. The current talk of "refuting" is because people do not understand that the established provisional nature is originally the Way. Therefore, they treat the Way as the Non-Way. Now, we simply make them realize that the Non-Way is the Way; thus we call it "refuting." In reality, nothing is refuted. 

Second, one must know that nature <note>inherent nature or svabhava</note> is itself the provisional. Ordinary people are deluded and claim that the provisional becomes nature. The Buddhas observe that nature is always provisional. Therefore, it is said that all worldly truth <note>conventional reality</note>, when viewed by the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Come One; the Buddha</gloss>,

<note original: "齊東">Qidong</note>

A hunter was lying in wait in the mountains at night when he saw a small person, about two feet tall, walking alone along the bottom of a ravine. After a short while, another person arrived of the same height. When they met, they asked each other where they were going. The first one said, "I am going to visit Yang the Scarred-Eye. I recently saw that his aura was dark and gloomy; he has many unlucky stars and his fortune is ill." The second one said, "I am going for the same reason. Your words are not mistaken." The hunter, knowing they were not human, gave a loud shout. Both figures vanished instantly. That night, he caught a large fox. On its forehead was a scar as big as a coin.

# The Dragon Plays with the Spider
<note original: "龍戲蛛">The Dragon Plays with the Spider</note>

Lord Xu was the magistrate of Qidong. In his government office, there was a tower used to store meats and cakes. Often, things were stolen and left in a mess on the floor. The family servants were frequently scolded for this, so they lay in wait to observe. They saw a spider as large as a bushel basket. Terrified, they ran to tell the Lord. The Lord thought it was strange. Every day, he sent the maidservants to throw food to it. The spider became increasingly tame; whenever it was hungry, it would come out and stay near

<column-break/>
</translation>

<translation page="166">
people, leaving only after it was full. After more than a year had passed, while the Lord was once reading official documents, the spider suddenly came to lie under his desk. Suspecting it was hungry, he was just calling for a servant to bring food when he saw two snakes flanking the spider. They lay there as straight as chopsticks. The spider curled its legs and shrank its belly as if unable to bear its fear. In an instant, the snakes grew violently large, becoming thicker than eggs. Greatly terrified, the Lord tried to run, but a massive clap of thunder erupted. The entire household was stunned and lost consciousness. After some time, the Lord regained his senses, but his wife and seven or eight maids and servants had been struck dead. The Lord remained ill for over a month and then passed away. The Lord was a man of integrity and honesty who loved the people deeply. When he was about to leave his post, the people collected money to see him off, and the sound of their weeping filled the fields.

The Historian Wu says: I always thought "The Dragon Plays with the Spider" was just a false rumor from the streets. Yet could it actually happen? I have heard that the strike of thunder must fall upon wicked people. Why then did a law-abiding and virtuous official suffer such a cruel and poisonous fate? Truly, the injustices of Heaven are many.
</translation>

<summary>A hunter encounters mountain spirits foretelling a fox's doom, followed by a story of a virtuous official whose kindness to a giant spider leads to a tragic lightning strike involving dragons.</summary>
<keywords>hunter, fox spirit, omen, Lord Xu, giant spider, dragon, lightning strike, virtuous official, Wu Shishi</keywords>

<translation page="50">
<meta>continues from previous page: "I understand words."</meta>
<note>The header text reads: Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries.</note>
"Knowing words" means being able to distinguish the right and wrong in people’s speech. If one exhausts the principles of things and affairs, then the mind becomes like a bright mirror. Only then can one use the Sage’s method of observing people to examine others.

### The Master said: "He who warms up the old and thereby knows the new is fit to be a teacher."

"Warming up" <note>original: 溫</note> means to seek out and unravel. The "old" refers to what was previously heard; the "new" refers to what is gained today. If in learning one can constantly practice what was previously heard and thereby always have new gains, then what is learned resides within oneself, and its application is inexhaustible. Therefore, such a person can be a teacher to others. If it is merely "the learning of memorization and recitation" <margin>pronounced "fu"</margin>, then nothing is gained in the heart <margin>Master Chen of Xin’an says: "with"</margin> and what is known is limited <margin>Master Chen of Xin’an says: "with"</margin>. This is the opposite of "inexhaustible application." Therefore, the *Record of Education* <note>original: Xueji, a chapter in the Classic of Rites</note> mocks such learning as being insufficient to make one a teacher of others. This is precisely the same point expressed here. <margin>Master Zhu says: "The learning of memorization and recitation, and warming up the old..."</margin> If one does not search within to find the principles, then remembering ten items is just ten items, and remembering a hundred items is just a hundred items. This is something dead. "Knowing the new" means seeing the principles within the very act of "warming up the old."

<meta>Volume Two</meta>
</translation>

<translation page="51">
<margin>Great Collection of Commentaries on the Analects</margin>
These principles become increasingly refined, surpassing what was known before. By extending them and applying them to similar cases, the knowledge remains constantly alive and never dies. <note>Gu</note> The *Doctrine of the Mean* mentions "warming up the old and knowing the new." This does not mean one does not warm up the old to know the new; rather, it means that by warming up the old, one gains the new again. <note>Qiu Mei</note> Regarding "warming up the old and knowing the new," if one only warms up the old without seeking the new, then one cannot "know the new" and is insufficient to be a teacher. Thus, the meaning depends on this distinction. If indeed there is nothing to "warm up," one is likewise insufficient to be a teacher. The emphasis of this phrase is on "knowing the new." This "knowing the new" is not about finding some bottomless principle, but rather that through constant and familiar practice, the meaning gradually emerges. It is like how principles all come from within oneself. When someone comes to ask about a principle, one investigates and deduces from that principle based on the person asking. Its application is then inexhaustible. As for the "learning of memorization and recitation," if one remembers one thing, one can only speak of that one thing and cannot produce ten. This is far from the meaning of "warming up the old." ○ Is this not also the principle of "learning what is below and reaching what is above"? What is contained in the Six Classics is this one principle; what is contained in the *Analects* and *Mencius* is also this one principle. By constantly warming them up and practicing them, one feels their flavor is deep and long-lasting, and new insights naturally arise. ○ It is also said: What was gained in the past...
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the Confucian concept of "warming up the old to know the new," contrasting genuine internal realization with mere rote memorization. They emphasize that true learning must be alive and adaptable, allowing a teacher to respond inexhaustibly to new situations.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Analects, education, warming up the old, knowing the new, Zhu Xi, memorization, teacher, principles</keywords>

<translation page="61">
<meta>continues from previous page: the envoy from Lu confirmed the fire had destroyed the temples of Huan and Xi.</meta>
The events followed the traditional records. The Marquis of Chen said to Zigong, "I now know why a Sage is so highly valued." Zigong replied, "It is not as good as being devoted to his Way and implementing his transformation." <margin>Revised following the Shuo Yuan</margin>

After Yang Huo fled to Qi, he then fled from Qi to Jin to seek refuge with the Zhao clan. When Confucius heard of this, he spoke to Zilu, "The Zhao clan will suffer from disorder for generations." Zilu said, "The fundamental power does not reside with him <note>Yang Huo</note>; how could he cause disorder?" Confucius said, "This is beyond your knowledge. Yang Huo is clever in his observations but not close to benevolence. He enjoyed favor under Jisun <note>the head of the powerful Ji family in Lu</note>, yet he plotted to kill him. Having failed, he fled to Qi. The people of Qi imprisoned him, but he escaped and returned to Jin. Thus, the two states of Qi and Lu have already rid themselves of their disease. Zhao Jianzi <note>the leader of the Zhao clan in Jin</note> is fond of profit and commits many killings; he will surely find Yang Huo’s talk pleasing and follow his schemes. The resulting disasters and defeats will not be limited to a single generation."

Ji Kangzi questioned Confucius, saying, "Today is the twelfth month of the Zhou calendar, which is the tenth month of the Xia calendar. Why are there still locusts <note>specifically, the migratory locust or katydid</note>?" Confucius replied, "I have heard that only after the Fire Star <note>Antares</note> has set do the hibernating insects fully hide. Currently, the Fire Star is still flowing toward the west <note>it has not yet descended below the horizon at sunset</note>." <margin>Note on the Zhengqi Hall edition</margin>

<summary>Confucius predicts long-term instability for the Zhao clan due to their employment of the treacherous Yang Huo and explains a biological anomaly using astronomical observations.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Zigong, Yang Huo, Zhao Jianzi, Zilu, Ji Kangzi, astronomy, Fire Star, locusts</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
The calendar official has made an error." Ji Kangzi asked, "By how many months is it off?" Confucius said, "By the tenth month of the Xia calendar, the Fire Star should have already disappeared. Since it is still visible, the leap month has been missed twice." <margin>See the Zuo Zhuan, 12th year of Duke Ai</margin>

King Fuchai of Wu intended to take Duke Ai <note>of Lu</note> to meet with the Marquis of Jin. Zifu Jingbo replied to the messenger, saying, "When a King assembles the feudal lords, the Earls <note>the Hegemons</note> lead the Marquises and Shepherds to appear before the King. When an Earl assembles the feudal lords, the Marquises lead the Viscounts and Barons to appear before the Earl. Now, as the lords meet, if your King intends to have our humble ruler meet the ruler of Jin, then Jin will effectively become the Hegemon. Furthermore, your staff summoned the lords in the name of a Hegemon, yet you treat your own King as a mere Marquis. What profit is there in this?" The people of Wu then stopped, but later regretted it and imprisoned Jingbo.

Jingbo said to Grand Vizier Pi, "In the tenth month, on the first day of the upper stem <term>Xin</term> <gloss>the eighth of the ten celestial stems</gloss>, Lu will perform sacrifices to the High God and the former kings, concluding on the day of the last <term>Xin</term>. My family has held official duties in this for generations; since the founding of Lu, this has never changed. If the ritual officials do not meet for this, they will say Wu is truly without ritual." Pi spoke to Fuchai, and they sent him back. When Zigong heard of this, he went to see Confucius and said, "The son of the Zifu clan is clumsy at persuasion."

<summary>Confucius explains a calendrical error regarding the Fire Star, and Zifu Jingbo uses diplomatic protocol and the requirements of ancestral sacrifice to secure his release from the King of Wu.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Ji Kangzi, calendar, Zifu Jingbo, King Fuchai of Wu, Duke Ai of Lu, Grand Vizier Pi, diplomacy, ritual</keywords>
</translation>

Since it is still visible, the leap month has been missed twice." <margin>See the Zuo Zhuan, 12th year of Duke Ai</margin>

King Fuchai of Wu intended to take Duke Ai <note>of Lu</note> to meet with the Marquis of Jin. Zifu Jingbo replied to the messenger, saying, "When a King assembles the feudal lords, the Earls <note>the Hegemons</note> lead the Marquises and Shepherds to appear before the King. When an Earl assembles the feudal lords, the Marquises lead the Viscounts and Barons to appear before the Earl. Now, as the lords meet, if your King intends to have our humble ruler meet the ruler of Jin, then Jin will effectively become the Hegemon. Furthermore, your staff summoned the lords in the name of a Hegemon, yet you treat your own King as a mere Marquis. What profit is there in this?" The people of Wu then stopped, but later regretted it and imprisoned Jingbo.

Jingbo said to Grand Vizier Pi, "In the tenth month, on the first day of the upper stem <term>Xin</term> <gloss>the eighth of the ten celestial stems</gloss>, Lu will perform sacrifices to the High God and the former kings, concluding on the day of the last <term>Xin</term>. My family has held official duties in this for generations; since the founding of Lu, this has never changed. If the ritual officials do not meet for this, they will say Wu is truly without ritual." Pi spoke to Fuchai, and they sent him back. When Zigong heard of this, he went to see Confucius and said, "The son of the Zifu clan is clumsy at persuasion."

<summary>Confucius explains a calendrical error regarding the Fire Star, and Zifu Jingbo uses diplomatic protocol and the requirements of ancestral sacrifice to secure his release from the King of Wu.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Ji Kangzi, calendar, Zifu Jingbo, King Fuchai of Wu, Duke Ai of Lu, Grand Vizier Pi, diplomacy, ritual</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Just as when a person’s illness enters the vital organs...</meta>
and is beyond what a doctor can save, then one must treat it using these methods. If the desired object can be obtained through effort, then exert that effort to obtain it. If it cannot be obtained through effort, there is no harm in providing it through trickery. For those so poor they cannot acquire wealth, one might borrow from a rich man and falsely claim it is a gift from a relative or friend, placing it at the head of the bed to give them this joy. This is the primary strategy for curing the illness of poverty. For those who have not yet attained office, one might urgently pay the grain tax <note>a method of purchasing official rank through grain contributions</note> or falsely claim they have been recommended for promotion. For those already in office, one might genuinely seek their appointment or falsely report their transfer. Regarding the longevity that the elderly desire, such news often comes from the mouths of astrologers, fortune tellers, or spirit healers; why should I be stingy with such words? These are all instances of using a person’s own ways to treat their own body. Nevertheless, while it is easy to treat various illnesses, it is difficult to treat poverty. The number of people in the world who worry about poverty until they fall ill, and whose illness becomes incurable, is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How can one possibly provide the grain from the Great Granary or the gold of Guo Kuang <note>Guo Kuang was a famously wealthy figure from the Eastern Han Dynasty</note> to everyone? People would all look to me at Mustard Seed Garden <note>the name of Li Yu's estate and publishing house</note>
</translation>

<translation page="106">
### Volume Six
<sig>4</sig>
to provide something joyful and make them suddenly and completely recover.

The Medicine of a Deeply Loved Person

The third category: a person whom the heart deeply loves <term>zhong'ai</term> <gloss>to cherish or concentrate affection upon</gloss> can serve as medicine. The private affections of the human heart must have a focus. It often happens that what a ruler cannot get from a minister, or a father from a son, is instead found in someone very distant or unworthy of love, upon whom the person’s spirit is focused and their very life depends. This is the object of their deep affection. It might be a charming wife or a beautiful concubine; it might be a close male companion <term>xiake</term> <gloss>an intimate guest or entertainer</gloss> or a favorite youth; or it could be a most intimate friend. If one longs for them but cannot have them, or has them but cannot be close to them, it can cause illness. Even if the cause of the illness is unrelated to this, once a person reaches a state of painful boredom and distress, they will inevitably think of the person they privately love. If they are suddenly brought together, like a fish returning to water, there is no one whose ears and eyes will not become clear and whose spirit will not suddenly become robust.
</translation>

<summary>Li Yu discusses using psychological placebos, such as fake wealth or status, to cure the sick, before moving on to the third category of unconventional medicine: the presence of a deeply loved person.</summary>
<keywords>psychology, poverty, rank, Guo Kuang, Mustard Seed Garden, love, companionship, healing, spirit</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: but Fayu failed to punish him with the staff, merely expelling him from the community.</meta>

Dao'an heard of this from afar. He placed a bramble switch inside a bamboo tube, sealed it, and sent it to Fayu. When Fayu opened the seal and saw the staff, he immediately said, "This is because of the monk who drank alcohol. I was not diligent in my instruction and leadership, which caused my teacher to send this gift of concern from such a distance." 

He then ordered the signal wooden block to be struck to assemble the community. Placing the bamboo tube in front of him, he burned incense and paid his respects. Lying prostrate on the ground, he ordered the <term>Vina</term> <gloss>the monastic administrator or disciplinarian</gloss> to strike him three times with the staff. He shed tears and reproached himself. Both the monastics and the laity within the region were moved to sighs of admiration. Because of this, the number of people who were encouraged to practice diligently grew very large.

The Eulogy says: Alas! If people today were to open a seal sent by an elder like Dao'an, those who would not smash the tube, break the staff, and speak arrogant words would be few indeed. Between the sagely teacher and the worthy disciple, even a thousand years later, I still hold these two gentlemen in high esteem.

### Performing Repentance Rituals for the Teacher

During the Jin dynasty, Faquang was a native of Xiapi. He lost both parents early in life and was known for his filial piety in serving his stepmother. Later, he left the home life and served the <term>Sramana</term> <gloss>monk</gloss> Danyin as his teacher. Once, Danyin became critically ill. Faquang prayed with utmost sincerity and performed repentance rituals for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw five-colored light illuminating the doors of Danyin's room. Danyin felt as if someone had shaken him with a hand, and his illness was immediately cured.

### Standing in the Snow Above the Knees

During the Wei dynasty, Shenguang's learning and understanding were unsurpassed in his generation. When Grandmaster Bodhidharma arrived from the Western Regions, Shenguang went to serve him as a teacher. Bodhidharma never spoke to him. One night, there was a great snowfall. Shenguang stood on the garden steps until dawn, by which time the snow had risen above his knees. Bodhidharma looked at him and asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what is it you seek?" 

Shenguang wept and said, "I only wish for the <term>Upadhyaya</term> <gloss>preceptor/monk</gloss> to open the gate of sweet dew <note>a metaphor for the nectar of immortality or the Buddha's teachings</note> and broadly deliver all living beings." 

Bodhidharma said, "The supreme and wonderful Way of the Buddhas requires diligent practice over vast kalpas, doing what is difficult to do and enduring what is difficult to endure. Even then, one might not reach it. How can you, with a light and shallow mind, hope for the True Vehicle? Your toil and suffering will be in vain." Hearing this instruction, Shenguang...
</translation>

<translation page="25">
...felt encouraged. He took a blade and cut off his own arm, placing it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma said, "When the Buddhas sought the Way, they forgot their own forms for the sake of the Dharma. Now that you have cut off your arm, your seeking may indeed be possible."

Shenguang said, "My mind is not yet at peace. I beg the teacher to pacify my mind."

Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you."

Shenguang said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is completely unattainable."

Bodhidharma said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you."

He then transmitted the Dharma to him, and Shenguang became the Second Patriarch <note>known as Huike</note>.

> The Eulogy says: The Second Patriarch obtained the Dharma truly because his sincerity was absolute and his karmic conditions had ripened. It was then that the needle and the magnet met <note>a metaphor for a perfect match</note>. It was not necessarily because he cut off his arm. If a foolish person tries to imitate this <note>literally "imitating a knit brow"</note>, they will eventually end up at the knife and chopping block. Alas! If transmitting the Dharma required cutting off an arm, then the patriarchs would have no intact skin. If becoming a Buddha required burning the body, then the holy ones would have no survivors. One should cut off the arm of afflictions and burn the body of ignorance. I hope practitioners of Zen will strive toward this.

---

### ->Self-Reproach After Leaving the Teacher<-

During the Tang dynasty, Qingjiang realized at a young age that life is like an illusion or a bubble. He took Vinaya Master Tanyi as his personal preceptor. He recited the sutras and laws, understanding everything he saw. Those who knew him said, "This is a 'thousand-mile colt' <note>a prodigy</note> of the monastic order." 

Once, he had a slight disagreement with his teacher, so he left and traveled to various regions. After visiting many Dharma assemblies, he reproached himself, saying, "I have traveled half the world, yet those who are like my original teacher are rare!" 

He then returned. At a time when the monks were assembled, he carried a bramble switch on his back <note>a gesture of asking for punishment</note> and called out, "This person <note>referring to himself</note> returns to submit to the Master once more. I only wish to be accepted." 

At that time, Master Tanyi scolded and insulted him. Qingjiang wept like rain while repenting and thanking him, saying, "In the past, my thoughts were ignorant; now, my heart has reached an awakening. I hope the Master will bestow great mercy and joy upon me." He begged for mercy repeatedly. Master Tanyi took pity on him, and they resumed their teacher-disciple relationship as before. After Tanyi passed away, Qingjiang served National Teacher Huizhong and was secretly transmitted the essentials of the Mind.

> The Eulogy says: To leave a sage and then realize one's error, and to endure scolding without retreating—this can be called both clarity and sincerity. That he finally received the Mind Seal, was it not because of this? Those of shallow faith leave forever over a small grudge and never forget their resentment over a slight scolding. To encounter a bright teacher in vain—what benefit is there in the end? It is like meeting an Emperor but failing to obtain a single office. How tragic!
</translation>

<summary>
These pages detail the extreme devotion of disciples toward their teachers, including Fayu's self-punishment, Shenguang's (Huike) self-mutilation to prove his sincerity to Bodhidharma, and Qingjiang's humble return to his original master. The text emphasizes that internal sincerity and the "cutting off" of spiritual ignorance are more important than physical sacrifice.
</summary>

<keywords>
Dao'an, Fayu, Bodhidharma, Shenguang, Huike, Qingjiang, Tanyi, filial piety, repentance rituals, transmission of Dharma, Zen, Mind Seal
</keywords>

The wind moves over the lake, creating the image of <term>Zhong Fu</term> <gloss>Inner Truth</gloss>. The superior man embodies the virtue of Heaven and Earth's love for life, and thus he deliberates on legal cases and delays executions. This is the meaning of Inner Truth. When a legal case is about to be finalized, he deliberates on it; when a sentence is about to be carried out, he delays it. Only then does he fully satisfy the hearts of men. To speak of "deliberating" on a case is to seek an exit from within the sentence; to speak of "delaying" death is to seek life from within death. <note>The author emphasizes the humanitarian aspect of the hexagram, linking legal mercy to the core concept of sincerity.</note> 

The Emperor Shun's anxiety over punishments, Yu's weeping over criminals, Tang's prayer at the hunting nets, and King Wen's burying of bleached bones—had these acts not proceeded from the sincerity of the original heart, who would they have moved? The Way of utmost sincerity can tread through water and fire, split metal and stone, and move Heaven and Earth. How much more so can it affect men? How much more so spirits and gods? The King hears the case, the Three Dukes hear it, and the Minister of Justice hears it: this is the "deliberating on legal cases." After ten days the officials hear it again, and after thirty days it is sent to the superiors: this is the "delaying of executions." Deliberating on cases carries the image of <term>Dui</term> <gloss>the Lake/Joy</gloss>; delaying executions carries the image of <term>Xun</term> <gloss>the Wind/Gently Penetrating</gloss>. 

Looking at the six lines of the hexagram as a whole, it represents "inner emptiness" <note>referring to the two broken yin lines in the center of the hexagram</note>. Taking the second and fifth lines of the two trigrams, 

<summary>This page discusses the ethical application of the Zhong Fu hexagram, specifically how a ruler's sincerity should manifest as mercy and careful deliberation in judicial matters.</summary>
<keywords>Zhong Fu, Inner Truth, legal deliberation, executions, sincerity, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="135">
it represents "inner fullness" <note>referring to the solid yang lines at the center of each trigram</note>; both are images of <term>Fu</term> <gloss>Trust/Sincerity</gloss>. Furthermore, the lower trigram is joyful to respond to the upper, and the upper is penetrating to comply with the lower; this also contains the meaning of Trust. 

Inner Truth is to have trust in one's heart. To have trust in one's heart is to have trust in the <term>Li</term> <gloss>Principle/Reason</gloss>. Having a vision of Principle and trusting in it is the means by which one trusts one's heart. Among the sixty-four hexagrams, there is not a single hexagram or a single line that does not use Trust as its pivot. If there is no Trust, then the center cannot be "empty," and how could it then be "full"? It is through emptiness that one attains fullness. The yielding lines trust in the firm lines; joy and penetration are the means to achieve emptiness. "Trust reaching even to pigs and fish" refers to the mutual resonance of emptiness. "Crossing the water in a wooden boat" refers to emptiness aiding emptiness. The "fullness" of it is Principle. Principle is Heaven; it is the reason why the heart is a heart. This is what is meant by "beneficial to persist."

<note>The hexagram symbol for Xiao Guo (Preponderance of the Small) is shown, consisting of the trigram Zhen (Thunder) below and Gen (Mountain) above.</note>
<term>Zhen</term> <gloss>Thunder</gloss> below
<term>Gen</term> <gloss>Mountain</gloss> above

<summary>The author explains that sincerity is rooted in the alignment of the heart with universal Principle, serving as the central axis for all hexagrams and human actions.</summary>
<keywords>sincerity, trust, Principle, emptiness, fullness, Zhen, Gen, Xiao Guo</keywords>
</translation>

# High-Minded and Accomplished Men Will Have Their Own Way to Correct This

## Instructions for Dong Zhiguang

The student Dong Sizhang <note>Dong Zhiguang's secular name</note> was born and raised in a wealthy and noble household, yet he developed the resolve to seek liberation from birth and death early on. This is surely due to the internal scenting power of the supreme conditions of <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> practiced in previous lives. He first studied under the Great Master Yunqi <note>the famous Master Lianchi</note>, who transmitted the Pure Land Dharma gates to him. Recently, he visited this old man at Shuangjing, wishing to receive the <term>Upasaka</term> <gloss>layman's</gloss> precepts. He also openly confessed that his sinful karma is deep and heavy, and he asked for the essentials of escaping suffering and how he should practice to extinguish his transgressions. 

This old man therefore instructed him, saying: Since you already know that the roots of your sins are deep and heavy, you should follow the ancient virtues who taught people to "dissolve old karma according to the situation, and strictly avoid creating new misfortunes." For sentient beings with heavy karma, the Buddha opened the gate of <term>repentance</term> <gloss>ksama</gloss>, which is the most effective convenience for escaping suffering. A verse says:

> All sins are like frost and dew,
> The sun of wisdom can dissolve them.
> If you wish to repent,

# High-Minded and Accomplished Men Will Have Their Own Way to Correct This

## Instructions for Dong Zhiguang

The student Dong Sizhang <note>Dong Zhiguang's secular name</note> was born and raised in a wealthy and noble household, yet he developed the resolve to seek liberation from birth and death early on. This is surely due to the internal scenting power of the supreme conditions of <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> practiced in previous lives. He first studied under the Great Master Yunqi <note>the famous Master Lianchi</note>, who transmitted the Pure Land Dharma gates to him. Recently, he visited this old man at Shuangjing, wishing to receive the <term>Upasaka</term> <gloss>layman's</gloss> precepts. He also openly confessed that his sinful karma is deep and heavy, and he asked for the essentials of escaping suffering and how he should practice to extinguish his transgressions. 

This old man therefore instructed him, saying: Since you already know that the roots of your sins are deep and heavy, you should follow the ancient virtues who taught people to "dissolve old karma according to the situation, and strictly avoid creating new misfortunes." <translation page="120">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
Water, fire, soil, and stone exhaust the substance and function of heaven and earth. This is distinctly different from the theories of various other schools. However, Master Zhang <note>Zhang Zai</note> says in his *Zhengmeng* <gloss>Correcting Ignorance</gloss> that water and fire are <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy</gloss>. Therefore, their properties of flaming upward and moistening downward follow the rising and falling of <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term>, and soil cannot constrain them. Wood and metal are the flowers and fruits of the soil. Their natures contain a mixture of water and fire. Thus, as for wood as an object: if soaked in water, it grows; if it meets fire, it burns; yet it never separates from them. This is because it obtains the flowering of the soil, floating at the intersection of water and fire. As for metal as an object: it obtains the essence of fire from the dryness of the soil, and it obtains the essence of water from the dampness of the soil. Therefore, water and fire depend on each other without harming each other. Even when melted, it simply flows without being consumed. This is because it obtains the solid essence of the soil at the boundary of water and fire. Soil is that by which things complete their beginning and their end. It is the substance of the earth and the finality of transformation. It is that through which water and fire rise and fall.

<summary>The author critiques standard Five Elements theory by citing Zhang Zai's view that water, fire, soil, metal, and wood are interdependent transformations of vital energy centered on soil.</summary>
<keywords>Zhang Zai, Zhengmeng, Five Elements, Yin Yang, Qi, metaphysics</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="121">
Soil is that which encompasses all substances without omission. Master Zhang's explanation of how metal, wood, water, fire, and soil are produced is an unchanging principle.

the fatwa of the person who issued a fatwa that it is permissible <note>Arabic: halal</note> to sell chickens to the Chinese <note>The context involves ritual slaughter and the use of animals in non-Muslim festivals</note>. Such is the proof.

upon the best of Allah's creation, and upon his family and his companions, the guides of the community, and upon the scholars who are the heirs <note>referring to the Hadith: scholars are the heirs of the Prophets</note>, and those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection.
To proceed: In Makkah, in the year of the Migration of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, <unclear>one thousand three hundred and seventeen</unclear>, I

However, some of them rejected my fatwa, specifically their leader <unclear>named Haji Madi bin Macan</unclear>, and he sought help from Haji Abu al-Hasan Palembang Talang Bali in Makkah. Then Haji Abu al-Hasan assisted him and also found two companions in Makkah, namely Muhammad Mansuri Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan. <unclear>Then Haji Abu al-Hasan immediately issued a fatwa of permissibility to Haji Madi bin Macan and he informed him that he had already asked the question to</unclear> Mufti Sayyid Ahmad bin Zaini Dahlan in the past, and the Mufti had issued a fatwa of permissibility as well. <column-break/>

Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan also permitted it. Such was the letter of Haji Abu al-Hasan from Makkah to Haji Madi bin Macan in Belebu. Then Haji Dat 
demanded <unclear>Raden Muhammad Arif Buyan</unclear> to immediately translate the letter of Haji Abu al-Hasan and send the copy to me at Pangkal Pinang. <unclear>Then I</unclear> 
immediately sent his letter to Makkah to be presented at Mantewei. On Friday, 5th of Ramadan 1323 <note>approx. November 1905 CE</note>, the Head Penghulu of Mantewei, Haji Marzuqi, showed the letter of Haji Abu al-Hasan from Makkah informing that he himself had issued a fatwa of permissibility for selling chickens to the Chinese, and that the fatwa of Mufti Sayyid Ahmad Dahlan was also permissible, and the fatwa of Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil was also permissible. </translation>
