<meta>continues from previous page: ...their mother.</meta>

<translation page="15">
Their males and females are equal in this because they are her brothers and sisters through her mother. It is well known that brothers through the mother, when they are with their sisters, inherit in this way. If they were to divide the inheritance of a son of a sister through the mother and the maternal aunts related through her, they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females. End.

The apparent meaning in both the <term>Tuhfa</term> <gloss>The Gift, by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</gloss> and the <term>Nihaya</term> <gloss>The Ultimate Goal, by al-Ramli</gloss> is that their statement "equally" is a condition for both the children of the child of the mother, and for the maternal uncles and aunts related through her. This is explicitly stated in the <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Garden, by Zakariyya al-Ansari</gloss> as you have learned from its phrasing. However, the matter is not like that; rather, their statement "equally" is a condition for the children of the mother's child only. In that case, the exception is clear. Then he mentioned the reason for the exception, until he said: As for the maternal uncles and aunts from the mother—meaning the sisters of the mother of the deceased and her sisters through her mother—they are excluded from the aforementioned rule as you have learned. Their exclusion from it necessitates that they inherit such that the male receives the portion of two females, because they occupy the status of the mother, as is explicitly stated in the primary texts <note>original: "al-mutun"</note> let alone others. If they were to inherit the share of the mother as if she were the deceased, they would divide it according to the number of their heads <note>equally per capita</note>.

<column-break/>

Jamal al-Ramli followed this in his <term>Nihaya</term>, and their teacher Zakariyya al-Ansari preceded them in <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term>. His phrasing is: And excluded from that are the children of the brother through the mother and the maternal uncles and aunts through her; they do not divide that such that the male receives the portion of two females, but rather they divide it among themselves equally, as will be known from what follows in his words. End.

I understood it as such so that we do not judge that it was an oversight. End. And God knows best. According to the Hanbalis, the maternal uncle is prioritized over all <term>dhawi al-arham</term> <gloss>uterine relatives/non-primary heirs</gloss>. If the male and female are from the same side, such as children of a daughter at the same degree, and one of them reaches the heir first, they are prioritized by that. Otherwise, they inherit through both, such as the daughter of the daughter of the daughter of the son of a daughter—as when the son of Zayd's daughter marries the daughter of his other daughter and they have a daughter. Or the daughter of a sister through the father who is also the daughter of a brother through the mother—as when Zayd's brother through his mother marries his sister through his father and they have a daughter. Or the daughter of a maternal uncle who is also the daughter of a paternal uncle—as when Zayd's maternal uncle marries his paternal aunt and they have a daughter.

Note: <insert>they are equal in it</insert> is taken from our saying "a branch."
</translation>

<translation page="16">
When descending generation after generation, etc., to the intermediary between the uterine relatives and the closest heir is considered in the first. It says in <term>Kashf al-Ghawamid</term> <gloss>Unveiling the Obscurities</gloss> by al-Sibt: The mother's father occupies the status of the mother, the father's mother's father occupies the status of the father's mother, and the mother's father's mother occupies the status of the mother's father. If the intermediary were not considered, the mother's father's mother would occupy the status of the heir, which is the mother, and thus she would be equal to the mother's father, but no one holds this view. As for what is in the legal opinions <term>fatawa</term> of the scholar Ibn Hajar regarding making the son of a maternal aunt equal to the maternal uncle, it requires further scrutiny. It is understood from our statement "according to his inheritance from him" as <term>asaba</term> <gloss>agnatic heir</gloss> or <term>fard</term> <gloss>fixed share</gloss> that the intermediary is considered in transferring the share of the heir to the uterine relative, since agnatic and fixed shares are actualized in the connected branches. It says in <term>al-Fath</term> <gloss>The Opening</gloss>: The summary of this is that you raise the lower descendant generation by generation, and for the higher ancestor, it is the opposite. End. Therefore, I said after that: meaning the share of the heir descends to his connected branches, etc. Also, there might be a uterine relative at the end of the branches, such as a daughter of a son of a daughter of a son, and a son of the daughter of that daughter. If the intermediary were not considered, they would be excluded because they are not an heir of this heir. But it is not so; rather, the share of the son's daughter

<column-break/>

descends to her branches through three, then the share of the son descends to his daughter, and the share of the daughter to her son. And God knows best.

The author—may God grant him enjoyment of it—said: This is the end of what I intended to transcribe from the aforementioned book during my journey to the Noble Mecca for the <term>Hajj</term> <gloss>Pilgrimage</gloss> in the year 1232 <note>equivalent to 1817 CE</note>, so that it may be a reference for me in case of need, as it is the summary of the core of that commentary. Because it was not possible for me to bring the original work with me, although the original is better as it contains more clarification and explanation, and mentions chapters on examples of the categories, their branches, their differences, the rulings of <term>radd</term> <gloss>the return of shares</gloss>, the principles of their legal problems and examples, and the school of the "People of Relationship" <note>the legal school specializing in uterine relative inheritance</note> and its branches. I ask God Almighty to benefit the people of Islam with both of them. And May God bless our Master Muhammad and his family and all his companions and grant them peace. Amen. M <note>abbreviation for 'tamma', meaning finished</note>.
</translation>

<summary>This page concludes the technical discussion on the distribution of inheritance among uterine relatives, specifically maternal uncles and aunts, and clarifies the role of intermediaries in calculating shares. The author concludes with a personal note about transcribing this work during his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1817 CE.</summary>

If they were to divide the inheritance of a son of a sister through the mother and the maternal aunts related through her, they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females. End.

The apparent meaning in both the <term>Tuhfa</term> <gloss>The Gift, by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</gloss> and the <term>Nihaya</term> <gloss>The Ultimate Goal, by al-Ramli</gloss> is that their statement "equally" is a condition for both the children of the child of the mother, and for the maternal uncles and aunts related through her. This is explicitly stated in the <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Garden, by Zakariyya al-Ansari</gloss> as you have learned from its phrasing. However, the matter is not like that; rather, their statement "equally" is a condition for the children of the mother's child only. In that case, the exception is clear. Then he mentioned the reason for the exception, until he said: As for the maternal uncles and aunts from the mother—meaning the sisters of the mother of the deceased and her sisters through her mother—they are excluded from the aforementioned rule as you have learned. Their exclusion from it necessitates that they inherit such that the male receives the portion of two females, because they occupy the status of the mother, as is explicitly stated in the primary texts <note>original: "al-mutun"</note> let alone others. If they were to inherit the share of the mother as if she were the deceased, they would divide it according to the number of their heads <note>equally per capita</note>.

<column-break/>

Jamal al-Ramli followed this in his <term>Nihaya</term>, and their teacher Zakariyya al-Ansari preceded them in <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term>. His phrasing is: And excluded from that are the children of the brother through the mother and the maternal uncles and aunts through her; they do not divide that such that the male receives the portion of two females, but rather they divide it among themselves equally, as will be known from what follows in his words. End.

I understood it as such so that we do not judge that it was an oversight. End. And God knows best. According to the Hanbalis, the maternal uncle is prioritized over all <term>dhawi al-arham</term> <gloss>uterine relatives/non-primary heirs</gloss>. If the male and female are from the same side, such as children of a daughter at the same degree, and one of them reaches the heir first, they are prioritized by that. Otherwise, they inherit through both, such as the daughter of the daughter of the daughter of the son of a daughter—as when the son of Zayd's daughter marries the daughter of his other daughter and they have a daughter. Or the daughter of a sister through the father who is also the daughter of a brother through the mother—as when Zayd's brother through his mother marries his sister through his father and they have a daughter. Or the daughter of a maternal uncle who is also the daughter of a paternal uncle—as when Zayd's maternal uncle marries his paternal aunt and they have a daughter.

Note: <insert>they are equal in it</insert> is taken from our saying "a branch."
pages.16:
When descending generation after generation, etc., to the intermediary between the uterine relatives and the closest heir is considered in the first. It says in <term>Kashf al-Ghawamid</term> <gloss>Unveiling the Obscurities</gloss> by al-Sibt: The mother's father occupies the status of the mother, the father's mother's father occupies the status of the father's mother, and the mother's father's mother occupies the status of the mother's father. If the intermediary were not considered, the mother's father's mother would occupy the status of the heir, which is the mother, and thus she would be equal to the mother's father, but no one holds this view. As for what is in the legal opinions <term>fatawa</term> of the scholar Ibn Hajar regarding making the son of a maternal aunt equal to the maternal uncle, it requires further scrutiny. It is understood from our statement "according to his inheritance from him" as <term>asaba</term> <gloss>agnatic heir</gloss> or <term>fard</term> <gloss>fixed share</gloss> that the intermediary is considered in transferring the share of the heir to the uterine relative, since agnatic and fixed shares are actualized in the connected branches. It says in <term>al-Fath</term> <gloss>The Opening</gloss>: The summary of this is that you raise the lower descendant generation by generation, and for the higher ancestor, it is the opposite. End. Therefore, I said after that: meaning the share of the heir descends to his connected branches, etc. Also, there might be a uterine relative at the end of the branches, such as a daughter of a son of a daughter of a son, and a son of the daughter of that daughter. If the intermediary were not considered, they would be excluded because they are not an heir of this heir. But it is not so; rather, the share of the son's daughter

<column-break/>

descends to her branches through three, then the share of the son descends to his daughter, and the share of the daughter to her son. And God knows best.

The author—may God grant him enjoyment of it—said: This is the end of what I intended to transcribe from the aforementioned book during my journey to the Noble Mecca for the <term>Hajj</term> <gloss>Pilgrimage</gloss> in the year 1232 <note>equivalent to 1817 CE</note>, so that it may be a reference for me in case of need, as it is the summary of the core of that commentary. Because it was not possible for me to bring the original work with me, although the original is better as it contains more clarification and explanation, and mentions chapters on examples of the categories, their branches, their differences, the rulings of <term>radd</term> <gloss>the return of shares</gloss>, the principles of their legal problems and examples, and the school of the "People of Relationship" <note>the legal school specializing in uterine relative inheritance</note> and its branches. I ask God Almighty to benefit the people of Islam with both of them. And May God bless our Master Muhammad and his family and all his companions and grant them peace. Amen. M <note>abbreviation for 'tamma', meaning finished</note>.

explicitly false. Rather, what drove the claimant to it was ignorance of its meaning combined with deception in the question, as will be explained later, alongside a lack of desire for divine reward and a love for ease and luxury. Consider this: if a sick person is able to endure a hardship equivalent to the hardship of walking in rain and mud, as previously mentioned, then how can a healthy person not endure a hardship that is less than that? This is an inescapable logical comparison. Indeed, if there were a distribution of <term>riyals</term> <gloss>currency/coins</gloss> in the old mosque, would you see the one claiming hardship staying behind due to an inability to endure the walk? Or would you find him the first to rush toward it? Success in returning to the truth is by God’s grace. Amen.

### The Ninth Matter: Clarifying the Ruling on the Impermissibility of Multiple Friday Prayers in This Incident
It is not hidden from any person of knowledge that our Shafi'i Imams <note>scholars of the Shafi'i school of Islamic jurisprudence</note> — may God be pleased with them — only permitted the multiplication of Friday prayers <note>holding more than one Friday prayer in a single town</note> when there is a need and necessity. This necessity is defined as the "certainty of difficulty in gathering" <note>original: "usr al-ijtima' yaqinan"</note>, as will be cited from *al-Tuhfah*, to remove the distress resulting from unbearable hardship. It is well-known that every necessity is measured by its extent. They have identified specific causes for the difficulty of gathering: either due to fighting <note>civil strife</note>, or the narrowness of the location given the large number of worshippers, or the distance of the town's outskirts. They have assigned restrictive conditions to each of these causes that must be certainly present.

The condition for the narrowness of the location is that there is certainly no place in the town of the Friday prayer that can accommodate them. Furthermore, the relied-upon view — as stated in *al-Tuhfah* and *al-Nihayah* — is that the consideration is based on those who usually attend the Friday prayer, not just those who actually attend, whether the location is a mosque or otherwise. The certainty of the lack of space is only true if there is no place for the Friday prayer at all, and it is impossible to expand the existing narrow location, and it is impossible to roof over an unroofed area if praying in the sun 

<column-break/>

results in a hardship that is certainly unbearable. The certain absence of these solutions is the "excuse" that our Master al-Ghazali <note>the famous 11th-century theologian and jurist</note> referred to when he said: "If their gathering in one congregational mosque is excused <note>literally: made impossible/difficult</note>, it is permitted in two mosques..." etc. This is because the meaning of "excuse" <term>ta'adhur</term> is the total lack of possibility, not merely a suspicion that the space is insufficient, nor a mere claim of narrowness without verification of the aforementioned meaning through certainty. Such claims are mere guesswork and a pursuit of ease and luxury.

Furthermore, the condition for the "distance of the outskirts" is either that the distance requires traveling from dawn until the time of the Friday prayer, or a distance from which the call to prayer <note>the Adhan</note> cannot be heard — as explained regarding the minaret in the Seventh Matter — or the presence of unbearable hardship according to the meaning passed in the Eighth Matter. Thus, the certainty of the difficulty of gathering is not established except through these mentioned restrictions and conditions.

Therefore, the statement in *al-Tuhfah*, "and the certainty of the difficulty of their gathering," means the existence of one of those causes with its conditions. The same applies to every statement by al-Ghazali. When the "need" is verified — meaning by the existence of what we have mentioned — they have regulated the difficulty of gathering arising from one of those causes by "unbearable hardship." It says in *al-Tuhfah*: "The criterion for difficulty is that it contains a hardship that is not normally bearable." The end. This hardship is what involves distress and necessity, as preceded in the Eighth Matter, and it will be mentioned here from al-Qamuli, who explicitly stated this with his evidence. From the legal opinions <term>fatawa</term> of our teacher, al-Sayyid Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Yahya: when al-Qamuli mentioned in *al-Jawahir* the permissibility of multiplication due to difficulty, he supported it by citing God's word: "He has not placed upon you in religion any hardship." This indicates that our scholars' permission for multiplication is solely to negate hardship. The end (abridged). This is also an explicit statement that the presence of distress and necessity is what is meant by "unbearable hardship."
</translation>

<translation page="13">
which is the regulatory standard for the difficulty of gathering that permits multiplication. It is not intended for the minor hardship of walking to the congregational mosque while seeking comfort and luxury.

**If you know** and have verified everything mentioned here, and you know what was stated in the Fifth Matter regarding the description of the old mosque, its spaciousness, and the vastness of its courtyard, you will then know and realize the absence of the cause that permits multiplication — which is the lack of a place that accommodates them. That is, accommodating those who usually attend, as is the relied-upon view of Ibn Hajar, al-Ramli, and others. This is because of the vastness of the mentioned mosque and its courtyard; look upon it again.

**And if you know** what was mentioned in the Seventh Matter regarding the distance between the two mosques — that it does not involve unbearable hardship in the sense mentioned in the Eighth Matter — and that the call to prayer is heard between the ends of the two mosque neighborhoods, let alone it being a distance requiring travel from before dawn until the Friday prayer time; **you will then know** and realize the absence of the cause that permits multiplication, which is the "distance of the outskirts." This is due to the short distance between the two neighborhoods and the absence of the aforementioned hardship.

**Thus it has appeared** and become clear to you now, through what has been mentioned and recorded, that the current situation does not permit the multiplication of Friday prayers because none of its causes certainly exist — let alone the certainty of any of them existing. All the texts of the Imams stating the permissibility of multiplication under specific conditions cannot be used as evidence for permissibility in this incident, which is void of those conditions. Similarly, the response of the Mufti of Mecca cannot be taken as evidence for the validity of multiplication here, because it mentions the restriction of "need" and "hardship," which 

<column-break/>

does not exist at all in this specific case, as has been established in these matters repeatedly and will be clearly known from the upcoming Eleventh Matter. And with God is success.

Regarding the dissemination of the characteristics of opposition displayed by those claiming the permissibility of multiplication in this incident. These characteristics clearly indicate their defiance of the truth and that they have no motive other than establishing multiplication by any means, through any path, and by any school of thought — even if it is through a void method, as will be known from their words. This is in addition to their motives of defiance, seeking dominance, arrogance, and cooperation in falsehood.

**Among these characteristics:** First, what occurred from the builder of the newly created mosque, as mentioned in the Sixth Matter, regarding what his soul previously claimed about building a mosque and establishing Friday prayer in it; that the previous judge prohibited him in the presence of the scholars, and that he seized the opportunity at this time. He and the judge wrote to us, requesting some texts from the scholars that they could use as evidence for the validity of multiple Friday prayers in the new mosque, by any means possible.

May God guide you; do not offer an excuse."

**Also among them:** His statement in that same paper: "And what is the point of the scholars' intent in preventing multiplication... if there is no way in the Shafi'i school, they should ask the scholars in

The ministers may be clever, but Alexander Nikolaevich <note>Tsar Alexander II</note> does not fully trust them. To assist them, he has called upon the famous doctor Liprandi <note>Ivan Liprandi, a high-ranking official known for his involvement in secret police work and suppression of revolutionary circles</note>, who treats with heroic remedies and will undoubtedly bring things to a tragedy sooner. The great consolation for governmental Petersburg now is the people and the people's attachment to the Tsar. They threaten the revolutionary youth with the people. "The Tsar only needs to wave his hand, and the students will be no more." Yes, undoubtedly they will be no more; but on the next day the nobility in all of Russia will also be no more, and along with the nobility, the entire bureaucracy will fall under the axe; you yourselves, my dears, will perish. Well then, try waving that hand! And there will remain the people and the Tsar. But what will this Tsar do with this people? For our Tsar is bureaucratic and aristocratic, not of the <term>Zemstvo</term> <gloss>land/people's assembly</gloss>. He himself will drown in noble blood, only to yield his place to some new Pugachev <note>Yemelyan Pugachev, leader of a massive peasant uprising in the 18th century</note>! Why not try the methods of Nicholas <note>Tsar Nicholas I, known for his harsh autocracy</note> instead: the whip, the gallows, and Siberia? Good methods. But they are unlikely to help you now. For fear has been killed in Russia. Nowadays people will go to the place of execution laughing at you. Even for the cowards, there is no reason to retreat before your terror. In Russia now there is a fear more terrifying—the fear of popular retribution. And if one must choose between the axe or the gallows, then certainly it is better to fall with the consciousness of a noble feat than as a victim of a fatal misunderstanding by the people.

You have one more remedy—war. A national war against the Germans, in alliance with Italy and France, perhaps even for the freedom of the Slavs, if only to avoid giving freedom to the Russian people. Yes, indeed, to go to war against the Germans is a good, and most importantly, a necessary Slavic cause; in any case, it is better than strangling Poles to please the Germans. To rise for the liberation of the Slavs from under the Turkish and German yoke will be a requirement, a necessity, and a sacred duty of a liberated Russian people. But you, enemies of Russian and Polish freedom, what kind of freedom will you give the Slavs? Or do you want to repeat the old, shameful deception for the hundredth time? Without satisfying anyone or resolving anything at home, what will you lean on? Even the army you will have to 
</translation>

<translation page="534">
maintain on credit through foreign subsidies. And you will only serve as a means for foreign goals; you yourselves will gain nothing, while you will ruin Russia completely. Or perhaps you are counting on her exhaustion? Do you think you can pacify her with hunger? Be careful not to miscalculate: war did not prevent the <term>Pugachevshchina</term> <gloss>Pugachev's rebellion</gloss> or the Novgorod riot in our history.

But all our efforts are in vain. Neither war, nor the tricks of the supposedly liberal (?) ministry, nor open reaction will help you. The people have awakened and are waiting for their hour; you yourselves contributed to this awakening. By flirting with them and inciting them against the young educated generation, you yourselves awaken in them a consciousness of strength, and they will take by force what you do not want to give voluntarily.

For a peaceful outcome to the current unavoidable crisis, there is only one remedy: a <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> <gloss>Assembly of the Land</gloss> representing all the people, and within it, the resolution of the people's land affairs. This is the sole saving remedy in the hands of the Tsar. But he does not want to use it. This means he wants blood.

When rulers ruin a country, private individuals must take up the task of salvation. To all true conservatives who have the mind to understand and foresee necessary events—to all merchants, priests, and nobles, to military and civil officials who love tranquility and peace and wish to preserve life, property, wives, sisters, and children, to all who hold dear the prosperity and glory of Russia—I would advise them to think hard about this. For not much time remains for free reflection. And it would not be bad if they, having come to an agreement, formed among themselves a vast conservative society, which I would suggest they call: "Society for the Salvation of Russia from Tsarist Myopia and Criminal Ministerial Charlatanism," and let them raise their voices in unison in favor of a <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> as the only means for preventing a bloody, destructive catastrophe.

And for us, the revolutionary party, what is to be done? We too shall unite and stand under the banner of the "People's Cause" <note>the name of Bakunin's revolutionary program and future journal, Narodnoye Delo</note>.
</translation>

<meta>continues from previous page: wonderful is in what it was given in its throat of wondrous songs and the...</meta>
melancholy, enchanting melodies; or in noble character, or the delicate craftsmanship of the paw, or strange guidance and useful assistance; or even in the harmfulness that invites intense caution and precise cunning. Thus, it is prioritized in mention for those reasons. And what is more wondrous than the <term>magpie</term> <gloss>Arabic: al-ʿaqʿaq</gloss>, the truth of its senses, the intensity of its caution, and its excellent discernment? There is no bird on earth that protects its eggs with more comprehensive protection or subtler knowledge than it. <note>The magpie is often cited in classical Arabic literature for its intelligence and perceived thievery.</note>

Uthman ibn Affan <note>The third Caliph of Islam</note>, may God be pleased with him, said: "Everything loves its offspring, even the <term>bustard</term> <gloss>Arabic: al-hubārā</gloss>," yet the bustard is used as a proverb for stupidity <note>The bustard was proverbially known for forgetting its own nest or abandoning its eggs</note>. Then there is the magpie, which despite its skill in means and speed of snatching, does not use this for anything beneficial. How many a heavy, precious necklace or a noble, exquisite earring has it snatched from people's hands, only to throw it away after circling in the air, or to hide it away and never look at it again!

Al-Asma'i <note>A celebrated philologist and naturalist</note> claimed that a magpie once snatched a precious <term>sukhab</term> <gloss>a necklace made of scented beads or cloves</gloss> belonging to some people. The owners of the necklace seized a Bedouin woman who was with them. While she was being beaten, dragged, and insulted, the magpie passed by with the necklace in its beak. They shouted at it, and it dropped the necklace. The Bedouin woman, recalling her safety after having been afflicted by another calamity, said:

> The day of the necklace is among the wonders of our Lord,
> It is as if He saved me from a wicked town.

She meant the settled people among whom she had been staying. There is no harm in mentioning what arises, as long as it does not belong to those long chapters containing nothing but bare analogies and pure dialectic, for such things are not easy on the ear and souls do not rejoice in reading them. A master of the craft or a seeker of reward and merit might endure that. Whenever we find a topic that can be adorned with witty, eloquent poetry and curious reports, we take the trouble to include them and narrate them all for the benefit of the reader.

For this reason, we permitted ourselves to say what we said in the chapter on Fire. I am writing to you after this—since I have perhaps bored you with lengthiness and set you upon the most difficult mounts and rugged paths by mentioning a significant portion of the discourse of the theologians—and I do not wish to increase your weariness or force you to exhaust your energy by starting the discourse on camels, cows, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and the like, which I will write for you eventually. Rather, I shall begin with small, short, concise, and pleasant chapters, so that you do not exit one chapter except with renewed energy for the second, and likewise for the third and fourth, until the end of what I shall write for you, God willing. We shall begin with what concerns the sparrow, then we shall take up the mention of the mouse...
</translation>

<translation page="57">
(51)

and the scorpion, and the enmity between them along with their other traits; then the discourse on the scorpion and the beetle and the friendship between them; then the discourse on the cat; the discourse on the hedgehog; then the discourse on mosquitoes and fleas; then the discourse on lice and children; then the discourse on the monitor lizard and the mastigure; then the discourse on the jerboa and the hedgehog; then the discourse on vultures and Egyptian vultures; then the discourse on the eagle and the rabbit; then the discourse on ticks and frogs; then the discourse on the bustard and its likeness.

Before mentioning this chapter, we shall mention chapters of witty poetry suitable for discussion, which inspire vigor and make one deserve to read the long books. Were it not for my low opinion of those who claim to seek knowledge in this age, and those who pretend to patronize books in this era, I would not have needed—despite the many benefits of this book—to employ this long discipline, or this frequent apologizing to humor them, attract them, reconcile their souls, and encourage their hearts. It is as if the benefit I provide them is a benefit I receive from them, and as if my desire for their improvement is the desire of one who seeks after their worldly goods.

Furthermore, I have not yet mentioned any of the long chapters. I have come to mention the distinction between the Jinn and mankind, between angels and prophets, between the female and the male, and the difference between them and that which is neither female nor male. This continues until the discourse extends to the virtue of man over all types of animals, and the mention of nations and eras, and the mention of fates and lifespans, and the measures of intellects through sciences and crafts. Then follows the discourse on the nature of man from the time he was a <term>nutfah</term> <gloss>a drop of semen</gloss> until anxieties consume him.

If you grow weary of the book and find the reading heavy, then you are excused. I have no trick for you except to depict it in the most beautiful form and turn you through various arts. Thus, you do not exit an argument from the Wise Quran except to go to a narrated Hadith; and you do not exit a Hadith except to go to authentic poetry; and you do not exit authentic, witty poetry except to go to a current, apt proverb; and you do not exit a current proverb except to go to philosophy and rarities verified by experience, brought forth by testing, and unveiled by proof—those wonders for which souls have a passion and towards which sound minds have a strong longing. For this reason, I wrote it for you and guided it to you, seeking reward through you. Look into it with the eye of an impartial peer and scholar, or the eye of a seeker of guidance among students and followers. If you find the book I have written for you to be contrary...
</translation>

<summary>Al-Jahiz discusses his editorial strategy, moving from the behavior of animals like magpies to a broader philosophical and scientific survey of creation. He justifies his use of poetry and anecdotes to keep the reader engaged through more difficult theological or technical passages.</summary>
<keywords>magpie, bustard, animal behavior, Jinn, Jili, Uthman ibn Affan, Al-Asma'i, pedagogy, Arabic literature, philosophy, zoology</keywords>

and the scorpion, and the enmity between them along with their other traits; then the discourse on the scorpion and the beetle and the friendship between them; then the discourse on the cat; the discourse on the hedgehog; then the discourse on mosquitoes and fleas; then the discourse on lice and children; then the discourse on the monitor lizard and the mastigure; then the discourse on the jerboa and the hedgehog; then the discourse on vultures and Egyptian vultures; then the discourse on the eagle and the rabbit; then the discourse on ticks and frogs; then the discourse on the bustard and its likeness.

Before mentioning this chapter, we shall mention chapters of witty poetry suitable for discussion, which inspire vigor and make one deserve to read the long books. Were it not for my low opinion of those who claim to seek knowledge in this age, and those who pretend to patronize books in this era, I would not have needed—despite the many benefits of this book—to employ this long discipline, or this frequent apologizing to humor them, attract them, reconcile their souls, and encourage their hearts. It is as if the benefit I provide them is a benefit I receive from them, and as if my desire for their improvement is the desire of one who seeks after their worldly goods.

Furthermore, I have not yet mentioned any of the long chapters. I have come to mention the distinction between the Jinn and mankind, between angels and prophets, between the female and the male, and the difference between them and that which is neither female nor male. This continues until the discourse extends to the virtue of man over all types of animals, and the mention of nations and eras, and the mention of fates and lifespans, and the measures of intellects through sciences and crafts. Then follows the discourse on the nature of man from the time he was a <term>nutfah</term> <gloss>a drop of semen</gloss> until anxieties consume him.

If you grow weary of the book and find the reading heavy, then you are excused. I have no trick for you except to depict it in the most beautiful form and turn you through various arts. Thus, you do not exit an argument from the Wise Quran except to go to a narrated Hadith; and you do not exit a Hadith except to go to authentic poetry; and you do not exit authentic, witty poetry except to go to a current, apt proverb; and you do not exit a current proverb except to go to philosophy and rarities verified by experience, brought forth by testing, and unveiled by proof—those wonders for which souls have a passion and towards which sound minds have a strong longing. For this reason, I wrote it for you and guided it to you, seeking reward through you. Look into it with the eye of an impartial peer and scholar, or the eye of a seeker of guidance among students and followers. If you find the book I have written for you to be contrary...

<translation page="19">
<meta>continues from previous page: Eventually...</meta>
when they are driven by a lust for power and are unable to obtain it through themselves and through their own excellence, they squander their fortunes, baiting and corrupting the masses in every possible way. Once they have made the common people greedy for bribes and handouts through this mindless craving for prestige, then democracy is abolished, and it is transformed into a rule of force and violence <note>original: "cheirokratia", literally "rule of the hand"</note>. For the multitude, having become accustomed to eating the property of others and having their hopes for a living based on the possessions of their neighbors, whenever they find a leader who is high-minded and daring, but excluded from the honors of the state due to poverty, they then establish a rule of violence. Then, gathering together, they perform massacres, banishments, and redistributions of land, until, having become completely brutalized, they find a master and a monarch again. This is the cycle of constitutions <note>original: "anakyklosis"</note>; this is the plan of nature, according to which things change and shift, and eventually return again to the same points in the stages of constitutions. If someone has clearly understood these things, he might perhaps err regarding the timing when speaking about the future of a constitution, but regarding where each one stands in its growth or its decay, or in what direction it will shift, he would rarely be mistaken, provided he makes his pronouncement without envious anger. Furthermore, regarding the Roman constitution, it is according to this method of analysis that we might best arrive at a knowledge of its formation, its growth, and its peak, and likewise of the change into the opposite state that will result from these. For if any other constitution, as I just said, follows this natural course, this one too happened to have its formation and its growth according to nature from the beginning, and will have its nature and its change into the opposite state likewise. This will be possible to observe through what will be said hereafter. For now, we will make a brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus <note>the legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>. For such a discussion is not irrelevant to our purpose. For he, having considered each of the aforementioned things

<summary>Polybius describes the transition from democracy to a rule of violence and the cyclical nature of political systems. He introduces the Roman constitution and Lycurgus of Sparta as case studies for these natural political cycles.</summary>
<keywords>democracy, rule of violence, cycle of constitutions, Roman constitution, Lycurgus, political decay</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="20">
<meta>continues from previous page: ...aforementioned things</meta>
being fulfilled necessarily and naturally, and having reasoned that every simple form of constitution that is established according to a single power becomes precarious, because it quickly turns into its own specific and naturally following vice. For just as rust is a natural blight on iron, and wood-worms and borers are to wood, by which things—even if they escape all external harm—they are destroyed by the very things born within them; in the same way, a certain vice is born naturally within and follows each constitution. For kingship, there is the so-called monarchical way <note>implying tyranny</note>; for aristocracy, it is the way of oligarchy; and for democracy, the brutal rule of violence. It is impossible for all the aforementioned constitutions not to make their shifts into these states over time, according to the argument just given. Lycurgus, having foreseen this, did not establish a simple or uniform constitution, but gathered together all the virtues and the peculiarities of the best systems, so that no single part, by growing more than what is proper, might turn into its natural vices. Instead, the power of each being pulled back by one another, the system should not incline in any direction nor tip heavily to any side, but being held in equilibrium and balanced, the constitution should remain for a long time like a ship sailing against the wind. The arrogance of the kingship is restrained by the fear of the people, who were given a sufficient share in the government. The people, in turn, do not dare to look down upon the kings because of their fear of the elders <note>the Gerousia, or council of old men</note>. These elders, having been selected based on merit, were always going to align themselves with what is just. Consequently, the side of the disadvantaged, by remaining true to established customs, always became greater and weightier through the influence of the elders

<summary>Polybius explains how Lycurgus designed the Spartan constitution as a "mixed" system to prevent the natural decay inherent in simple forms of government. By balancing the powers of the kings, the people, and the elders, stability is maintained through mutual restraint.</summary>
<keywords>Lycurgus, Sparta, mixed constitution, political stability, checks and balances, kingship, elders, democracy</keywords>
</translation>

# Chapter Five

Root Text—Through constant practice, one certainly sees it within three days. By the mere sight of it, the practitioner burns away the multitude of sins. || 190 ||

Commentary—One should contemplate that <term>Niranjana</term> <gloss>the stainless/the void</gloss>, known as the swan with rays of nectar and possessed of sixteen digits <note>phases of the moon</note>, located in the cavity of the skull within the head. By performing this practice continuously for three days, the manifestation of the Stainless One will certainly appear to the practitioner. By merely having this vision, the practitioner will burn away all fallen acts. || 189 || 190 ||

Root Text—Knowledge of the future manifests, and purity of mind truly occurs. Even if performed for a moment, it burns away the five great sins. || 191 ||

Commentary—By performing this meditation, an intuition of the future <note>original: "anagata-vishaya", things not yet come to pass</note> will arise; that is, matters that have not yet occurred will be revealed. The mind will become pure, and through this meditation, the practitioner will instantly burn away the <term>pancha-mahataka</term> <gloss>five great sins</gloss>. || 191 ||

Root Text—The planets become favorable, and all calamities perish. Obstacles are pacified, and one attains victory in battle. || 192 || Through the vision of the moon of milk, the <term>Khechari</term> <gloss>moving in the sky</gloss> and <term>Bhuchari</term> <gloss>moving on the earth</gloss> powers are attained. Through meditation alone

<summary>This page details the benefits of meditating on the lunar Niranjana within the skull, including prophetic vision, purification of sins, and planetary favor.</summary>
<keywords>Niranjana, future vision, five great sins, planetary favor, skull cavity meditation</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="182">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
everything is achieved; there is no need for further deliberation here. || 193 ||
Through the yoga of constant practice, a human becomes a perfected being. Truly, truly, and again truly, he certainly becomes equal to me. This supreme science of yoga grants success to yogis. || 194 ||

Commentary—By meditating on the moon situated in the head, all planets become favorable, all calamities are destroyed, obstacles are calmed, and victory is gained in battle. The <term>siddhis</term> <gloss>supernatural powers</gloss> of <term>Khechari</term> and <term>Bhuchari</term> are attained; there is no doubt in this. By continuously performing this yoga practice, the practitioner certainly becomes a <term>siddha</term> <gloss>perfected being</gloss>. O Parvati! I say truly, truly, and repeatedly, that he will become equal to me, of this there is no doubt. This supreme yoga is the giver of perfection to yogis. || 192 || 193 || 194 ||

### The Description of Raja Yoga

Root Text—Above that is the divine thousand-petaled lotus. It stands outside the body known as the <term>Brahmanda</term> <gloss>the egg of Brahma/the universe</gloss>, and it grants liberation. || 195 || Its name is <term>Kailasa</term> <note>the sacred mountain home of Shiva</note>, where the Great Lord dwells. He is called <term>Akula</term> <gloss>beyond form/lineage</gloss>, imperishable, and free from decrease or increase. || 196 ||

<summary>The text concludes the benefits of lunar meditation, equating the practitioner with Shiva, and introduces the Sahasrara lotus as the external Kailasa where the Lord dwells.</summary>
<keywords>Siddha, Shiva, Raja Yoga, Sahasrara, Kailasa, Akula, liberation</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="54">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
As for knowledge, it is divided into two aspects. One is that which is called knowledge according to common convention <note>original: "urf"</note>. The other is that which is not called so according to common convention. Yet both types are considered part of the category of knowledge by the Masters of Truth <note>the Sufi metaphysicians</note>. This is because they witness the permeation of the essential knowledge of God, glorified be He, within all existing things. 

Regarding the second type, for example, which is not conventionally regarded as having knowledge, we see it <note>an inanimate element like water</note> distinguish between high and low ground. It turns away from the high and flows toward the low. Likewise, it penetrates into the interior of a body and arranges the manifest form of the body to be revealed, and so forth. 

Therefore, it is a property of knowledge that it flows according to the requirement of the capacity of the recipient and does not act in opposition to it. However, in this specific rank, the rank of knowledge has manifested in the form of Nature. By this same analogy, knowledge permeates all other existing things; indeed, all perfections permeate them.

<summary>Jami explains that divine knowledge permeates all things, even inanimate nature, which demonstrates a form of knowledge by following its natural inclinations and capacities.</summary>
<keywords>divine knowledge, permeation, nature, capacity, spiritual truth</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="55">

|---|---|

| Through the attributes that were hidden within it | Even if all the entities of the world were separated |
| The secret of the description from this, which was receptive to it | Became manifest according to the capacity of the entity’s acceptance |

Just as the reality of Existence, by virtue of its absolute purity <note>original: "sarafat-i itlaq"</note>, permeates the essences <note>original: "dhawat"</note> of all existing things in such a way that it is identical to those essences within them—just as those essences were identical to it within itself—so too do His perfect attributes, in their totality and absolute nature, permeate all the attributes of existing things. 

This occurs to the extent that, within the context of their attributes, His attributes are identical to theirs, just as their attributes were identical to those perfect attributes within the essence of those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the context of the knowledge of one who knows particulars, is identical to the knowledge of particulars; and within the context of the knowledge of one who knows universals, it is identical to the knowledge of universals.

<summary>This page describes how divine existence and attributes permeate all things, becoming identical to the specific qualities of creatures based on their individual capacities.</summary>
<keywords>Existence, divine attributes, particulars, universals, permeation, essence</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="13">
<meta>continues from previous page: The text follows the description of the groom's grandfather, a consul in Memmingen.</meta>
The son, having entered into the footsteps of his dear father,
Bestows many benefits upon my fatherland.
He presides over the afflicted, and kindly helps
Needy men, and is ready to bring aid to the wretched.
He once provided green pastures for my Muses <note>The Muses here represent the author's poetic and academic pursuits.</note>
And continually favored my studies.
In exchange for these things, Almighty God, may you grant him
The heavenly joys of eternal life at some time.
You will skillfully imitate these examples of your clan;
Illustrious groom, express the character of your ancestors.
Thus your praise will grow, thus your lineage will become
Brighter, and thus your fame will be perennial.
But since you reflect on these things more wisely by yourself,
Let our songs cease from their own admonition.
Just as a strong horse born of strong seed
Does not fear noises, nor flees mournful weapons;
In no other way do you follow the deeds of your famous parents,
Nor do you allow your own character to degenerate.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
Not even if I should surpass the Pylian Nestor <note>Nestor of Pylos, a figure from Greek mythology known for his great age and wisdom.</note> in speaking,
Or if I were greater in eloquence than Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator regarded as the master of Latin rhetoric.</note>,
Could I recount all the things that the glory of such a groom
Demands to be brought forth according to his merit.
Why then, my Muse, do you not rather leave the young husband,
And seek the face of the chaste maiden?
</translation>

<translation page="14">
Hail, illustrious nymph, the ornament of feminine modesty;
Hail, great glory of the virginal choir.
May He prosper the most holy laws of your bed,
He who was the first patron and author of the bridal chamber <note>Referring to God as the institutor of marriage.</note>.
He who first discovered the marriages of the sweet torch <note>The "torch" (taeda) is a classical symbol for marriage ceremonies.</note>,
And who is said to love the sacred lights of the marriage bed.
May He peacefully bless the treaties of your bed,
Euphrosyne <note>The name of the bride, also the name of one of the three Graces in Greek mythology, representing joy and mirth.</note>, a girl worthy of so great a husband.
Your face is rare, and the excellence of your beauty
Is so great it makes you surpass all other women.
You lift your blue eyes toward the sublime breezes
Quite often, and you shine entirely with a golden-red color.
Such as there often is from the shining light of the opposing Sun
When the clouds have been stained;
Or like the frosty mother <note>Likely referring to Aurora, the Dawn.</note> who drives away the stars of heaven
And leads the day from the Eastern axis.
Such a color is seen on your face; lilies tinted with
Purple blood barely blush so much to my eyes.
Divine modesty decorates your beautiful countenance;
You are mild, and you lack all rusticity.
An ivory neck lets down golden-haired locks,
And flowery wreaths polish your hair.
Your arms are whiter than snowy privets;
Each individual limb displays its own adornment.
You also, Groom, be cheerful; be glad with your whole heart,
Because she seeks your embraces.
</translation>

<summary>These pages of the wedding poem praise the groom's virtuous ancestry and the bride's exceptional beauty and modesty. The author uses classical references to Nestor, Cicero, and the goddess Euphrosyne to elevate the status of the couple.</summary>
<keywords>marriage, epithalamium, ancestry, virtue, beauty, Nestor, Cicero, Euphrosyne, modesty</keywords>

This famous bath is heartily good for the <term>calculo</term> <gloss>stone</gloss>, for it softens and drives out kidney and bladder stones, sand, and grit, as many honorable persons besides myself have experienced in fact. For <term>cholericis</term> <gloss>those afflicted with bile</gloss>, or the jaundiced, it is also excellently suited, from whom it has expelled a mass of foul humors, the witnesses of which are for the most part still living at this time. Many parched, consumptive, and lung-diseased persons have been brought there in litters due to weakness, who, after completing the cure, were able to ride home on horseback fresh and healthy. To a corrupted and indigestible stomach, it brings again an excellent appetite and creates a desire for eating. It <term>acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and clears the eyes most wonderfully, so that many persons who had to use glasses or spectacles before the bath cure could afterwards write, read, and perform other business without them. He shall lay low the bodies of the Trojan-born with his hostile sword.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
The waves of the Scamander <note>a river near Troy</note> shall be witness to his great virtues,
Which spread far and wide into the rapid Hellespont <note>the strait between Europe and Asia</note>,
Whose path he shall narrow with heaps of slaughtered bodies,
Warming the deep rivers with mingled blood.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Finally, the prey given over to death shall also be a witness,
When the smooth tomb, piled high with a lofty mound,
Shall receive the snow-white limbs of the struck-down maiden <note>Polyxena, sacrificed to Achilles' ghost</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
For as soon as fortune gives the weary Achaeans <note>Greeks</note> the power
To loosen the Neptunian bonds <note>the walls of Troy, built by Neptune</note> of the Dardanian city,
The high sepulchers shall be moistened with the blood of Polyxena,
Who, succumbing like a sacrificial victim to the double-edged steel,
Shall drop her headless body on a sinking knee.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Therefore come, join the desired loves of the soul,
Let the husband receive the goddess in a happy covenant,
Let the bride be delivered at last to her eager husband.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Her nurse, revisiting her at the rising of tomorrow's light,
Will not be able to encircle her neck with yesterday's thread <note>a sign that the marriage was consummated</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Nor shall the anxious mother, saddened by the separate sleeping
Of her discordant daughter, cease to hope for dear grandchildren.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
The Fates <note>original: "Parcae"</note>, speaking such happy things for Peleus,
Sang these songs from their divine breast in times past.

<summary>The Fates conclude their prophecy regarding the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, foretelling the military prowess of their son Achilles and the fall of Troy.</summary>
<keywords>Achilles, Scamander, Polyxena, Fates, Troy, Peleus, Thetis, marriage prophecy</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="197">
# ON CATULLUS
For the sky-dwellers <note>original: "Coelicolae"</note> used to visit chaste homes in person
More often in the past, and show themselves to the mortal assembly,
When piety was not yet despised.
Often the Father of the Gods <note>Jupiter</note>, revisiting his shining temples,
When the annual rites arrived on festive days,
Beheld the chariots of the Cretans racing across the land.
Often wandering Bacchus <note>original: "Liber"</note> from the highest peak of Parnassus
Drove the Thyades <note>female worshippers of Bacchus</note> crying "Euan!" with flowing hair,
When the Delphians, rushing eagerly from the whole city,
Received the god joyfully with smoking altars.
Often in the death-bearing contest of war, Mars <note>original: "Mauors"</note>,
Or the mistress of rapid Triton <note>Minerva</note>, or the Rhamnusian virgin <note>Nemesis</note>,
Being present, encouraged the armed throngs of men.
But after the earth was stained with unspeakable crime,
And everyone banished Justice from their greedy minds,
Brothers soaked their hands in brotherly blood,
The son ceased to mourn his dead parents,
The father wished for the death of his young son,
So that he might freely possess the flower of a virgin stepmother,
The impious mother, casting herself beneath her unknowing son,
Did not fear to defile the sacred household gods <note>original: "Penates"</note>.
All things lawful and lawless, mixed in a wicked madness,
Turned the righteous mind of the gods away from us.
Therefore, they do not deign to visit such assemblies,
Nor do they allow themselves to be touched by the clear light of day.

<summary>Catullus contrasts the heroic age, when gods interacted with virtuous humans, with the current age of moral decay and familial depravity.</summary>
<keywords>piety, Bacchus, Delphi, Mars, Minerva, Nemesis, justice, moral decline, household gods</keywords>
</translation>

(13.) Whether from the same principle, namely, the <term>Alkahest</term> <gloss>a universal solvent or primordial substance</gloss> (which, in my opinion, I might rightly call fire reduced to a center), the perpetual fire of the ancients can be conveniently restored. of reason, or even the neglect of a single required circumstance, is sufficient; a point they express with the common saying of <term>Dionysius</term> <gloss>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher</gloss>: Any singular defect causes evil, yet good is caused only by an entirely intact cause. One must, however, observe a distinction here among the circumstances themselves. Some of these transfer a moral act into a new genus of malice, while others leave it in the same genus, but nevertheless increase the degree of the sin. 

Thus, the example of fornication, which <term>Aquinas</term> <gloss>Thomas Aquinas, a medieval philosopher and theologian</gloss> brings forward, consists in this: that a man has relations with a woman who is not his own. However, if this circumstance is added—that he exercises his lust upon another's spouse—the act is then transferred into another genus of sin, namely into injustice, insofar as a man usurps the property of another. For this reason, adultery is called a graver offense than fornication. 

An example of the latter would be an angry person who becomes angry when he ought not, and at whom he ought not, and with an improper gesture; this trio of circumstances certainly renders this anger graver than if only one of them were violated. Just as a sickness is graver which infects more parts of the body. It happens, however, sometimes, that a certain circumstance does not add a new deformity, but merely increases that which had originated elsewhere. Just as taking the property of another constitutes theft; but if this is added, that he takes a great amount of another's property, the sin will be graver. 

Nor is there any reason for someone to say that a circumstance, if it is evil, constitutes a specific kind of sin by itself. For this is false, or at least not universal, since it can add a degree of malice within the same species. On these matters, see <term>Thomas</term>. 

<margin>1. 2. question 73. article 8. to 2.</margin>

We add at least this, since it can also be listed among circumstances: how often <note>one sins</note>, whether properly—which <term>Cajetan</term> <gloss>Thomas Cajetan, a 16th-century Italian cardinal and theologian</gloss> denies—or by analogy, that this also must not be overlooked in the weighing of an offense. 

<margin>Cited passage.</margin>

Whence <term>Grotius</term> <gloss>Hugo Grotius, a Dutch jurist and philosopher</gloss> says: A greater depravity also appears if someone has sinned more often, because habits are worse than evil acts.

<summary>This page discusses how circumstances change the severity of a sin, either by making it a different type of wrongdoing (like adultery versus fornication) or by increasing its intensity within the same category.</summary>
<keywords>circumstances, Thomas Aquinas, Dionysius, adultery, fornication, Grotius, moral acts, sin, malice</keywords>
</translation>

# THESIS XI.

## Eighthly, the gravity of vices differs according to the dignity of the virtues to which they are opposed.

<margin>1. 2. question 73. article 4.</margin>

<term>Thomas</term> proves this from <term>Aristotle</term>: The Philosopher <note>a common title for Aristotle in medieval and early modern texts</note> says that the worst is the contrary of the best. In moral matters, the best is the greatest virtue; the worst, however, is the gravest sin. Indeed, since the dispute over the mutual comparison of virtues—specifically which one holds the leading place among them—is not yet settled, it will not be possible to determine anything definitive regarding vices in this respect. 

To be sure, all virtues shine like stars, and our world of darkness is made bright by their rays. However, <term>Piccolomineus</term> <gloss>Alessandro Piccolomini, an Italian humanist and philosopher</gloss> confesses that it is not easy to judge which of them shines more brightly or stands in relation to the others like the sun. 

<margin>Philosophy of Morals, Grade 4, chapters 47 and 49.</margin>

And for each individual virtue, he himself brings forward something in light of which they might claim leadership with sufficient probability, which he confirms both by reasons and by the consensus of the wise. He warns first of all that, according to the diverse condition of men, judgments concerning this prerogative vary greatly: those placed in the magistracy prefer justice; leaders of armies and soldiers prefer fortitude; men of noble birth and education prefer magnificence, and so on. 

Notwithstanding these points, we consider that a settled opinion can be established regarding which virtue is preferred absolutely. This we prefer to express in the words of the most celebrated Doctor of morals in Italy already praised, rather than in our own:

<margin>Philosophy of Morals, Grade 4, chapter 51.</margin>

> Since that virtue ought to be judged absolutely best which possesses the best grounds for excellence; the most excellent grounds for dignity are to be sought especially from the end <note>the purpose or goal</note>. The end of virtue is action. Of actions, those are most excellent which proceed from justice. Rightly, therefore, justice holds the leadership. That the action of justice is the best is clear: for its duty is to organize our actions toward others, to govern others appropriately, to gather together scattered men, to preserve those gathered, to bind together Republics and groups of men—both small and large—with golden bonds, to benefit all, and to harm no one, which is the highest characteristic of virtue.

These are

<summary>The author argues that the gravity of a vice depends on the importance of the virtue it violates. Following Piccolomini, justice is identified as the supreme virtue because of its social and governing functions.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, justice, virtue, Piccolomini, moral philosophy, gravity of sin, social order, ethics</keywords>
</translation>

76. Likewise, is a mother excluded from her legal inheritance through an express <term>pupillary substitution</term> <gloss>the appointment of a substitute heir for a minor</gloss>? We affirm this as well.

->Donellus on the law "By prayers" in the Code on the substitutions of minors and others.<-

77. A man can make a testament by military law both for himself and for his son, or for the son alone even if he has not made one for himself; this testament will be valid if the father happened to die either during military service or within a year of his service.

->Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph "likewise both for himself" in the Digest on military testaments.<-

78. Finally, a soldier can appoint an heir by his bare will, even through signs, in whatever way he wishes or is able; likewise, he can appoint one heir for a certain time and another after that time.

->Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph 1, and paragraph "a soldier" 4, in the Digest under this title.<-

79. Here a question can be proposed: Why can an heir be appointed by a civilian <note>original: "paganus," referring to a non-soldier</note> under a condition, but not from a specific day or until a specific day? We shall investigate the reason.

->Law "Under condition" 73, Digest on the institution of heirs, laws 3 and 4.<-
->Digest on the institution of heirs: Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding<-
->military testaments, folio 325.<-

80. Hence, although soldiers have neither employed the legal number of witnesses nor observed other formalities of testaments, they nevertheless make a valid will, provided it is established that a testament was made.
<margin>at the beginning of the Institutes on the military testament.</margin>

81. If, therefore, a soldier about whose goods there is an inquiry before you, having called people together for this purpose to witness his will, spoke in such a way as to declare whom he wished to be his heir and to whom he would grant freedom, he can be seen to have made his testament in this way even without writing, and his will must be held as valid.

->Law 24, paragraph "If therefore" in the Digest on the testament of a soldier.<-

82. Indeed, if he should note anything on his scabbard or shield with letters glowing in his own blood, or should write in the dust with his sword at the very time when he leaves the lot of life in battle, a will of this kind ought to be stable.

->Law "A soldier" 15, Code on the military testament.<-
</translation>

<translation page="19">
83. Just as a soldier can grant an inheritance by bare will, so also he can take it away.
Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph "Just as however" 5, Digest on the military testament.

84. Thus a soldier is permitted to make several testaments; but whether he made them at the same time or separately, they will certainly all be valid if he has specifically expressed this: nor will a prior one be broken by a subsequent one.
Law "It was asked" 19, on the military testament.

85. An elegant question can be debated here as the occasion arises: Is the previously perfected testament of a civilian broken by a later imperfect one, in which those who would succeed by intestacy are appointed as heirs, if a son was passed over in the later one? Having inspected the legal truth in this matter, we shall strive to defend the negative position with all our strength.
Law 7, Digest on children and posthumous heirs. Law 16, paragraph 1, Digest on common substitution.

86. A soldier's testament is also not broken by the <term>agnation</term> <gloss>legal birth or adoption into the family line</gloss> of a posthumous child, provided that when the soldier passed over the posthumous child, he knew his wife was pregnant.
Law 9, Law 10, Code on the military testament.

87. Likewise, even if he was unaware that his wife was pregnant, yet was of such a mind that he wished whoever might be born to him to be disinherited, the testament is not broken.
Law 7, Digest on the military testament.

88. A soldier's testament is also not broken if he has adopted a son, or if a grandson has succeeded to the place of a son.
Law "the same is" 8, Digest on the military testament.

89. Thus if a soldier who is a <term>paterfamilias</term> <gloss>head of a household</gloss>, having made a testament regarding only his camp-acquired goods, should give himself over to be adopted, his testament is nonetheless valid, as if by a new will.
Law "the same" 23, Digest under this title.

90. However, these mentioned benefits concerning the making of last wills are granted only to those who are occupied in expeditions.
The penultimate law. Code on the military testament.

91. It is debated whether those soldiers who are in camps, in the trenches, or in winter quarters, or stationary camps, in garrisons, away from the battle line, and away from the danger of battle, are permitted to make a testament by military law? And we judge it more true that it is permitted.
Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding the military testament.
</translation>

<summary>These pages detail the exceptional legal privileges granted to soldiers regarding their wills, including the validity of oral or informal testaments made in battle and the rules governing the appointment or disinheritance of heirs.</summary>
<keywords>military testament, inheritance, pupillary substitution, posthumous heirs, legal privilege, military law, Roman law</keywords>

Written from my study at Altdorf <note>original: "Museo Altdorphino"</note> on the day before the Academic Festival, held in the church sacred to Saints Peter and Paul, at which time this most flourishing Academy was to pass into a University on the following day. I pray and vow from the innermost fibers of my soul that it may thrive and flourish in that flower and honor forever. 

In the year of restored Salvation 1623.

-> To the Kind Reader <-

I confess indeed, wise Reader, that many—nay, very many—errors are present in this collection. These are not merely slight, but even serious and offensive to Grammatical purity (such as that in the 5th decade regarding <term>tēs eudaimonias</term> <gloss>concerning happiness</gloss> in the introduction, where "infamis" appears instead of "infamibus"). These errors arose from the haste of the typesetter and a lack of correction. Due to other business and frequently poor health, it was not possible for me to correct them or to append a catalog of them here at the end of the collection. You will therefore grant me pardon and, according to your own integrity, amend the errors yourself. I hope they will be very easy to correct from the coherence of the text, and you will soon find the sense obvious, even if it is somewhat frequently darkened by the shadowy covering of mistakes. I would especially ask that where an error occurs in the words of the authors themselves, you go to the sources. Particularly regarding the passage of Aristotle from book 2 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 4, in the 4th Decade of *Concerning Happiness*, section 3, which is enormously corrupted; you will soon have the truth clearly. With these words, fare very well and favor me kindly.
</translation>

<translation page="12">
-> To the Most Excellent Man, the Master <-

# MASTER GEORG FRIEDRICH Blinsig
## FAVORABLE FRIEND.

<note>A small decorative initial letter Q begins the following poem.</note>
Whom shall I call you, FRIEDRICH, so skilled?
With what titles shall I adorn you, FRIEDRICH,
Worthily enough? Amazed indeed,
I know not, I doubt; amazed indeed
That you are more blessed with divine genius,
More blessed with divine judgment.
What? Should you not deservedly be called—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*?
By Pollux! You are not undeservedly called that one—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*.
Do you wish it? I shall show you, and you will give faith to my words.
What, I ask, is celebrated *Sophia* <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>?
Is she not the pious mother of the liberal
Arts, and has she not brought forth 
More beautiful daughters; whom you seize 
With a more celebrated love of a more celebrated mind?
In form, especially, more sweet,
And also more virtuous than the others,
*Dejanira* <note>In mythology, the wife of Hercules; here used metaphorically for a branch of knowledge or virtue</note> is in all your limbs
</translation>

<summary>Page 11 concludes the author's dedication from Altdorf and provides a disclaimer regarding printing errors. Page 12 begins a laudatory poem addressed to Georg Friedrich Blinsig, comparing his intellectual labors to those of Hercules.</summary>
<keywords>Altdorf University, errata, Aristotle, Georg Friedrich Blinsig, Hercules, Sophia, Wisdom, academic dedication</keywords>

I confess indeed, wise Reader, that many—nay, very many—errors are present in this collection. These are not merely slight, but even serious and offensive to Grammatical purity (such as that in the 5th decade regarding <term>tēs eudaimonias</term> <gloss>concerning happiness</gloss> in the introduction, where "infamis" appears instead of "infamibus"). These errors arose from the haste of the typesetter and a lack of correction. Due to other business and frequently poor health, it was not possible for me to correct them or to append a catalog of them here at the end of the collection. You will therefore grant me pardon and, according to your own integrity, amend the errors yourself. I hope they will be very easy to correct from the coherence of the text, and you will soon find the sense obvious, even if it is somewhat frequently darkened by the shadowy covering of mistakes. I would especially ask that where an error occurs in the words of the authors themselves, you go to the sources. Particularly regarding the passage of Aristotle from book 2 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 4, in the 4th Decade of *Concerning Happiness*, section 3, which is enormously corrupted; you will soon have the truth clearly. With these words, fare very well and favor me kindly.

# MASTER GEORG FRIEDRICH Blinsig
## FAVORABLE FRIEND.

<note>A small decorative initial letter Q begins the following poem.</note>
Whom shall I call you, FRIEDRICH, so skilled?
With what titles shall I adorn you, FRIEDRICH,
Worthily enough? Amazed indeed,
I know not, I doubt; amazed indeed
That you are more blessed with divine genius,
More blessed with divine judgment.
What? Should you not deservedly be called—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*?
By Pollux! You are not undeservedly called that one—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*.
Do you wish it? I shall show you, and you will give faith to my words.
What, I ask, is celebrated *Sophia* <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>?
Is she not the pious mother of the liberal
Arts, and has she not brought forth 
More beautiful daughters; whom you seize 
With a more celebrated love of a more celebrated mind?
In form, especially, more sweet,
And also more virtuous than the others,
*Dejanira* <note>In mythology, the wife of Hercules; here used metaphorically for a branch of knowledge or virtue</note> is in all your limbs

### XLIV.

Furthermore, the Jews, in order to maintain the same course of the seasons in individual months, add an entire month whenever the number of <term>Epacts</term> <gloss>the age of the moon on January 1st, or the difference between the solar and lunar years</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The Epacts are the eleven days that represent the difference between the Solar year of 365 days and the Lunar year of 354 days. It is necessary for these to increase subsequently if we allow several such years to flow from a single common beginning without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus that Lunar year arises which I previously called <term>Embolimæus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. Since it is so tempered by the motions of the Moon, the months even of common years are restored in some way to the laws of solar revolutions for the enjoyment of the perpetual seasons by its benefit; the entire form of such years is rightly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be held neither as purely Lunar nor as solar, but as Luni-Solar.

### XLVII.

Finally, Civil years are more free than others. Those of the <term>Olympiads</term> <gloss>Greek four-year periods</gloss> are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes in 361 or 362 days, and others in 390, 391, or 392 days. The <term>Nabonassar</term> <gloss>referring to the era of the Babylonian King Nabonassar</gloss> or Egyptian years have 365 days, just like the common Julian year, but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, that reckoning of years is quite wandering if compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a certain and perpetual beginning there, but after every four-year period has passed, it differs from the Julian by an entire day because of the intercalary day, which every fourth Julian year receives, while the Egyptian does not admit it.

### XLIX.

Hence its head <note>referring to the New Year or start of the year</note> runs back through all the months of the Julian year until, after 1460 Julian years are finished, 1461 Egyptian years are completed. For then both return to one and the same common beginning.
</translation>

<translation page="11">
### L.

These things I had to say concerning Time, according to the nature of the undertaking, concluding with the verses of Master Cramer:

> If you always measure fleeting time to your fingernails <note>an idiom meaning to measure with great precision</note>,
> time will never pass away in idleness.
> Tomorrow’s hour is not yet here, yesterday’s cannot be recovered
> with a thousand talents: if you wish to live, live today.

---

You burn with love for <term>Eusebia</term> <gloss>Piety</gloss> and <term>Sophia</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, as well as for virtue;
therefore you discourse on TIME. Well done!

->Endure and persist, this labor will benefit you one day.<-

->JOHANN FRIEDRICH SCHARF, Doctor<-
->Dean of the Philosophical College at this time.<-

---

The matter is indeed true: most excellent virtue is pressed down,
yet it is by no means crushed, but finally rises on high.
This, FIEDLER, you testify abundantly by your example,
while you yield to no one, even though your means are small <note>original: "curta supellex", literally "scanty furniture", a metaphor for limited wealth</note>.
I praise your efforts. May the Deity prosper your undertakings,
so that your native soil, by whose sweetness everyone is led,
may welcome you back and your labors.

->MICHAEL WALTHER,<-
->Public Professor.<-

<note>A faint circular library stamp is visible in the upper right corner.</note>
</translation>
